TWTM is an extremely enjoyable game, comparable to that of Rexaura while also having a community that can create maps for users to play on; a community not lacking in creativity as well. The puzzles in TWTM are multidimensional and require very creative and unconventional uses of the time machine, leading to more of a lateral thinking experience on my part. the level also for the most part took around an average of 20 minutes for me to solve with no prior knowledge, so the game itself should take around 2-3 hours. However, the amount of intriguing maps the community creates keeps me coming back to this revamped version of Portal 2. Not only does TWTM have admirable gameplay, but it also has impeccable graphics and spends all expenses on making this game enjoyable from every facet. The game, despite being short, does compensate with its difficulty level, leading to a larger sense of reward when completing an ostensibly challenging puzzle. 9.5/ 10 game(0.5 is taken away due to the bugs that the clones you make can have while interacting with certain areas of the environment, but even these mistakes are minute.)

If you like Portal 2, you'll probably like this game. It has all of the mechanics of Portal 2 including the workshop but it also has a "time machine" you can use during gameplay to record yourself for a seemingly infinite time &, when you play your recording, a duplicate of you does everything you just did. Combine that with the other Portal 2 mechanics & you get some amazing puzzles.
One of the few problems is that, because the game was made by a team of modders for free, there are, predictably, some weird glitches & oversites. Your recording can do things it shouldn't be able to do that are basically cheating which wouldn't be a problem since you could just refrain from doing it but the problem is that some map creators will expect you to exploit those oversites which can lead to some frustrating puzzles when you don't realize you're supposed to cheat or you don't know the "cheat" the level creator wants you to use.
Another downside is that you can't disable the time machine &, although you probably wouldn't want to because you'd basically just be playing Portal 2 if you did that, it does mean you can't make a level where people have to earn the time machine. This means some ideas that would be puzzling in Portal 2 can be easily bypassed with the time machine. If you know how to use Hammer to make levels, you can probably find a way to get around this problem &, really it hasn't bothered me yet so it's probably not a big deal.
Another small downside is that the campaign is really short, the story is extremely lacking, & certain mechanics are strangely entirely absent from the campaing. The campaign doesn't use turrets or gel a single time, for example. The workshop is the real reason to play this game though.
In my opinion, the gameplay of this game might actually be better than Portal 2. It's like Portal 2 but with even more variety. What's not to like?

Where do I begin?  Ok, first, the lead dev seems to have some kind of thign against the normal intuitive controls used by games liek minecraft ot Robocraft. I saw a youtube video from Robbaz and thought "that looks great".  So there I was not quite standign , but not quite floating on a cell shaded hull of a weird floating house on massive rollign swells of the ocean.  I dont' knwo what I pressed that disconnected me from the little robot body, but I wasn't in build mode, because I coudl switch into it.  The fly speed is set way high so strafing was disorienting as hell.  Up and down ofted plunged me into the ocean.  There were signs identifying systems, which was great!  But control indicators were awful.  I hopped into the little skiff.  I figured out how to start the engine.  Yay.  Then i figured out how to control it.  But the littel robot hopped in and I was still floating abouve the skiff.  The UHJK keys worked.  Thats a weird combination when you could just use asdw and a locked cameral.  Whatever, so I quickly accidentalyl drove the skiff off screen.  When i caught up I killed the engine manually, because who thinks to hit T+G to kill the engine.  I dunno about you but I have a single button brake in my car and I figure that is as intuitive as it comes.
Clearly I wasn't ready for a campaign, so i quite out of that, which took a nausiating length of time readign white text on light sea blue background.
I went into the vehicle designer thinking surely that would be somethign liek the Robocraft garage.  hoyl hell, that was worse.  I was suddenly on a 3X3 raft with the little robot and the waves were crazy.  Ok, so i built out some pontoons and it got more stable great.  The turtorial on engine building was awesome, but again not mouse friendly.  I felt like I was back to the old rubber ball mice I had to pick it up and reset it on the pad so many times.  The best is when a part would spawn for the tutorial, it woudl reset the view (damn thats disorienting), spawn in a cloud of black smoke, and spawn behind other parts so I could never tell what had just spawned.
Long story short I flipped my skiff as soon as I tried to drive it.  That caused the build mode to flip to, but the little robot was still right way up and spinning.  so as I was tryign to fix my skiffs orientation, the world was spinnign and the waves were rolling. This game is a fantastic adaptation of the mechanics of Terraria (side note: I get thatg everyone compares this game to Terraria) in a space setting, and I thoroughly enjoy it. However there are some problems I have with the game, technical and preferential.
I greatly enjoy this game, don't get this wrong. But I would like to point out a few bugs that I have come across recently, as both a tip to the creators and a warning to others.
- On a fire planet - you know, where fire rains from the sky - I found an Avian village and was walking through it when some fire landed and burned off a bunch of banners from a wall, and the villagers immediately accused me of stealing them.
- Not sure if this is on purpose or not, but enemies who are targeting friendlies will not under any circumstances cease targeting those friendlies, even when I'm blasting at them with an ex machina and the other guy is running away.
- Occasionally when I destroy wild farmable plants that are immediately above caves by about a block or two, their drops will appear in the cave instead of on the surface. This also goes with other drops as well.
- In platforms within Apex science facilities, if I jump down onto a platform that is rising upward, most of the time I just fall through the platform. I assume this is because the player's code checks a certain distance below the player for a solid object to land on, but the platform gets out of the way too fast so no solid object is found.
- This one is a bit lengthy. So I am used to my own keyboard configuration where "w" is the jump key instead of space. This works fine unless I get in a mech suit in zero gravity. Usually I would set jump to "Space, W" and move up to "W" so I can use W for both actions. However in a freefloating mech suit, this does not work - when I press W, the suit does not go up. I think this is because the suit is trying to jump instead, but the suit can't jump in zero G anyway. I have had to solve this problem by getting used to using Space to jump. So far I have only died twice from this recalibration.
- This one I actually like - sometimes when you eat food, you don't consume the food item. This appears to only happen on very specific frames of the game.
- In the Hunting Grounds where the Floran relicis, one of the boulder traps sends boulders uphill instead of downhill. This is from awhile ago and may be fixed by now.
Now for a few preferential things - stuff I find slightly problematic with gameplay, and the fixing of which I would find as an improvement.
- Rain makes the game incredibly laggy at times.
- Many of the animals, especially flying ones, glitch from one place to another as if I were on a server with substantial lag. (This may actually be the case for all I know.)
- Food items such as chocolate and chili peppers are priced very high for their commonness. I have a massive plantation of chocolate from which I have created tens of thousands of pixels worth of chocolate bars in the same timespan it took to only have just found my first neonmelon. Actually, you know what, don't fix this, I kinda like it now that I think about it. Maybe we just need oculemons to be more expensive is all.
- Fine movement is difficult because if you barely tap a directional key, if you're on flat ground you barely move at all but if you're on the edge of a block you fly right off of it at a pretty high speed.
- There is a large amount of animals that attack unprovoked but a very small amount that don't attack unprovoked, and seemingly none that actually run away (besides small birds). It would be interesting to see more wildlife that you need to sneak up on.
- Learning about the existence of mech suits after completing a large portion of the game first results in a lot of progression feeling as though it has been lost, or pointless, since you need to go back to low-danger areas to farm items to upgrade mech suits when those same low-threat areas on planets are long behind being difficult for late-stage weapons. As such I think it should be made at least slightly more obvious that mech suits exist to new players, instead of simply labeling areas in space as "requires mech to deploy", since I had no idea what that meant. (I originally thought that mech was mechanical components you add to your ship; I don't watch anime so I'm not that familiar with mech suits, ok?)
Everything else I can think of is well-balanced, in my opinion. Thanks for creating and updating this game, it's really fun!

This game is pretty good as far as tower defense games goes. It's not great, just good. It has a slow, boring, start that makes most people likely quit. A friend and I tried it out and it took us maybe two hours to get into it. It has so many avoidable issues, bad designs, that makes the game less user friendly and a tad overwhelming. Because there is so much thrown at you, the game has a very bad first impression.
The game allows you to customize your mech, in this game called a "Trench," customizing its core (body) that then allows you what emblacements (defense towers) in varrying types and quantities in trade off for various weapons sizes and quantities. You are able to pick from a healthy enough variety of weapons and can pick some really powerful weapons if you so choose to sacrifice emplacement options for it. You also can choose the legs of the "Trench" which gives varrying abilities that will accomodate some playstyles.
There is not an overwhelming large variety of emplacements, there is maybe slightly more than ten. However, like the weapons, there is different variants of each emplacements from quality of weapons. For example, there is "advanced" versions of weapons or emplacements that need to be unlocked through progression (such as leveling up and earning money) to purchase it through the store the game has or getting it by chance in the so very common loot crates.
The weapons uses an inventory system which means if you want two of a weapon on your mech.... you need to own two. Some things however have no need to have multiple variants of, such as emplacements or cores, but you seem to be able to get them anyways which is always disappointing if you get them from loot drops. Also a negative point, the store makes it difficult for you to know what you already have, meaning you need to exist the store menu and check inventory just to be sure.
The story is mediocre, it's not bad but not good, but it gets the job done. The story is more of an excuse for the gameplay, which is just fine considering many tower defense games, including Dungeon Defenders, do. The gameplay allows players to have more emphasis on emplacements or gun combat, something I think is a good design choice. The enemies are diverse and create many challenges I am sure in the late game that will need good team coordination. However, as of right now, the game is very easy and has virtually no challenges.
The game has a bronze, silver, gold, grading system that grades you based on time. I am sure this will generate mild replay value, some gold scores being overwhelmingly low compared to our bronze finish which hints we are suppose to come back later with very good "trench" mechs. If it can keep our attention long enough for that, I am sure we will appreciate the something to do. I do think that such a system is bad design, nothing is more fun than playing with overwhelmingly powerful mechs on lower levels to complete trivial tasks just to finish a grade for your gold collection.
The game is far from perfect, I would argue it deserves a 7/10. It's enjoyable, just not for the default price. I am very glad I got it in a bundle long ago. Get it for under $10 with some friends, only then would I say it's worth it.

If you like hitting the undead with an array of melee weapons, Shooting round after round into advancing hoards.
Or simply scavenging for supplies and rescuing survivors. Then you should absolutely check out State Of Decay.
I enjoyed this game a lot. Searching for supplies never gets old and I think that is because the loot varies, from basic food supplies (coffee, snacks, ect) to medicine or ammo, melee weapons of all sorts and guns. Who doesn't love finding a stash of ammo for that one favourite gun of yours? Searching for supplies feels natural in this game. And it really adds to the survival element.
State Of Decay is slow paced compared to a lot of other zombie games and a lot of the time you'll have to take your time to really assess your group of survivors and the base as even when you're not playing, the game itself is still active. I left off with good morale within the group and came back the next day to find one of the survivors had fallen sick and another had died. So the game really keeps you on your toes and is constantly changing.
In the game you'll be able to complete a lot of missions, you'll pretty much always have something to do however if you ignore missions for long enough or simply get occupied doing other things within the game certain missions will solve themselves, not always in a good way either. Fail to help a fellow survivor kill a certain zombie, or find a lost survivor and they might die doing the mission on their own. So the game really encourages you to constantly be active. However this doesn't happen for every mission so if you prefer just exploring and doing supply runs, then do your thing.
The game is far from perfect and there is honestly a few things that could have been polished further, the driving mechanics feel clunky and occasionally the AI will do a few silly things. However playing the game I found myself looking past those things and instead simply enjoying the world and gameplay and of course fretting over my survivors. Stop getting sick ya'll!!!

The music is decent, but I love the art style. Lea and the alchemist gal's designs are fantastic in my eyes. The gameplay itself, however, didn't really do anything for me, despite the fact that I enjoyed that retro-styled 2D Scott Pilgrim brawler game a few years back. You're locked to a screen which will fill with enemies coming in from off-screen to the left and right, and must throw punches and dropped items to defeat the enemies. If you do, you advance to the next wave, and if you don't, Death itself (grim reaper rascal) spawns and starts chasing you around the screen (though he's pretty easily avoidable; more of a minor annoyance and storyline element than anything).
I cannot fault the game itself for anything other than my jump-kicks being very fickle about working, resulting in me touching an enemy without attacking, and in the tradition of old-school games, touching an enemy means taking damage, so the controls not working would often cost me 20% of my health. If it works well for other people, then that's good for them.
The gameplay itself simply does not appeal to me, as the things you can purchase in the shop appear to be temporary power-ups as opposed to equipment like long-term weapons or character upgrades, and there isn't much in the way of story after the intro to keep me intrigued. I'm pretty terrible at the game as well and cannot complete the very first level, so for me there is nothing to like other than the music and graphics. Would I recommend this game to
? Of course, and I would also recommend some of the worst games on Steam to certain people, because there's someone out there that would love them. Therefore, clicking that we recommend a game because we can imagine
would like it is inherently wrong.
The best solution I have found is deciding "would I recommend this game to the "me" in the past, taking out time travel/time loop/history-changing problems, etc., if I could? Or would I tell me to avoid this game?" This way, my own lack of enjoyment with a game is statistically taken into account with all other reviews, and that gives players a better idea of the overall Steam community opinion of a game, since people who like the game can do much the same. If I clicked that I would recommend it to
(which I covered why that's not in the best interest of all Steam users), then I would be contributing to the problem and not doing my part to convey accurate information to potential buyers.
This is not a perfect system, of course. Other things could be implemented like Steam setting a rigid numerical 1-10 rating scale for various categories, but even then, that's difficult to really handle properly because of the nature of certain games. What I'm trying to say is, I don't hate this game, but it's not for me, and not recommending it is the ethical thing to do to benefit potential buyers by giving them a better idea of if people like this game or not by me avoiding recommending it and making a potential buyer see so many thumbs up and assume all those people liked the game, when in fact they did not.

'Catch A Falling Star' was initially off putting to me as I tend to avoid clicker style games. After viewing the video and seeing multiple friend's reviews about it I decided to get the 99 cent game. 8 hours of teeth gritting, leaning in the direction the star is falling, and collecting tea cups full of stars later, I feel I can give my impressions about it.
The fun of this game is held entirely by it's connections to Steam and Steam achievements for me, aside from the aesthetic appeal of bright, colorful and cute graphics. Without the goal set for me to achieve 5000 points, open up all the basket options, and save up 2,500 coins I might have stopped playing this game hours ago. The game is deceptively challenging behind it's simplicity. There are many techniques one begins to learn as you crawl up the point gain to combat ice, catch a star, and use the very edge of your bucket to bounce a negative power up. Some of the negative (red) power ups begin to seem appealing as one can use them strategically. The game also seems to completely change after hitting 2K, 2.5K, and 3K points, but I can't be exact in what numbers bring about this change. Suddenly stars are dropping more quickly and on opposite sides of the map. I can go from a full bar of health that I've built up until this part of the game and drop out before I can deposit a bucket of stars. So after I've almost reached every achievement and definitely gotten my money's worth of playtime and entertainment from this game, an entirely new challenge appears out of the woodwork.
The graphics and music are also pleasant. I have really enjoyed getting the Steam badge and emoticons. They are the same appealing graphics of the game and quite affordable for those interested. My favorite background being 'Japan' which is pink cherry trees with a lovely mountain backdrop. I also like the teacup, coffee cup, suit case, present box, cookie jar, and most of the other cute baskets. The other unlockable backgrounds were unremarkable to me, although I can see the appeal for fans of those games they represent. My only other qualm would be that not all functions seem to be fully available yet, such as the 'Bubble Time' power up which doesn't seem to do anything when caught as of this review. I can foresee this power up being a game changer once it is instilled.
Overall, 'Catch A Falling Star' is affordable, a boredom killer, “relaxing” for some (ha, not me!), a hidden challenge and something worth playing.

Catch a Falling Star is another great example of an indie game done right. It proves even with a low budget and a personal edition of Unity, great games can be made. It has a great soundtrack, addictive gameplay, and a perfect way to break up the monotony of playing AAA games. I cannot recommend this more.

I thoroughly enjoyed this game (and all my many, many playthroughs). Its artwork is beautiful, and there's a lot more going on story-wise than you can first see on the surface.
What I enjoyed most was that many characters aren't what they seem. There are many secrets, and after enough playthroughs, you start to learn things that are never outright mentioned in the game... you start to identify causal relationships between your choices and events that may have originally seemed random.
Your choices matter immensely, and many will ultimately kill you. Every skill is valuable to your survival, but you don't have time to learn them all... benevolence is a viable route, and so is killing all who oppose you. You can study the art of war, or you can focus on... well, art.
The possible routes are nearly endless, and the story as a whole is far more intricate than it seems on the first go.
Highly recommended for those players interested in the story, especially for those who will play several times looking to find all the secrets.

Fantasy JRPG meets Empire: Total War in a VN-esque fashion.
If you ever ventured into one, two or maybe all three of these gaming styles before, I believe it's easy to see why Long Live The Queen is so well rated here.
Despite having completely different themes and gameplay, the joy of playing this kind of games comes from the same things:
(a) they can be extremely funny when things go wrong;
(b) nothing feels better than a well executed plan.
So why not mix them all into a single product and see why happens?
This indie 'The Sims: Medieval Days' you're now skimming through searching for funny reviews and considering if the price is worth it, is the cute, adorable –but at times infuriating– offspring of a merciless strategy game with a naive Role Playing Game.
(Speaking of which, if you're not self-inserting as Elodie, our troubled protagonist, you're doing it wrong).
It's common to read folks praising this game for its "complex strategy" but truth be told, it's not THAT awesome. It took me about 5 hours and little more than 4 saves to (successfully) get a crown placed above my head, which was kind of a bummer since things were getting really interesting by the end. That said, the "strategy" complexity and difficulty of actually "beating" the game -as in reaching coronation day- is nothing remarkable. The variety of ways you can achieve that, however, is what makes playing this game over and over worth the time.
There's a reason you have literally dozens of save files slots, and if you enjoy the game, you'll likely fill most of them, where, depending on your mood, some are likely to end up with exotic names, i.e:  "Save File #16 - Should I execute this maggot?", "Save File #21 - Survived the chocolate".
The masterpiece lies within the development and execution of the (a) and (b) items previously mentioned where,
You'll die. You'll die in funny, unexpected ways.
Characters will say funny stuff before you die.
And your epitaph will always make you giggle.
Alongside brilliant characters with the most alluring behaviors which will show you that,
Training some skills on the wrong order will prove extremely disastrous.
Everyone has awkward, impossible-to-remember names.
You'll eventually give up trying to memorize their names.
You'll notice it's easier to just call it whatever is easier to remember (Talasse -> Tallahassee)
If there are any negative aspects about this game that I can point out, it would indeed be its short length. Had it been a bit longer, it would make an outstanding awe-inspiring Journey™ instead of just an above-average afternoon play.
Anyway, point is,  stop wasting your money with stupid COD releases every year and support this deviant, creative game.
Oh, and don't use guides. It spoils the fun.
For me the game was interesting enough to keep trying after every death

'From the Depths' is, by some margin, the most unique and refreshing voxel-based game I have played in a great deal of time.  With a surprisingly appealing mixk of block based polygonal structures as well as curved and rounded shapes, the visual appeal does well enough.  However, the game shines in the level of complexity and smoothness of the vehicle and fortress building systems, that feature custom AI units, engines, shields, cannons, missles and more.  The tutorial section also feature several methods by which to learn how to use and implement these mechanics.  Unfortunately, the game does suffer from a rather steep learning curve, and it will take several attempts before new players are able to properly string together the components to properly build a formidible vehicle.

First off, do not buy this if you intend to see the funny moments and gruesome humor that was POSTAL 2. The humor in here is minimal and not nearly as frequent as even just standing still on P2.
This game is VERY serious and dark, but in a good way. For 1997, it was pretty realistic as well.
It was made from 95 percent brutality and shock factor and 5 percent humor.
:
This game is very dark in contrast to the sequel, the art is grimy looking, you really get a feel that the guy you're playing as is VERY psychotic (mainly from the daily Journal entries on the loading screen before each level) partially from one of the few spoken lines of the Postal Dude; "I regret nothing." before shooting himself in the head (after killing hundreds of innocents!!!)
***NOTE: There is a suicide key (K) which acts as a way to restart the level.***
This is one of those games that was highly controversial. One of the reasons was how it executed its "violence" within the game. Reason being; it was as realistic as the dev team could make it for the time. Adding on to that, children can also be killed, and executed while incapacitated.
:
+ The gameplay is amazing fun (isometric shoot em up, with some decent strategy needed)
+ Has the 'Special Deliery' add-on included which adds 5 new levels
+ Lots of features for a game that's simple and from 1997
+ Very unique and nice hand-drawn art style
+ Gives an unsettling, horror vibe (see below for details)
+ Quite a nice arsenal of weapons for an old mass-murder game, all weapons feel different and some explosive weapons have varieties of ammunition
:
- Controls may be hard to get used to for some players
- Not quite a straight-forward, linear story, but the Postal Dude's inner-thoughts are expressed clearly through the Journal entries (loading screens), and throughout the game he mutters lines, as well the last level shows just how mentally unstable he is (it is a cutscene)
The game truly takes you on a trip through the mind of a mentally ill man who feels the need to purge the world of every living human. It might shock some, sure, but it really is an amazing game for how simple it is, yet allows you to have so much fun killing time AND people. The story may not be heavy in terms of spoken dialogue and many pages worth of text, but there is an underlying surreal feeling while playing the game that makes it clear that the story is just how psychotic the "Postal Dude" has become.
You can easily get used the controls, create your own cozy setup, master the controls in 10 minutes, and have a BLAST playing this. Disregard my Steam playtime as I have played at least 30+ hours before the Steam release.
9/10   //   4.5 out of 5

State Of Decay - (SOD) Wow! In short - BUY IT NOW! Its great!
The Long version... A great game that I can highly recommend. Its not too scarry 'horror-wise' (blood and gore), but it will keep you on your toes and running to survive. Perhaps even make your heart race faster..
I enjoyed the openness of the missions. True open world - do it as you like, without any real penalty for deciding not to do any particular thing. Only that, you need survivors and if you don't save / rescue them in time, you will lose them. I'm not sure if they ever return.
Obviously, on the opening missions of any game, the game leads you around a bit. (I hate that), but its just to get you started. After that, you are free to do what you want basically. I like that the most.
There is a nice range of weapons - and their availablity is just about right -  I found.
A lot of these types of games don't give you enough tools or conversely you find stacks of ammo and weapons laying all over the place.
I think there could have been more scope - (and in the future), to let you do more in the game, like use tents and sleeping bags + other camping gear, that are littered all over the game, But, nope - you have to sleep on the floor or take turns in a bed when your residency capacity is overflowing.
The graphics are great!  - Graphics in any game is not about the newness and shiny things and how pretty it all looks. Graphics is about the atmosphere the images create. I feel as though I'm watching myself on a TV program about the zombie outbreak.. (If that makes sense)..  It's like a grainy and colorful setting..
There is no rain - wind etc. Just night and day. That's enough for now - perhaps in later future game?
Perhaps we could have had more scavenging of building materials that were real physical things like fences and wood to board up windows. (Where does the wood (nails and hammer), come from when we just decide to nail boards over a window?  They mysteriously just appear.. It should be a collect inventory thing..
You can only carry a certain amount - but can bet a bigger rucksack to carry your stuff in! Also, I liked to take a vehicle to keep more supplies nearby. You can also leave them out and about, no one else will steal them, Stuff you can back at camp can be brought back in another vihicle.
As a TIP: I used to use a cop car for storage and emergency - that way - I always knew which vehicle was my store and escape vehicle. The best vehicles for trasnporting are pickups, some have 4 or 6 seats, and can take up to 6 storage in the back. They should have let us use busses and vans or lorries too, but they weren't drivable in the game. (Maybe next time)!
You will have a lot of fun moving to new bases. But I think you should be able to have them all and just expand into the next base rarther than have to pack up and move. Then you'd have more missions to do, transporting resources between the bases etc.
There could be more explanation of why there are so many zombies and where they are all coming from. e.g. - You are in a small groups of towns off the highway, and the Z's are coming from the cities, where there are millions of them; Looking for 'BrainZ' food.. Moving out of the city by the dozens daily.
There are plenty of items to make and repair, although you don't actually make the repairs or build anything with your own hands. I think this could be a nice addition to the game.. Currently, you just park your vehicles outside your base; for instance and they can be repaired overnight if you have the mechanics shop built and a resident mechanic.
Other horror games I play - are usually on console, like "Silent Hill" - Now there's a horror game for you.. But you don't get a chance to build and play like you do in State Of Decay.. I really want to have more to do in the game. Actually building and making things and transporting things around - all with the constant threat of zombies getting you..
About people you save...
A tip or two: I like to sacrifice the odd player. Ones without any real sikills when you get them. You don't have to get rid of people until you have too many and your facility is overcrowded,
So, take the person you want to sacrifice, perhaps because they have no skills for fighting or medical / other skills etc.  Or perhaps you just don't like the look of them. Take a tool to fight with, something you don't want or can afford to loose, take no medical supplies and go out and fight to the death with the biggest, badest dude you can find,
Always look for and go for the next new person that needs rescuing, you never know what skills they might have. You can always take them out alone and get them killed later.. Suicide... Mission.

If you're looking through Steam reviews before buying this game, take note that most of the negatives are based on technical part of the game. Yes, some of it are downright atrocious in this day and age. However, if you do not consider yourself as part of the "PC MASTER RACE", then know that most of the technical problems were fixed and some of the other problems are basically nitpickings from the so-called "PC MASTER RACE".
So if we looked beyond the technical problems, how does the game fare? Well, it's a 2004 game. If you've already played "Tales Of Zestiria", then this game is the watered down version. Unless you're wearing nostalgia glasses, you'll notice that the gameplay doesn't age well. Newer generations of gamers who were too young to play this back when it got released will probably get bored with how the game played within a few hours.
Story is also not something to write home either. Sure, back when I played this all those years ago, the story feels amazing and rewarding but that's probably my 12 year old mentality speaking. It's not as good as I remembered it. It's cliche and predictable. Perfect for early teens but not for fully grown adults.
Characters are your standard JRPG stereotypes. A hot headed MC, a ditzy female MC, a shota, a loli, some older male who is obviously smarter than the MC, etc. If there are people calling these characters "deep" or "fleshed-out", they are either b*llsh*tting you or have a serious case of nostalgia fever. They're not, trust me.
Why would you buy this game? Well for starters, it's probably because of how a lot of people seems to point out that ToS is among the best JRPG to-date. Debatable but that's up to you to find out.
RECOMMENDED: For those who played it back in the day and for JRPG lovers
NOT RECOMMENDED: For PC elitist who can't stand 30 fps

Disclosure: I haven't "Completed" the game per se but have played enough to understand it.
Luftrausers is a game where you play as a single plane taking on a near impossible task. It's you vs everything. The entire game is essentially a massive "Objective: Survive".
There are roughly 9 different enemies in the game. The consist of different things like planes, "Aces" which are super-powered planes, and (Blank, not putting the full name, since it makes it a tad obvious what they do.) aces which are super powered aces. (Scary♥♥♥♥♥♥. There is also boats, battleships, submarines and the acemarine. (Real scary♥♥♥♥♥♥. Then you have the blimp. You're on your own to find out what each of these things do how ever.
The game has a form of loadout system, using 3 parts. The gun, the body and the propulsion. Part of the fun in this game is finding different insane combinations and seeing how long you'll last. The body will for instance make you slower, but with more health, or faster with little health. I personally like to play as a glass cannon, going at mach speeds, but get scratched and I die. Can lead to some fun or frustrating playthroughs.
There's enough variation to keep the game fresh how ever I can say from personal experience that I feel that it's a "Go To" game. When you have moments where you just want to hop on and play a game. No story or anything like that, just pure gameplay. Each playthrough is relatively short and depends on your skill. Sometimes a minute, sometimes 10. All depends on you.
The standard music is pretty great. You'll be flying down from the sky, about to take out a battle ship and the music peaks up. It really feels great, when moments like that happens.
There's 2 difficulty modes from what I can see. SFMT and Normal. Essentially, hear sirens and cry. You can periodically unlock new colour schemes for the game but I didn't think any of them match up with the original, how ever if you're looking for a new experience after playing for a while. Maybe just changing the colours is all you need.
Conclusion, if you're looking for a game which you can keep coming back to, that doesn't take a lot of your time, yet has enough replay value for multiple playthroughs then this is a pretty decent game. I reccomend trying it out, and if you're still skeptical then wait for a sale. It was roughly 2-3 pounds when I bought it, which is a pretty nice price.

I really want to like this game, but I put it down for very long lengths of time and when I pick it back up to try and play again I'm reminded of why I don't like the game. Would I reccomend this game? I wouldn't. Not for full price, anyway.
First I think I should delve into things I do like about the game. The music, the visuals and the overall aesthetic are really nice-- it's what attracted me to the game in  the first place. The music is brilliant with memorable tracks. That being said, I haven't gotten past the first stage so I've potentially only heard three or four of the total number of tracks.
The thing I don't like is the actual gameplay itself. I don't mind the fact that it's a brawler with enemies swarming near constantly. I'm used to it as I've played games like Castlevania where enemies continue to respawn. But What I don't like is the movement lock when your player character attacks an enemy with a lot of health. It's fine if you only have to press the attack button once, but on enemies that take two or three punches it's irritatingly unfair to be locked in place without the ability to push them back with your attacks. Either the attacks should be better weighted, or you should be granted the ability to move while attacking.
The largest problem for the mechanics of this game is that punching and kicking is essentially all you do which make the mechanics more glaringly frustrating and grueling. EDIT: It's also worth mentioning that the item pick ups add another layer of frustration. You must choose between attacking with your body, attacking with a very perishible item that may only eliminate one enemy from the screen, or healing if multiple items and enemies pop on you.
It does have multiplayer but I prefer playing alone and since this game does have a singleplayer option, I don't feel as though buying a miserable, unplayable time by myself makes any sense.

My recommendation is mostly positive, but with some large reservations.  As a 10-wave, single-screen survival brawler, Curses 'N Chaos is enjoyable, and the pixel art is impeccable. Many users have reported performance issues ranging from running too slow to running far, far too fast, and while some of these problems have been fixed via a patch from September 2015, the endings remain glitchy.  As a fan of the game's art assets, it pains me to see artifacting like that of a failed ROM check spewed across the screen after a successful playthrough, and so I say to you: if you don't have a Playstation 4 or Vita, then buy this and hope for a patch to clean things up a bit, but stay away otherwise.

The mechanic of time travel is interesting and makes very unique puzzles, but the storyline is nigh-nonexistant and sometimes random. It also has an terrible learning curve, going from patronizing tutorial, to simple puzzles, and then all hell is releases. Thankfully, though the campaign is short, the community levels are nearly as good as the campaign levels.
It is worth getting, mainly from gameplay.

Pros:
It's a great twist on the basic Portal idea. The time travel mechanic adds an extra layer of complexity to the puzzle solving that really does feel like a progression in the concept of Portal.
Fascinating and devious level design that takes good advantage of the new mechanic.
It's Portal, simple and fun, minimialist puzzle solving and this is a worthy attempt at expanding the game.
Nice polish of the look of Portal, less bland and just uncluttered enough to not get in the way of the problem solving for the most part.
It's free
Cons:
It's rather unstable. I've suffered multiple crashes and there are in game bugs and glitches that need to be sorted out to improve the game play experience. Most of these are during direct interaction with your double like when climibing on it to reach high places.
It could use a better tutorial system. The animations force you to go back and forth a lot which is frustrating. Most of these instructions could have been done more fluidly through audio or prompts I think though for replays it does at least mean they don't get in the way. The game is a complex enough advancement from the original Portal idea for this to be important.
Given the huge scale of some of the levels it can be very hard to see what to do. Some more visual clues, say more obvious portal surfaces could lessen the frustration of simply working out the mechanics of the more complex levels (the last one for instance is a huge two parter where you can't see all the relevent componants as they're a huge distance apart on a couple of occasions. Things like the ceiling switches are not obvious how to interact with, things like that need clearer flagging as to how those compnonants work.
It's surprisingly short. Yes it's free and that's certainly not unappreciated but the game ends before you know it. The game crashes for me after the Glados cutscene (level 9?) so if there's anything else then I'm missing it.
-------
To summarise, great game, an interesting twist on Portal thats marred by stability problems,  minor issues with level design and a short length. I'm sure extra levels through the workshop will address the last point to some extent though those are never quite the same as a continuous story. I think this has great promise though as a way forward for Portal should a full scale game be made so congrats to the devs for adding something very worthy to the Portal universe. Hopefully it'll lead somewhere interesting in regards to an official release. It's free, so it's most certainly worth a look if you can't get enough Portal.

There's not much I can say about Dark Souls that hasn't been said already, because this is such a prolific game. It's known for being overly difficult, but once you get to know the game better, you understand that the game is challenging in a very fair way. It's not difficult because enemies do too much damage, or some other arbitrary number they flipped in the code - it's difficult because it challenges you pay attention to what you are doing, be intentional about your actions, and practice the mechanics to get better. However, no game I have ever played has given me the sense of satisfaction this one has after beating a boss, or in some cases, just a normal enemy. The environments are both dark and beautiful, and the world that has been created is mysterious and wonderful.
The downsides to this game are also well known. Running back to a boss fight after dying can be so tedious that some people call this game a running simulator at times. Many of the mechanics are never explained, such as how to build your character's stats or how covenants work. It's worthwhile to join a community like Reddit's /r/dark souls, or even read some build guides or a FAQ if you get stuck or want to know more about how something works. Sometimes, it's the only way to really understand what's going on in the game.
The game is also showing its age, but this is easily corrected by mods. Make sure you pick up DSFix, Wulf's Dark Souls Connectivity Mod, and PVP Watchdog at the very least. You can also up the graphics to 4k and do other things to make it look nicer and bring it up to date, but there are whole guides on how to do that, so I won't talk about it more here.
In any case, love it or hate it, I think this is a game every serious gamer should play, as it really challenges players in a way that games haven't done in a generation, and gives you the sense of a world much bigger than you are. Even with all of its flaws, this is one of my all time favorites.

Make no mistake, Dark Souls is a game that's going to test your wits, skills, and above all else patience.  Prepare to die couldn't be more applicable here.  Newcomers to the Souls games, like myself, will experience a tough-as-nails approach to third person combat that will require you to analyze each and every enemy you face in order to survive.  After you die every enemy with the exception of some tougher ones, mini bosses and regular bosses, will immediately respawn so that is something to take into consideration. Reaching save points known as bonfires will also respawn enemies after the bonfires are lit.
On your first playthrough expect to die, die again, and die some more.  Dying is basically the theme and it can become frustrating unless you begin to understand WHY you're dying.  Success is strictly dependent on how well you adapt to the enemies.  There is no hand holding in Dark Souls and this may be offputting to new players.  It took some time to get used to but there is something special about overcoming absurdly difficult challenges and with Dark Souls, that's what you'll get.  Everything from the story to the combat and everything in between is something you will have to figure out yourself - nothing is spoon-fed to you.  Exploration is mandatory in order to find good loot like new armor or weapons.  Of course, there will be options to purchase loot from certain NPCs, however, it is all very pricey seeing that the currency used to purchase the loot is also used to level up your character.
I am enjoying my time with the first game in the series even though it can be quite frustrating at certain points.  The formula for this game is unlike anything I've ever played and for that reason alone I can recommend giving this a shot.  It is however not for the faint of heart or the easily rage-induced.  If you are easily upset because you are always dying in games and are looking for a relaxing and casual experience, this is not the game for you.  Find something more... forgiving.
One last note, a controller is strongly recommended to play.  It makes the experience a hell of a lot better.  I have tried mouse and keyboard and it just felt too clunky and awkward.  I use a 360 controller and the gameplay is how it should be.    Aside from a controller being pretty much required for a solid experience, this port is fantastic.  It works flawlessly and I have yet to encounter any technical issues running on windows 10.

State Of Decay - (SOD) Wow! In short - BUY IT NOW! Its great!
The Long version... A great game that I can highly recommend. Its not too scarry 'horror-wise' (blood and gore), but it will keep you on your toes and running to survive. Perhaps even make your heart race faster..
I enjoyed the openness of the missions. True open world - do it as you like, without any real penalty for deciding not to do any particular thing. Only that, you need survivors and if you don't save / rescue them in time, you will lose them. I'm not sure if they ever return.
Obviously, on the opening missions of any game, the game leads you around a bit. (I hate that), but its just to get you started. After that, you are free to do what you want basically. I like that the most.
There is a nice range of weapons - and their availablity is just about right -  I found.
A lot of these types of games don't give you enough tools or conversely you find stacks of ammo and weapons laying all over the place.
I think there could have been more scope - (and in the future), to let you do more in the game, like use tents and sleeping bags + other camping gear, that are littered all over the game, But, nope - you have to sleep on the floor or take turns in a bed when your residency capacity is overflowing.
The graphics are great!  - Graphics in any game is not about the newness and shiny things and how pretty it all looks. Graphics is about the atmosphere the images create. I feel as though I'm watching myself on a TV program about the zombie outbreak.. (If that makes sense)..  It's like a grainy and colorful setting..
There is no rain - wind etc. Just night and day. That's enough for now - perhaps in later future game?
Perhaps we could have had more scavenging of building materials that were real physical things like fences and wood to board up windows. (Where does the wood (nails and hammer), come from when we just decide to nail boards over a window?  They mysteriously just appear.. It should be a collect inventory thing..
You can only carry a certain amount - but can bet a bigger rucksack to carry your stuff in! Also, I liked to take a vehicle to keep more supplies nearby. You can also leave them out and about, no one else will steal them, Stuff you can back at camp can be brought back in another vihicle.
As a TIP: I used to use a cop car for storage and emergency - that way - I always knew which vehicle was my store and escape vehicle. The best vehicles for trasnporting are pickups, some have 4 or 6 seats, and can take up to 6 storage in the back. They should have let us use busses and vans or lorries too, but they weren't drivable in the game. (Maybe next time)!
You will have a lot of fun moving to new bases. But I think you should be able to have them all and just expand into the next base rarther than have to pack up and move. Then you'd have more missions to do, transporting resources between the bases etc.
There could be more explanation of why there are so many zombies and where they are all coming from. e.g. - You are in a small groups of towns off the highway, and the Z's are coming from the cities, where there are millions of them; Looking for 'BrainZ' food.. Moving out of the city by the dozens daily.
There are plenty of items to make and repair, although you don't actually make the repairs or build anything with your own hands. I think this could be a nice addition to the game.. Currently, you just park your vehicles outside your base; for instance and they can be repaired overnight if you have the mechanics shop built and a resident mechanic.
Other horror games I play - are usually on console, like "Silent Hill" - Now there's a horror game for you.. But you don't get a chance to build and play like you do in State Of Decay.. I really want to have more to do in the game. Actually building and making things and transporting things around - all with the constant threat of zombies getting you..
About people you save...
A tip or two: I like to sacrifice the odd player. Ones without any real sikills when you get them. You don't have to get rid of people until you have too many and your facility is overcrowded,
So, take the person you want to sacrifice, perhaps because they have no skills for fighting or medical / other skills etc.  Or perhaps you just don't like the look of them. Take a tool to fight with, something you don't want or can afford to loose, take no medical supplies and go out and fight to the death with the biggest, badest dude you can find,
Always look for and go for the next new person that needs rescuing, you never know what skills they might have. You can always take them out alone and get them killed later.. Suicide... Mission.

This game is a fantastic adaptation of the mechanics of Terraria (side note: I get thatg everyone compares this game to Terraria) in a space setting, and I thoroughly enjoy it. However there are some problems I have with the game, technical and preferential.
I greatly enjoy this game, don't get this wrong. But I would like to point out a few bugs that I have come across recently, as both a tip to the creators and a warning to others.
- On a fire planet - you know, where fire rains from the sky - I found an Avian village and was walking through it when some fire landed and burned off a bunch of banners from a wall, and the villagers immediately accused me of stealing them.
- Not sure if this is on purpose or not, but enemies who are targeting friendlies will not under any circumstances cease targeting those friendlies, even when I'm blasting at them with an ex machina and the other guy is running away.
- Occasionally when I destroy wild farmable plants that are immediately above caves by about a block or two, their drops will appear in the cave instead of on the surface. This also goes with other drops as well.
- In platforms within Apex science facilities, if I jump down onto a platform that is rising upward, most of the time I just fall through the platform. I assume this is because the player's code checks a certain distance below the player for a solid object to land on, but the platform gets out of the way too fast so no solid object is found.
- This one is a bit lengthy. So I am used to my own keyboard configuration where "w" is the jump key instead of space. This works fine unless I get in a mech suit in zero gravity. Usually I would set jump to "Space, W" and move up to "W" so I can use W for both actions. However in a freefloating mech suit, this does not work - when I press W, the suit does not go up. I think this is because the suit is trying to jump instead, but the suit can't jump in zero G anyway. I have had to solve this problem by getting used to using Space to jump. So far I have only died twice from this recalibration.
- This one I actually like - sometimes when you eat food, you don't consume the food item. This appears to only happen on very specific frames of the game.
- In the Hunting Grounds where the Floran relicis, one of the boulder traps sends boulders uphill instead of downhill. This is from awhile ago and may be fixed by now.
Now for a few preferential things - stuff I find slightly problematic with gameplay, and the fixing of which I would find as an improvement.
- Rain makes the game incredibly laggy at times.
- Many of the animals, especially flying ones, glitch from one place to another as if I were on a server with substantial lag. (This may actually be the case for all I know.)
- Food items such as chocolate and chili peppers are priced very high for their commonness. I have a massive plantation of chocolate from which I have created tens of thousands of pixels worth of chocolate bars in the same timespan it took to only have just found my first neonmelon. Actually, you know what, don't fix this, I kinda like it now that I think about it. Maybe we just need oculemons to be more expensive is all.
- Fine movement is difficult because if you barely tap a directional key, if you're on flat ground you barely move at all but if you're on the edge of a block you fly right off of it at a pretty high speed.
- There is a large amount of animals that attack unprovoked but a very small amount that don't attack unprovoked, and seemingly none that actually run away (besides small birds). It would be interesting to see more wildlife that you need to sneak up on.
- Learning about the existence of mech suits after completing a large portion of the game first results in a lot of progression feeling as though it has been lost, or pointless, since you need to go back to low-danger areas to farm items to upgrade mech suits when those same low-threat areas on planets are long behind being difficult for late-stage weapons. As such I think it should be made at least slightly more obvious that mech suits exist to new players, instead of simply labeling areas in space as "requires mech to deploy", since I had no idea what that meant. (I originally thought that mech was mechanical components you add to your ship; I don't watch anime so I'm not that familiar with mech suits, ok?)
Everything else I can think of is well-balanced, in my opinion. Thanks for creating and updating this game, it's really fun!

I really like this game, and the concepts in this game.
An alternate-history, post-WWI apocalypse, where a radio signal has created hordes of telivision-themed monstrocities that threaten humanity. And to combat them, Heavily-armed walking tanks, called Mobile Trenches, are invented and deployed to stop them.
I ♥♥♥♥ing LOVE mechs when they're walking tanks. Forget the Gundam mechas, this is the REAL good♥♥♥♥♥♥
However, this game suffers. A lot.
First off, thanks to Games for Windows Live, this game has had a lot of problems pop up. The Removal broke the multiplayer, making it so that you can't connect with ANYONE online. (Or, at least, I haven't been able to.)
The entire game can be beaten by yourself, but it can be an uphill battle at times, and pretty frustrating.
The game also has no way to reset your progress in-game. If you want to reset your account and start from square one, tough luck, because ther'es basically no way to do so. There's SUPPOSEDLY ways to alter the game's files to reset your progress, but so far, none of the methods have worked for me, unfortunately.
The game also appears to be locked at 30 Frames per Second. This is mainly due to how the game's engine is set up. As a direct result of the engine, you can't manually unlock the framerate via the game's files, so you're kinda stuck there.
Those 3 1/2 problems can be kinda off-putting at times in the game, especially since there's no real replayability after you've beaten the game. If the multiplayer worked, I believe THAT would make this a much more replayable game, but thanks to Games ♥♥♥♥ed by Windows Live, that's almost impossible, and the patch Double Fine put in hasn't seemed to fix it, either.
This game is good, don't get me wrong. It's a decent game that you could spend a long time playing, even in singleplayer. But you're not going to get the full value of the game due to the bugs left behind by Microsoft's terrible attempt at a PC gaming program.
tl;dr, Buy it when it's on sale.

Normally, I would start a review with my conclusive thoughts in a less blunt manner. However, I'm sure people won't bother read further if I don't mention the port.
It's another one of many Tales of Phon(ing)-in-a-game:
I don't think PC gamers are entitled for expecting more, but here's the thing:
(I did have one or two issues around the 40 hour mark, missing voice-acting and one unexplained crash.)
All of this is to say I'm more focused on the merits and the problems about the game than its technical details. (They are problems, but none I would think as damning).
ToS's core gameplay focuses around its active-time battle-system which can be played with 1 - 4 players. (Or 0 if you want to play it like a traditional JRPG similar to FF13.)
This game doesn't require you to have friends (local) to enjoy it as the AI is "bearable" with minor baby-sitting. Nor does every character seem tailored for players. However, the novelty of playing a cooperative JRPG of 45 to 50 hours is what makes the feature stand out.
As for the gameplay, it's enjoyable, though too simple when you look for depth.
In spite of the variety of 256 enemies--with a lot of color-palatte swaps--and nine heroes, it's becomes obvious how there are only three enemy types for the whole game: Sorcerers/casters, melee fighters and rangers. (No hero acts like the last type.) Bosses also all fall within these categories, which makes them feel easier than cheaper enemies like mimics.
Simple enemy behaviors are not what makes the combat too simple. It's actually the battle-system itself.
Every engagement becomes a giant mosh-pit. You cannot move freely in battle--you can move forward and back, and change the camera if there is more than one enemy. The 2D movement results in every engagement converging to the center, which makes the tactics feel pointless. A simple fix would be to use the shoulder buttons to strafe around enemies.
The system also presents the problem when you get backed into a corner by the camera. You have no control over it, which means enemies can obscure your character if there is only one enemy on screen.
All these issues do not take away from the visceral combat--if you stick with the melee fighters. Their move-sets are the best because they have the most fluid combat and they have the best combo potential.
It's not a surprise to me now that when my stepbrother and I played this game we always stuck with Lloyd, Kratos, Sheena and Zelos. (Colette, Presea and Regal all feel too clunky.)
If you never played a Tales of game before (or haven't in a long time), I wouldn't expect this battle-system to be exceptionally innovative. It's competent in comparison to the game's lacking mechanics.
One might say I should temper my expectations of playing a game from over a decade ago, but it's surprising how many of these extra features are undeveloped or shallow.
The exploration of ToS is good for about the first half the game (20 - 25 hrs) without the Reyiards. You have to manuever around enemies, find monuments to make the travel-time smaller, and you have to explore the continents with some non-linear play.
(The funny thing is that the game itself is very fast-paced and linear if you pay attention to names.)
Once you get the Reyiards, which comes shortly after obtaining the boat, there is less exploration involved and more so of moving from A to B with no obstacles. It honestly feels like these machines were meant to be saved for the end-game to quickly tie-up any side-quests.
The exploration is at least passable, which is what I cannot really say for the menus/systems in the game.
The Gald system is so easy to obtain money that you can avoid grinding in the game with some exploration to just upgrade your characters, restock your items, and even then waste 200K+ on Luin with a lot left over. (The only reason I gave it away is because I didn't have any other use for the money.)
I am honestly okay with this system because I never once felt like I had to grind, but I would like more uses of my money. What I avoid buying where the EX Gems and the Cooking materials because you more often find them as you play or you'll forget about them because they add little to the game.
The Cooking system becomes worthless when you can buy Gels for dirt-cheap. The meals don't provide really any bonuses to the game. (They restore health and magic--like gel.) The recipies aren't obtained through experimentation but of finding the right ingredients for your limited recipies.
EX Skills are a little more useful as they provide perks that can make your party more specialized. But, again, you'll find more than enough through exploration than you would using your Grade Points. (Something you should save up for NG+ if you want to go for Mania mode.)
I don't hate these sytems, nor are they broken; they feel tacked on for extending the game. Much like the game itself.
I'm not going to mention spoilers; instead, I'm going to criticize ToS' storytelling faults and positives.
What stood out to me about ToS's archetype cast is how most (with the exception of two characters) feel necessary for the plot. Almost every character could be seen as the protagonist. This is usually a problem for other series, but here it goes a long way to establishing the cliche moral "You can't save the world alone."
It's also no surprise that the two characters (Presea and Regal) whom I question why they are in the game are also a part of my problem with this game's mature themes. They feel out of place and are often poorly handled.
The game constantly talks about sacrifices, deaths, conspiracies, and other darker subject matters without committing to some message. These issues often feel shallow or underdeveloped.
For example, if the message was one of "You cannot always save everyone", then why does the game have situations where you do save everyone? It's not like Valkyria Chronicles where they emphasized the actions of the characters to commit to a message.
It's ironic how a cynic like myself praises the game's lighter/egalitarian themes of friendship, equality, the problems with overcoming discrimination and the problem with ideals. There are some well-thoughout stuff written here.
By far the biggest problem of the narrative is how often it reguritates itself.
Far too often in both cutscenes and the "skits" (voiceless talks for English), characters have to repeat information that was either said a few mins ago. Or it was established way back hours ago. Or at the very beginning of the game.
It becomes a problem because there are some exchanges that are worthwhile to listen to, but you have to sit-through a lot of repetition to find them.
Then add-on the confusion of the organizations' names, double-crossings, and the power-play game around you. In the end,  I don't find myself understanding a grand conspiracy but finding a mess of a story.
The game also suffers from some serious padding. If nostalgia won't let you leave, the game sure will pad itself out to keep you playing for 45 - 50 hours.
I might come across as not liking the game, but I honestly still love it; it's hard to look past its faults. Still, you should definitely play it. Maybe elsewhere if the port isn't for you.

Thinking with Time Machine brings you the new concept (unless you already knew about The Talos Principle) - Record & Rewind  (or Time Tewind)- which really works here in Source engine and it does expand the thinking with portals to a whole new level, thus props to the devs who made it possible! And it also has some creative puzzles along the beautiful Tron-ized layouts.
However, I WARNED new players better get used to the concept by playing the community-made maps first! Or at least be an intermediate player in puzzle games!
Here is the deal though... This game is very rushed and unbalanced
1. There is a little bit of story, however, when it gets interesting it just ends right there
2. And It is very short! Only 9 Chambers!
3. There is no difficulty arrangement at all! At the beginning you just learn the basic ideas, from chamber 2 to 4 you must learn to think twice of it. And from chamber 5 onwards suddenly the difficulty went straight from 0 to 100 real quick, especially chamber 6 which is seriously overspiked in difficulty. The reason is that it requires your accurate timing, however, the time designed in the level itself is too tight and just one minor mistake you failed the whole process - which is impossible for new players to catch up immediately
4. Frustrating level design and polishing. In chamber 5 there is a possible case you shut yourself into a closed room and there is no way out but reload, actually there is a button for that case to open the door, but you don't know what are the clear conditions for it to show up!. For the second half of the chamber 6, the aerial plate will confuse the hell out of you as it does not launch you close to the button as destinated but random direction. Even if you did succeed then you wouldn't be able to notice fast enough to act, and by the time it is done you would realize you missed the cube at the ceiling and forced to REDO EVERYTHING from the start, unless you saved before that.
5. The unclear in explaining record & rewind mechanic. R to begin the record, Q to mark the end of sequence and F to play the whole thing which is very simple, isn't it? But the game does not tell you that whenever you press F to play the sequence all the portals you shoot before would be resetted!? and that would cause the stuck case in chamber 5!
And for the past and current time shown on the tablet, that is unnecessary as we only need to know how much time we have been recording, for easier calculating our actions, which is really important for chamber 5 and 6 for example, Therefore minutes along the seconds do well enough, no need for year, month, etc... Besides, I don't have time for subtraction here, might as well just count it in my head then (again what is the point of the past and current time indicator then?)
6. Unoptimized rewind action showcase. You can clearly see the bug, the weirdness when your past-self interacts with objects. Luckily, this does not affect you much in solving the test but mainly the reason 4 and 5
That being said, the new concept works, the game does have the cool looking except the story, and in terms of level design and difficulty balance they are not polished very well, still have bugs here and there that devs need to fix them. Therefore I will give this a 7, it could drop down to 6 due to its super short, yet how fortunate as there are workshop for this so I can continue to enjoy the game for much longer as I really like this time rewind concept.

The game used to be better and more stable, but now it's just a mess. I like adding new things to the game, but they really need to work on the bugs first. When there is a bug, you're stuck with it for months until they release a whole new patch that either ignores that bug or makes it worse. For example, a while back, there was a bug that made it so you could only cook one food item over a campfire. If you tried to put another one over it, it would just cook forever. The only way around this was saving and quitting then rejoining. Rather than fix this very problematic bug in the next update, they chose to ignore it until a later update. Fast forward a few versions and they made the water extremely choppy. Not like a normal choppy water. I mean that if you paddled, your camera would bounce all over and you couldn't see a damn thing. This made traversing shark infested waters damn near impossible. Then they include a map editor. While a really good concept that could enable players to make and share great islands, it instead is buggier than the game and causes extreme lag if you're near an island that has a bit too many objects on it. Not only that, but each update breaks older maps so any downloaded map would not work for different versions of the game which would render those maps completely useless. The least they could have done is put up a workshop page for islands, but instead you have to sift through dozens of discussion pages to find a map that ends up not working for your version.
Each update they release, while interesting, just breaks the game more and more. For every problem they fix, they create 3 more. It's a shame because the game is a really good concept, but it's just so damn broken that it's virtually unplayable. Keep in mind I can run Skyrim on Ultra graphics with 200 mods with no lag, but then I get severe FPS drops in this game if I decide to move. Devs need to spend the next few updates fixing the game and improving performance instead of adding new things that will break the game.

Japanese folklore is loaded with strange and fascinating creatures. From demons who can be defeated with beans to flying-head vampires, they run the gamut from hilarious to horrifying. Yōdanji hopes to fall somewhere in the middle, stuffing a bunch of bizarre spirits known as yokai into a traditional roguelike structure of exploration and death. It’s an inspired idea that could get a lot of mileage out of its unique characters, if it had any sort of depth or balance to match.
There’s unfortunately no story to hook on here (probably their first mistake), just an assortment of folklore critters and a dungeon to send them into. Yōdanji has 20+ yokai to play as but they must be unlocked by finding scrolls in the Yokai Hunt mode, essentially a finite, collection based version of the game’s Endless mode. Each floor of the dungeon has items to find and enemy yokai to battle, hopefully granting you enough power to overcome the greater challenges on lower floors. You’ll have to rely on your chosen yokai’s skills to see you through, and leveling them up will be key to victory.
Your skills are essential, in fact, because there’s barely any other depth to the combat. Levels in Yōdanji are mostly featureless except for obstacles like boulders or trees, and none of the characters are designed to take advantage of them. Most yokai are melee fighters, and while there are plenty of status effects they’re the common can’t move/can’t act/take damage ones that provide no tactical complexity. That leaves your skills to do the big damage and grant what few new combat options there are, but I can tell you after an hour of playing the base classes that you’re going to find an ideal 1-2 punch of skills and just use that forever and ever. Oh, and you don’t level up normally, but instead track down a will-o-wisp enemy on every floor that gives you a skill point for killing it. That means combat is meaningless except to gate off access to places you need to go.
The other kicker here is that combat hardly lasts long enough for any kind of tactics anyway. Your health is usually going to be measured in single digits and regular attacks can do up to 4 damage, so most fights are resolved in a scant two turns. This also means effects like paralysis and merely being outnumbered can easily be the kiss of death in a single turn, and indeed all my deaths in the last half-dozen attempts have been in one of those manners. Yōdanji may bill itself as a coffee-break roguelike but you can’t afford to flub a single move here, which may be more stress than you prefer over your French roast.
Items play an important role here, but their design still lends itself more to irritation than interest. Powders can heal you or provide powerful effects, and charms held in your inventory take the place of equipment by imparting key boosts like defense or attack bonuses. But your inventory is limited to five items, and you also need food items to keep from starving to death as you explore. Most of your journey is going to be spent juggling items and guessing whether healing or buffs will be more important in the near future, and often being wrong. Worse still is that the three scrolls you need in Yokai Hunt mode to unlock a new character also take up space, so the further in you get the less valuable inventory space you have to work with.
I’ve tried over a dozen times to unlock even a single character in Yokai Hunt with no luck, and even on the easier difficulty I can’t get more than one scroll before death claims me. I’d be more inclined to keep trying if there were any variety to the combat, or any interesting levels to explore, or any story to follow, or any interesting use of the source material at all. Purchased the game in the Double Fine bundle, which is the only way it's worth your money. It's a passable Tower Defense title set in an alternate timeline where World War 2 is waged between giant mecha and psychokinetic, electric monsters. Customization options are surprisingly deep: you can select a character, modify the chassis and weapons of your "Trench" (the bipedal walking tank that carries you into battle), and the selection of turrets you want available for construction on the field. The gameplay itself is shallow and poorly balanced. Iron Brigade, like many other Double Fine games conceived during Amnesia Fortnight, is a generic game too reliant on the classic Double Fine charm to appeal to gamers.
The most obvious comparison would be Dungeon Defenders, a game that offers similar gameplay mechanics, but with much more varied monster and level design. Unilke Dungeon Defenders, Iron Brigade hardly acknowledges the third dimension, with generally flat levels and straightforward monster pathing. Turrets are separated into offensive and support turrets. Weapon and turret progression is so poorly balanced that you can progress through much of the game with simply support turrets to slow monster advancement. Though the concept of combining Mechwarrior and Tower Defense is a fresh one, it's poorly executed. Was unable to test online capabilities as the player base is non-existent.
If you're looking for a 3D TD-Shooter hybrid, Dungeon Defenders II offers greater community, more robust gameplay, and a better pricepoint (it's Free-to-Play). Though Iron Brigade will be an enjoyable, if occasionally tiresome, few hours of your time, it's impossible to recommend you spend your money when a better, free alternative is available.

Tales of Symphonia is one of my favorite games of all time. I love every single party member and I always loved the art-style.

All in all this is a very lovable RPG which only downside now is the fact that it is a port. So I recommend the game, and the port is not unplayable, but it's lacking.
