Quest of Dungeon originally got my attention simply for the funny trailer, however as I sank a few hours in, I felt like it was the devs that got the last laugh. This is not worth your money at all. And here's why in this long list of issues.
-The game is overly simple. The game throws at you ton food items that any experienced Roguelike player would expect them to serve a greater purpose aka hunger. Here, their only purpose is simply to (restore a bit of HP). They are basically just lesser Health Potion. Also, The only strategy involved with any character is to spam skills whenever they are available. There's no wands of teleport or rings of polymorph to be found here. No fun silly deaths that you'd find in other roguelike eitheir. Here.
(But you had no way of knowing prior).
- One design choice of other turn based Roguelike is to walk or pass a turn to restore HP, usually you can fast foward this to make this take second and you can't do it forever or you will starve. In this game however. It becomes a gigantic issue that ruins replayability.
As the Warrior. You gain a very small chunk of HP by walking 5-6 steps. It takes about 2 minutes of walking back and forth aimlessly in a room to be fighting fit again. THIS IS THE OPTIMAL WAY OF PLAYING. THE GAME ENCOURAGES YOU TO DO SO SINCE THERE'S NO HUNGER SYSTEM. So if you're playing on Hard difficulty. You'ill want to save as many health potion as possible for later. So after every encounters. You should be ready to do the tedious task of regenerating HPs. By walking in a circle around the room. Also, enemies that doesn't appears within your view range just doesn't move at all. So you'ill never be taken by suprise by doing this tedious task. By the way, The Mage character only restore MP while walking around, not both. Enjoy the tedious task of spinning right 'round the rooms for MP instead of HP.
-Quest of Dungeon encourages grinding, as much as possible to progress. The anwers to everything is just to have a stronger character instead of having more knowledge then a less experienced player. The only thing to learn are the way to cheese the skills you learn trough randomly dropped books. Basically. All the Warrior's skills has a cooldown after use. (He doesn't have MP to worry about) Let's say your Bleeding Hit skill failed on the boss, You now have a 50+ turn cooldown before you can use it again. You know what that means? You're gonna be running around in circle around the room some more until the skill is available again! Superb! 10/10 gameplay right here. Also on a lesser note, trough the dungeons are stones that activates quest. But there's only 2 variety of quest. Quest A: Kill that boss. Quest B: Find an item that just randomly spawned around the dungeon. Both serves the only purpose of making you revisit the entire floor again with a vague hint of (The item or boss is situated north). You HAVE to do these quest if you want to survive on Normal or above. Pretty lackluster for a game called Quest of Dungeons.
Now on to the smaller stuff...
-Unlimited skill slot, at no point you will have to make a choice of having a healing spell above stun effect spell. The only anwers is just to read all the spell book you can find until all further books you find becomes (Book of Nothing) which you can sell to the merchant for a quick buck.
-Pointless traps that are always in plain sight. In other Roguelike, traps would be invisible to the player until they stepped on it, or had a method of finding them. Here, you will want to step on the spawn monster trap. So you can grind more XP.
Also the game features props like a shelves, pots, boxes and other thing that can be destroyed or search for gold or items. And sometime breaking a pot will inexplicabably trigger a trap that makes enemies spawns from the ceiling. (I guess these skeletons were really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥I just broke their favorite pot?) One last thing about special tiles. There are invisible stash that can be walked on that yeild more gold, but those are stumbled only trough pure luck, or walking on every tiles of a dungeon. But you'd have to be crazy to do that.
-Equipement makes no friggin' sence. Very rarely weapons has additional attributes like (More gold) or (2+ Crits). There's a multitude of weapon sprite, however, that sweet crystal shield you just found could be beaten by that random wood buckler you had laying around in your inventory stats wise. Don't get me started on the equipement name etheir. In the same playtrough, I've got two exact looking pair of boots. One was named (The Boots) with 12 point of DEF, the other pair was named: (Damaged Boots) with 16 points of DEF.
This is explained by the fact that all piece of equipment you find seems to have random generated names, it slaps random adjective to the item, so you'ill get things like (Dark Sigil Sword Seeker). Way to confuse new players to think there's actually depth to be found here.
-Enemies with ranged capacities are the bane of your existence. And if it's a boss with spells or a bow. Run, and pray that you don't get immolated by that fireball or get a random crit from that arrow. You can ultimately trick them to follow you around the room like other melee bosses, but first you got to walk up to them, and by then you're already on the brink of death.
-Item menu, as far as I know, cannot be used with arrow keys or keyboard imput, you have to use your mouse. Same goes for choosing a skill. It would have been nice to be able set the skills to the F1-F6 keys instead of clicking the spell book every time you want to switch.
-Along gold, you'ill find gems along the way, there's at least 8 or so sort of gems that are worth maybe 15 to then 20 GP each. Each kind of gem stack with each other, but if you find 6 sort of gems in a row and you're short on inventory space, you'd rather just leave that gem there and avoid the clutter, because ultimately, finding just one random piece of equipement will make those gems feel like chum changes when you realise that even the worst shield can be worth 1000+ GP.
-Enemies sometime spout some random lines like: (The cake is a lie) or (You should have taken the blue pill) or even worst (I am your father). Too bad that the humor stops the moment you step in the dungeon. Because the trailer and intro was really funny in comparaison.
-Your sprite will never change to reflect the equipement you've equipped and that's really unfortunate and lazy.
- Last and more important. It's a roguelike where you have to grind and it's never fun to die.
Ultimately, I can't recommend this game to veteran or neophytes alike. At best this game is a good distraction while watching something on the side or eating...
If roguelikes are something you might be interested in, go for a free Roguelike like POWDER which is made by one guy and is much more deep. Or you know, dish more money for a roguelike worth it's salt like FTL or Darkest Dungeon.

Quest of Dungeons
About The Game: Quest of Dungeons is a turn-based, rouge-like, RPG. The object of the game is simple, DON'T DIE!. Navigate the dungeons killing monsters, gaining exp, and collecting loot. You can switch out your equipment but leveling up just gives strait stat boosts. Skills come in the form of tomes you find. Some skills work better for some classes than others. The dungeons are randomly generated and can have multiple stairways. Some of the doors take keys to open them and there is no garantee that you will find that key on that floor. Backtracking to open a door on a previous floor might not be worth it since loot matches the floor you are on and not your level.
Pantsu's Rating (out of 5)
Graphics: 2.5 Nothing special here. 8 bit characters and monsters. The map shows what keys you need to get through the locked door but sometimes they are hard to see.
Playability: 3 With WSDA movement and some changeable hotkeys you are never confused on what to do.
Fun: 2 Perhaps it is because I chose the archer for my first run, but after the challenge of the first boss I didn't have much problems. I only died because I gave up caring. The game also trolls you right at the start with a sign showing a skull. I clicked on it looking for lore, instead found instant death.
Sound: 3.5 Even though the game is in old school graphics they actually tried with the background music. Different tunes play when you enter certain rooms and floors.
Replay Value: 3 There are 4 classes to play so there is some replay by challenging yourself on how far you can get with each class. Plus randomised maps and loot make each attempt a little different.
Final Score: 2.75
Final Thought: At $4.99 definitely wait for a sale. I believe I got this game for 49 cents.

Each level has slightly different layouts, or a slightly different goals (e.g. make 20 words using the letter A). There is a surprising amount of levels (I'm about 95 in and the end is soon, I think). There's challenges on each level too, for completionists.
The story is amusing, if nothing to write home about. The game itself is solid, and I do like that the focus is on intelligently finding words rather than short timers and forcing you to make 3 and 4 letter words over and over.
Highly recommend this.

Trapped in
a non-descript generic everyday tall skyscraper that has no visual similarities to any well-known tallest buildings, you and a small group of co-workers must (a) get out of the skyscraper and (b) work out what on earth happened in the first place. Both of these things are accomplished through a boggle/bookworm type word-game that becomes progressively challenging.
One of the usual complaints I have with these type of word games is the "obscure Scrabble syndrome" where some otherwise nonsensical word hidden away in the deepest darkest less frequented pages of a dictionary always score you some points. This game still has some of those, but less frequent that it becomes unnoticeable. Forming words is a nice challenge with some occasional obstacles or stage rules, f.ex. having to include character tiles as you form words so their health/oxygen bars don't run out; freeing character tiles from 'debris' tiles; using timed letters in words to clear a level. All these little challenges add to a word game that otherwise could have been like every other word game out there.
In story mode, there is a definite story happening - it has cheesy dialogue; comedic at times; and is really just a nice touch of fluff to a word game. There is a challenge mode as well, which if you happen to be playing story mode and manage to unlock/complete a challenge, you do get credit for it. Something I thought was nice to have.
There is a friendslist leaderboard and a global leaderboard that pops up after each level so you can see how well you are doing compared to others, or as a reminder you have no friends with similar interests. Your choice!
However way you play it, escaping from
the generic looking no relation to the tallest building skyscraper is a nice side-story to a word game that offers some casual play on a commute, during a server maintenance or to fulfill some achievement hunting.

NOTE: If the game won't start, try turning of DeepGuard (assuming that you have that as part of your antivirus program, of course.)
The first thing you see upon entering the game is Story Mode and Chimp Challenges.  Once you choose one, you'll be able to access Settings.  Options are separate mute buttons for music and sounds, plus Windowed mode or full-screen.
Gameplay consists of chaining together letters to form words, usually with the goal of dropping everyone to the bottom of the screen to "save" them.  When you include the characters from the story in a chain, it will give you access to letters you otherwise wouldn't be able to get to, but there's more to it than that.  Characters will soon run out of air if you don't use them in a word with an air (blue) tile, there are battery cells that have to be used within a certain number of turns, or they'll explode and everyone will die from toxic gas.  There can be fires to put out, debris to clear, and/or glass to break before you can move on, and you only have a certain number of turns to save everyone!
Each character has an ability that will help you out of a tight spot, ranging from instantly breaking a tile that would otherwise take 3 turns to destroy, to swapping letters on the screen, to showing you the longest-possible word on the screen.  SUPER-helpful... but use these abilities wisely, as each time you use them, you'll lose a certain number of turns!
Making 5+ letter words will give you a small red bomb, which takes out all of the tiles touching it (8 tiles), and making a 7+ letter word gives you a large gold bomb, which will take out an additional row of tiles surrounding it (24 tiles).
The early levels will give you hints if you stall for too long, but no worries... That doesn't continue once you progress in the game, and neither does the super-easy-to-pass nature of the levels. Every word you make gets you points, and of course longer words give you more points.  Chaining together multiple characters in a word will net you some bonus points, and there are also some tiles that include multipliers.  If you're an achievement-hunter like me, simply passing a level isn't good enough, as you're going to want to get the most points possible in order to get three stars, and if you're competitive, there are leaderboards for each level, too!
All levels have a hidden timer for the purpose of stats, but there are a good 10 levels (that's a guess) that have a visible timer, and which you have to complete within 2 minutes or less... and a few of those levels have number tiles instead of letters, with challenges such as "Link tlles to add up to 40." GAH!
Every level has a goal that must be met before you can move on, and 64 of the levels include an additional challenge in the form of "banana" challenges.  An example of a banana challenge would be, "Make a 6+ letter vowel-heavy word."
There are:
- 36 achievements - If you're having trouble with the Codebreaker achievement, you'll find the secret on

- 111 story-driven levels
- 64 "banana" challenges
- 12 chimp challenges
The story was surprisingly interesting for the most part, and although I had figured out an important point pretty early on in the game, there were some surprises thrown in, and I found myself rushing through the latter levels just to see how it would end... And there came another surprise!  There are
possible endings! :O  NICE!
Overall I found Highrise Heroes to be a delightful word game, with an engaging story and nice bonuses.  I love the achievements and extra challenges to complete, and the difficulty level -- once you get past the early stages -- was enough to make me re-play over and over again to get my three stars, but (with the exception of the number levels) not enough to make me want to pull out my hair.
Definitely recommended to lovers of word games, the competitive, and those who love achievements (eventually, I'll have them ALL!  I WILL defeat those number levels!)  Muwahaha! XD

This game definitely belongs to my top 3 favorite games of all time. I keep replaying it over and over and over again, and I still have as much fun as I did on my first playthrough back in 2012 or so on the Xbox 360.
The fun of exploration is unparalleled, the combat is among the best you will find in a 3rd person action game, the diversity of character builds you can do is staggering, and the best of all: the game has absolutely no hand-holding. The absence of hand-holding makes the experience feel authentic and immersive. You won't find waypoint arrows or other unimmersive modern amenities.
The game has tons of optional content to the extent that you're likely to miss a lot of things on your first playthrough. This gives the player a real sense of discovery when they find a big hidden area.
Dark Souls is infamous for its difficulty, but don't be fooled: the difficulty is just one small piece of the puzzle in what makes this game so great. Killing the boss after struggling for a while feels extremely rewarding, and if you can't progress otherwise, you can always summon in some help via the co-op feature. Dark Souls is good not only because of the difficulty but because all the design elements come together and form a truly amazing work of art.
The only gripe I have with this game is that the level design starts to decline towards the last 20% or so of the game, but that's a minor issue in the grand scheme of things.
9.8 game. It's sad that Dark Souls 2 and 3 couldn't even come close to DS1's greatness.

The short: You control two characters in a well-made puzzle-platformer that expects you to be VERY proficient at controlling them by the end.
and you like the anime aesthetic; otherwise, you probably ought to pass.

*Note: I played the game before it was released on steam, hence the low playtime.
The long: Reverse x Reverse (RxR) is a puzzle-platformer with the core gameplay mechanic of simultaneously managing two characters, each with their own unique ability (one can dash, and the other can double jump). The first few stages provide a gentle introduction to the game while the player gets used to controlling the pair. These intro stages are followed by a steady stream of new gameplay mechanics, which are accompanied by an initially reasonable difficulty ramp... but the last world is a monster on its own, so be prepared to endure a lot of frustration.
Additionally, there are several puzzles that will require you to think, react, and execute rather quickly and precisely, especially if you choose to pursue high scores for each stage, so keep that in mind when considering a purchase.
Most importantly, in my opinion, RxR passes all of the checks for a good puzzle-platformer: good stage/puzzle design, tight controls, steady introduction of new mechanics (and combinations of old)... combined with good artwork, music, spritework, and voicework, this was genuinely one of my favorite games of 2015.

Here is my "First Play on Launch Day & Review" video:
Very relaxing game where you simply try and catch falling starts that fall while trying to catch power ups and bonus coins to help you buy cool stuff between games.  All the while you need to try avoid catching ice chunks which will slow your movement down.  There are also several negative effects that you want to try and avoid, that are colored red and orange, red being the worst of the two.
You start each game with 3 hearts of out a possible 5, and if you miss any falling stars, you lose a heart.  Hearts can be caught in the form of power-ups, but they fall pretty rarely.  Lose all your hearts, and it's game over.
The game slowly but progessively speeds up, so what starts out very casual will eventually turn pretty frantic, and while the game is very casual in nature, things like high winds blowing either left or right can definitely increase the difficulty enough to keep you from falling asleep to the amazingly tranquil music playing in the background!
Scoring is only accumulated when you dump your basket on either side of the screen, and the more stars you collect and dump, the more bonus points you can aquire.  Upgrading your basket from the default 5 star capacity to a maximum 10 star capacity with gold coins is my recommended highest priority over other things you can spend your coins on that are cosmetic only such as different designed baskets or different backgrounds to choose from when you play a game.
Add in the ability to compete with players of this game world-wide to see who is the most epic falling star catcher in the world is a very nice touch as well.  (Top 15 scores is kept)
I know, I know.. this is a long review for such a simple game.. but I think it helps you understand that this game DELIVERS for the price, especially if you tend to like casual games once in a while.
This game scored an impressive 88% from me in my video linked above, mainly due to a maximum "value" score, along with good "fun" and "controls & bugs" scores.
Great job to the developer(s) of this great casual game!

I think this game is a prime example of a case where if people didn't know the game specs and just played it, then it would be an enjoyable experience.  Instead we know what the specs are (or rather are not) and that's colouring people's perspectives.  Yes it's locked at 30fps instead of 60 (which, I'm not endorsing and is a shame) and some people have had resolution issues (I personally have not but I know how frustrating it is when you can't adjust this setting).
But, specs aside, the game plays fine on my laptop and it's really fun.  I never played the original version so I can't compare but I do have Tales of Zestiria on Steam and Symphonia is a much more enjoyable experience.  The combat is quick paced and fun, the story is cheesy (a good thing when playing Tales games, imo), music is good and graphically the game looks great.  I've only played for 3 hours, but no bugs or crashes yet so that's a plus too.  The only downside about that actual game for me is the voice acting - the person who voices Lloyd also did Max from Dark Cloud 2 and it's a jarring enough disconnect for me that I actually turned them off (but that's just a personal issue, the voice acting itself is okay).
Bottom line, if you care about the specs then be aware that this is locked at 30fps.  If that doesn't matter to you then the game itself is pretty solid port of a great game.

Unlike Postal 2, this one is a bit more serious. There is no real narrative, but the game is darker and more menacing in tone in comparison to its infamous sequel. It also features a top-down isometric view instead of a FPS style view. The game is solid enough; the sounds are very clear, and are probably the most impressive part of the game (say, for example, you walk up to a light on a building, there is a buzz from the fixture there; sounds of nature are well placed; people's screams and terrified shrieks sound real at times and sometimes just silly). The graphics are surprisingly hand-painted, which add somewhat of a depth to the game. The journal writings of the Postal Dude are relatively disturbing, demented, and dark, and are a contrast to the witty yet sadistical Postal Dude in Postal 2.
This game is also a game you didn't want your mom to see you playing back in the 90's, but today some of the violence is pretty tame as there really isn't any gore to speak of, just blood. It does involve killing innocent people, so it is definitely not a game for the easily offended.
Also, press F1 to progress to the next level. Just saying.
All in all, it's a solid game in terms gameplay and sound. 7.5/10

This terraria-inspired platforming survival epic has you bounding across space, discovering new solar systems with semi-unique creatures and presence. I have played both Terraria and Starbound to a very high extent. "Which is better?", I cannot say for anyone. Personally, I enjoyed this game much more as i valued the more in-depth story, along with the amazing sprite animation and high-quality/polished gameplay.
I would say that Terraria has a much more concise and compressed design, meaning it has very focused goals and events. The world is much more condensed, allowing for much more compact level design.
However, unlike its counterpart, Starbound also has a very concise feel to it, as all the planets have there own geological presence and ambience. When you travel to another world, you expect a different experience, and that's exactly what you get. There are different creatures and ores scattered across the world's core that can be discovered. Starbound also brings a new sense of high-quality exploration, as there is more than just one wolrd to explore. This game feels like a much more amped up version of Terraria with it's futuristic setting and broad exploration.
Although this review was not soley about the game itself, I feel like its still holds value to those who are debating about getting this game or Terraria.
It's terraria in space with some nice progression and exploring.

An extremely repetitive game with almost nothing to unlock.
In this game, you choose a character, you choose dungeon, and you progress between floors by killing enemies, looting stuff, finding keys, opening chests, killing bosses and finding stairs. (Be sure to read this list well. It's all you'll do in this game.)
There are two dungeons in total plus a custom dungeon mode. No story at all, almost no text or cutscenes.
Each floor works exactly like the last. Only the colors and the enemies change slightly.
Also, all enemies are basically the same. Some have a ranged attack or a special ability, but most of the time it doesn't change anything.
Bosses really are stronger than other monsters but they're still not interesting at all.
There are five playable characters in total.
They can gain new abilities during the course of the game. One 2 hours game where I explored everything was more than enough for me to unlock ALL my character's abilities.
Also, most of these abilities are pretty useless. Your first ability will always be the main one. Most abilities aren't even subtle or interesting; it's mainly just "deals more damage in a larger zone but costs more mana and has a longer cooldown". There's almost no strategy at all in this game.
Some games have a bad repetitive gameplay but are still fun. That's because in these games you can unlock things, which is a nice perspective for players who like to collect things or access to new ways to play. Others have a nice story or atmosphere and make you dream. But this game doesn't have any of that. It is both boring and pointless, and its gameplay is almost inexistant.
Your first game will be nice. But as as soon as you finish it and read the achievements, you'll understand that you have nothing more to do here.
Don't buy this unless you can have it for $1 and you have a lot of time to loose.

Having linked my copy of this game to my Steam Account in the middle of a haiatus (I played it extensively prior to it appearing on Steam), I'm finally back to playing this game, and it's every bit as excellent as I remember.
This is essentially a princess raiser/visual novel hybrid. Your character is Elodie, fourteen-year-old princess of the blood royal, who has just lost her mother, the late Queen of Nova. Your task is to guide her from the day she returns home from boarding school to the day of her coronation, on her fifteenth birthday. On the way, she will face a host of challenges: some political, some social, some physical, many quite deadly. You will lead her to her death many times before successfully navigating the dangers of noble life.
The artwork and character design are adorable. This adorable artwork juxtaposes well with the seriousness of the situations this would-be queen must face. The music is simple, but highly suitable. The plot is simple... but navigating it is anything but.
Gameplay proceeds in weeks, and involves three phases of decision making. First, you must choose what skills Elodie will study this week. Second, a plot event will occur, choices will have to be made, and what choises are available to her (and which ones she can actually be successful at) are governed by her skills (and her previously established level of cruelty). Third, you must decide how she spends her weekend. Some weekend events will advance certain plotlines, but mostly they are used to manipulate Elodie's mood, which determines how fast she will learn specific skills. Then the week finishes, and you're back to picking skills to learn. There are 42 skills. She will not learn them all. She will not succeed at all checks.
Equally cool is how after her coronation, there's a section where you get to read about her legacy. This will differ every playthrough, depending on what skills you developed, what checks you succeeded at, which ones you failed, and so on. For instance, I just finished what I like to call an "academic" playthrough, in which after she was raised to the throne Nova essentially started the Enlightenment. But this is not the only path...
Adorable design, intricate gamepley, and incredible replay value for just ten bucks. Why haven't you already bought this?

This is a variable thumbs up.  Which is to say, this game is not for everyone.  It appeals to a certain venn diagram demographic of people who grew up building castles with Legos and then finding ways to wreck them.  Which I imgaine is a pretty big group, it is true, but still isn't everyone.  Lucky for me I'm in that group.
Be warned, however, that it requires that certain obsessiveness when it comes to building things most commonly seen in Minecraft players who live logged into the game from inside their life support pods, being feed through IV drips as they continue the sixth year of their quest to recreate, in 1-to-1 scale, the Taj Mahal
it's surrounding gardens.  If you're not that insane, however, you're in luck - the integrated Workshop is already overflowing with more prefab designs of varying degrees of "That's no moon!" than you can imagine, so honestly you'll never really
to design anything if you don't want to.  And if you
that kind of crazy, thanks!  We really appreciate all that neat stuff in the Workshop.  Well done!
Then comes the fun part - destroying everything in sight.  Once you get your Insane Flying Battleship of Laser Doom finished it's time to head out and see what it's got.  Thankfully, do to an amazingly complex AI system, at this point you can just sit back and watch your engines of destruction curb-stomp inferior NPCs all day until you find yourself drooling and yelling "Smash Beetles!"
Ah, but eventually the game difficulty will ramp up, the NPCs will start fielding their own doomships and from there the battles will look like a Minecraft rendition of "Star Blazers" as kilometer long dreadnauts butt heads against each other in battles worthy of Godzilla's applause.
There is, of course, some downsides: If you're actually playing the campaign, good luck in actually getting any of those super-dooper ships assembled in anything less than five hours, because the gap between a player's campaign starting resource generation and the ambitions of the Workshop gnomes can be measured in parsecs.  Picking out the cheap, practical stuff can be a quest in itself... unless you want to make it yourself, and that leads to the other problem: The AI system.
Woe to he who does not spend several hours learning the many intricacies of the AI modules & system, and I don't just mean the tutorial stuff.  Making AI do anything more complex than "fly in circle and shoot stuffs" requires something resembling actually programming ability, and is not for the faint of heart or lacking of scripting skills.  Mastering that can make building your first
laser cannon seem simple in comparison.
However, again a lot of people who
handle that probably fall into the same venn diagram area I mentioned at the beginning of this review, so it's not
big of deal.  Yeah, the game almost requires a certain mindset but then it appeals most to that mindset to begin with.
Now as for the "Early Access" thing: The campaign system still need some work but it's functinal.  In fact, everything in the game is functional right now.  From here my prediction is that development will simply be bug fixes and refining the many rough edges of what is already in the game.  Right now it's kind of like a perfectly functional car without any paint, trim or dashboard lights.

I initially posted a very negative review. Now that I understand the game better I’m enjoying it, but I also have more criticisms, which I won’t post here because it is a long and detailed list.
At its core, the concept of this game is amazing. There are many unique aspects which are inspired genius. It’s apparent that a lot of thought and a lot of work have gone into the game's mechanics.
From my perspective the developer has taken the construction style of Minecraft, minus the landscaping and crafting, and nothing as complicated as red stone logic gates (expect maybe LUA blocks), and combined it with the vehicle design aspect of Kerbal Space Program, with more focus on weapons and defence and less on physics (e.g. no orbital mechanics!).
There is an RTS style capaign in which you mine and use resources to spawn the voxel based vehicles you design and have AI pilot them.
There is also a first person aspect, as you interact with the world through an avatar, which I believe is superfluous and detracts from the game with unnecessary added complexity, especially considering you can move the camera independantly and still interact in all the same ways without the avatar. On top of that there's a levelling system and a skill tree.
It has probably the steepest learning curve of any game I have played, but that's not due to the concept, its due to UI design, controls and at times infuriating camera controls. I spent the first 5 hours or so hating the game. Sheer determination got me through. I still felt I had a lot to learn after 30 hours.
I think the game could have broad appeal, but that will ultimately be limited by how well the developer can address the usability problems and simplify the learning curve. The in game tutorials are good, but not detailed enough. I hope links to external videos are removed from the game in favour of more tutorials.
As an RTS, there may also be inherent limitations to what can realistically be simulated but I’m confident the developer will work how to balance the game’s performance (without forcing the player to manage that).

Word puzzle games can be deceptively simple. They can also be ambitious, but that doesn't mean it should feature a long uninteresting story (a visual novel format would have been best here), endless repetitive levels, and top it off with unforgiving timers. Seriously, many of the levels just like to add insult to injury by forcing you to take many parameters into account (oxygen levels, moving rows, moving villains, forced tiles, timer, etc.), all the while expecting you to find words long enough that you'll get your 3 stars or complete an extra challenge.
Sure.
My first impression wasn't too great because the game doesn't have a great soundtrack and it's overall a lazy mobile port, which many UX problems I could have done without. Halfway through Highrise I just stopped caring, and it's only my judeo-christian education that prevented me from jumping out of a virtual window instead of going through each of these floors one by one and hearing stories about how that boring girl lost her stupid china cat and wants it back at the cost of another annoying level.
And while I'm sure it'll have its fans (I myself am a big fan of the studio's way more relaxing Quell Memento), it hurts me to say I simply can't recommend it if you're looking for a quick fun game to play between two tasks. Unless you're really planning to devote 50 hours into it, but you could finish Letter Quest 3 or 4 times instead, which sounds a lot more exciting to me.

I bought Highrise Heroes in the steam sale after enjoying another word game called Letter Quest: Grimm's Journey and while I still prefer Letter Quest this game makes a considerable effort to give variety. There are more than just your basic find words challenges, timed challenges and even a few number challenges (which I loved!). The story while not amazing is certainly quite humorous in places and I was eager to progress to see the next part mainly for the humour.
As a few reviewers have commented on, this game really does start to crank up the difficulty very fast, even when working together with my partner we struggled with some levels for nearly 40 minutes, Some of the later ideas and how to's aren't greatly explained either which led me to take a break from it.
Overall if you liked boggle or word games im general I can recommend this title. I certainly hope there are more like it sooner rather than later.

Here’s a word game that I enjoyed at first, but then grew to strongly dislike once I reached the later levels. Its mobile roots are very obvious, especially when trying to scroll up or down since the mouse wheel doesn’t work. You’ll need to click and drag instead. I don’t mind making that motion from left to right, but up and down does not feel great. Fortunately, the actual game doesn’t require any of that, just the main menu.

Once you start playing, you’ll notice how words are formed by drawing an unseen line through letters adjacent to each other or by clicking on them individually. The letters will have arrows indicating the direction you took through them. I didn’t have trouble for the most part, but I did find accidental word submissions annoying when I was trying to adjust a word by clicking a letter in the middle of the path. Canceling words requires clicking on the X off to the side when a word is started or by clicking elsewhere on the board. It’s all very functional when going at your own pace, but timed levels can increase the chance to make an error with word creation.
One of the most enjoyable aspects of this game is the leaderboard. Having that in the game really encourages replays and score chasing as you try to outdo your friends. There are some scores posted on there that are impossible, so I recommend having friends with the game or setting a goal such as Top 100 for yourself.
The game isn’t just about making words. Where the words are made are important and there are many obstacles and hazards introduced as you make progress down the building’s 90 floors. At first, you just have letters and survivors that need rescue. Blocks with various hit points then make their way onto the board. You’ll also run into water tiles, fire tiles, oxygen levels, and more. To help out, survivors have abilities that can manipulate the board, but they come at the cost of turns or time. The game starts out pleasant enough, but eventually, you’ll hit a wall depending on how good you are. Still, it’s fun to create words that end up creating explosions and wiping out strategic sections of the board to rescue everyone. The game also keeps the experience varied by changing the goals and boards of some levels such as linking numbers to add to a specific amount or using specific letters.
The difficulty really ramps up at the end of Chapter 3 and beyond. I remember spending 2 hours on building level 27 (you start at 90) due to the number of different mechanics I had to keep track of including lethal gas letters with turn times, fire letters that spread and take two turns to clear (one to put the fire out and the next to destroy the normal tile), keeping track of oxygen for the survivors, and reinforced blocks. Some levels can require an early restart if you have a bad draw if you want a decent score or want to win. You cannot control that aspect, so when you’re dealing with many different things, it just feels extremely frustrating at times. The difficulty spike also hurt the leaderboards where friends are concerned because I noticed a large drop off at the very end of Chapter 3. They just gave up. The following screenshot shows a board that has indestructible blocks, moving rows, destructible blocks, and protected letter tiles at the bottom.

The further I went, the more the game became more unpleasant. I started encountering more and more timed levels which are some of my least favorite. I found myself restarting much more often, sometimes to just have a strong beginning if the letters aren’t in my favor such as having a consonant block that can’t be cleared with using up many turns. Most of my playtime was spent on the second half of the game until I finally stopped some levels after reaching Chapter 5.
This game has a strong first impression with a frustrating second half depending on well you can handle everything thrown at you. It relies heavily on word making and strategy which can be fun and appealing to many. It’s an approachable word game for the beginning portion and you could probably have some fun leaderboard chases, but the later levels killed my enthusiasm for this title.

Amazing game. Definitely darker than Postal 2 and 3, but so much fun. Don't let the isometric graphics scare you away - I have to say, this is probably the best 17-year-old game I've ever played. Normally games that old feel clunky and terrible on newer computers, but Postal still feels up-to-date and fun, even though the graphics are old style.
Literally 10/10, would shoot cops for days! :D

Yeeahhhh childhood memories.  A must buy for anyone who's played the game in the past as it'll be fun as a blast from the past!  It might not appeal to anyone who hasn't played it before but it is interesting to say the least!

Despite the fact that I finished Postal, it is a bad game.  Even by 1997 standards it looks and plays lousy, not to mention the arguably offensive content.
The only reason I was able to play this game is because I went into the file called "Postal Plus.ini" and manually tweaked the controls enough to get the game feeling smooth.  The in-game key binding feature wasn't good enough to map the mouse and some of the keys on the keypad.
The graphics are all hand-drawn and are (hopefully) intentionally lousy. This style makes the game more visceral and gritty while at the same time making the game less serious.  If the game looked good I think it would be much more disturbing blasting one's way through a shanty town, a department store, or a retirement home.
One area that the game shines is the weapon selection.  There is a good variety of things to try out like throwing moltov cocktails, heat seeking rockets, and even an automatic shotgun.  Unfortunately this is lost on dumb enemy AI and the point at which I can't recommend this game.
In fairness to the developers it seems they are still updating the game for Steam users that bought Postal Plus.  It's one of the few late 90's games that have achievements, and that is impressive to me.
This game is sub-par and only serves to fill a basic need for a violent action game when all the other classics have been finished (DooM, Blood, Duke Nukem, Quake and so on).  If it comes to you in a bundle give it a try, but don't buy it.

It doesn’t really have a plot (unless you have the booklet that came with the game in 1997 or the Dude’s little diary bits before each level). But for the kind of game that Postal is, it doesn’t really need one. It’s just mindless fun. And you know what, that’s okay. The game is played in a top down, isometric point of view (kind of like Sonic 3D Blast or Command & Conquer). This is actually pretty cool. The camera is neither too far away or too close. You have a good sense of where you are and where enemies are. So it’s not hard to plan things out. It’s best if you play the game tactically. There is however a drawback to the whole bird’s eye, isometric view. It’s a bit hard to line up your shots with an NPC. And it can get frustrating (especially when the NPCs move which they will do by the way). But it’s forgivable seeing as that it doesn’t take much to kill an NPC. You have a selection of about eight weapons. Your default weapon which is a weak assault rifle, a stronger assault rifle, a shotgun, a grenade, a missile launcher, a molotov cocktail, a flamethrower, and an RPG. You even get a few specialty weapons such as land mines.
You play as a character called The Dude. No, not Dude from The Big Lebowski but The Postal Dude. The only way I can describe The Postal Dude is that he’s a smoother, less muscular version of Duke Nukem. He also shouts catchphrases like Duke. Catchphrases Like “Buttsauce” and “don’t be a sissy”. Though, he can also be described as a more tragic version of Duke Nukem as well. If you are following the games (almost non-existent) plot, it turns out that The Dude has gone insane and is under the impression that everyone in the city has a madness disease. So he takes it upon himself to exterminate everything that moves. I won’t give away the ending. But I will say that it is pretty satisfying.
So in conclusion, all I can say is that Postal is mindless fun. It’s really just a pick up and play game. It’s also a good way to relief stress after a grilling day at work or school.  This game gets the official Redneck grade of G for good.

Y'know, I had high hopes for Symphonia's PC release after seeing how good of a PC port Zestiria was. Boy was I mistaken. The thing is, it isn't inherently the game that is the problem here, it's the PC port and it's such a massive let down to see how lazy Bandai have been with porting it. As someone who is a big fan of the franchise, I can't help but be dissapointed with how awful it turned out. I think it's best we start with the biggest issue and that is the state of the PC port, because it's bloody awful.
First things first, the frame rate is locked to 30FPS with no way to increase it. Some have managed to it get it to 40FPS but don't hold out hope for it to run at 60FPS. It's rather amusing really that a console which is more then 10 years old (The Gamecube) can run this game better then modern day powerful PC's and have the game run at 60FPS.
The resoltuion is also locked to 720p even though the game gives you the option to have it go up to 1920x1080. Putting it in 1920x1080 doesn't increase it to 1080p at all, it stays at 720p with no way to increase it without help from Durante which I'd like to point out, managed to break past the resolution lock in 14 minutes and raise the it to 4K. Yes, Durante is currently working on a fix for the game but it is starting to get to the point where we have to rely on a single person to fix something an entire company of people couldn't be bothered to do and becuase of that, they should ashamed of themselves.
There is also hidden DRM built into the game called VMProtect which creates a new *.exe file everytime you run the game which continues to baffle me still as to why that is there.
It's hard to think of all the things they messed up in this broken PC port, how about the localization? Yep, they messed that up also with differentl languages being completely broken, hell, even the english is broken with words being mispelled.
But the one thing they messed up the most, the biggest thing which I personally couldn't believe until I saw it for myself is the steam badges. They even got the steam badges wrong, which is completely unforgivable. I think that is what ruins this PC port on every level. Let's also not forget about all the crashes that stop people from down right playing the thing.
As far as PC ports go, this is by far one of the most insulting ones I've seen in a long time. They seemed to show absolutly no interest in the port which in turn, made the game worse for it and has led to a lot of unhappy customers.
The thing is, I would have loved to recommend this game, I really wanted to, but I can't with how terrible the PC port is and that hurts coming from someone who grew up playing this game 12 years ago (Did I mention this game is 12 years old?). It's unbelievable that we still have to deal with awful PC ports such as this and expect to like it or wait for someone who cares about the PC community to bring out a fix FOR FREE when an entire company who's job it is to fix this, y'know, the companies we give hundreds to every year, can't be bothered to do anything about it.
That's it, I can't recommend this as the PC port is just so awful which hurts such a great game, because behind it all, Symphonia is a great game that could've been brought to a much larger audience and introduced the series to more people as one of the best Tales Of games. Unfortunately, seemed that Bandai couldn't care less and for that, they can go felate a bee hive for all I care.

: Since this review's getting hits, might as well make it more proper.
This game was launched with many issues, such as:
As of this writing only the menu delay seems to be fixed...for me, most of the time. It returned _once_ about 4 hours into a binge, but has otherwise not been an issue. It looks like they're fixing issues but if I were considering to buy this product, I'd wait until they produced a few more updates before actually purchasing this port. It seems the bad press is forcing Namco to act. This is sad, since Zestiria's port was actually pretty good. A little rushed and buggy, but not in any way that disrupted gameplay.
Tales of Symphonia itself is a classic Tales game from 2003, and it's the first ever 3D Tales game. This port is a more or less the remastered PS3 version ported to PC.
Like all Tales games, it uses the Linear Motion Battle System where you move your character in real time across a 2D line on a 3D battlefield -- between yourself and whatever enemy is selected. It plays much like a fighting game or a brawler in that you make real time attacks, perform combos, and need to defend or evade like you would in a brawler. Of course like an RPG, you have 3 other AI controlled party members and you can order them occasionally, but usually they'll just do their own thing. This game's unique gimmicks are Unison Attacks and Overlimits, the former being a bonus attack similar to QTE's and the latter just seems to happen randomly. Unfortunately those Unison Attacks use a PS3 controller interface and I can never seem to get all four to execute.
It's pretty awkward compared to current Tales games...the most notable aspect is this game came out before free roam existed, but while jumping was still an option. So you can't run around to flank enemies, but there are aerial abilities you can perform to achieve the same effect. Having played Phantasia before any others in the series, it wasn't too difficult to pick up on. It's still the awesome battle system that got me hooked on the series.
I had issue with the controls...it might be my 360 controller, but navigating the map was a pain since it uses push sensitivity for walk/run and I'd often find myself walking. It's probably since I'm a PCphile that I settled on using keyboard controls. The default controls are for people whose arms are 3 inches apart, but after switching to WASD + numpad I found gameplay to be pretty enjoyable.
I'm not going to comment on the story until I get further through. 8 hours is too few to judge...but so far it's a mix of a pretty lighthearted party in a pretty bleak world.
Graphics are...720p. They're a notable improvement over the Gamecube graphics but still seem a generation behind for the most part. Also they're quite blurry, being locked at 720 arbitrarily. Bit of a weak point for the game.
The soundtrack is the kind you'd actually make the effort to purchase separately. Not only do I prefer melodic over ambient, I love Motoi Sakuraba's style.
Anyway, I plan on changing my thumbs down into a thumbs up,

Where to start...
I still have the game on GameCube and that is thoroughly one of the most enjoyable gaming experiences I've had in my 23+ year career as a gamer.  With that in mind, you can easily tell how hyped I was when I heard about this coming on PC and for 20€ no less!
The hype is hype, though.  While the game functions well enough (haven't gotten through the first dungeon yet, though) in that it starts, runs and functions well enough, I can see why people are callign this a disastrous port.  There are significant instabilities that CAN be avoided, if you know what they are.
For instance, the game crashes for me when I enter the configuration menu from the start menu (logical first step with any new game) and the loading times for save menus is abhorent *by modern standards.*  The config menu does work while in the actual game, it just takes nearly a minute to get in.
I can accept that this game is a port of a previous gen port, especially since I've never owned any other console than what Nintendo's produced.  I like the additional motion in the skits, I look forward to the added Anime cutscenes (which I know are in the PS3 version), I love that the redone japanese intro is in the game and I especially like the option of playing the game with japanese voice work.  That last one breathes new life into a game I've already played through multiple times with 40-80h on each playthrough (damn metal spheres...).  Best of all, I can play this game with an XB controller.
To address what people are really complaining about with this port are the graphics, the instability and the DRM.
I've been a gamer for over two decades, well into my prime for 16.  Graphics are something I don't particularly care about.  As long as it looks good, I like it.  That's why I grind through multiple classic games and occasionally revisit my Nintendo library.  Then again, 1080p is better than 720p, but that's more like a bonus to me than anything.
The instability is a big minus, especially since my antivirus detects each .tmp file the game creates when I try to change the settings before going into the campaign, promptly leading to an irresponsiveness crash.
The DRM....  When will devs learn that DRM doesn't do jack squat?
So to sum up my feelings about this port....  It has problems.  Boy, does it have problems, but it works.  And as long as it works, I'm willing to bend around them.  And since it works to my satisfaction, I give it a thumbs up.  A 51/49 thumbs up, but still.
Tl;dr I recommend this game for those who want a classic JRPG experience and are willing to forgive technical issues, especially those who want to ride on GC nostalgia.  If you're a graphics junkie who wants something modern and without technical issues, you might want to think twice before buying this.  And even then you better have a controller, since this thing is NOT meant for keyboard+mouse.  PS3 port owners shouldn't bother.
===POST UPDATE===
Lot of instability fixed, menus work well; still getting annoying F-secure popups about the .tmp files, though.

This is a very interesting concept, and I think it could be a really great mod.  The only issue is that it feels really inconsistent with its new mechanics, and it seems to end the tutorial a bit early.
I stopped at the first test chamber that didn't have a tutorial screen because of this.  The point of the chamber seemed to be using all the various new mechanics together, but they needed to be used simultaneously, which it had given no indication was possible.  Or how to do it.
It looks like the developer/modder has put a lot of time and effort into this, and it definitely shows.  Sadly, the seemingly incomplete tutorials make it difficult to progress, and the seeming inconsistency of the new mechanics make it extremely frustrating.
I would recommend ether extending the tutorial screens for at least one more chamber, or recording some voice over dialogue to add to what you have currently.
All in all, Great start!  Keep working on it.  I look forward to seeing where you go with this in the future. (Assuming you are still looking to work on it more)
Edit:
After thinking about the puzzle I stopped on, I figured out how to solve it, and decided to give the game another shot.  And for a bit, it was interesting, all be it, a bit boring.
The level design of the later test chambers was so convoluted, it quickly stopped being fun.  This was made worse by the fact that there isn't as much as background music through the whole thing, until you get to the final cut scene.
I found what was the briefest outline of a story, but it only was shown in three points in the entire game.  Literally, the beginning, middle and end.  And you never get any real explanation as to what's going on or why.
I will reiterate my previous recommendations for additional voice work, though now, to infer story rather than mechanics.  And will add a recommendation to rethink and rework the later test chambers, and to add some background music in.
Sadly, as it is now, I can't recommend this mod/game.  I applaud the developers efforts and accomplishments, but this still needs ALOT of work.

Thinking with Time Machine expands on Portal 2 with a new ability to record and playback player actions, and then interact with the recording (similar to one of the tools in The Talos Principle). Essentially allowing players to create doubles of themselves for a short time and play coop alone. The mod does not take full advantage of this new mechanic, though, as it is way too short, with only a handful of test chambers. This is partially remedied by player-created levels in the workshop, but playing disparate custom levels is a hassle and does not quite provide the same experience as a wholesome campaign. It seems the author tried to tie the mod into the Portal story with a few cut scenes and scripted events, but these attempts feel feeble and never really go anywhere. But this does not take away from the thoroughly enjoyable content, enough for about 2 hours of gameplay, with fairly easy puzzles and a brand new tool to play with.

This game has excellent potential. But for a game in early access, it has surprisingly few flaws.
1. Thirst drains too quickly and there is mainly one source of water: Coconuts, which rapidly run out, and don't seem to respawn, making it difficult to settle on one specific island if you have to continuously move to have a continuous supply of water.
2. Graphics are stunning, but unless you have a newer computer or have a computer built specifically for gaming, the game's framerate will suffer. Especially if you are on an island with cliff's, the framerate may drop dramatically.
3. The fish don't appear to serve much purpose (unless you can cook them in a specific way other than having a fire spit)
4. I would suggest that new items like driftwood, tarps, etc. Drift upon the shores of islands every other morning so you don't have to row/swim to other islands every day to get a handful of random supplies that the island may or may not have.
5. Plants that should contain fruit do not grow.
The fact that food will eventually spoil adds realism. Having the character speak is interesting to add.
Overall, the game really does give you the struggles and hardships of survival, and I am eager to see what is added in future updates.

If you think that it's "just like Terraria, but in space!" — you're dead wrong. Every single activity is a routine and thanks to ridiculous amounts of downtime you spend waiting for something to craft only makes it a depressing slog as the more time passes. In early days of Starbound beta you actually could just leave desired workstation (Well, at least Furnace) to continue crafting stack of items you chose on itself. But alas this feature is no more. Considering that you can't make an armor, say with just 5 ingots and 1 leather — like in minecraft, — and have to use
workstations for this: every activity becomes more and more tedious.
"Well, but you don't have to only craft and build! It's an infinite universe of endless possibilities to find and explore!" — you'd say, and would be wrong again. There was a potential for something special here. But dungeons are scarce and even after so many content patches they are still overly repetative. AI is braindead, and without a dedicated mod, it can't even use terrain to get to you. Procedurely-generated quests are as boring as you can imagine if you had dealt with this system before. And, again, every activity is nothing but a routine.
Main quest and story are nothing special too, but even then they have an audacity to rely on randomly generated dungeons for you to explore in between missions to "gather info about X race" (yes, the goal always remains the same). I understand that it's made to encourage exploration, and help player find better equipment. But since changes to weapon system were introduced in recent patches, finding a good new weapon on every tier of progression is not mandatory anymore. And enough ore to craft a next tier armor can be found within minutes of digging.
Add to all aforementioned shortcomings some real problems: like constant freezes in multiplayer (and even in singleplayer) when the game loads a new chunk of land (and it's a long-running problem that occurs on
PC), and you'll get a product that I truly can not recommend.
I don't even know, how I managed to play this game for so long. Probably it was due to a fact I constantly tried to love it, giving it another chance every time a new patch came out. However it all feels like a hazy dream, a distant memory of an autistic trance in wich I've spent four hundred hours. Whereas in Terraria every hour was filled with pure fun and joy.

This terraria-inspired platforming survival epic has you bounding across space, discovering new solar systems with semi-unique creatures and presence. I have played both Terraria and Starbound to a very high extent. "Which is better?", I cannot say for anyone. Personally, I enjoyed this game much more as i valued the more in-depth story, along with the amazing sprite animation and high-quality/polished gameplay.
I would say that Terraria has a much more concise and compressed design, meaning it has very focused goals and events. The world is much more condensed, allowing for much more compact level design.
However, unlike its counterpart, Starbound also has a very concise feel to it, as all the planets have there own geological presence and ambience. When you travel to another world, you expect a different experience, and that's exactly what you get. There are different creatures and ores scattered across the world's core that can be discovered. Starbound also brings a new sense of high-quality exploration, as there is more than just one wolrd to explore. This game feels like a much more amped up version of Terraria with it's futuristic setting and broad exploration.
Although this review was not soley about the game itself, I feel like its still holds value to those who are debating about getting this game or Terraria.

Ignore the amount of time spent on this game. I played this when it came out on Xbox.
What is the gameplay?
Well, you are in a mobile 'Trench' that can hold weapons on it. There are different "Chassis" which give you a certain amount of weapon slots on each side. A "big" chassis gives you 3 weapon slots on each side. A medium would give 2. A small would give you 1. Certain weapons take certain amount of slots. A machine takes 1 while a artillery will take all 3 on the one side. Snipers take 2 slots. Also, the weapons get stronger as you progress in the game, some getting "special" abilities. For example, an artillery that has shock, which stuns the monovision. Second thing is there are turret slots. Like machine gun turrets, Sniper turrets, land mines etc. they each take a slot and depends on what type of slot. There is a support, light, and heavy slot. Snipers and land mines are heavy, machine guns and shotgun turrets are light, a support would be a repair crane, Dampening Genarator, or a Magnet prong.
What am i fighting?
They are called monovisions. Essentially, its kind of like an alien life form, but look allot like electricity and blue wires. There are unique monos that target certain things, or attack in certain ways.
All in all, i bought this game out of Nostalgia (i think thats how you spell it) and dont regret it at all. the game has replayability for the achievements, loot to find, and even has survival mode. *Kinda like Zombies on Call of booty* how long can you last. You even get loot from the survival mode. There are 3 survival maps from what i know. I got to 56 on one, 76 on another, and my favorite map, i got to 100.
Truly, if you are into strategy, and want to use defences and even your own trench to protect a building, drill, or gun. Then you arent far from finding an amazing game. Look up some youtube videos and watch. Good luck on finding the game you want.

LUFTRAUSERS is a fun, challenging little game with suprisingly good replay value, given that the game essentially consists of a single stage with endless waves of enemies. LUFTRAUSERS is the most basic of arcade shmups in that you play until you die and hope to get a high score. However, it has more depth then most games of that type thanks to a range of interchangable parts that greatly effect your Rauser's performance in combat. You may choose from weapons, fusilages and engines, each with very different behaviors. Each of the many, many combinations has its own name and there is an achivement for trying them all once, by far the most time-consuming one. You can also change the game's color palette away from its default, deliberaitely monochromatic sepia tones, though most of these alternate schemes will wear on your eyes. The music also changes to match each configuration of your Rauser, and the game comes with the seperate audio tracks to create your own remixes. While thin for its list price of $10, the game is well designed, with responsive controls that challenge you rather then hamstring you, and an overall stylish presentation. Well worth getting on sale.

It's SUCH a fun game, if only multi-player worked reliably, which it does not. SO much potential lost of this fundamental problem!
Despite the confident Dev claims from a couple of months ago, playing in multi-player mode, one or more players WILL lose their connection at random. Thus, you get a long way into a Mars mission, only to have one or more players disconnected, and then everybody else quickly dies while the unlucky one(s) try to rejoin: Failed mission.
After several retries like that, it gets frustrating that the maps are designed for multi-player, certain achievements are based upon multi-player, but the game engine CLEARLY does not yet solidly and reliably support multi-player. So, until it is truly fixed, my friends and I are tired of the frustration and wasted time of trying to beat hard missions and having key players dropped at crucial moments.
People contemplating buying the game should understand that multi-player is NOT fixed nor reliable yet, so there is a core frustration to the game (particularly on the harder settings) that make it more luck (will everybody's connections hold?) than skill whether you'll be able to complete particularly the Mars maps.

From the Depths (or FtD, as I shorten it to) is a game where you build ships, tanks, planes, spaceships, space stations, flying fortresses, and submarines, among other fantastical sh!t you can make. The building, while originally counterintuitive and clunky to new players, quickly becomes engrained in the muscles, making it very easy to begin building once you master the controls and read a few guides.
Gameplay- 9/10
The game plays incredibly; it's fun, relaxing, and exciting all at the same time, depending on what you happen to be doing. It is, however, marred by occasional frame issues. I myself have not had many, but I have built myself a godrig, so consider your hardware carefully before puchasing.
Audio- 6/10
Arguably the weakest part of the game, the audio and soundtrack (of which there is none at time of writing) is very generic, with almost copy-pasted wave crashing effects, firing sounds, and propeller and engine sounds droning on. Many people, among them myself, have learned to ignore it, but it still is a weak point in an otherwise good game. It will most likely be rectified as the game progresses (it is an alpha, after all).
Visuals/Graphics- 8/10
The game doesn't look terrible, despite its indie roots and early dev. stage. In fact, many of the best looking areas in gaming that I have seen come from me dicking around on small skiffs on the highest graphical setting. Most of the time, however, it looks fairly standard. As stated above, it might challenge some older/weaker PCs, but it will, most likely, be fixed over time.
Overall- 8/10
The game is a quirky, fun, and addicting building game, where the inner engineer in you can come out to play in a voxel based world, where very little cannot be overcome by a little bit of thinking. It's very new, however, and may seem rough to those not familiar with it. The price point, another weak point, hovers around $20. It is worth it, but be careful, and seriously consider what type of gamer you are.

Is AdVenture Communist same as AdVenture Capitalist? Njet! AdComm is true idealism! Do not discuss such silly things, is obvious!
In all seriousness, the two games, while having similarities for obvious reasons, are different. In adCap (last I played it, might have been changed since) you have money and you can buy everything with this. In adComm, you have potatoe and you buy farmer with potatoe to harvest potatoe for you. Then you buy worker with farmer, then you buy miner with worker, eventually getting camps to generate farmers etc. Unlike adCap, there is no one all-important currency. Rather, every currency remains relevant for a while still.
Pros:
-More engaging playstyle.
-Actual minor choice of strategy (f.e. whether you want to get a nurse early-game to build up meds).
-No restrictions by making the other currencies unlockable, you can click them right from the beginning.
Cons:
-Less clicker-game because you'll need to swap between menus to get more of a resource before you can get more of a different resource. Especially early game you cannot rely on auto-generate.
-Has a bit of a dip in gameplay between the start and the part where you get to real auto-generating resources.

Highrise Heroes is a boggle-style word building game where you match adjacent tiles to make the best word possible, triggering various score bonuses and explosions based on the strategy you went for. Whilst a story may seem like an unlikely addition to this type of game, it does actually have an element of mystery and discovery as you try to figure out what exactly went down in this bizarre skyscraper. In between each of the levels there is dialogue, which is a little bit tongue in cheek bad. I thought it was actually well written, but with characters that are designed to be obvious tropes and the writer was clearly looking for groans and facepalms along the way. Nothing too serious and it did actually make me laugh a few times.
As the game unfolds you get more and more characters, each of which has a special ability. The characters you get on each level are story-based, so you don't get to choose. Some levels include things like saving a teddy bear, or mopping up some water along the way. There are also a lot of monkeys, collectible flag-based bananas and a character named Captain Amazeballs, because why not.
In addition to the regular word challenges, there are occasional number levels where you need to match combinations of numbers, both positive and negative which I found surprisingly fun. Not fun enough to want a whole game based around it, but enough to keep it fresh every now and again.
Some of the levels are incredibly simple, but others, especially the timed challenges, are incredibly hard! There's a little bit of a disconnect in difficulties, but generally speaking as you progress to the end of the game, it gets harder, and harder and harder... I would say that this is probably one of the more challenging word-based games to complete that I've played and at times, a little frustrating, but I got there in the end.
Overall the amount of strategy, different level types, different challenges and increasing difficulty makes this one of the most feature-complete word games I've played - with a lot of replayability in the star and score system, including global and friend based leaderboards. It's not just another clone, it does bring originality so it gets a thumbs up from me.

Highrise Heroes is superior to any of the other word games on Steam.
First off, the basic gameplay is akin to a Match-3 game where you need to destroy normal tiles to allow important tiles to reach the bottom, but instead of matching colours you're creating words. This simple premise alone wouldn't have sustained the player through 90 levels so thankfully we have lots of other minor mechanics and distractions to stir things up. There's admirable attention to detail everywhere, in the menus and storytelling as well as the game levels. The game even accepts US and UK spellings.
An update rolled out today (Feb 4 2016) is the option to turn off the timer without being penalised. This is most welcome as my only grumble prior to this update was the unnecessary (IMO) pressure of a time limit on some levels. Now you just uncheck the timer box on the level info screen and take your sweet time. It won't even affect your achievements.

Highrise Heroes is 10/10 if you're a word game junkie.

It’s strange to think that XCOM: War of the Chosen was the catalyst for me to try the origin of its Nemesis system, Shadow of Mordor. Not to be easily confused with its sequel, Shadow of War, as the second most derivative name ever, SoW is a surprisingly superb game with obvious influences from the Arkham and the Assassin Creed series. As an avid fan of both series who acknowledges their shortcomings, SoW manages to improve on their lack of challenge before the final act tumbles on itself with the same issues of its predecessors. If anything, the attempt to make a game that is more than mere imitation makes it worthier of praise than the criticism of its unoriginality.
However, as much as SoW is enjoyable on its own with tons of additional content only for movie fanatics who don’t care about the lore, the sad truth that becomes more apparent as you play is that it showcases the writing on the walls of its future Games As Services model. It doesn’t have any bearing on the game itself as the GOTY edition includes everything bundled together, yet it cannot help but overcast its proverbial shadow of a game by the constant realization, “I Cannot Believe It’s Not Microtransactions.”
If Shadow of Mordor has answered any one question about gaming, it’s made me realized that 3D platformers/collect-o-thons have never truly died. Instead of fading away into Kickstarter obscurity, these games have become repurposed into 3D person action games of all variety. The emphasis on exploration and platforming has been reshaped into “Play Your Way”/”The Ubisoft Game” approaches to sandboxes emphasizing action, stealth and a combination of the two with the fundamentals of simply collecting everything on the map as a checklist. It’s only after not playing one of these kinds of games for so long following Yooka Laylee that the transition is more apparent than ever.

Unlike collect-o-thons, however, many of these types of collectables often offer no practical value or sense of reward save for bloated features, and SoW is an example both of their good and bad qualities. At its worst, many collectables are “Collect X things because Achievement Y” where they add nothing to the game except a minor distraction for longevity. At its best, the early/mid game progression encourages the player to hunt these bonuses down to meet the ever-impeding odds. The rewards from defeating Nemeses offer mainly stat-based benefits to make them easier to handle and make the player’s growth feel more in the player’s control.  Upgrades truly do allow players more diverse tactics as they play. All these systems benefit the player with truly becoming familiar with these environments through repetition as the entire game consists of two maps, and, if played in controlled bursts, this progression system is satisfying the more you become familiar with the gameplay.
Some might decry these features and the limited overworlds as signs of bloated content with a paltry attempt of reused assets, yet the difficulty for two-thirds of the game is benefited from these distractions to encourage the sandbox storytelling these games often forget. It’s such a shame that at its greatest moments the Nemesis system is often a forgotten feature that is criminally underused because of how overused is its implementation.
Sandbox games like Shadow of Mordor attempt to bridge the linear storytelling of AAA games with the non-linear, open ended approaches not only for the sake of longevity but also for more replayability. Compromises like scaled-to-player enemies, plot-threads with little to no time pressure, etc. are all attempts to keep the uncompromising marriage of storytelling and gameplay in check from making any real commitments. SoW attempts to fix this mess through combining various story-levels with its implementation of a system generating randomized enemy orcs with unique quirks to make every Nemesis its own memorable threat. Death is never a game-over but merely a new rising conflict for the player to add to their overall journey to make for what should be a unique experience for every player based on their skill.
At its better moments, this design shows its merits with the level of detail put into this system. Orcs never seem to say the same lines twice, which leads me to believe most data for this game is audio files in sheer numbers. Chief Lords all have their names chanted to signify their presence. Lines are written to remind players who they are and give players the satisfaction of vengeance or a reminder of failure in every confrontation. There is a great illusion given to this system that makes it more beautiful in its appearances than what is truly underneath its guise.
The problem in hindsight with this implementation is that when every orc is a randomized obstacle, none are memorable after the hundredth orc you slay. Perhaps this is why XCOM only has three randomized enemies that show up multiple times to enforce their presence rather than making every enemy randomized. In the fifthteen hours of gameplay, not one orc stood out from me other than RatBag as the difficulty often would result in me simply killing the orcs than being killed by them. Whether you are dying often in the beginning when Tallion is at his weakest or you are massacring Nemeses by the dozens, the fundamental issue of there being too many antagonists makes everyone forgettable. It did not even occur to me that some orcs were resurrected until the orc said this was the third time I had slain him. Ultimately, a system designed to generate player-based enemies only makes the player their own worst enemy as the repetition will make every orc look, fight and sound all the same.
For any other game, Shadow of War would easily be on my horizon, but Shadow of Mordor is the only game that I can safely recommend, and it’s a shame. Everything from what I have seen and heard about the sequel appears that Monolith truly have ironed out the issues of its Nemesis system by making orcs into caricatures to make them memorable. Combat and the sheer numbers of enemies also seem to greatly improve on the original’s shortcomings where upgrades begin to have diminishing returns on the difficulty of the game, yet it’s still highly likely to become too easy unless you game the system rather than removing the stat-based elements entirely. As a whole, it’s difficult to truly appreciate Shadow of Mordor when there are moments here and there of brilliance where everything comes together, yet it never succumbs to the temptations of power to make shortcuts at any cost.
In an ideal world, SoW would be admirable for laying out the groundwork for an even better game, yet with the shoddy end-game simply reusing the same objectives as well as giving the player the late-game ability that is the central focus of its sequel Shadow of Mordor is more bittersweet than it should have been. (Ironically, this is the same damnable offence that would plague its sequel for different reasons.) It is one of many things that makes me wonder how much greater Shadow of War and Mordor could have been or if Shadow of War was their intentions all along that were never seized until they had enough followers.
