This game is the farthest thing away from what I usually take and interest in as visual novels normally bother me.
That being said, this game is genius. Pure Genius. It's morbidly funny, mind numbly difficult at times and the cutesy graphics actually add to the game rather than take away from it. I think I laughed so hard I cried the first time I played through it. Poor Ellodie. Why is it so satisfying to see her fail?
I still have yet to get to her coronation but half the fun is exploring all the options. I even gave this to my fiance and he -hates- visual novels. He spent 2 hours trying to keep Ellodie alive. And he's hooked too.
The sugar-fluff appearance hides the truth about this game. You have an obscene amount of classes you have to balance along with her moods. To make it more difficult, her moods affect how fast she learns certain things so you'd better keep a close eye on Ellodie if you want her to succeed!
Unfortunately the complexity of the game is also it's downfall. So much going on at once can be overwhelming and hard to keep track of. I suggest keeping a little notepad by your computer when you pick this game up, just in case.
The soundtrack is simple in the game and pretty at first but becomes a bit grating the longer you play.
Those small gripes aside, the game is a good, solid choice for people who like a bit or dark humour, court intrigue and puzzles. Don't let the pink frills fool you. Ellodie will die. Repeatedly. And you'll giggle every time. A solid 7.5/10
TL;DR:
A visual novel-esque game with a morbid flair and a delicate balance.
Pros:
=====
+ So many ways to kill poor Ellodie
+ So many options to choose to keep her alive until coronation
+ A storyline that you really have to focus on with a huge cast of characters.
+ A more intelligent take on the life of a royal. Less princess gowns and pretty princess, and more royal duty and demands.
+ Choices really do matter. Will you be a polite and gracious ruler? Or a war-hardened tyrant?
+ Great humour and surprisingly good writing.
Cons:
=====
- The soundtrack gets rather grating after a while.
- Sometimes the choices can be a little too numerous
- The story can fail to make sense if you don't train in certain skills and thus become really confusing.
- The chocolate.

The road to being queen is long, bloody, strewn with the bodies of yourself in your many failed attempts.
While Long Live The Queen looks like any generic anime style game on steam, in reality it is a decently written hyper-lethal choose your own adventure story with you trying to help your little princess survive to be crowned by any means nessicary. Each day you adjust her mood via little events and try and groom her in the skills you can only -guess- that you'll need. Those points in medicine may not be enough to secure an alliance with a foreign dignitary, but they may be enough to stop your own assassination attempt a week later. With no way to see what skills you need in the future, you will fail alot, and you will die alot in your first few playthoughts. This is were the micromanagers dream comes in.
Each time you fail (and you will fail) just makes you wanna try again to help survive another day or try a better route. There are several paths to the end game, especially after the free update to add more options and ways to win, but even after you do, you'll wanna come back again and again to see what else works. The event you missed may have led to something new entirely, or maybe even working for the villian.
For what it is, it's short, fun, cheap, endlessly replayable, and well worth however much time you choose to sink into it. Long live the queen!

DISCLAIMER: This genre isn't exactly my cup of tea, I got this game from a bundle, and so I'm presumably terrible at it.
That said, it doesn't seem like this game would be much fun even for someone who knew what they were doing. After a couple of introductory missions (one air combat, one as the door gunner), I was given the task of defending the allied base from a few enemy fighters that were exactly the same as the ones in the tutorial (after a few decent cutscenes). Which seemed reasonable enough for the start of the first real mission. Except after I wandered around the expansive map for long enough to chase each one down (tedious, but that might be mostly my fault), a few more identical fighters appeared. This exact scenario played out about eight more times - with some vague plot explanation as we moseyed between the base, some oil fields, and the location where an ally was forced to eject - before the mission was mercifully deemed successful.
To be fair, it might get less repetitive later on. But on the other hand, it seems fair to say that some things won't change much - the sloppy controls, the disconcerting and unnecessary kill cam, and the overall tedium. In several areas, it's at least a decent game. The overall design, though, leaves it as not a particularly fun one.

For all his supporters and enthusiasts, Dark Soul is one terrible game, perhaps the worst I have ever played. I like the idea of a game so brutally difficult as to inspire camaraderie among its fanbase and allow people to boast about their achievements. But "difficult" should mean "fair, playable, and fun", not "unfair, clumsy, and hideous" (let alone quite ugly to look at). Playing through Dark Souls is a truly masochistic experience that offers no other reward than the pleasure of beating the game -- the same as, say, trudging barefoot through a thorny field to eventually say "I've made it". If you want a difficult but fair game, take a look at Darkest Dungeon instead.

Great game with almost 600 hours. For the price I can definitely say even if I stopped playing today it was well worth the money.
When I first played the game, I was rather overwhelmed by the UI and how the game worked. To the point I got a refund. (I know silly right but nerd rage is a powerful thing).
Pros -
Well clearly the freedom you have in which to build things. From flying monstrosities that bring love in the form of rainbow colored lasers. Subs that shoot missiles and torpedos or harpoons, because dragging someone under the water is fun. Satalites rain now large amounts of cannonfire (cannons being given and update and now you can build even more fun artilary gun pieces, or railguns) :D
Boats that fire hundreds of missiles, lasers, guns, and bring love and peace to all that resist, resistance is loosely classified.
Oh and there are the death fortresses.
There is a campaign mode, while not the greatest, it can be pretty fun to test out your designs against other armies. The campaign mode is a mixture of RTS and arcade boat / flying game. Where you might control a single vehicle entirely (or let the ai control the guns), while having the rest of the fleet controlled by the AI.
The biggest pro how ever, and which likely kept me with the game for so long, is the epic community. while somewhat small everyone is so helpful, often willing to look at your designs and help you fix problems. Give tips, and tricks.
There are many more improvements in the making so I am looking forward to seeing what comes in the future.
Cons -
Remember this is alpha so hopefully these problems with be fixed in the future.
FPS and crashing. By far the biggest and worst thing of the game, it does not like large fleets, Up to around 25000 blocks the game works fine with some slow downs. But after that you can expect the game to come to a grinding halt, followed by crashing randomly. This can be highly annoying especially in campaign mode when you have to fight an enemy fleet that has many vehicles.
Too many missiles and bullets willl also bring down the FPS.
The other problem is AI. While you can deal with it, especially if you work out how to use LUA code, and or the automated controllers. (I use the automated controllers to do a lot of different things to over come the limitations of the AI).
While you can make subs, and spaceships, there is no proper AI which can make setting up fully AI controlled Subs and spaceships rather hard and frustrating.
So yeah I highly recommend this game. and am rather glad I over came my earlier frustration to give this game a second go. The learning curve is steep, as in clith like steep. But there is so much you can do, and once you learn the basics From the Depths (heh) of this game It becomes great fun.
I just wish I could learn to build more restrained but hey I like explosions and rainbow deathray lasers.

I'm writing this review for one of my favorite games ever. I own the game on every possible device it has been released on. I own the GC, PS2, PS3 and now the PC version of the game and have poured probably thousands of hours into this title. You would think that as the time passes and technology progresses that these old games would only get better when they are remade for newer console. But that's not the case with Tales of Symphonia. To put it shortly the PC version is just one ugly mess.
Pros:
- Dual audio
- PS2 version extra content, few skins and bunch added hi-ougis (or mystic artes as they like to call them)
Cons:
- Locked 30 FPS even if the very first version on the Gamecube was solid and smooth 60 FPS
- Capped internal resolution of 720p (the year is 2016 btw and this is PC we are talking about)
- Crashes at startup, crashes when trying to access the customize menu, crashes alt+tabbing, crashes whenever it feels like
- Horrible translation errors in coding, letters missing or generally completely bugged menus
- Some kind of VMProtect to act as an additional DRM (yay) which changes the running .exe name and prevents stuff form Nvidia cp AND makes it even harder for modders to fix the damn game
- No support for mouse and keyboard
I would NOT recommend this version of the game to anyone. It's just a shameless act from Namco and no one should give them money for this kind of blatant robbery. I love the game itself, I really do. As I mentioned in the beginning I have it for every system and if you truly want the DEFINITE version of the game then the original Gamecube version if the way to go. It does lack a tiny amount of content (not a big deal, few skins and few mystic artes), but it's simply the most solid and smoothest experience of the game. Dolphin with the grapchical enhancements has been the most wonderful experience I've had with this game.
tl;dr: The game itself is one of the best games I've ever played, but the PC port is one of the worst ports I've ever played. DO NOT BUY!
~Refunding the game ASAP

The alt-tabing isn't great but that seems to be the case for anything not running borderless windowed mode which I hope they include in a patch otherwise I'll have to find a way to force it. The FPS for me hits 30 consistantly.

For those that don't know, the PS3 version is based of the Japan only PS2 release not the Game Cube which is where the bulk of the extra content comes from as well as the slightly increased dificulty.
Story wise still as great as it always was, got it for christmas when if first came out and have put in well over 1000 hours over the years. Most characters aren't static and grow and change throught the story and makes you actually care about the characters and what happens to them. The story sits between sterious and whimsical, having moments of both but neither becoming overbearing. Definitly one of my top two Tales games along with Vesperia.
*note* hours played isn't too accurate, I mostly play in offline mode and Steam doesn't record offline hours
*Edit* Running the newest Windows 10 public build and the latest Nvidia drivers

This game is essentially a remake of the 1991 Sega classic "Fatal Labyrinth", which is also available on Steam. Quest of Dungeons adds a few elements to the formula, some good and some bad, but doesn't really aspire to improve it so the few flaws that Fatal Labyrinth had are still here in Quest of Dungeons.
This game adds more loot and a store to sell and buy items. But most of the loot is just junk to sell anyway, and there is nothing worth buying except healing potions. Quest of Dungeons also tries to add personality to the player character and the monsters, but fails completely. The character says random things like "This game was made with C++" and "This game was made with OpenGL". The monsters say equally weird things, according to another reviewer they are mostly references to movies that have nothing to do with the context of this game.
Like in Fatal Labyrinth, the only way to heal between battles is to run around a bit. In this game the healing is a lot slower so the running around just to heal yourself gets even more tedious after a while.
I quit playing soon after I got to the 4th floor of the dungeon. There you encounter monsters who steal stuff from your inventory. This is another "feature" that was present in Fatal Labyrinth as well. But again, Quest of Dungeons makes an annoying feature worse. In Fatal Labyrinth the monster sometimes stole an item from you, in this game they almost always succesfully steal from you, so you see the few good items you didn't sell before going to the 4th floor disappear from your inventory at an extremely frustrating rate. And you can't get stolen items back from the monster after killing it. Within a few minutes I lost the three keys I had in my inventory (the most important items in Quest of Dungeons and not easy to find) and the better part of my gold. This is such a cheap mechanism to make a game more difficult (and Quest of Dungeons has a few of those) that it made me decide to quit playing.
Conclusion: the premise of the game is good but we saw that 25 years ago already in Fatal Labyrinth. And Fatal Labyrinth is still the better of the two games: it's longer, more balanced, less frustrating and annoying, it doesn't have the weird and even childish atmosphere and it has a "continue" system (if you play it via the emulator that comes with the Sega Megadrive Classics / Sega Genesis Classics collections, you can even save at any point). So I don't recommend this game but if you're looking to play a game just like it that doesn't have its flaws, I recommend Fatal Labyrinth instead.

I bought this game last summer during the sale. I have not "upgrade" to Year One, and don't really plan on it. I have yet to find any bugs that will impede my gameplay so far. The most I have run into are zombies getting stuck in walls/ the floor/ a fence somewhere. Other than that, I love this game. Not even for the actual game bits (doing missions and such). I love how it feels to me. I feel like I'm playing in a great zombie thriller.
One of my first missions, I was trying to help a fellow survivor who got overwhelmed by Zeds. By the time I broke the door in to help, he was dead. So there I was, face to face with a group of about 10 Zeds in this little house, with more approaching outside. I started fighting through them, but quickly became overwhelmed and low on stamina. They knocked me down, but I got back up. I dove through the window in the living room and began running for my truck. The Zeds were hot on my trail. They were covering my Norma. I started driving away, throwing my door open in a futile attempt to rid the Zeds from my ride. I was in such a chaotic state that I didn't even realize I was spinning my camera every which way. As I straightened my camera out, I had about 3 seconds to realize that I was headed right for a ravine. Without being able to stop, I drove in head first. I was thrown from my truck, which flipped onto its top. Fortunately for me, many of the Zeds who were still on my truck were pinned. (Could've been a bug, but whatever). Having been my first car accident scenario, I started to run away, only to hear my truck explode in the ravine behind me. I turned around and paused for a moment, watching my former vehicle burning, cooking Zeds all the while. I legitimately felt like I was watching a movie or something. After snapping back to reality, I slowly and carefully started heading back towards the Church of the Ascension. The only ♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing about this story is the fact that my fellow survivors didn't really care about what happened to me.
I would recommend this game. I have enjoyed it so far (having only played for as long as I have). Sure, what happened with the YOSE is♥♥♥♥♥♥ but I purchased the original SoD for dirt cheap, so I'm not complaining THAT much.

I picked this game up on the 2017 Steam Summer Sale. I knew it was a great game, but never had a chance to play it. I Ended up buying for like $4 or something like that, and didn't even play it for about 4 months. Reading whatever I say won't give you any new information that you haven't probably aready heard. But either way, I'll just leave my experience with this game. I enjoyed it enough to write this review, just to give my own 2 cents on it and hopefully convince other hesitant people that it's worth getting. Pretty much everything I write will be subjective when it comes to my own experience.
This game runs incredibly well, this clearly wasn't just a port to PC in terms of performance. I ran it with literally every setting up on max. In windowed borderless (1920x1080) no less. On my 144hz freesync monitor, I was usually seeing between 55-95fps (FX-6300 overclocked at 4.0Ghz, 16gbs of DDR3 ram, and a stock RX480). However (in my opinion), the keyboard controls are terrible. I played the game using only the default keyboard and mouse bindings, I got used to it and it ended up working alright. I guess they're just more awkward than anything else. Spacebar to spring? Shift to sneak? CTRL in interact?? Might be alright for some people, but it took me a while to get used to. Also trying to do precise things like stealth kills or running next to a wall is weird sometimes. Also, riding Caragors is pretty bad. I only ever did that when the game made me. I didn't like it.
This game is really fun. Like, really fun. It makes you feel bad@$$. The Orcs are extremely unintelligent, and that's great. They should be, right? Executions always feel great. Fighting dozens of dozens of orcs at want works great. Unlock the combat brand ability and get half of those dozens fighting for you. After your team of organized Orcs is done, press one button and murder all your newly-made allies in a instant. When you're busy fighting a hoard of Orcs and a Captain shows up. While you're focusing down the Captain, another Captain shows up and interrupts your fight. Then another Captain shows up. Then... another Captain shows. Announcing themselves each time. It gets so chaotic and hilarious. I had possessed a Warchief and created a power struggle between him and another Captain. They both showed up with 12 Orcs each, ready to fight eachother. They gave their opening lines and then not even 2 seconds after the battle beginning, the enemy Captain ran away. He had a fear of Conflict. All that build-up, the missions leading up to it. I haven't laughed that hard in a single player game in a long time.
This is a great game for completionists, like me. There's 2 areas to explore in the game. There are secrets, collectables, plant gathering challenges and hunting challenges. I completed EVERYTHING there is do accomplish in the base game. And did it in about 21 hours. I wouldn't say it's a long game, but it's long enough without overdoing it. There aren't TOO MANY collectables or sidequests, which is important. It never got tedious. I definitely got my money's worth, and had a great time with it. This game is amazing, and loads of fun.
If you're like me before I bought this, eyeing it once in a while. Contemplating whether or not to get it or if you'd like it. Reading the reviews over and over to see if it's really that great. It is, and it doesn't overstay its welcome. You get two relatively small areas to explore and then you're done. There's 20 story missions, and they're short, and not particularly that fun. Get it for the combat. Pick it up for $5 some time and finish it in 20hrs. If you're not like me, you'll likely finish it in less than 10hrs. But it's even worth it then. You'll enjoy it like I did. And now that I've gotten 100%, I'll be un-installing it, and likely never have a reason to go back to it. But I had a blast with it, and it'll always be one of my top recommendations for single-player games.

A fun and immersive island survival game that's worth a shot for any fan of the genre. Right off the bat you dig yourself out of a plane crash and into a world of isolation. Oh, and you just so happen to be the lone survivor of that crash.
From then on, aside from the help of an optional tutorial, you're left to survive how you see fit. And that process will most likely involve tiger sharks and the dark depths of the mysterious ocean engulfing you. So if you're afraid of the sea, or otherwise being lunch for a shark, well then all I can say is good luck!
Seriously, this is a great game and it's only going to get better. Definitely worth your time. But nothing is perfect, and there is still definitely a few improvements to be made here. These include:
- Much, much larger maps with bigger islands and more to explore below the surface.
- Make sharks a rare experience so that we can actually explore the ocean, and when we do encounter them we are in real danger of dying, but can still escaspe with some determination.
- Add more secrets to explore such as MASSIVE shipwrecks and other plane crashes.
- Add a fuel system for the boat motor that is challenging but not ridiculous.
- Maybe add a sanity feature where players have to maintain their mental health or risk going insane.
-Introduce caves for us to explore (not just underwater) that are full of mystery and wonder.
- Make the building system more in-depth (right now it restricts you certain types of roof designs, etc)
- Maybe add dynamic fire so a player can burn down an entire island if they're really bored.
Lots of things that would make the game even better!

Overview: Third Person Tower Defense
The Good:
+ The main feature of the game is that you can customize a mech in a variety of different ways. First you choose the chassis which allows you to carry more weapons or tower placements (but not both) . Then you choose the type of weapons you want to use: machine guns, shotguns, sniper rifles etc. More powerful guns require more weapon slots. Then you choose the type of towers you want. Different maps require different load outs. Experimenting with different weapons and towers is part of the fun.
+ Plenty of weapons and towers that can be bought or found
+ Lots of enemies that require you to change up your tactics, some enemies target your towers, other target you etc.
+ Killing enemies and completing levels allows you to level up allowing you to use more powerful weapons and towers
+ Good voice acting
+ Full controller support
+Coop
+Removed GWFL
The Average:
Maps that require only one area to defend can feel repetitive because the basic strategy never really changes.
Big difficulty spike in the last few maps
The Bad:
- multiplayer/coop is dead and thus completing certain achievements will be hard
Conclusion:
A fun if not short tower defense game that focuses more on third person shooting than actual tower placement. A fun diversion.

Now, there are admitedly 2 things I'm not a huge fan of in this mod.

This is game is very engaging, and all the more so if you're a fan of contemporary martial aviation. The graphics are great, which does nothing to harm the feel of flying a decent selection of different air craft from different parts of the world in either third person or♥♥♥♥♥♥pit mode. I'm a big fan of Russian war planes, and this game delivered for me from the MiG-29 to the Su-35 and 37. If you like F-22s and F-15/16s and stuff, or are into European advanced fighters like the Raphael or Eurofighter or something, it will suit you fine as well.
The feel of the controls took time for me to get used to, as it's a strange way of doing a flying game for me. I found myself making customized controls for some time before i found something I got comofortable with. Also, I take issue with the apparent need to go into this close-up cinematic combat flight mode that becomes an important part of the cmapaign very often; sort of takes away from the advanced manuevering skills players need to hone that come with just flying around shooting hostiles in air to air dog fights with no assistance but a radar lock. It seems somewhat optional otherwise, as the game has plenty of hostiles that can be taken out in the more fun manner of dogfighting.
I'd give this game either a 7/10 or an 8/10; depends on how much you're into contemporary dogfights and military aircraft stuff. It's pretty cinematic, sometimes the levels can be a little boring or reptative, but the flights themselves are still pretty cool.

10/10! Fun. Like Minecraft / Robocraft / Space Engineers / Kerbal Space Program / Starmade / Garry's Mod but with RTS fleet control, engaging resource harvesting and management, and competent AI nations to fight in epic naval/air battles. It has a steep learning curve, especially to those who haven't played the above games, but is well worth it, and is one of the two most addicting games I have played in my life.
What to expect in a single-player campaign battle (similar events actually happen with regularity):
You are in a small custom jet fighter, and spot a large enemy fleet approaching. You call for reinforcements, but as the daredevil action hero you are, you decide to engage them first, even though their fleet has 20x the amount of firepower you have, and 100x the size. You are not intimidated, not as an ace pilot, dodging heat-seeking missiles and cannonballs/bullets/flak by inches and firing your own custom barrage back at them. Significant damage is done to the enemy ships before something hits your engine. Your craft is now falling, but you guide it to an enemy ship. You jump from your craft right before it is destroyed in an explosion by incoming missiles, jumping like a frickin action hero and landing in an enemy ship. After boarding it, you take out its defenses and blow up its AI mainframe, hacking the craft, seconds before it warps away. Your reinforcements arrive, your own AI blasting lasers, cannons, torpedoes, and missiles at the enemy ships. They down the enemy mothership, a giant flying battleship (much like a heavily armed helicarrier). However, repair bots start fixing it quickly. It starts to go airborne again, but right before it leaves the water, you swim to it and jump with your rocket boots to a ledge on its back, barely with seconds to spare. You blast a hole in its hull and blow up a grenade in its ammo room, creating a massive explosion, which you use to divert the repair bots attention while you hack the AI mainframe. The battle is finished quickly, with your fleet and the two ships you captured. You then scrap the captured ships and use the materials to make a monstrosity of your own.

I've been waiting for a free game like this, and this is so much more than I hoped for.
Some people are saying that this is too simalar to adventure capitalist or that this game is all about micro transactions, and those people haven't played the game.
The only simalarity between Communist and Capitalist are are their names and graphics. They're completely different. Capitalist is more of a play ever week or so and click a couple times. Communist is more grindy, but if you don't play for a week, you can still advance through the game. And to those people who say this game is too clicky, that's the point. And the micro transactions are just there for the company to make money off of people who want end game at the beginning, I haven't even though of buying something once.
There are other clicker games for free on steam, but they are nearly as good as this. With other games, it gets repetitive very quickly and you don't want to play again. With Adventure Communist, you keep wanting to progress through the game, and you move through stages very quickly.
I think what people don't understand about the game is how clicky it is and that you don't have a lot of "scientists" in the beginning. (Scientists are the buyable currency used to upgrade). If you keep clicking long enough or come back to it eventually, you will be getting scientists by the dosen.
Overall I LOVE this game, and if I did have to buy it, I would.

A lot of people have been reporting difficulties and issues with opening the game up. I had no such issues, but that may have been because of a patch I missed. You can rebind your keyboard controls which is cool for keyboard users and supports 360 controller fully, even having the correct buttons on screen. At a constant 30 FPS for a low-tier machine, the game is still incredibly smooth. So smooth that if someone tinkered with files to put it to full 60 FPS it would make the game not break, but not look good. If you have played a Tales game before, the combat will feel familiar to you. Story is take it or leave it. I personally have no issue with it, the typical hero must go on a journey to save the world, etc. The english voiceovers are well done, something the Tales game is pretty solid at with each game, however you can choose Japanese voiceovers if you want to.
Cons:
-Everything looks a bit too large in terms of proportions (as in the models, the world, etc.)
-The story if you don't care for it.
Pros:
-Runs smoothly
-No major gamebreaking bugs have been reported.
-Combat is fun and intuitive.
-Opens up fine for me, but seems to be a common issue.
-High customizable controls for both controller and keyboard.
-English voiceovers are well done.
In my opinion, this is a very well done port, and for 20 bucks is worth it. At the very least, worth trying it out.

This game checked so many of my boxes it was kind of a guaranteed sale. It spans many of my favorite genres, has plenty of content, co-op! I will just list things :)
* Tower-defense, more so when playing single
* Shooter, more so when playing multiplayer
* Mech-game with customization; weapons, chassi, legs, towers, paintjob
* Character progression, challenges, achievements, all doable without much grind outside of completing the game.
* Customizable player character, only cosmetic, but fun when running around in the lobby before starting a multiplayer game.
* The multiplayer lobby is the same as single player, other people just loads up in the empty slots on your ship. It's great design really, and you can look at other people's mechs and gesture at their characters :)
* Anyone you have invited to a multiplayer game ends up in your regiment, which has separate challenges to complete, it just happens automatically and it's kind of great :o
* All customization on your mech and character are visible immediately in game, has custom animations and models, so nice :3
* Many of your towers can actually be killed, and they are not at all used to build labyrinths, you cannot block enemies with towers. It's just different :)
* The whole game design seems built around quirky humor, at first it's quite odd but after a while I just ran with it. Game mechanics sold me on the experience.
* An overhead map, on some symmetrical levels it can be really tricky to know where you've placed towers, makes for quite a bit of running around. It does make sense though as the player characters probably do not have any radar och satellite to provide map data.
* In the shop I would love to see if I actually own an item already, especially the cosmetics for the marine, it's a minor gripe but it felt like an obvious feature.
* Playing during a summer sale makes Steam a bit glitchy, several times one or several were disconnected from Steam during multiplayer which boots them from the game. Sadly you cannot rejoin, this was kind of annoying in Survival which can take 1-2 hours depending on your success. There were no issues while the USA was asleep though.
* Some maps have places where you can get stuck, and you cannot jump or even walk over very low  walls, this is pretty annoying when it happens. But then I always try to get to places I'm not supposed to go :x
* I took me a while to realize why this felt exactly like playing on a console, I think the game is locked to 30 fps, which is kind of a bummer when using a 120Hz monitor.
All in all I was very impressed by this game, I was looking for another tower defense game, saw this in a short clip on YouTube, and kept an eye out during a summer sale. Played it for an entire weekend with my brothers and a friend, great times was had :P

Iron Brigade is definitely one of the more enjoyable experiences from DoubleFine in the gameplay department. You pilot a Mobile Trench Unit (basically a pair of robo-legs with guns) and fend off incoming beasts built out of TV's and electronics, with the aid of some deployable towers and possibly a friend or two. You gradually unlock bigger and better guns and turrets, and it's great fun to just slap an artillery cannon on your trench and blow♥♥♥♥♥♥away. It's a decent game in solo, and a much better experience with other people who can run loadouts that complement yours.
Which brings us to the issue of multiplayer. Sadly, despite GFWL finally having been stripped from this beast years after the fact, the netcode is still tempermental at best and outright shoddy at worst. You can usually get a 2-player game going without much issue, but attempting a 3 or 4 player session has ended in crashes, hangs, and disconnects within minutes for me every single time I try.
2 players insofar works just fine and dandy though.

The worst game in the franchise by far.
TL;DR: to summarize: Unsalvageable music and story, horrible and long non-jet missions that play like completely different games even though you bought Ace Combat to play Ace Combat, and the only good part of the game (the jet flying) is mediocre to just about okay. I bought this game for 3 bucks and I still feel ripped off.
Stay away. Play the classics (even Infinite, which isn't good, is much better than this) and wait for Ace Combat 7.
FULL IMPRESSIONS:
The story is completely nonsensical. I'm more than halfway through and I have absolutely no idea what I'm doing, who I'm fighting, why I'm fighting or even who I am and who I fight for!
The only actually memorable music is the one that plays in the intro mission. It's absolutely fantastic, even, but then the game immediately drops the ball. I can't remember liking (or even remember, period) a single tune beyond the opening stage.
The helicopter, door gunner and AC-130 missions play like something straight out of Call of Duty. Totally unbearable and play nothing like Ace Combat (which, y'know, is the game I want to play if I buy a game called Ace Combat). You'll force yourself to get through them just so you can go back to actually playing Ace Combat. They simply shouldn't have been there at all: Their problem is not that they are done wrong, it's that they couldn't have been done right. They're the equivalent of having a first person shooter segment in your racing simulator.
When you get to the actual jet flying, the game is actually pretty decent. It's still the worst Ace Combat has ever been, but even then it's still okay. I could see myself finishing and even mildly enjoying this title if it had nothing but jet missions. By far the worst part of the flying is the infamous DFM (Dogfight Mode, sometimes referred to as the more crass equivalent of "Dogpoop Mode"). Basically, it locks your view onto an enemy fighter and puts your general flight trajectory on-rails so that you are always flying behind the other pilot. You can still move the jet, but only a little bit so that you can aim the guns and have a fragile illusion of control.
It would't be so bad if it was optional, but ace pilots (marked as TGT_LEAD on your screen) dodge everything like madmen and are sometimes straight-up invincible to gunfire and deploy infinite flares when chased by homing missiles, literally forcing you to use DFM. But even with those enemies that do not technically require using DFM, some of them still dodge like absolute gods even on the normal difficulty. It's just very obvious that they designed the game around DFM itself, and that's a huge blemish on the gameplay.
Not a flight sim. Not even an acrade flight sim. You don't even get to fully control the direction your plane flies in. Utterly abysmal. Avoid.

I can't recommend this game because it is just generally boring and unfun.

Very Brief Summary:
Obligatory Minecraft reference - using blocks to build ships, planes, spacecraft, floating fortresses and really really really stupidly big guns that may or may not look rather phallic.
Important Points:
* The install size is very small, and the game is very stable and smooth. Loading times are minimal.
* Your constructions will not wobble! Even as they're being shot to pieces, flying through the air or diving across the rolling waves, your creation will not wiggle and the parts will not look like the glue hasn't dried. Once you stick it together, it behaves like a proper, solid object.
* The physics are robust. Whether you're ramming another warship, or just trying to make one that doesn't sink the moment you put it in the water, you can rely on the physics to make sense.
* The combat is fantastic, whether you're manually aiming a weapon or leaving it up to AI modules that don't actually suck. Imagine Homeworld's colourful, trail-filled battles with Eve's general ship control, but with the added bonus of being able to walk around your ship and man the guns yourself.
* You will spend too much time in this game, and neglect your wife/job/personal hygeine.
Important features:
* Comes with a huge list of pre-built vehicles, from tiny submarines to flying fortresses.
* Weapons systems that can be customised in painstaking detail - if you want, you can build a cannon that runs the entire length of your ship, or an automated missile turret with 20 laser-guided missiles.
* Single missions that act like challenges, which can be played with default vehicles or your own creations.
* A campaign mode that's like one big RTS game, where all the units and structures can be designed by you.
* The game is full of tooltips, documentation, visual examples and prefabricated components.

But in its current state, I can't recommend it to anyone quite yet. I'd love to change the review to something more positive once some of the most glaring issues have been addressed, many of which have been mentioned by other reviewers:
Please fix the crashing issues especially, Bandai Namco, and please take into account what people are saying about this game's port. A lot of people, myself included, are huge fans of this game, love it dearly, and only want the best for it so both old and new fans have better access to it from the start.

While this is one of my favorite games of all time, and having beaten it countless times on the Gamecube and a couple times on the PS3; I can't recommend it in it's current state
this is the only platform you can get it on. The game is riddled with DRM and is causing multiple issues for users (the DRM in question is VMprotect).
It should be noted that this is a port of the PS3 version of the game, not the Gamecube version. The PS3 version was a port of the PS2 version (only released in Japan). The PS2 (and in turn PS3 and PC) version did not have cell shading as the GCN version had, some textures are lower resolutions (very noticeable on the world map), and the frame rate is locked at 30FPS (Gamecube was 60 when certain spells like Cyclone didn't kill it).
There are no graphics settings whatsoever. Not even FXAA, the one antialiasing type that generally comes with PC ports (MSAA would have been wonderful).
The internal resolution doesn't seem to be affected when you change resolutions, instead it appears to just render at 720p and stretch to your chosen resolution as adjusting my resolution to native and above did not help with the aliasing issues.
After adjusting my resolution above my monitor's native resolution the game would no longer launch, instead giving me an error and crashing (it's likely a problem when changing resolutions above native at game launch). I had to manually adjust the resolution to 1080p through the CustomConfig.conf in the game folder in order to have the game launch again (if this happens to you just open the file with notepad and edit the resolution).
The game is great, but this port is as bare bones as it can get. I was really hoping this would be the definitive edition of the game, but the lack of options is an utter disappointment. Visually and performance-wise, the Gamecube version is the best. Content wise this version is on par with the PS3 version (a few more costumes, abilities, and improved secret dungeon).
But if you already have the game on GCN, PS2, or PS3 it might be best to not pick this version up just yet.

TLDR: Don't buy this game, it's bad. Instead consider playing Tales of Maj'Eyal or Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup.
Quest of Dungeons is not a roguelike, it is a roguelikelike. It is a dumb, poorly made abomination that merely contains elements that an ignorant may ask and be told, probably from a bored and indifferent source, can be found within roguelikes.
This insipid program is a mannequin of a roguelike. There is next to no variety in abilities or items. Most gear is a flat upgrade, additional stats are rare and usually as significant as +1% crit chance. It has draped itself in the trappings of a roguelike but nothing more.
It lacks many basic features such as auto-exploration, travel to landmark, or rest till fully healed. And may the Good Lord in Heaven have mercy or your wretched soul if you should even attempt to make use of the click to move feature.
Clicking on a square causes you to move to that square, even distant squares that take many turns to walk to. In those subsequent turns you get to watch your character get mobbed to death without you being able to stop it. Yes, this game lacks the basic feature of stopping auto-walk when an enemy appears or you take damage. The first time I had a character die to this I had to immediately kill off a few more just to convince myself that yes, this game is just that badly made. Had the developers placed into this game any sort of love, care, attention, or to be frank, competence, then they would have caught this.
No love was put into this game, and I presume only minimal effort. Where are the random and unindentified potions, scrolls, and wands? Where are the whacky item egos and curses? Where is the innovation? Where is the fun? Where are the things that people who love games hold so dear that they want to dedicated a significant portion of their lives just for the chance that they can share them with the world? Where is this game's voice? Oh no, not That Friend's voice. But yes, it is, and we will discuss it.
Throughout the game monsters will say famous quotes from pop culture. “Welcome to your doom.” You might open a door and see a walking tree that announces “I am your father.” No reason, no joke, no connection to anything. “The cake is a lie.” These things are just said and said and said, repeated constantly through the game. “Run you fool.” It isn't funny.
Say you find yourself, despite all good efforts, alone in a room with That Friend. You know of whom I speak, we all know That Friend.
“Do you remember Portal?” he asks, then guffaws. Using his thumb he counts down the greasy fat fingers on his other hand. Star Trek, Terminator, Lord of the Rings, Scooby-Doo. Each punctuated with a false high pitched screech that his dim mind approximates to laughter before moving down the queue to the next reference. No jokes, no punchlines, just references to the existence of pop culture icons. And then braying.
Grabbing you by the shoulders, That Friend pulls his oily face within millimeters of yours, dilated eyes blood shot and half mad, spit foaming in the corners of his filthy unwashed mouth, he screams his putrid breath into your nostrils: “Do you remember Star Wars?!” And then the noise, which you will never forget, not laughter, but a robotic repetitive pronunciation of a syllable without variation, screamed at the top of his lungs, into your face, into your rattling suicide-contemplating bones. “HA HA HA HA HA HA HA HA HA HA!”
These syllables are devoid of humor and the halls that they echo through are indelibly darkened, even memories of mirth and joy past are erased.
This game is bad.
It was made by bad people.
But it was not made for bad people.
It was made for no one.

, many people complain that the game is too random, they cannot properly predict how to play the game or how to get through the game.
Even without making any actual choices within the narrative, the game's events change the moment you choose Classes for your queen to have. Medicine, art, singing, military, economics...Choose one over the other, and the way the game flows will change -- which destroys any further predictability.
Some people hate that, but personally? I found it very interesting.
Life, is random. You go to highschool, enter a major, study the eccentrics of the world and entertain a hobby or two. Throughout all of these experiences, our future outcomes hold very little regard to what we did in the past in absolute necessity -- more times than not, you'll hear people say "If you asked my past self, he'd never think he'd be where I am", and LLTQ captures that randomness within the narrative and game mechanics.
You have very little control, you have very little understanding -- and that's okay, the game is more about experiencing the difficulty in making a Long Living Queen out of an innocent and impressionable princess, rather than minmaxing a character by save scumming. It's an interactive story about the collapse of a kingdom, with a small spark of success within numerous paths to disaster, and you have to learn all of them individually.
That being said, if you want to 100% the game, the points I presented might be inconsequential, as it is for anyone who wants to acquire every single achievement.

=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=STORY=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=
Tired of Russian-as-bad-guys story? I've played all CoD and BF games, and no, this one isn't as cliche as the 'haters' imply. Check youtube. I've played all kinds of naval, fps, and flight games. From Microsoft's Simulator to Warthunder's multiple modes. This one is ARCADE.

If you buy this, do NOT buy this expecting a traditional Ace Combat experience, instead buy it expecting a blockbuster action experience similar to Call Of Duty in the means that it has some on-rails gameplay and deviates from the gameplay that is known for the rest of the series.
What's changed?
Alot! I went into this seeing the mixed reviews and I expected alot of change but didn't know what... for starters, the game is very story driven, there are Metal Gear-esque cut-scenes at the bunker, quick time events during combat, helicopters missions and infared bombing missions. It's strange to see Ace Combat goes this route. The music is no longer Steve Vai/Joe Satriani stuff but is that orchestral moody stuff you'd expect to hear while playing something like God Of War.
Alot annoyed me at first but the gameplay is addicting as ever!
The multiplayer stil functions and is acrually pretty awesome.
It's okay, I like RaidersSphere4th better but this was passable after getting used to the changes. If this didn't have the name "Ace Combat", it would have recieved much better reviews from the player base. It's not bad, it just does things differently.

Positives
-HUD is very nice, as is usual with Ace Comabat games
-Still somewhat has the feel of the Ace Combat series
-Nice graphics (nothing to write home about, but it lets you feel like a pilot)
-Still fairly fun, especially the air combat missions
Negatives
-Short Campaign
-A story about as complex as a fanfiction written by Donald Trump on a power trip
-Literally 0 emotional attachment to any of the characters
-Awkward controls on the keyboard (customizable but still not too great)
-Controls sometimes feels stiff
-Number of helicopter missions that are really boring (basically just point and click)
-Final boss is abosultely stupid. Basically a "♥♥♥♥ You" from the game. You learn a bunch of skills and tricks through out the game, and the final boss just negates all of those skills. You learned how to counter manuver? You cant do that without being hit. You learned how to follow a counter manuver? Cant do that here. You thought that being on someone's six means you're safe from enemy fire? ♥♥♥♥ you, there are 5 homing missles coming at you OUT THE BACK SIDE. Literally all the skills it has you learn slowly through the game is useless. All you can do is attempt to follow it and rely on you reactions and not any learned skill.
-No real replayability
Final Verdict
Dont buy it unless you are a super fan of Ace Combat OR you really like plane sim + CoD

Build your own ships, planes, helicopters, submarines, satellites, fortresses, tanks, aircraft carriers, etc with a hugely customizable array of blocks.
The game allows you to custom tune your engines, weapons, armor, etc. to perform a certain way and every design choice has advantages and drawbacks. There is no single best way to build anything. There is always a way to build it better.
The lead developer, Nick Smart, is very helpful and dedicated to improving the game.
There are updates every week, unless Nick is working on a huge feature.
The building mode is very well thought out and is as efficient as possible. Vehicles can be 10,000+ blocks in some cases, so the mirror line, fill tool, and pre-fabs are essential. The optional, but recommended, keyboard based building mode can be significantly faster than the traditional point and click mouse building mode. This gives you more time to adjust and optimize your vehicle.
This game asks for a lot of learning to fully enjoy it. The many customizable systems can be mastered through trial and error, learning from others makes the process faster and more fulfilling.
I consider the excelent community FTD has on the official forums (
) and on discord part of the full game expirence.

Are you willing to spend 1-2 hours learning this game?
If so, it will become your Skyrim. It will become your World of Warcraft. It will suck your life away. You will think of new designs, new crazy things to build, weapon systems to obliterate your opponents and AI systems that can get the job done under any circumstance.
You will reminisce the possibilties of fleet management, what forces you need where - which resource zones you need to suckle upon to better your advances against the incoming factions. You will bribe with oil and crystal, why be enemies when you can be friends? And then you will backstab the very faction you befriended, because this is From The Depths and you need all the precious resources you can get.
When you are taking a shower, you will contemplate just how to get your orbital bombardment of custom made ICBM's raining down on your rivals with unprecedented insanity and accuracy. You will ponder over your cruiser and if you really need those massive drills spinning at 50k RPM on the front, do you really need to drill into every enemy ship and watch them explode in majestic fashion? Yes, the answer is always yes.
You will board enemy ships and attempt to destroy whatever you can with the weapons of your choice. Minigun? Hrmm, maybe. Grenade launcher? Yes... that feels right. Blow up their mainframes, disrupt their AI connections, take out their command center, or just launch into the ammo storage and watch the fireworks. Every part of this game is destructable, and this makes me smile.
I own a lot of titles on steam, and this is my new Skyrim.

I'm sure everyone who put a positive review before me has already mentioned what I'm putting here, but what's that to stop me from singing my praises?
First and foremost, the aesthetic of this game is gorgeous, with each texture or object being unique and visually appealing. The hybrid low/high quality artwork maintains its beauty while still being rather light on processing to suit lower-end computers, such as my own. The soundtracks and FX create equally pleasing soundscapes that add even more to each environment the player traverses. The races that populate Starbound's universe are especially diverse, with large differences between both each race and each individual, including the player themself.
Second, Starbound's storyline is quite interesting, and gracefully manages to take a backseat when the player wants to create, explore, or simply goof off. When it's brought to the spotlight, however, it leaves most of the control of pace to the player and their capabilities. If you want to charge headlong into the final battle butt-naked with nothing more than a flimsy stick with a rock at the end, not one thing is stopping you.
Third, the game sees constant attention from both Chucklefish and the community alike. The Spacefarer Update shows that Chucklefish is, and will continue to be, invested in their game. The community is just as ingrained, with many users having poured their own hearts and souls into workshop addons for the game. Some of these can be a small tweak to a certain asset, while others can be so huge they alter the game on a fundamental level.
What I'm trying to say here is, this is a great game. Great looks, great play, great community, and most importantly,

This game can be be great fun alone or with friends(though if your friends think in any way like you with character creation, you
have to rescind the previous statement of diverse characters) and can lead to many hours going by without so much as a second thought. I along with many others highly recommend this game, and I also have a second recommendation: once you've let the vanilla game run its course, head to the workshop and subscribe to
. This is one example of the aforementioned fundamentally altering addons out there, and practically turns Starbound into a brand new game to play.
And with that, I bid thee good luck on the hunt for new games to enjoy.

Fast-paced arcade-style action. The concept and gameplay are quite simple -- piloting a plane in 2D with a single weapon fighting maybe 6 different types of enemies. As you progress you unlock a handful of weapons, body types and engines, adding up to >30 different loadouts which potentially play very differently (fast, low armor, slow but high-damage bullets, versus slow, heavy, high fire rate, and everything between). Each run can take a few seconds to a few minutes at most. The later unlocks and achievements become difficult if not impossible, but the ability to return to the action almost immediately after dying makes the difficulty tolerable. Definitely worth a few dollars if you enjoy arcade-style play.

STRANDED DEEP
This is a game that is for players who like a lot of survivalist stuff in their games. The premise of the game is simple: you survive a plan crash and take a life raft to a nearby island and try to survive long enough for help. Sounds kind of fun yeah?
At first I was really liking the idea of surviving on a tiny island with some resources and having the need to take your raft island hopping to get more resources to further your chances of survival.... until I played the game. Everything plays against you on a grand scale. From what I have played so far everything is 100% randomized on the start of a new game. So one island you start out on in one game won't be the same in the next. The items you need to craft, tools, structures, etcetera, are also 100% random. During one playthrough I needed to make a refined knife, a task within the first 5 minutes of the game, I searched the island and there were no more rocks because I needed to make a basic knife first!! This means I needed to hop into my raft and head over to the nearest island a good 10 to 15 minutes away....7 minutes from shore a massive fog appears and blots out ANY islands I could see previously in 360 degrees! The fog lasted until I died! The problem here is in order advance further you need to have craftable items. Sure the whole game has you island hopping to get these craftable items, but damn it, withing the first 5 minutes of the game!?!?
Furthermore, if you mess up just 1 time your good as screwed! Time is also a against you as well. During one playthrough I was busy crafting when suddenly BAM! It was pitch black and I could not see a damned thing! The day and night transition is non-existent! It's like someone just flipped a light switch! I turned my brightness level to 100% and it did NOTHING to help!!!!
To make the urgency of how critical of a situation you are in, you can watch your vitals drop...and boy do they from your watch. They are in sequence with how fast the time flies in this game. Literally this game really ends up ****ing you right up the pooper from the get go. It seems the game is only geared to end up screwing the players over. This is the WORSE $15 I ever spent! I do not suggest this game to anyone except those that hate themselves and like to cause self inflicted pain.

Okay, enough of the "Poetry". Dark Souls is a medieval role playing game, featuring a variety of monsters and equipment with which to dispatch them, as well as an elusive story with deep lore. However most notoriously, it boasts great difficulty. To the uninitiated, and even still on occaision to the already initiated, the game delivers on that promise. By all means it's a wonderful game. I can't go as in depth as I'd like, it would take forever, and I'm no master of the game anyways. However, I will try to say as much as I can. So let's get started, shall we?
At it's core, I would say it's a Hack & Slash game, featuring Stamina management. It feels like an understatement, but I struggle to find an alternative way to describe it. The game will have you traveling through the kingdom of Lordran, on a quest to slay all that stands in your way to rekindle The First Flame ( Or let it die out, the choice is yours.) Alternatively, you could ignore all the lore and story, and just make it your mission to kill everything, regardless of whether there was a point. (Sorry Dark Sun Gwyndolin and Crossbreed Priscilla, I knew you were bosses, you had to die.)
As you travel through the land, you'll come across friend and foe alike. Unfortunately for you, foe is much more common. Killing these enemies will grant you souls, the games currency. You can use these souls to level up your skills, purchase various items, or to reinforce your equipment, though you'll additionally require titante for the reinforcements.
You have a variety of ways to dispatch enemies, and are usually given the luxury to formulate your own plan of attack depending on how you choose to play, and this, personally is where I feel the game shines brightest. You can focus your points into strength, fight like a beast unleashed and lay the smack down on enemies with heavy hammers and greatswords, or place your points into dexterity to fight swiftly and elegantly with daggers and rapiers. Perhaps you'd like to shine above the rest, investing points into intelligence or faith, and unleash the true power of magic and miracles. However you choose to play, the game has equipment to accomodate you. Just remember, you're not a god, you can't take everything head on, sometimes you'll need to roll if you wish to survive, and some enemies and bosses are weaker to some styles more than others.
As for the story, I honestly can't speak for it. It's rather elusive, and the most comprehensive bit of what's going on, I've already mentioned above. I couldn't do it any justice by attempting to retell it, so I won't even begin to try. I will however say, that if you're interested in learning, all you need do is pay attention to the items you find throughout your journey. Much of the worlds lore can be found right under your nose, in item descriptions, and if you're willing to delve deep enough and connect the dots, it makes the already bizzare world, all the more interesting. As you go from the  decrepit rooftops of Undeadburg, to the dark night and lush green of the Darkroot gardens, all the way to the golden city of Anor Londo and the burning ruins of Lost Izalith, the world never feels stale, and the bosses you face, while varying in size and difficulty, all dominate and demand your respect as you focus on their attacks, and attempt to learn how to best exploit their openings and weaknesses. Patience and a keen eye are a virtue, as well as your key to success. (Except for Pinwheel, that guy's a pushover.) That's not to mention the fantastic music that acompanies each battle, you will never tire of hearing it, no matter how many times the boss wipes the floor with you.
Within which you can join one of the games many covenants, invade the world of another player, and kill them for rewards. In some cases, such as the Forest Hunters Covenant, upon joining you will recieve a ring that will automatically summon you into the world of a player who has entered a certain area of Darkroot Garden, given only one task. Kill the player and protect the grave of Sir Artorias. (Read as: Try to keep that player from progressing in the game). What kind of rewards do you earn for these actions? I have no idea, I never participated beyond one Forest Hunter summon, but I assure you, there are rewards!
Dark Souls is quite a special game. I wouldn't go as far as to call it a masterpiece, though it's certainly an exceptionally good game. By all means, I'd consider it an instant classic. If you've got the time, and a bit of patience, I suggest you give it a go. A stubborn attitude helps too.
I'm sure there's plenty of things I've left out, but as I said before there is simply no way I could cover everything there is to cover. I do however hope that what I did manage to put into words, was able to help those of you uncertain about the game.

Quest of Dungeons isn't the most complex Rogue-like you'll ever play. It lacks the in-depth skill system of a game like Dungeons of Dredmor, and from what I've seen there's only one kind of trap, and what it does is spawn more monsters, which isn't necessarily a bad thing when you're trying to grind out a little more XP. And yet, even though its simple, and at times just a tad bit bland I still find reasons to recommend it.
Perhaps it's because QoD is so focused. You have four classes to choose from, and there's nothing in the way of stat points to allocate. You can loot and equip items but the stat system for the randomly generated loot is easy to read, and so for those who aren't theorycraft extraordinaires knowing how to build a character is as simple as making sure you have level appropriate gear.
The focus then becomes knowing when to use your skills and keeping a supply of food items and health potions to keep yourself alive. There is a quest system in the game, but there are only two types of quests: Kill enemy X, or Find item Y. There's a definite necessity to complete these in order to keep up with the escalating level of the dungeon enemies from floor to floor.
The game does feature four difficulty levels, and there is supposed to be an update soon which will add a new dungeon. The game is not devoid of content but much of what is there is grindy and similar. For some that will work (I like to play this game in between sessions of hardercore, more mentally taxing games) but those who seek something that will constantly crank up the Wowfactor and throw lots of curves at you might fair better looking elsewhere.
I'd recommend this game to those who are new the sub-genre, or else can't stand the complexity that some of us masochists relish in the more hardcore rogue-likes. Those who have already defeated Dredmor a few dozen times and completed Nethack a hundred times over might want to wait for something more complex to come along.

I'm sure everyone who put a positive review before me has already mentioned what I'm putting here, but what's that to stop me from singing my praises?
First and foremost, the aesthetic of this game is gorgeous, with each texture or object being unique and visually appealing. The hybrid low/high quality artwork maintains its beauty while still being rather light on processing to suit lower-end computers, such as my own. The soundtracks and FX create equally pleasing soundscapes that add even more to each environment the player traverses. The races that populate Starbound's universe are especially diverse, with large differences between both each race and each individual, including the player themself.
Second, Starbound's storyline is quite interesting, and gracefully manages to take a backseat when the player wants to create, explore, or simply goof off. When it's brought to the spotlight, however, it leaves most of the control of pace to the player and their capabilities. If you want to charge headlong into the final battle butt-naked with nothing more than a flimsy stick with a rock at the end, not one thing is stopping you.
Third, the game sees constant attention from both Chucklefish and the community alike. The Spacefarer Update shows that Chucklefish is, and will continue to be, invested in their game. The community is just as ingrained, with many users having poured their own hearts and souls into workshop addons for the game. Some of these can be a small tweak to a certain asset, while others can be so huge they alter the game on a fundamental level.
What I'm trying to say here is, this is a great game. Great looks, great play, great community, and most importantly,

This game can be be great fun alone or with friends(though if your friends think in any way like you with character creation, you
have to rescind the previous statement of diverse characters) and can lead to many hours going by without so much as a second thought. I along with many others highly recommend this game, and I also have a second recommendation: once you've let the vanilla game run its course, head to the workshop and subscribe to
. This is one example of the aforementioned fundamentally altering addons out there, and practically turns Starbound into a brand new game to play.
And with that, I bid thee good luck on the hunt for new games to enjoy.

I'm bit ambivalent about this game, to be honest. It's hard not to reccomend with a fully realized resource system, single-player campaign, regular updates, and a truly bewildering array of components that puts Space Engineers to shame. That said, it's also hard to reccomend this game, at least solidly, due to the many technical limitations.
Don't get me wrong, I'm aware that it's incomplete and that work hasn't been finished and that, given the track record so far coupled with my own personal (if limited) interactions with the developer, it's very likely that this WILL see a final release. That said, you can'y play it right on anything beyond a dedicated gaming rig. The preveiws would have you believe that it's a game that's filled with epic clashed on the sea, in the sky, and among the heavens beyond... AND IT IS! But... they can only be realized by machines that can handle that sort of thing, and since (as of yet) the game still runs on 32-bit, so no one on a moderately powerful lappy willl likely ever see them.

As an Assassin's Creed and The Lord of the Rings fan, I was extremely hyped for this game before it came out. Sadly, I didn't get to play it at launch, only 2 years later.
So here I am. Holy maccaroni, I loved Shadow of Mordor.
First of all, everything in this game looks amazing. The graphics are on par with games like The Witcher 3 and Star Wars Battlefront. Extremely high quality models, textures and effects even on medium settings!
My biggest fear was that it wouldn't run properly on my machine, but surprisingly, it did! The game is extremely well optimized.
Now, the combat. It is, in my opinion, the best combat system in a game ever made! Period. Fluid animations, brutal executions and blows that actually feel like they have impact.
The Nemesis System is simply the cherry on top. Each enemy feels unique, some are so cool you actually begin to like them. Each one is special, I couldn't help but want to recruit them into my army.
The story is Shadow of Mordor's biggest downside. It absolutely DEFECATES on Tolkien's established lore of Middle-Earth, adding unnecessary edgy villains and strong independent women cliches into this universe. Not only that, but they also inventend a hanful of new species of creatures that supposedly roamed the land of Mordor, not being mentioned ever again in any other Lord of the Rings work. Monolith goes a step further in Shadow of War, by adding SJW tropes into Middle Earth. The storyline is boring.
That being said, Shadow of Mordor is a gem. It's gameplay is what it makes it one of the best games of the last few years.
But, the crappy story brings the score down.

Feels like ultima online with a way way way better game engine. And when I say it feels like ultima online that's not an understatement or exaggeration. Sometimes when I'm playing this game I feel like I'm having some sort of fever dream of an alternate reality where they made a sequel to UO.
GIANT PRO-TIP that should be in the opening tutorial but isn't: if you time your movement *perfectly* you can hit most mobs without them getting a chance to attempt a hit back. This allows you to fight stuff without using all your healing items (which are plentiful, potent, and easy to use) so you don't have to keep running back to town and/or have 200 heals on you all the time. It's also really fun to try to keep your timing right instead of just standing there hacking on mobs and getting hit back. Player movement during mob encounters is the literal diference between losing an encounter by 90% (and using 30 heals) or winning an encounter by 90% (and using 3 heals). Some special attacks have extra distance, and some larger fast mobs are hard to do this with, but just use your eyes and figure out what works.
Anyways, check it out. Biggest con is that the world population is super low but they haven't been advertising because it's been out 6 months and they still feel they're working through some big issues even though the game itself feels solid and complete. Another RPG maker game review. The result of this RPG maker game is much better than the last RPG maker game that I reviewed.
Usually good RPG maker game on steam that we all love are good story telling ones such as “Mad Father”, “To the Moon” and “A Bird Story” simply because it take really a lot more commitment to recreate JRPG game than simply story telling ones. It’s really near impossible for small indie studio to produce and complete masterful JPRG like FF6. A lot developer like that last RPG maker game I reviewed “Secret Of Magia” lay out the foundation of a good JRPG but they failed follow it though and it ended up like uncompleted high school project.
This game however was very well done with a very usual plot that beginning with a failed hero party and rescue by a small abused goblin monster. You don’t play as the hero party but in every chapter you play as one of the NPC they encounter and everyone is dealing with an impending doom of end of world. Every chapter play as a different aspect and view point and they are completely different than rest of the chapters. Since most JRPG offer happy plot and ending this game is in reverse. Betrayal by trust, Blame by villagers, Lost of friend, everyone running away, World dying with some surprising twist, turns and questions.
Each chapter is about 2-3 hours long and last 2 chapter feels a bit rushed and shorter than the rest.
It’s a bit unsatisfying that you play for a few hours starting getting attached to the NPC player that you control after upgrading, leveling then the next chapter start and you start completely from beginning again with different character and items. (There is only 1 equipment that get transferred from chapter to chapter).
Simple item upgrading system with a whole bunch of weapon and equipment. The combat system to calling friends for help is quite unique and weird. Music, Graphic, Sounds and plots are good enough to be enjoyed. There are a bunch of achievements that are all pretty easy to get but some of them can be missed if you are not careful.
8.0/10. IF you hunger for some good indie JPRG fun that was made by indie developer using RPG maker. This one is for you!

It's never quite clear how your choices are going to affect your survival chances--until it's too late, leaving you scrambling for a save file where you didn't make that seemingly innocuous fatal error! Really keeps you on your toes, but it also takes a certain weight off decision making, because you really can't plan that far in advance, so you don't have to worry about making too "wrong" a choice. That isn't to say you can't be strategic. The game is balanced in that as long as you cover several bases, you can come back from almost anything (provided you have a close enough save point :P).
2) The impressive depth of the story (various important characters don't even show up in certain playthroughs) also allows for massive replayability, with different routes feeling like very different experiences. This has the additional perk of making the chasing down of the many simple but sometimes elusive achievements not like a chore and more like a treasure hunt.
Basically, Long Live The Queen is a really well executed choose-your-own-adventure game that I keep playing over and over again, trying to get that 100% completion, all the while having a great time and being majorly impressed at how it doesn't seem to be quite the same game every time I go through it.

Summer-Rain

You kiss her cheek,

I've never played the older AC games (I don't have a gaming console), and granted I got this game while it was on sale (I had my eyes on this game for a while, and was waiting for a sale), but I'll say this: Sometimes companies decide to take a different approach to their franchises for a lot of different reasons, and it's either you'll love them or hate them for doing it. From the reviews of the game by fans of the old AC games I've read, many are absolutely appalled by it. I don't think they're wrong - they're seeing a franchise they've been with for a very long time change into something they're not used to. (I had the same feeling when the Total War franchise decided to go into Warhammer, for example, and I felt the same disappointment, too.)
But that's not to say those fans are right either. Project Aces was obviously trying to test out something new, and I think it's quite brave of them to have given it a try (after recovering from the initial disappointment, I feel the same of the Total War franchise now).
Now, for those that are still deciding whether to buy the game or not, here's the best way I can put it:
(1) DFM takes quite a bit of getting used to, but it'll feel rewarding when you tail another fighter and gun them down.
(2) It's nothing like the old AC games (from what I can judge from the Let's Plays I've seen people play), but it's an interesting spin on the genre.
(3) If you don't like the campaign, see the story as a massive tutorial that teaches you what you'll need to know to be effective in multiplayer.
(4) Judging from the mechanics, the game was originally designed with multiplayer as more a core feature than single player.
In the end, a game's a game - some of them we love, others not so much. The franchise titles represent something significant for some people, but not so much for others. I understand those grieving for what AC's become, but I'm personally happy that there's an AC game on PC, and agree with those that enjoy the game for what it is.

i've played so much of this and it's honestly still one of those games i can keep coming back to. you can /feel/ the effort and love put into this game, from the quirky descriptions of every single item to the lovingly handmade sprites for the food. did i mention there are well over 100 different food items? this game isn't even focused on cooking.
the visuals:
stunning. it's pixel art for sure, so it's not everyone's taste, but god damn are some of the scenes astonishing to look at. this game really shines in arctic regions, but even the scorched wastelands that were once city planets have their charm. no planet feels the same, and it's always a new adventure to explore one.
the gameplay:
very, very solid. from underground challenge rooms hidden throughout caves to spice up exploration, to finding small dwarf cities including people you can pick up and throw around (har har), you'll find it here. combat will sometimes feel repetitive and in some cases even unfair; your enemies will remain strong, but you yourself will eventually run out of weapon power - danger is serious in this game.
the music:
listen to it. it's beautiful.
multiplayer? easy drop-in via steam.
vehicles? somewhat iffy to use on most worlds, but nonetheless also fun.
mods? TONS.
this game is easily worth four times what they're charging, but the price remains untouched. it's a masterpiece of a game and the gold standard for building & sandbox exploration.
