This game is amazing.
Yes, the PC port is bad. But with some time and a few excellent steam guides it works great. The graphics are a bit dated but now bad. I hardly noticed them. I have been told that a controller is reccomended but I played with KB+Mouse with little trouble. The MouseFix GUI was very helpful, and with some tweaking and personal preference the controls worked well. If anyone is having trouble feel free to message me.
Yes, this game is challenging. Some bosses or areas will take many tries to beat, then you can look back with the sense that you learned every aspect and beat the challenge. Death becomes a learning experience. Boss stun-locked you to death? Your dodge was timed poorly, or you didnt watch your stamina levels. Eventually, you will learn how to time your attacks and movement depending on the enemy. Overall, the gameplay is (mostly, there are exceptions) fair.
The mechanics allow for much customization of your appearance, playstyle, weapon choice, ect. There is a world of weapons, upgrades, and magic to explore and learn. For me everything was complicated at first, but over time (and with a few guides) I learned what it meant.
Probably the best thing about this game is the level design and overall world design. The areas are connected in amazing ways. Exploration is rewarded, not just with items but the discovery of shortcuts.
Right from the start, the game begins building a world full of lore. The opening cutscene sets the stage excellently. With a little dilligence in talking to npcs and reading item descriptions, more information is found. This game may be a masterpiece just for creating a detailed and amazing world using small pieces. Even characters are built up to be unique after only a few lines.
Overall, this game is a masterpiece. Anyone who hasnt played is missing out on a world of lore and skilled gameplay.

The game has been in development for a long time it has made some impressive graphical leaps and a lot of new content has been added. However the actual game itself hasn't had the attention it deserves. You can spend a lot of time in the creator making your machines of war and what it seems to be is just a proof of concept. A fun one though you should buy it on a sale just for that.
The campaign is where the meat and potatoes of the game really is. It pits you up against an entire world filled with multiple factions and you have to defeat them all. It is fun getting into a few battles but then you begin to notice the bugs in the UI and the limits placed on the number of blocks you can have in a battle even if you have a great PC.
The game suffers from some serious limitations that may have to be addressed with a revision of gameplay and world-size. I think a map with you vs another faction would be more appropriate.
In the campaign you may be asked if you want to start a battle with an enemy, you can or you can retreat. If you retreat you lose your boat so you fight, however the enemy doesn't spawn for whatever reason because of either the block limit or a glitch, I don't think 50K blocks where in-play at the time. So you can't actually fight but if you retreat to restart the battle you will lose your ship.
The game has many annoying bugs like this and I was only on my 2nd base when I ran into this one.  There is a lot of content in this game and a steep learning curve, the tutorials aren't very helpful so you have to go to YouTube to figure anything out and with the updates those tutorials are many-times out of date.
The game suffers from an incomplete main-game, the developer is still adding things such as land vehicles and extra cannons so who knows how far out this game is. I have a feeling that it's going to drag on until the game becomes too bothersome to figure out and people stop playing/buying the title.
Buy on sale if you want to play with its impressive creative mode, that's about all that works.

This game would be a hell of a lot more fun if the dev's hadn't decided to make it completely unplayable. The game continues to play when you're not playing, meaning that if you have things like a job or children, you will come back to food being missing, people disappeared, and storyline quests going by. The dev's argue that no one is supposed to die and storyline is not supposed to progress, yet I have come back after a week at work to find several people gone and the "You just missed storyline" radio broadcasts going off. As well as -430 influence and several of my resources empty. There IS a client loader that's supposed to fix it, but I believe the programmer for it quit the project, and the dev's updated the game so it no longer works.
If you have no life and WANT to put the time in, it is a fantastic game. The storyline is meh, but the gameplay is some of the best I've ever seen (with mods to fix certain things of course). It's far too dark at nighttime, but the base building and upkeep with survival management is something I'd love to see in more games.
Graphics: 8/10. Seriously fantastic.
Sound: 8/10. The voice acting in great though a bit repetitive, the music is actually mood enhancing, and the ambiance creepy.
Storyline: 5/10. It was honestly hard to tell what was going on most of the time, as there was too much going on, and you always feel like you're missing out on something.
Gameplay: 4/10. Incredible gameplay, but the fact that it continues to progress without you while you're not playing makes it unplayable.
I would still recommend this game, but with a warning.

Oh man, oh man, oh man! I love me some flashy japanese arcade jetfighter action!
I got into Ace Combat with AC4 back on the PlayStation and have played every single game since, enjoying each and every one. Assault Horizon is no different, although it is a fairly heavy departure from the series origins. Gone are the Estovakian warplanes and other fictional nations, replaced with the real world, NATO, Russia and terrorists, but with that lovely over-the-top Ace Combat flavor added on top.
First things first: I REALLY love the sound design. The music (especially the dogfight music from the intro level, which evokes old musical ques from the past games) is mind-shatteringly GOOD, the explosions and screeches and sputtering of dying aircraft, the BRRRRRT of cannonfire and whooshing of missiles, all accented by the lovely cacophony of both friendly and enemy radio traffic, with calls of "Fox two", "Break, break!" and "I'm hit!" all mixing together. Just writing about it gives me the chills!
The game itself is mostly the standard Ace Combat -affair, with you flying a fighter jet, shooting down utterly unrealistic numbers of enemy planes with missiles that simply don't seem to ever run out. The realistic look of the game at first glance is a lie: Assault Horizon is arcade madness with "flight simulation" naught but a fanciful idea to the dev team. In addition to the usual flying, you are required to challenge enemy aces into dogfights, frantic challenges where you struggle to match speed and keep the enemy in your sights long enough for your infrared -tracking missiles to achieve a lock (again, completely unrealistic, but who cares at this point? LOOK AT THE EXPLOSIONS!).
The somewhat baffling storyline has you also flying bombers, AC-130 -gunships and helicopters, so there is a surprising amount of variety on offer for an Ace Combat -game. The game isn't too easy, either, with some missions demanding some pretty damn quick flying in order to reach all your targets in time, let alone to catch and down some of the late-game enemy aces.
All in all: I freakin' love this game! As a matter of fact, I think I'll go and listen to the soundtrack right now. Cheers!

Later in the game, you gain access to a unique army-building mechanic that tacks onto the already-established army-assassinating mechanic (the Nemesis System, as it's called). I always recommend people at least make progress on the second land before giving up on the game if they aren't enjoying it, because I personally went from "bored" to "in love" after I started recruiting at the second stage of the game.
With how cheap this game gets, I highly recommend it. The second game has its problems with microtransactions, but this game is free of that and WELL worth paying for. This game is hilariously fun. Those of you familiar with Tim Shaefer and Double Fine Studios wll already be familiar with the kinds of quirks their games provide and this is no different.
Its essentially a tower defence game only its fought in the third person and you control an active unit on the battle field, a massive hulking robot called a Mobile Trench. In each area you have several areas to defend and a certain time limit to set everything up before the enemy come in. Rather than do this from an overhead view, you stomp your trench around and set up assorted turrets on available building platforms, trying to create the right sort of deadly crossfire.
You have to think on your feet once the attacks starts as they foes will becoming from all directions and you can only be in on place at a time, so what do you rebuild? Your own trench is heavily armed and can be upgraded between missions. You can collect loot boxes that drop from powerful enemies that can give you powerful new equipment to customise your mech with.
The games atmosphere is an over the top setting remeniscent of a fictional world war one with anachronistic technology. The sense of humour is kinda crazy, I chose as my character a dapper British dude whose trench came equiped with a humidor for his cigars, at the end of every battle he would light up a cigar.......with his pistol.
It also has multiplayer an immensely fun co-op mode for up to four players. Get it.

Pleasingly reminiscent of classic tactical RPGs.  The dialogue and story development is light but sufficient.  The battle and character development mechanics are inspired by Final Fantasy Tactics. Every character has a main class they gain experience for after battle, but have access to the skills of a secondary class.  New and more powerful classes are unlocked through progressing through a combination of lesser classes.  Unlike FFT, character statistics are developed by spending star points that which you gain in parallel to experience.  After 30 hours of gameplay I’ve unlocked every class across my four characters.
The encounter and exploration systems are more like Chrono Trigger though.  You can visit towns and ransack an NPCs house with impunity.  You can see enemies on the map and can buff and strategically engage them.  Unlike CT, the inventory system is bag-based, much like the Divinity series.  Like Divinity, there is also an inventory based crafting system. For example, using shears on a blanket creates a bandage for healing minor wounds.  New armor and weapons are commonly gained through crafting.  In fact, using tools and spells outside of combat for exploration is a large part of the game.  Also unlike CT, the great majority of encounters do not respawn.  To grind, you have a choice of only a few repeatable encounters which become dull quickly.
I would highly recommend to anyone looking to satisfy a craving for FFT and willing to tolerate the graphics.   However, the rudimentary Earthbound-esque look of the game belie a varied environment filled with myriad secrets.

This game is pretty great for a small tactics rpg, scratched an itch for a niche I haven't been able to in a while.
I only had a few real complaints about the game.
Cons:
- The game doesn't have decent controller support. I went into it hoping to just hack it with custom keys linked to my button presses, but there is just way too much mouse interaction to make it work well.
- The game has too much emphasis on inventory management. Imagine Diablo II x 10, without the fun of sorting magical equipment. You have 4 separate character inventories whilst most things don't stack as well as bag-inside-bag nesting. It gets quite out of hand.
- Healing items felt pointless. I imagine they'd be essential to a mostly physical party, but considering magic users seem to be the best classes, you'll probably gravitate to having 2 casters. This means you'll get all your health and energy healing from them instead of items.
Pros:
- Character creation is pretty fun. No character is pidgeon-holed into their starting class, making it easy to change your mind if you don't like a certain class.
- Complex magic system is really sweet! I loved drenching a battle arena in water and then electrifying it shocking all the  enemies still standing there.
- A lot of the music is really good, it's a shame there were so many "quiet" area or places with ambient rumbling when there was plenty of good music when it was playing, but when the music did kick in it was pretty awesome.
- Non linear areas are pretty awesome, you can play much of the game in any order you want. You can even fight the end boss and beat him way before the end of the game. One of the best uses of this I've seen in a game like this.
- Lots of classes dedicated to 4 major playstyles. I took a Melee/Ranged+Stealth/Mage/Healer party and still had to make some tough choices about how they were kitted out. There's 18 classes in the game with a sub-class system which is really awesome.
If I didn't have to spend so much time dealing with the literal piles of gear on the ground this game would have been a solid 8/10 for me. Otherwise I just knock it down to a 7.5/10.

The music is surprisingly solid throughout and few tunes even stick in your head afterwards.
The only real bug I encountered I made a post about and had a response within a day or two from the dev (even though it was a pretty minor bug in the sceme of things). The game has an interesting inclusion of using shovels, picks, and other tools to interact with things on the map, sometimes obviously and sometimes secretly. The only real negative I have is that inventory management is kind of annoying, but I say that as someone who hates inventory management in literally every game that has it (Diablo, Fallout, etc.) so grain of salt there.
If you are out for a tactical RPG, this is a great one to give a shot. It might not look flashy but there's a lot of depth to uncover here.

What a fun little journey!
Absolutely worth the money.
The story hits that sweet spot of nice little background snippets and a fluid pace. The game never bogs you down with too much dialogue or heavy handed story dumps. Lean and efficient storytelling.
The variety of classes and abilities is impressive, the synergies between them even more so. You will frequently surprise yourself with moments of ingenuity and improvisation.
You will however never feel overwhelmed by the number of options as the game staggers new classes and abilities nicely across its length, so you can get used to them one after another.
Similarly you will discover the spire one area at a time with no predetermined order. There are however several metroidvania style tools that will unlock areas formerly unaccessable.
At the end of my experience I feel fulfilled yet yearning for more. More backstory, more gameplay and more adventures in this fantastic world. Wholeheartedly recommended!

TL;DR,  Communism is easier to win than capitalism.
Very similar to AdVenture Capitalist but more difficult.  I have been playing AdVenture Capitalist for almost a year on Android.  It seems much more managable for a phone game.  This game requires a significantly greater amount of clicking and babysitting.  There is not much autoplaying and few perks.  Progress is very slow and it seems to be only sped up with paying for "scientists" which are used to increase click rates/amounts.  It would take maybe a hundred hours of game play to make enough progress to get to the point that the scientist regenerate themselves.  Even with an autoclicker it will take a few weeks of constant play.  I'll probably keep playing and see how it changes because these type of repetitive games seem to suck me in.
Some tips for the new players...
Save your scientists!  Get at least 5 to get the All Industries perk which will save a lot of time.
You can get 2-3 bonus bundles of items in land mines in each resource each day (just click a lot).
Don't open up the side panels too quickly.  You need a lot of supplies to make any progress on those so use your scientists for something else.  Once you are ready, start with the potatoes and work up.
Medals don't do much but the unlocks will help you speed things up.
So far the overall wealth doesn't do anything except look pretty.
There is no need to invest heavily in bullets or medicine until later on in the game.  You need the potatoes, land, and ore much more.
EDIT:  100+ hour review
After playing over 100 hours with an autoclicker, I have about 100 scientists regenerating.  I got my first potato scientist at about 50 hours.  Scientists can be collected after 4 hours for the potatoes, 3 hours for land, 2 for mines, 1 for weapons and medicine.  These must be collected by hitting the claim button and do not automatically add like everything else.  I've been investing them into the industry perks which are one and done perks.  I have saved up 100 for one of the state perks (10x multiplier).  These you can click multiple times so it is worth it to save for the higher multipliers more than dumping into the lower ones.  The trial multipliers don't seem very useful aside from the "Dearest upgrade" trials.  These are extremely expensive though.
By now, clicking is almost pointless and the game is doing better just playing itself with me checking every now and then to see what needs upgrading.   I'm finding ore and bullets to be my bottle neck.  In case you haven't opened up the medicine side panal, it creates more of your farmers/workers/miners/soldiers rather than medicine resources.
Edit #2:  Somewhere around 8.99X10^307, everything becomes infinity and the game is pointless.  If you keep going, you get to the point where you can't buy anything.  Look at my screenshots if you want to see the end.  A bit fun while it lasted but glad to be done with it.

I played through the game on normal with the warrior and enjoyed the variety of skills I acquired for him. Not a ton, but enough to add some strategy and keep a ~3 hour game interesting. I'm assuming the other three classes have their own set of skills, which adds some potential replayability.
One thing to keep in mind before starting a game is that 'normal' difficulty was rather easy for me and I never had any shortage of money. If you are adept at rogue-likes, you may want to play on a higher difficulty.
This game isn't amazing, but it is a fun and simple rogue-like that is very accessible. It retails at $5 so it would be a very reasonable purchase on sale.

Disclaimer: I received a key from the developer for the purpose of beta testing. I have not been compelled to leave positive feedback and have judged this game by my own standards.
OH! RPG! comes from the same people who brought you Epic Quest of the 4 Crystals, and right off the bat, I will say that it's likely an improvement over said game. The intro at the start of the game made me feel this way almost instantly, and it isn't long before you are chucked right in at the deep end, straight into combat.
The music is improved here, and there's a great combination of guitar and a more traditional sound for the genre.
Graphics seem better too, especially environment graphics which are rather well detailed. Character graphics are probably a bit lacking, and the animation, at least in exploration mode, isn't a lot different from their previous effort. Combat mode is better, when it comes to character design, especially with enemy characters.
This game is still a sort of send up of JRPGs in general, or at least that's the feeling I get, as obvious references are made to Harry Potter and other franchises, but thankfully they seem to have left out a lot of the crude, sophomoric jokes this time. In fact dialogue as a whole seems to be less, at least initially (I have admittedly not spent a lot of time with it; it may get worse - or better depending on how you look at it - as you go along) and just limited to quick conversations which are good if you don't want your game constantly interrupted by long, drawn-out banter.
I found the game to be a bit harder than Epic Quest, even though there is a bit of hand holding going on as members of your party attempt to give you tips in combat. This is especially true because of the faster start with this game. There's no moving about and getting acquainted with things -- you are thrown right in and you have to learn the ropes on the fly. Don't expect any sort of training or a lull at the beginning here.
One thing I find that is much better is the interface. It doesn't have the same disjointed feel like with Epic Quest. You just press escape and you can access anything you want from the in game menu. That said, the interface, although it looks better, isn't very intuitive and it will take some experimenting and trial and error before you figure it out.
Overall, I would say this is as good if not a bit better than Epic Quest, but, and perhaps I am biased seeing as RPGs, especially JRPGs aren't really my thing, it's once again not a game that I would spend an inordinate amount of time playing. It's the same recipe as far as basic JRPG gameplay goes, but it seems more streamlined and polished than Epic Quest, so I think it's at least a step in the right direction.

Ah yes, Dark Souls. Originally a cult classic, for x360&ps3, ported to GFWL (games for windows live), and later ported to steam. This game is considered by many to be "one of the hardest games ever", and it's honestly true. Dark souls has clever world design, many weapons to try with various different movesets. Most bosses in the game are designed fantastically with various different attacks of their own that you must learn to dodge and find the openings to deal some damage. I can go on and on but many other reviews can tell you why the game's fantastic.
The main reason you're even reading this review right now is you're either a curious individual, or your friend challenged you to play this game. I'm gonna tell you right here and now, the difficulty of dark souls isn't a reason you shouldn't play it. I've heard countless stories of people playing this game for their first time, ready to hop in, dying like twice to the same enemy at the start of the game, and never touching the game again. I'll stop you right there and say I can blast through this game in 1 session easily, and I didn't really have a hard time picking it up when my friend gifted it to me early January of this year. I blasted through the game in 3 days with his help and a couple days afterward beat the game on my own on a new character.
I'll quickly touch on the multiplayer mechanics of this game, it's buggy as hell and the PVP isn't exactly the most fun thing in the world since it's just a backstabfest. The game induces lag so the host doesn't get a clear advantage. Nobody's lagging if everyone's lagging, eh? This game was their first real attempt at an online mode because Demon's Souls' online was a joke, so if you do play this game, give the pvp the benefit of the doubt, it only gets better pvp wise in the next games.
Another quick reminder, I don't give a sheit if Dark Souls 3 is on sale, pick up dark souls 1, and then play them in the order of dark souls 1 then 2 then 3. This is so you can best appreciate the changes the series made over the evolution of the series.
To me this game is a 10/10 without a doubt.

PROS/CONS for four categories: Gameplay, Graphics, Story, and Music/Sound.
Again I STRONGLY RECOMMEND this game so take the negatives with a grain of salt.
Gameplay
+ Really unique. Combines things from Ultima, Metroidvania, and Turn based SRPGs. The part that’s Ultima is the interface with drag and drop interaction. The part that is Metroidvania is exploring a fairly large world with TONS of secrets. It restricts from you from going to later areas at the start by needing certain items or abilities. There are quite a few areas at the start that can be completed in any order. The part that is “Tactics” or  turn based SRPG is the battle system like Shining Force. Final Fantasy Tactics etc
+ Lots of interactable objects within that system.
+ The level design is well thought out with nice shortcuts that help with backtracking.
+ A lot of the secret areas are logical. I fought an Enemy that exists on a wall after defeating it I pick axed that wall and found a secret area.
+ Secret areas reward exploration/use of the interaction system.
+ Most battles are with less than 10 enemies so nothing drags on too long.
+ Perfect length (20-30 hours on first playthrough) doesn’t pull JRPG ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to pad game time.
+/- The tactics gameplay relies heavily on positioning your enemies by use of walls/turrets to be able to cast AoE magic spells.
– The inventory is straight from Ultima 7.  drag and drop nightmare
- Items won’t always stack if you have them in another bag within your inventory.
- It’s a Metroidvania in level design. Although its mitigated by shortcuts, there is backtracking especially if you’re stuck
- Some of the secret areas are really obscure wall hugging/pixel finding stuff.
- Enemies can take a really long time on their turns planning out their actions.
Graphics
+/- So it does use pixel graphics. They are on par with early Super Nintendo stuff (sprites are flat colors with little shading). At first I felt like everything was way too big and blocky at 1080p. But as I played it grew on me.
+Overall it was consistent nothing feels out of place within the world.
+ Not typical fantasy
+ Character Races are interesting and offer some customization.
+ Enough variation in areas and enemies to keep it interesting and made me want to see what was next.
+ Weapons change appearance. A couple of accessories actually show on your character.

- The accessories that do change your character is limited to (I think?) one or two. You can loot a cape that will show on your character but its right before the final boss.
- Different armor just changes the color of your character’s armor. Again other than one or two accessories /class changing your armor stays the same other than color.
Story
+ It has some cool ideas. Doesn’t have some Characters as completely good or evil.
+ There are some choices. (Though there are a couple that can make the difficulty sky rocket.)
+ Good length
+/- Moves at a good pace. Good flow of story events. Nothing drags or gets in the way of exploration/combat.
+/- Not typical fantasy but just barely.
- The story was “ok” at best.

Music

Despite a great number of reviews praising this game already, I feel compelled to leave another glowing review.  Voidspire Tactics, especially having purchased it 50% off during this Summer Sale, has been one of my favorite games played in the last few years.
The combat is indeed strategic and tactical.  You have access to view every statistic and class, both of your characters and enemy combatants, and the time/ATB is very transparent to ensure you know when an action will happen, is going to happen, and what area(s) of the field it will affect.
Although the game gives a great deal of flexibility to your characters, it does not feel grindy or as though you are punished for choosing things poorly.  I played on the standard Veteran difficulty, and found the game to be challenging but fair throughout.  I almost wished at times that the game had more opportunities to earn xp, to beef up characters just a bit more or to experiment with classes, but the pace is set very nicely.
The art is charming to me, and I think it has a ton of style.  Coupled with the music choices, many places have uniquely identifiable atmospheres that are memorable and fun to explore.  On that topic, there are quite a few things to explore, by virtue of having items that can expose and help you gain access to new pathways.  The exploration is put together very creatively, and allows you at some times to make shortcuts by dropping a rope, or forcing your way through a cave wall via pickaxe.
The story is interesting and engaging, with quirky humor and dialogue choices that give you at least the illusion of inclusion into this world.  Using the Look feature gives some useful information, but also fills in a lot of backstory to add depth to the experience.  It took me about 13 hours to complete, though to be fair, I did reference the guide here on Steam periodically which may have shaved some time off.
If I knew getting into this game how much play time I would get, and how much fun I would have, I would not have bothered waiting for the Steam sale to pick this game up.  I greatly look forward to trying the spiritual successor, Alvora Tactics!

It's like Final Fantasy Tactics combat with souls-esque exploration/level design.
If you're like me, not much scratches the SRPG itch quite like FFT did. I've tried everything from Disgaea, the spin-offs, hard-mode mods (In fact an FFT mod forum is where I discovered this) and consider myself an enthusiast of the Strategy RPG genre overall. When I played this game it scratched that itch and MORE. Hands-down, this quickly became one of my favorite games of all time. The feeling of wonder as you combine tools and discover new locations is so gratifying.
The best part is how seamless the open combat merges with the exploration. Grow plants that act as ladders, dig through walls and discover hidden tunnels, freeze the water and find that you can walk into a new area. Voidspire has created a robust and addicting system that isn't overwhelming, and encourages a child-like sense of experimentation.
When I say open combat I really mean it. The dual-class system allows for extremely creative combinations. Things like teleporting your elemental sword attacks across space, setting up turrets behind magic barriers for a zombie shelter, or improvising a trap with corpses left on the battlefield are all possible. You can really come up with so many playstyles and strategies, and yet the power curve is still very hard to break. This is in my opinion, one of its best traits. While it is an RPG, the stat-crunching aspect is heavily underplayed in exchange for small damage numbers and controllable difficulty. This leads to very consistently challenging and exciting battles that while never frustrating, will always encourage you to play intelligently.

Iron Brigade is a great game that you should not buy. The concept and gameplay are great - tower defense plus mech action is a great combination, especially in such a clever and amusing setting.
But the bugs and other problems make it nearly unplayable. The game is locked at 30 frames per second. There are persistent performance issues that cause frequent half-second pauses (the infamous "scrap stutter" bug). Sometimes scripts don't trigger and you have to erase all of your progress (manually, since the game autosaves frequently and doesn't have an in-game option to clear your data) because the game has been rendered unfinishable. And it uses Games For Windows Live, which Double Fine has "no plans" to remove, despite the service's impending shutdown in the middle of this year.

Gameplay: Luftrausers is an arcade-style shoot 'em up based around completing objectives (e.g., score 5000 points, kill a battleship at max combo). Your aircraft's weapon, body, and engine are customizable, which encourages development of different tactics. Enemy spawn inconsistency adds variety to gameplay, but leaves certain objective completions largely in the hands of chance. Given the short life of a typical game (a few minutes), this randomness is tolerable, but I wish they would have toned it down. A high level of skill is nonetheless required, but you might have to burn though several dozen attempts before enemies spawn conducive to your current objectives.
Controls: Compact and elegant: left, right, accelerate, fire. Body/engine build choices yield different maneuverability, all of which feel beautifully responsive (some more than others for intentional balance reasons). Controls are the highlight of Luftrausers, and fans of arcade classics will love it for its feel.
Presentation: Its simple graphics are immediately readable, and aircraft-specific musical adjustments make me feel like an angel of death. Menu navigation feels a bit clumsy. My biggest presentation gripe is during the "hardcore" SFMT mode, where you are continuously exposed to a blaring air raid siren. The only in-game way to eliminate that overwhelming sound is to disable sound effects, which are crucial to high-level gameplay. The appealing minimalist aesthetic is offset by flaws which could have been easily addressed.

Despite it's simple graphics and gameplay, this little game has a lot of character and replay value. It's also pretty unforgiving, if you're into that. No matter how often I die, it always seems to urge me on, compelling me to try more death-defying mid-air acrobatics and kamikaze tactics. 7.5/10.

Im going to review this game. Not the fact that I put it away for a while to allow for the many many bugs...including the lack of screen support making the guns fire to the left of the target, be fixed. I come back to find this mess has been abandoned and "remastered". More likely they realized what a mess it was and just decided to cash in their chips. Heres the deal. Core gameplay problems is what I will concentrate on. Nothing about the developers screwing the fanbase over because there are a thousand of those rants right now.
To start with. This is not a survival game. Its a resource collection game with arcade physics thrown in to give you something to do while youre trying to keep your little base alive. You WILL spend most of your time wondering why you can just carry a damn bag in the trunk of your car. See....the game mechanic is this. Break into house. Random loot is in random places. Lets say food. You pack it up into a bag and carry it on your back.....to the car....that you drove there in. Now. Common sense says "Hey. Ill throw a bag in the trunk or the passenger seat.", or "Hey, I got a truck. Ill throw the bag in the bed of the truck and I can bring more stuff so I can play the game a bit and not worry about the food situation." Now we cant have that can we? 1 bag at a time sir. Regardless if you brought a pickup truck or a muscle car. The method of delivery is 1 bag at a time.
While youre collecting those bags youll come across radio traffic in the form of side missions. usually its "Survivor X located at Y, go save them." That sounds simple but when youre literally in the middle of a mission and carrying a pack of supplies...its pretty much impossible to get there in time. Innevitabley they die and because of the "I hate your decisions" system built into the game, your damned squad gets MAD AT YOU FOR FAILING TO SAVE PEOPLE YOU HAVE NO TIME TO SAVE!!!!
So you say forget them. Ill just go back to base and turn these supplies in. All will be forgivien. Just about right. Except now that youre back the base is under seige. Right about the time that you come back. You have very little time to run back and forth, nailing boards to windows while your NPC buddies fire away, destroying the boards and....not really damaging any zombies that are crawling through. Eventually you get a few hits and some damage. Then survive the night. The "Seige" is what its called. Oh...but dont forget to kill ALL THE ZOMBIES!!! If you forget just one...anywhere...they will not stop the seige mode and more will come. I had a zombie stuck in a staircase that I couldnt kill and the seige just kept on until...well....I lost all my crew and myself. Lets assume for the sake of brevity that you manage to save the idiots standing around...I mean, your team mates. You have a broken leg. How? Zombie punched you in the arm maybe...who knows. Now we come to....
Tired and worn characters. Not only are your resources limited the characters you get to control are also depressive, unskilled, and sometimes just better off holding a grenade and running toward the largest hoard you can find. So here you are. Youve had the black dude with the vest or the military chick the whole time. Theyre the starting characters and quite frankly the best ones Ive found. LOVE the black dude in the vest. He weilds a sledgehammer like an anime warrior swings a mystic too big to hold sword at demons to split them in half! However...here you are. Unable to walk very far and tired. So you have to trade in. Cool...cool. Ill just use someone else. Its here that the game reveals just how hard it can push when it takes a dump all over you. See...the other characters in the game arent really all that useful. There are a few here and there that are ok but theyre all random when you get them. The way you mainly get them? Remember earlier when I said you gotta rescue people? Yeah. So anyways. Youre now forced to use some old lady thats an alcoholic chain smoker and has "A general knack for cleaning"........great.
Well you use the old bag lady who clans house. You kill zombies and raid houses. Every 12 minutes a call comes through to "Return to base. We have a horde incoming!" Yay.......another siege. Its only been like....10 minutes and you just got to the actual story mission area. Nope. Head home and battle more zombies. Well now that youre finally here and collecting supplies while playing through a mission....boss fight. Great. Your bag lady just got killed. Now its back to the wounded guy from earlier. You use him and...well....you were too slow and now hes dead. You decide....Ill take a break.
You come back from said break, unaware that while youre gone...the game keeps on. So you come back to a game where some survivors took supplies to trade with other survivors, they didnt get back because they were trapped by a zombie horde, theyve lost your supplies, and now youve got to take "Jim Boscoe" to save them. Jim is a derelict, chronic alcoholic, that wheezes like an old school bus muffler and coughs up just as much when you rev the engine. Hes armed with a pole that he picked up and smells like a bag of feet. Go get em Jim!
Thats the biggest issue, The character "story" is generic as all get out. The intricat relation you thought you had between the military chick, black dude in the vest, and white dude in ugly shrt? Yeah...thats all for nothing as the dialogue is written in such a way that not only is it not changed....its CONTINUED IN EXACTLY THE SAME MANNER AS IF NO ONE EVER DIED!!! The story just chugs along like an Austrailian land train convoy! No impact. No repercussion , except that now instead of having an actual "hero" character...youre in control of a useless whino. Yeah...because thats what I want to be in a game. A whino with a length of rebar!
Lets just say for the sake of things you decide to run with this....you should consider getting tested at this point...youve had warning and I didnt. By the way...at this point can you tell this is  100 percent MY ACTUAL EXPERIENCE WITH THE GAME?!?! So youre Jim...the whino savior of the badlands. You climb into your muscle car and you just want to do a mission. You find the location is on the other side of the map and go. Because youve got no skills you decide to just use the car. Doing so destroys the car and when you get out to switch you find the "stealth" element to Jim is severly lacking. There is NO DAMNED STEALTH ELEMENT! You are either behind a wall or you are seen. End of. The people who claim there is a stealth element are lying. Period. There is a stealth element attempted but not implemented all the way. So what you get is guess work instead of applied skill. I guess it adds to the "intensity" but at this point the "intensity" is annoyance. You get to the mission area....youve thus far ignored at least 2 cries for help, a person trapped in a siege building, and a siege at your own base...because screw it you just want to plod on with the mission!
Final problem. Joe is underpowered. Yeah. See. Games like Da-Z, Project Zomboid, H1Z1, The Dead linger...theyre all like this game in some ways. Theyre all worse and better so Im not advocating any of them individually, however, they did get one thing right. See. State of Decay has zombies that ar at different difficulty to kill. The Big'uns are FAR harder to kill and the Shrieker is the highest priority to kill. Well. The characters that are capable, the ones you worked on to get to that level, the ones you spent the last 6 hours of gameplay on....theyre all dead. Jim has a lenght of rebar to fight 2 armored zombies, a Big'un, and a shrieker....who are all in front of the mission building. You say "Screw this. Im running these cats over!" Then you find out that hitting the Big'un destroys the car. Now your car explodes and Jim is dead.
This, unfortunately, is the game.

Played Binding of Isaac until you can see it when your eyes are closed? Good news! This game is exactly what you hope it will be.
The Slimeking's Tower is incredibly fleshed out for being so new, it even has a few features that i wish BoI had. A pet system that persists between runs, where you upgrade monsters as pets, who will ultimately grant you an extra ability when equipped. A store that allows you to buy items to send in on the next run. An in-run XP system where you gain levels that grant additional stats or features. A large cast of characters with very individualized perks/flaws that make them all feel truly different.
The game moves fast, and has many of the features that BoI players might expect as well. You have secret rooms, item rooms, shops, and a multitude of special hearts. Ghost hearts, shield hearts, gold hearts, recharge hearts... just, look... this game is as close to a different version of BoI as I've ever found, and it's done well. There are a few issues and bugs to contend with but keep in mind that this game has been out less than a week as of this review.
In short, it's incredibly feature-rich for such an early stage, and it will scratch that Isaac itch in a fun way. Plus, look at the price! This game is worth every penny.

Every floor has a mini-boss that after you defeat it, it will gives a key for you to open the boss room,that's the room to advance to next floor. The game has 5 different modes to choose from.

I would look at Vaelsh's review because he goes indepth on what to expect and helped me decide to get it. I love this game and i would reccomend it, but keep in mind it is an early access game. So it does have its problems. And since Vaelsh goes over all of the great aspects of the game, i'm going to go over just a few things that are negatives. First there isn't full controller support, so you can play the game itself with the controller no problem! but when using the main menu or pause menu to look at the items you picked up (with the description) you have to go from controller to mouse. Second is that you can only look at your items up to a certain point. So it is like isaac in the sense that it has alot of item that change the way you play. So you are always picking up new items and wanting to look at them. Well you have four lines in a box where you can do so, but if it fills up, you can't see any items you pick up from that point on unless you drop or remove items that come before that. which is really annoying and a hassle. Third is that you have to be careful when fighting a boss. Because once he dies, a stair case will spawn in the middle and if you are standing there or running down the middle when he dies, you will automatically get teleported to the next level and miss out on the item. Really annoying! and when you beat a couple high bosses later in the game, one will drop a crown and one will drop a mustache. I recommend not picking up either because you don't get any achievement from doing so and it just ends the game when there are more levels to enjoy and play through. If any of this will annoy you or if you don't like early access games then i suggest to wait and see where it goes. With all of this said, i enjoy playing early access games and deffinately would recommend this game! with these annoyances the game itself is alot of fun, there are some cool characters to unlock, and the devs want to keep adding to it and working on it! I just wanted to let you know some of the minor issues in case that is a problem for you.

The Slimeking's Tower is an exciting action roguelike shooter game in the same vein as The Binding of Isaac. Where to start describing this game's features...
-Multiple game modes including a daily run
-Challenges similar to Isaac's challenge list
-Around 9 unlockable characters to play as, all with their own weird and sometimes wonderful perks and quirks
-Great music and sounds
-Very heavily inspired both looks-wise and function-wise to Zelda and Isaac
-Secret rooms similar to Isaac, but only one per floor
-Mimics (*shudder* mimics...)
-Nice mimics! These will accept keys to give you items/character upgrades or money for xp
-It is a rogue-lite with xp leveling on a per run basis including passively gaining more health, strength, etc. randomly from leveling up (xp is gained from killing monsters)
-Like Isaac, there are more floors than the initial set (similar to the Womb levels and onward in Isaac)
-There is a closet to store a starter item that is in the starting room of each floor. If there's an item you prefer to start with, you can save and buy it for your closet
-Pets! You can equip a pet and level it over time and get perks to help your character out on the run that the pet is with you!
-Each floor has you kill a mini-boss to get the boss key (like Zelda) then when you are ready, you can go for the boss
-Sacrifice rooms (similar to the spike sacrifice room in Isaac)
-Shops including ones where you have to buy items with red hearts instead of gold
-Multiple extra heart types (some I have no idea what they do) including skull hearts, shield hearts, gold hearts, recharge hearts and time hearts
-All original sprites and a funny premise that is quite likeable from the start
-Different difficulty settings to play on
-300 or more items to discover and use
-Once you pick up an item for the first time, you can look up the item and see what it is/does
-If there item effects you don't want to keep using (such as throwing bombs everywhere), you can go into the items area of the pause menu, find the item and hit the DROP button
Really one of my only suggestions for the devs on this game is even though it can be played quite well with a controller, please let us navigate the menus and lists in the game with controller instead of having to switch over to mouse when we want to look at something. Also allow us to have a scroll wheel or continuous page to look at all the items we have so we can tell what they all do at all times.
Overall, I highly recommend this wonderful little Isaac like game. I think you will find it fun and a great value for it's price. Also with the promise of online multiplayer coming soon, there is not much reason to not pick this up and at least try it out.

Starbound is sort of like if someone turned Team Fortress 2 into an adventure game, its fun for the first hour or two when you find new weapons and items, but after that all thats left to do is gather cosmetic items because of the incredibly limited selection of functional things.
almost every item in the game is purely cosmetic, without any functional purpose. that weird thing on the wall that you think might do something? it doesnt. its just a weird thing you can put on the wall.
Besides the lack of items, the game also suffers from convoluted and uninteresting progression. The player is left with no real idea of what to do beyond questing, which eventually just stops out saying "very good equipment recommended", with no indication of how to get it. Tungsten is the last part that a player can reasonably figure out as beyond that resources are gated by environmental hazards such as radiation, extreme heat, and extreme cold, none of which have any sort of indication of how to survive them.
Questing itself is also rather boring, consisting almost entirely of "fetch" quests or cooking quests.
Larger progression such as ship upgrades is extremely tedius as aquiring crew, which is necessary for ship upgrades, requires doing an incredible amount of the boring random quests until someone asks to join your crew. (though this can be skipped for a large fee)
Even if you can move past these problems, you will find many parts of the game just feel "soulless", there is nothing that attaches you to anything its just something you can get. the "combat system" its basically just mash left mouse until the opposition dies while also healing. which is not terrible, but its far less than one could ever expect from a game that promised so much. Along with that, the game may offer alot of options but none of those options feel complete. the mechs are very tacked on and look honestly just very very very stupid.
Even mods cant really save this game as its flaws are fundamental, the most damaging aspects as distributed evenly to where a whole new game would have to be made to correct all of the obvious flaws this game has.
To be clear I was one of the first people to preorder starbound. I watched its development go YEARS over what we were told it would, hoping that would coincide with an increase in quality. It didnt. even at 1.3 the game feels half finished and the universe feels empty.
TL:DR
Starbound is a game about making a pretty home, not about questing, fighting, or even just exploring as the store page would have you believe.

Pro's:
There is a very detailed ocean to swim around in and explore
Very nice graphics, fantastic sound effects, fairly large world.
Interesting depth to the survival mechanics
Cons:
There's not really any point. You just kind of exist for the sake of existing.
The tutorial is brain dead, not giving you enough information to the point where you still have to guess what to do
The controls are 100% aimed at using a controller, using a mouse and keyboard you will feel like a second class citizen
Some of the interactions are nonsensical (why do I need to use a knife to forage for potatoes? you should be able to pull those out of the ground by hand...)
Arbitrary difficulty: they are simultaneously trying to make the inventory system realistic while also making it so small as to be painfully useless; coupled with the terrible control requirements your primary interaction with the game will be fighting with the game to do what you need it to do
Poorly worded instructions: hold mouse0 to do X, hold mouse1 to do Y. How about you use normal English and designate left and right mouse buttons?
Mechanics without feedback: right click to drag a piece of meat and hold it over a fire to cook. For how long? How am I even supposed to know it's done?
No HUD in the user interface, sure this makes for a pretty game. But here's the problem: in reality you know when you are about to run out of air underwater, you know if you feel an injury and need to get medical help, and so on. In a game, you can't "feel" these things and you need a user interface to communicate with the player that something is going on with their character. You get none of this in game, you just have to guess what your oxygen levels and health are at. Or you know, die because the game didn't bother to tell you that you feel something wrong.
---
I'll summarize my 4 hours of playing:
Start game, get lost in menu because I'm an idiot and decide to explore the cartographer option as if that was something a new player should be touching. Yea, dont, you don't know what those settings do until you play the game. My mistake.
Start new game. Watch helplessly as my plane falls out of the sky. Fumble with the controls until I figure out how to swim out of the plane. Well that was interesting, so... now what.
Use raft to find an island. Spend the next several minutes trying to figure out what buttons to push because the game won't let me pull leaves off plants, or harvest potatoes or do anything really because it can't be bothered to tell you what the controls are for interacting with things.
Realize you can't interact with anything unless you have a tool. Decide to try and follow the tutorial and begin looking for rocks. Find rocks, find sticks and than.. wait I need some kind of binding. Game doesn't bother to tell you where the binding comes from (it's not part of the tutorial)
Spend way too many minutes browsing the very cluttered, confusing, crafting menu that can't even be bothered to be in any kind of order (not alphabetical or any semblence of order that I could figure out) until I finally find the recipe for the binding thing I needed.
At that point I clicked on the tool I was supposed to make, I have no idea why it bothered to craft it. I hadn't actually found any binding at that point, I was clearly missing an item to make it. It made it anyway.
Then had to figure out from there that you needed to use the tool to cut up plants to get fibers to make more binding to make a better tool. Still unsure how I made the first tool without binding if I needed a tool to get the binding. Confused, but whatever...
Spend some time finishing the rest of the tutorial, most of it cursing at whoever named mouse0 and mouse1 instead of left and right mouse buttons. Hating whoever decided that right click drag to cook meat was a good idea.
By now I've got my campifire, I know how to catch and eat crab (or do I? I'm still not sure I've been holding the meat long enough over the fire, there's no feedback on whether its cooked and my character seems to get sick if I eat it. But I get bored of just sitting there holding right click over the fire for several minutes waiting for it to cook, was it done or not? No one knows, I certainly don't)
I know how to drink from coconuts. Yay I won't dehydrate. And I've got my little shelter thing set up (required to save your game).
I click sleep, spend the night (it's too dark to do anything) and wake up to a tropical storm. Appreciate the sound effects and twiddle my thumbs while the tutorial finishes and just says: go survive...
I used my raft to visit a few more nice looking islands. I swam around underwater and marveled at the broken shipwrecks. I ate more crab, drank more coconut.
Explored the crafting menu long enough to realize whoever chose this layout was probably drunk and built a few more things from it by gathering materials.
But after a few hours I'm asking myself: now what?
Surviving is hard mostly because the controls stink. The actual keep yourself alive part is easy enough with crabs and coconuts everywhere.
Exploring looks nice but honestly after 4 hours of looking around, these are deserted islands. What more am I going to see? Shipwrecks? check, Turtles? check. A scary shark in the distance? Better get back to land and stay out of the water for a while.
You can build a bigger hut, you can make different rafts but ... the question that will haunt me is: now what?
You may be wondering with all of those criticisms why my review is still positive, and it's this:
The game doesn't lie about what it is. If you read the description it's very clear that it's just a survival game that strands you on an island. It meets that claim and it does so with a very pretty world and some nice sound effects.
My complaints are there only to provide context: do not play this game expecting it to be more than it is.
You've heard of walking simulators? This is a swimming simulator with survival elements. If you just want a relaxing experience where you hang out in pretty oceans and do some crafting you might even really like this game.
And if you play it with a controller you might not even hate the controls.
Bottom line: play it for what it is and you might have fun here. Expect a bunch of features that it doesn't advertise, and you are very likely to be disapointed.

Ah yes, Dark Souls. Originally a cult classic, for x360&ps3, ported to GFWL (games for windows live), and later ported to steam. This game is considered by many to be "one of the hardest games ever", and it's honestly true. Dark souls has clever world design, many weapons to try with various different movesets. Most bosses in the game are designed fantastically with various different attacks of their own that you must learn to dodge and find the openings to deal some damage. I can go on and on but many other reviews can tell you why the game's fantastic.
The main reason you're even reading this review right now is you're either a curious individual, or your friend challenged you to play this game. I'm gonna tell you right here and now, the difficulty of dark souls isn't a reason you shouldn't play it. I've heard countless stories of people playing this game for their first time, ready to hop in, dying like twice to the same enemy at the start of the game, and never touching the game again. I'll stop you right there and say I can blast through this game in 1 session easily, and I didn't really have a hard time picking it up when my friend gifted it to me early January of this year. I blasted through the game in 3 days with his help and a couple days afterward beat the game on my own on a new character.
I'll quickly touch on the multiplayer mechanics of this game, it's buggy as hell and the PVP isn't exactly the most fun thing in the world since it's just a backstabfest. The game induces lag so the host doesn't get a clear advantage. Nobody's lagging if everyone's lagging, eh? This game was their first real attempt at an online mode because Demon's Souls' online was a joke, so if you do play this game, give the pvp the benefit of the doubt, it only gets better pvp wise in the next games.
Another quick reminder, I don't give a sheit if Dark Souls 3 is on sale, pick up dark souls 1, and then play them in the order of dark souls 1 then 2 then 3. This is so you can best appreciate the changes the series made over the evolution of the series.
To me this game is a 10/10 without a doubt.

This game is amazing.
Yes, the PC port is bad. But with some time and a few excellent steam guides it works great. The graphics are a bit dated but now bad. I hardly noticed them. I have been told that a controller is reccomended but I played with KB+Mouse with little trouble. The MouseFix GUI was very helpful, and with some tweaking and personal preference the controls worked well. If anyone is having trouble feel free to message me.
Yes, this game is challenging. Some bosses or areas will take many tries to beat, then you can look back with the sense that you learned every aspect and beat the challenge. Death becomes a learning experience. Boss stun-locked you to death? Your dodge was timed poorly, or you didnt watch your stamina levels. Eventually, you will learn how to time your attacks and movement depending on the enemy. Overall, the gameplay is (mostly, there are exceptions) fair.
The mechanics allow for much customization of your appearance, playstyle, weapon choice, ect. There is a world of weapons, upgrades, and magic to explore and learn. For me everything was complicated at first, but over time (and with a few guides) I learned what it meant.
Probably the best thing about this game is the level design and overall world design. The areas are connected in amazing ways. Exploration is rewarded, not just with items but the discovery of shortcuts.
Right from the start, the game begins building a world full of lore. The opening cutscene sets the stage excellently. With a little dilligence in talking to npcs and reading item descriptions, more information is found. This game may be a masterpiece just for creating a detailed and amazing world using small pieces. Even characters are built up to be unique after only a few lines.
Overall, this game is a masterpiece. Anyone who hasnt played is missing out on a world of lore and skilled gameplay.

Overview: Visual Novel
Under normal circumstances this is a game that would never appeal to me: cute anime characters, little interaction, and cute music, yet underneath all this is a game filled with a lot of choices and difficult decision to make that affect the outcome of the story. With multiple ways of dying, upgrading your character and choosing how the story plays out, this game is filled with lots of replay-ability.
In LLTQ you make three types of choices. After every week you can participate in an activity that alters your mood. Depending on your mood, you get a bonus or penalty to certain skills. The second choice you make is the types of skills you want to learn on a week by week basis. The story has a series of skill checks, by passing or failing these skill checks you are given more information or choices in how the story progresses. The third type of choice you make is directly related to the story, you decide who lives or dies, weather you should go to certain events etc... all of this drastically affects the story in multiple ways and leads to various outcomes...some good....some bad.
This game is all about playing the game over and over again trying out different skills and choices and see where the story takes you. Though I'm not the biggest fan of visual novel games, this game is worth checking out.

It is hard to believe, but I think I've finally found it! I've probably played...dozens... of RPGMaker titles on steam and this is the first time I've actually felt like somebody put some real time, effort and HEART into their RPGMaker game.
Pros-
-The premise is amazing; seriously original, and the setting is a new twist on old hat. Good story. Sadly... I don't usually have the patience for JRPGs... but I really want to find out where they take the story! This one might sway me to finish it once I get Fallout 4 out of the way...
-Art and assets are nicely done
-No typos or bad spelling, grammar, etc!!! Sadly, this issue must be addressed in the RPGMaker arena. Anyway, this game clears the bar!
-Funny dialog, not corny crap like others of this ilk. Self-aware dialog, but used sparingly, so it doesn't break the 4th wall and get silly.
-Characters are actually interesting! *SPOILERS* but you get a ghost friend, a lady with multiple personalities and you get to control an enemy character. It kind of has a Chrono Cross feel to it, in that way.
Cons-
-I wish the combat were a little quicker. I know you can remove the combat animations in the options, which would help a little, but it just feels like it drags a little in the early part of the game when you fight 1 v 3 enemies and they all take a second to hit... and then you have to set your cursor over again
-Some aspects of the game could use a little better explaining, like the 'user level' or whatever it was called. The bonus given when beating an area. Not sure I understand the different levels and how its calculated. Also, the item and armor upgrading is a little mysterious and cumbersome since you can't be currently wearing the item you wish to upgrade (Update: they fixed this upgrading nusance)
*Disclaimers*
I played on Easy mode in order to get as far as possible in a limited time (it is the holidays, after all), so I can't comment on the "standard" difficulty, and;
I received a free copy of this game in exchange for my honest review.
Bottom line: I'll admit, JRPGs aren't really my bag anymore, I was really into them about a decade ago, but this one really has some fresh ideas for the genre. Seriously though, this is one of the best RPGMaker JRPGs I've ever played, it's totally worth it for the full price of $3, and if its on sale, definitely give it a go for the current sale price of a buck and change.

Compared to their last game Epic Quest of the 4 Crystals(which was also good), RosePortal Games have made some major improvements in their new game Oh! RPG.
First thing I have to say is that the setting of this game is much darker than the previous, but the story is much more engaging as well and characters are more compeling and interesting, at least to me. I won't get into any spoilers here but let's just say that our main character is not our usual "hero" and his inner struggle is what makes this game so different.
Once you start playing this game you won't be able to stop (At least I barely took my hands of my laptop).
And not only because of the story, but also because the maps and the world inside the game is much bigger, so it might take a while to finish a chapter or a part of the story, since there are so many areas to explore and secrets to uncover.
The combat system has also been improved, however enemies are much harder to beat from start, on normal mode, so you will have to invest in crafting and upgrading potions, weapons and armor, and develop fighting strategies. (Luckily there is a button to try the fight again if you die)
That being said the crafting system has been majorly improved as well.
Lastly but not least important the artwork in Oh! Rpg, looks even better than in RosePortal's previous games. It looks so very well designed, when it comes to both the characters and enemies. Even the whole world looks more realistic and 3d like compared to other rpg makers.
Overall I think that this is one of the better rpg maker games made by now and at this price it is a definite must buy! :D

Low in style, heavy in substance
this SNES 16-bit reminiscent turn based RPG is more than it looks. to make long story short, the game basically is a 16 Bit version of Divinity Original Sin with fun and varied classing and a great soundtrack to boot.
the main appeal of the game is the combat and spell system where the focus  is to use the elements against your enemies and solve puzzles. dowse your enemies with puddle of water, zap it with electricity and everyone in the area got zap. repair a bridge with wooden planks, use growth spell to re-grow cut tree so you have infinite supplies of wooden plank (or painstakingly scour areas for wooden planks or hit wooden furniture with ax to get wooden planks, etc there are probably a thousand way to get wooden planks in the game)
the level of interactivity in the battlefield is one of the best i've seen. your battle will leave permanents mark on the battlefield. cube of ice, schorched ground, puddle of water all will litter and mark the mayhem you've caused to your poor enemies.
of course, that level of interactivity isn't just wasted in combat. it place a crucial role for your party to discover all the secret items and bosses that litter the world. in 2D-zelda like traversal system, players are free to roam each part of the world, digging ground to find buried treasure, blasting annoying bushes to with explosions to make path, mining ores and glowy mushroom to craft things, or even regrow dead tree to give you fruits that increase HP permanently. the game is full of cool secrets that makes it worth to explore and visit multiple times.
of course the robust combat, skills and spell system are supported by satisfyingly varied amounts of enemies, where most encounters and hand crafted and offer unique situations. there are humanoid warriors that can have the same classes and use the same skills as the player, to giant magic bears that can leap at you with great speed to giant spider and rock people.
the class system is interesting. you start with 3 classes, warrior, scholar, and scout and you earn XP with each main class you "equip" there are 2 slots for classes, the main slot is the class that will gain XP, and the second slot won't net you exp, but you can use the skills you unlocked in that class. for example, to get sage class, you have to have 250 XP in scholar class, so you equip scholar class as your main, gain XP and get the sage class, then you set your main class to sage, and it will gain experience for you to spend on skill points and unlock more class. more advanced class like balancer, gatekeeper, breaker, mechanist will need multiple classes EXP to unlock, so  you are encouraged to try a different classes to experiment and combine. it is a robust system on itself on top of the already mention skills and spell interactivity that no other game has rivaled except maybe divinity original sin.
if you are looking for a turn based RPG with amazing combat and class system, on top of awesome groovy soundtrack this game is for you.

If you like Divinity series or Final Fantasy Tactics, you'll like this.
Pixel art graphics look dated, but under the hood this game is a ton of fun.
Tactical fights, like X-com with magic and swords, are done well and progress nicely in difficulty. Your ability to control your guys makes all the difference. You're not just watching stacks of hitpoints go down. There's a lot of interplay in the skills your guys learn, and how and when they use them.
The game lets you explore far and wide, so you can find encounters that really challenge you.
The puzzles are engaging in the intuitive way. They ramp up over time, and the same bits and pieces are used by the crafting system. There's a lot of 'aha!' moments. Without spoiling anything, they use common sense a lot.
Character progression is deep and fun. I was worried that I mis-created my party, when they didn't start out with the classes I wanted, but class-switching is effortless and you can't make a mistake. All XP is useful. Advanced classes require many beginner classes so if your warrior started as a scout, no big deal, that scout xp will come in handy later. This is very valuable, you can't screw yourself with a bad decision - at least early on - it might be different in late game, but I'm not there yet.
Crafting reminds me a lot of divinity, where you combine objects in mostly obvious ways to make new things out of them.
Those empty bottles at the beginning are useful. But don't buy them yet. When you find them, save them for later.
So now onto my 3-star rating system.
Does it have elves? No.
Does it have swords? Hell yes. Swords are very well done in this game.
Does it have pvp? No. It's a single player game.

Hello, here is my review for Voidspire Tactics.
Very nice little tactical rpg in the vain of final fantasy tactics. I enjoyed the time with the game.
Nice grafics rpgmaker niveau with custom made tilesets, excellent music and workable sound effects. There is no voice acting.
The difficulty is quite challenging on normal difficulty, but you can grind your way to victory. If you do not it is quite difficult. You get xp for killing monsters and invest them into classes and new skills on the fly, there is no level up, you only invest your earned xp into the skills, the prices get more expensive the higher the skill is. Gameplay is turnbased with initiative. The exploration is open world like, from the central area you can explore the spire as you like. The exploration part of the game is quite good, there are many secrets to be found in the enviroment. Many items in the enviroment can be manipulated or searched. You get lore entries for everything you find. The first contact with the world gave me a little oldschool ultima vipe, but it is not that deep. There are many tiers of items available, the power progression is more incremental.
My first playthrough without grinding is like 15 hours. It can be shorter if you know what you are doing.
Very nice game for fans of tactical Jrpgs or rpgs in general.
Thanks for reading, have a nice day.

Now, on to the inevitable Terraria comparison. So similar on the outside, yet completely different on the inside. IMO, Terraria is like this huge, massive NES game that never was. While Starbound is like an equally massive SNES or Genisis game. From the look and feel of the game, to the soundtrack and effects, to me, personally, Starbound feels a lot more polished and packaged. (Not to mention it doesn't crash all the freaking time, but I try not to hold that against Terraria.) That's not to say it is definitively a better game, they are so different that they might as well be at opposite ends of this Genre. (Whatever the survival/mining/crafting/building/exploration/metroidvania/genre is....)

I've seen people say the combat is better in Terraria... meh. Minute to minute, Starbound feels a lot better to me. With better animations, dual wielding, and actually targeted attacks (oh no, the mob is one block lower than me, I'm gonna die!!!! <-- Terraria). While Terraria has it's boss fights over Starbound, and they are actually scattered throughout the world, vs Starbounds story mission only bosses, but meh. Terraria's bosses still feel more like you are just trying to out tank them and hit them with the biggest wepon you have. But take that from someone who always cared more about regular gameplay than the bosses anyway.

Also, Terraria is just a sandbox. Starbound is a world (many of them, in fact) with NPCs, Towns, cities and Lore with multiple races. The 'Dungeons" feel a lot more realistically layed out, with varying rooms and coridoors, as opposed to 'tunnels' and randomly placed, perfectly rectangular rooms scattered around the underworld. Terraria end game, you pretty much have to build a skyway or subway, and a hellevator if you don't want to spend a ridiculous amount of time traveling. Or you create multiple small worlds, and try to keep track of them (small worlds never have as much stuff in them, obviously.) Starbound you can mark anywhere to teleport to, even in another star system, and easily explore as many or as few worlds at a time as you want.

There IS a difference at race selection, in spite of many claims to the contrary. Somewhat minor, but your scan tool (ala Metroid prime) features inner thought explanations of nearly every item in the game, which differ depending on your race. There is a definite immersion factor in exploring a world/town as a Glitch or Apex, that you are seeing the universe through their eyes. And NPC reactions do change depending on your race. I'm not even sure what other things people expect race selection to do.

I wondered why this game didn't have "Overwhelmingly Positive" rating, and saw a bunch of complaints about how the developer came to their house and murdered their kittens. Or, apparently, how they tested and removed experimental features that the devs feel didn't work. Remember how I said this game feels a lot more polished than Terraria? Yeah, that's probably why. I applaud the Devs for trying new things, and for removing them if they didn't fit their vision for the game.

On its own, this game could be "passable." But as an Ace Combat game, it's nothing but disappointing.
Yes, it fits well under the guise of "Call of Duty in planes" and that's what's wrong with it. Combat and missions are repetitive, the story is as cut-and-paste as it gets (OMG the Russians have a superweapon... again. 'Murica to the rescue!) and pretty much everything that made the old Ace Combat games great have been removed (New Game Plus, wingmate commands, plane EXP to unlock jets, etc.).
Ace Combat used to take place in a distinct world that resembled our own but had unique lore. This time around they chose real-world locations so instead the story world is filled with boring real-world characters and a boring real-world story - Just like Call of Duty!
Dogfight mode is a new on-rails addition that makes you semi-cinematically chase after and shoot down more skilled pilots that, simply because the game doesn't want you to, can't be shot down by conventional methods. A successful hit rips apart the enemy jet and leaves your plane splattered with oil and shrapnel and looks cool... the first few times you do it. After about mission 4 when you realize you have to do this A LOT in EVERY MISSION it gets old real fast - just like Call of Duty!
Thankfully, the campaign's missions in planes are intermittently broken up by missions where you either pilot a helicopter, man the turret on a helicopter, or man the guns of a gunship. Oh, and there's one where you fly a bomber. Problem is, the control schemes were not optimized very well at all compared to when flying a fighter jet. The bombers handle like beluga swimming through jelly, and to add insult to injury they make you basically do an obstacle course in that aircraft for the one mission you get to fly it. Meanwhile the helicopters can maneuver decently but for whatever reason can't rotate left or right while precision aiming at targets, so you're left with no choice but to fire randomly while strafing. Also for some reason they think helicopters can barrel-rol without their propeller blades ripping into each other. And, of course, turret sections are, well, turret sections that add nothing to the story and are effetively action-packed story padding - just like Call of Duty!
Oh, and there's a mulitplayer feature. But with how late this game's PC port was to the party, and the fact that it used to use GFWL, there's basically no one online.
TL;DR: Bottom line, the trailer shows you pretty much everything the game has to offer. If that's what you like, then by all measn enjoy. But if you're a fan of previous Ace Combat titles like me, steer clear and wait for either a PC port of Ace Combat Infinity or for Namco-Bandai to finish milking Dark Souls so they can come back to this franchise. GET IT ON SALE, DO NOT BUY FULL PRICE.

This was probably one of the most painful action games I've struggled through. The first struggle I had was buying this game when it still had GFWL included which is probably why I never bothered to finish it until recently. Thankfully that intrusive DRM has been removed and the game is now exclusively Steam based with achievements. The second struggle was painfully getting through the almost infinite number of enemies during each mission.
Now all the mission objectives in this game are great and fun. I loved the story and the gameplay is easy to enjoy. The variety of jets and bombers available to fly is also satisfying. The biggest issue for me was the sheer number of enemies during each mission. It made each mission feel excessively long and excessively repetitive. The fact that it takes multiple missiles to kill each enemy didn't help matters either. I get the arcadeness of the game and that aspect actually made it more enjoyable over a realistic flight simulator. But enemy after enemy after enemy after enemy after enemy...you get the point. There is a moment during each mission where I found myself asking, "Good Lord, when is this going to end?"
Ok so that is pretty much all I didn't like. That aspect left some battle wounds and those scars will likely never fully heal, but I loved the game overall. The story is excellent. There are a wonderful assortment of mission types and objectives and it is generally a fun game to play.
