This is a great game. I've spent hours of my life playing this game alone or with friends. Whether exploring, questing, crafting or fighting a boss, I always go back to Starbound at some point. The co-op is good, sound design is good, graphics are pixelated but not in an overused minecraft way, the gamplay is smooth, and while it is mostly a "hack-'n-slash" the combat system is there. The bosses are challenging, but not so hard that you want to throw your computer out of the window because you can't get past the first boss. What this game does really well is progression. At the start of the game, you feel kind of helpless, and monsters can do quite a bit of damage to you if you're not careful. This, compared with late game, where you can kill those same monsters in one hit, and take 0.01 damage from them, really makes you feel like you have progressed and become better at the game. Not to mention, the setting. Space! Who doesn't like a game where you have your own ship and can fly to entirely different galaxies in the push of a button? The planet types are extremely varied, from sizzling hot magma planets, to bitterly cold tundra worlds, Starbound always seems to have something new to offer. Overall, Starbound is an amazing game, and although the story is lacking a little bit, the lore is rich, and the developers have put so much time into creating their universe's backstory through codex's and strange places scattered among the stars. Starbound is truly a great game.
And for the record, Starbound is definitively better than Terraria.

Greetings!  At its core Particle Fleet: Emergence is a simple game; sort of like playing against a virus.  You slowly capture territory and build ships while the enemy spreads out in all direction with an endless supply of particles (duh).  You will spend a good deal of time overwhelmed and barely holding on but this is part of the charm of the game.
Difficult but Fair:  I almost consider this game a ‘souls-like’ game, the difficulty can be high but it is far and you will need to repeat some levels to adapt and understand the best approach.  Some tactics that work wonders on one level will be useless at another.  You have to evaluate your location, land mass, energy mines and the way your opponent is coming at you.  This ends in a satisfying victory when you do finally accomplish it and doesn’t take too long to pick up and put down.
Simple and effective:  Every bit of this game is efficient and effective, no, the graphics aren’t award winning but they accomplish the game’s purpose and I’d argue that better graphics could ruin the game.  The music is amazing and although it would be nice to have a bit more I love the score that is in this game.  Mechanics are solid and so are the controls; overall just no real complaints.
So, what’s bad:  I can’t really say that I have any part of this game I dislike?  Well, now that I think about it sometimes you get a point where the game is yours but it is going to take another 5-10 minutes to slowly make your way to victory.  This can be a bit boring at times but I don’t really see a way around it.  Overall, I love this game, especially for its price.  The story could be better but wasn’t really expecting anything on this front.
All in all, if you like tactical games, especially those that are easy to pick up and a decent difficulty to ensure a satisfactory victory (or defeat) get this game.  It is well worth the play through and if you are like me you will find yourself picking it up from time to time.  Enjoy!

An unenthusiastic yes. I bought this game because I spent a significant amount of time with Creeper World 3 and enjoyed the gameplay and story. It took me a while before I decided to, however; the game didn't look that great. The gameplay is similar to CW3, but with obvious significant differences, and that gave me pause.
Ultimately I tried it, and enjoyed the game, and then... it was done. There's very little game to this game. I blew through the 'campaign' very quickly, and the other whatever you want to call it that looks like a campaign but isn't, but while I'm still working through the hundreds of additional levels in CW3 I've completed this one in a day or two.
Sure, you can design your own block-by-block ships, but the campaign does a good job of giving you the ships you need when you get them, so unless you design similar ships, good luck to you.
And that's the sad thing: there's no easy way to use your own ships in a game to test them out. Randomly generate a level and it gives you a selection menu to pick from the real ships only. Launch the game, and then you can set the game mode to sandbox and pick your own ships.... but only after clearing the default loadout and manually adding your ships one by one, and don't click the wrong place or you'll be dragging ships back in order constantly afterwards.
The game favors making your own ships and maps, and you -can- download maps to play made by other players, but I've had more crashes than completed games that way, and it's not like CW3 where exiting gives you an auto-save. Prepare to lose progress.
Ultimately I'm disappointed. I liked going through the premade material, but that's where the game dies for me, and it's not really worth the price I paid.

This is Assault Horizon, NOT an Ace Combat game.
This is 60 FPS Arcade Aerial Combat at its finest.
Assault Horizon is a very under-rated videogame that was shunned by it's Ace Combat fanbase, worth it solely for the multiplayer experience.
This was an experiment by Project Aces to solve the QAAM Spam from Ace Combat 6's Multiplayer.
The game is niche, and Ace Combat players hate it for the DFM mechanic. I don't fault the Ace Combat players in that anything hurting their precious singleplayer experience is to be hated on immediately, but I can't blame them because DFM is so forced in the game that it hurts the overall feel of the game, but all you need is 1 playthrough. 3 max if you're 100%ing the game.
If you're new to the game you'll see that the DFM mechanic is very forced in singleplayer, this is to prepare you for the main bread and butter of the game; Multiplayer. It's what Assault Horizon was built around, and it's a fine tuned experience.
Unfortunately Multiplayer is deadish, only very few hardcore dedicated fans stick around, and the community is very small bringing in under 150ish aces platform wide, with about 15 of them being top tier, and about 5 out of that tier being active.
I'd aliken AH to Quake in that skilled players online will dance circles around newbies, nobody wants to play when your only opponent is a guy that can beat you blindfolded, right? It's a game that's rewarding to master, and it shows.
If you're looking to achievement hunt this game, get it and download a 100% save, then flesh out your achievements.
If you're looking to buy this and play singleplayer hoping for JETS and AWESOMENESS, then pass it up. You'd be better watching a Youtube Let's play of it. Trust me, you're not losing much by missing out.
If you want to play a 60 FPS arcade jetfighter game with some hard-core veterans, then download it and pop me a friend request. I'd be more than happy to play with you.

I love the Ace Combat series, it has always been a good blend between sim and arcade. I feel this latest iteration the series has leaned much more towards arcade. My biggest complaint is toward the dog-fighting mechanic. Yes, it makes for great cinematic but it is often too difficult to really see what is going on and the controls only makes it worse. I have tried playing with a controller and flight stick, neither feel great for this game.
Typically I would just ignore this “feature” altogether, however, you can't. The game forces you into these cinematic dogs fights and certain enemies cannot be shot down unless in dog-fighting mode. The entire thing just feels “off” to me in a modern aerial combat. Don't get me wrong, I don't love the Ace Combat series for it's realism, I love it for it uniqueness and story. I loved the crazy and sometimes frustrating boss battles. I love the characters and stories it told. The game could be dull at times but I enjoyed just flying around. Unfortunately, in their attempt to make something new and interesting, to me, it just feels like a series of gimmicks.

This game is quite a collection of terrible design decisions. First, there is no first-person perspective in a game that involves shooting. Also, you cannot fire a gun unless you first hold down the RMB to aim, which does weird things to the camera. The bizarre perspective changes that result from trying to use a gun in this game may cause motion sickness. During melee combat your character's "finishing move" sometimes causes  random teleportation. The melee combat system is almost workable despite that, but this game also includes "endurance" as a character stat, which is set to "couch potato" by default. You can swing a weapon only four or five times before needing a nap, and your character is helpless while your endurance slowly recovers.
The character's AI is abysmally bad. Most characters in this game are not NPCs, they are playable characters once you get them back to your base. The problem is that the characters not currently being played are helpless imbeciles. Sometimes they run right into hordes, sometimes into infestations, sometimes into special zombies. They are also unblievably bad at fighting, and sometimes do absolutely nothing to defend themselves, which often results in their deaths.
Another thing that often results in character deaths is that zombies will literally spawn next to you in large numbers. They will appear out of thin air in groups already almost close enough to grab you. I did not read that this game included ninja zombies, guess that's a bonus. Since you only have enough "endurance" for a few swings and guns are unusable in close quarters, when that happens your character is guaranteed a quick death.
This game's save system is bizarre and broken. It tells you that there is no quick save function, letting you know right off the bat that the devs couldn't be bother to create a save system that actually works. The game attempts to save your progress after you complete a mission, but nothing is like you left it when you go back to the game later. Vehicles are moved around or missing, supplies in your base are different, characters may be missing. I do not know what logic is behind the save game function in this game, nor do I care. The save game function must save the state of the game exactly as I leave it, anything other than that is not acceptable. Every character, every piece of equipment, every vehicle, every mission's progress must be saved exactly as it is when I quit playing or the system is broken.
The final nail in the coffin was the game's requirement that the player beat on their keyboard. If you are grabbed, the game prompts you to "tap c repeatedly.." The game mechanic that requires a player to rapidly hit a key is a terrible idea, has always been a terrible idea and always lowers the quality of a game that includes it. I absolutely will NOT beat on my keyboard like a chimp with epilepsy for any game, ever.

I bought this game along with the Breakdown DLC for 15 euros (give or take), after watching a few gameplay videos on Youtube. As a result, I've spent over 150 hours playing SoD so far, and I suspect I'll keep coming back for more at every chance.
So, here's what SoD is:
The story begins shortly after the zombie outbreak, and you need to group up with other survivors in an effort to...survive (strength in numbers and all that). No long backstories and explanations, no pseudo-scientific mumbo-jumbo. It just happened, and those responsible are obviously in no position to stop it. And neither are you.
The location is an idyllic valley, somewhere in the US, which is open for you to explore as you prefer. The landscape is very well designed, and features 3 separate settlements/towns with all sorts of areas in-between them. Farms, lakes, rivers, cliffs, you name it. All of them dotted with sites of interest that you can search for supplies, materials, or other survivors to recruit or assist.
As for the characters, there's a lot of them, and each one comes with different skills and traits. The 4 basic skills are common for all, and determine their amount of stamina, their stealth/scavenging performance, and finally their melee and ranged fighting ability. The more you use them, the more these skills level up (just like in the Elder Scrolls series). And then, there's all sorts of crazy extra skills! Some will add to your fighting efficiency, even by adding moves or abilities when leveled up. Others are only beneficial if your base includes a corresponding facility that would require them. Some affect the group's mentality, and some are utterly useless in post-apocalyptia!
There's really a lot to say about the characters, especially about the mechanics that drive their relationships and mood swings, which can make or break a situation, mainly in the beginning, when you don't know how to handle them. And, even when you do, the various random events that happen in your absence, or simply a mission gone wrong, may be enough cause for a survivor to blow his own brains instead of waiting for the undead to do it.
And speaking of death, it's permanent (permadeath, as it's often called). The game autosaves whenever you do something (or something's done to you), so prepare for moments of grief and shock when a beloved hero is literally torn apart in front of your eyes. I'd never experienced it in a game before, and took me quite a while to get used to it. Makes you think twice before firing without a silencer attached.
While fights feel very different than those of -for example- Dead Rising, they are frantic and very entertaining. Animation-wise, it's all I could ask for and more. Especially in melee, you can feel the impact of each strike, the finishing moves are great to look at, and it's very rewarding to beat the odds in almost choreographic ways. Not that gunning down the zombies, blowing them up, burning them, or running them over isn't satisfactory, but since both ammo and vehicles are not infinite, they must be used sparingly, if at all in some cases.
You will have the chance to see a bit of everything in the game's story mode, which is fairly simple and short, but it's the Breakdown DLC which pushes you to new limits. In Breakdown, your objective is to find an RV (a large vehicle), repair it, select 6 survivors, and move on. You can do this at your own pace, as it's more of a sandbox mode. However, when you choose to leave the valley, what happens is that the map resets, and you're starting over. You need to re-establish a base and scavenge for some supplies, but this time amidst a larger and stronger zombie population.
I left the visual part for the end, as I'm sure you've seen enough footage by now. The textures and anti-aliasing leave enough to be desired, and as a PC user I feel that the developers could, and should have gone the extra mile to upgrade these aspects accordingly. I believe SoD was developed with the Xbox in mind, but I cannot see that as an excuse. Fortunately, the game runs flawlessly, there are no fps drops, no bottlenecks, and the art direction makes up for a lot of the technical shortcomings. The flashlight's a little "funky", and, surprisingly enough, only the character you control will have one. Makes for some harder-than-they-need-to-be night fights.
Audio functions wonderfully, with great sound design which provides all the cues and warnings you need at every given time. I can't say much about the music score though, as it's been months since I muted the game's music in favor of my own.
There's plenty more I'd like to write about, but these are more or less my impressions after playing SoD for this long. I definitely recommend it, and I hope you'll have as much fun as I had -and still having- if you get to play it. :)

There may be a few problems, but overall, this is literally the best game to ever be made. And no, that's not an exaggeration.

Quick review since I'm going through the trilogy just to finally give my thoughts on it.
Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition is a very truthful title for a game. You'll die a lot. Many being utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, many being your fault or you missed a dodge, and the rest being because you misjudged a height.
Arguably the magnum opus of Miyazaki and From Software as a whole, Dark Souls deserves most of the praise it gets.
I'll be looking at this game as its own, without looking at what DS2 and 3 do better than it or worse.
Pros:
+ Unique style of gameplay that is extremely engaging
+ The setting, atmosphere and layout of the world. The world is connected perfectly and feels like it was planned from the start.
+ Story is quite simple and decently done and has quite a good amount of lore behind it
+ Designs of characters, enemies, etc are all done well, capturing a great dark fantasy look
+ A good amount of the bosses are well done, such as Artorias, Manus, Ornstein & Smough, Four Kings, and the final boss to name some.
+ Music is quite unique and does things almost every other game fails to capture. Has what is honestly the best final boss theme in any video game.
+ Many characters are quite well done and have interesting storylines.
Cons:
- Many of the bosses are extremely poorly done and lazy, such as Ceaseless Discharge, Asylum Demon and its two copies, the ♥♥♥♥ing BED OF CHAOS, Nito's gankfest, etc.
- The level design, mostly the latter, can be absolutely horrible. Lost Izalith/Demon Ruins is a painful eyesore, the Crystal Cave is a major annoyance, Blighttown is ♥♥♥♥ing Blighttown, and Tomb of the Giants is a massive pain. These levels are challenging without any fun to it.
- Very limiting when it comes to builds and whatnot. No form of respec unless you cheat, the odd endurance weights, and the fact that if you aren't fast rolling you're asking for your deaths.
- A ♥♥♥♥ing horrible PC port. DSFix doesn't fix everything (at least not for me, dropped to 30-40 fps in many places) and From saying "people wanted it on PC so we gave it to them!" is such a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ excuse.
- Has aged quite poorly in some aspects. Animations are poor, some delayed controls, character faces are pretty ugly, but armor and weapons manage to still look good both model and texture wise.
All I could think of as of right now. Overall a pretty great game after looking past some small♥♥♥♥♥♥

Looking for a new twist on some classic arcade style dogfighting shoot-em-ups? Look no further than Luftrausers. This slick 8-bit style shooter can keep you entertained for a long time, whether you're trying to unlock every part and achievement or trying to up your highscore just that little bit more. Plane customization, finding that perfect combo of weapon, body, and engine for your play style also adds to the depth and replayability. And the music! Different combinations of parts also change up the soundtrack, all variations on a common theme. Many a times I had to fight the urge to break into goosesteping while rocking out to its tunes. You'll get a lot of bang for your buck in Luftrausers and well worth any price it’s at, sale or not.

Luftrausers is a game where you engage fighter planes over sea. Made by Devolver Digital and Vlambeer, it has a delicious arcade feel to it, meaning it can be played for 5 mins or 5 hrs, depending on the mood you may be in. Multiple enemy types to destroy, many leaving the player with a great feeling of satisfaction (I'm looking at you, battleships and blimps).
There are lots of different parts available to the player for the customization of their rauser. There are also many unlockable color palettes to choose from, which allow you to change up the flavor of your rausing here and there. The difficulty is perfectly scaling, increasing a little more with each kill, each passing second of your continued survival. The one big drawback I've found with this game is no multiplayer option. Even a local VS mode would help add so much more variety to this already immensly addicting game.
If you like techo/electro music with a sort of diesel influence, you will love the soundtrack of Luftrausers. It has a great selection of tracks which perfectly match up to the setting of your aireal combat. If you are looking for a mobile-esque timesink, look no further than LUFTRAUSERS!

Ok, this sandbox game, THIS sandbox game, THIS SANDBOX GAME, right here, if you are in to SANDBOX GAMES, this is it for you! The developer is doing an insane job with updates, and he is truly building an outstanding sandbox game *with an awesome mix of campaign/strategy gameplay* that just blew my mind away. I play minecraft, terraria, starbound, space engineers, etc etc, and this one took me from all of them. Absolutely awesome game, great updates on a routine basis, open minded developer, great player community, and a fun and interactive experience to keep you looking forward to playing when you get off work huzzah!!! I highly HIGHLY recommend it, big time kudo's to the dev.
*Adding notes*
Mk so, reading my review, I realized it doesn't really, give a great review. It's just me being like, super excited because I love the game. So i'm gonna go for a more 'in depth' approach to some things i've come to love and the things i enjoy but, don't love....yet >.>
First off, the pro's and cons.
Pro's
1 Great building interface, with 2 ways to build, keyboard and mouse. Both of which have their own pros/cons. It also boasts a significant variety of blocks making every creation truly unique in it's own way.
2 Sub assembly system - Ever build something on something else, and wish you could take that something off the something else, and put it on something else? Well, in this, you can. Say you make a kick♥♥♥♥♥turret on one ship hull, but realize the hull just wasn't the right style, and couldn't hang. Well, damn, you don't want to rebuild that turret all over so, you make the hull work, right? Wrong, you can save subassemblies so that when you build more ships later you can add the same things to them w/out having to do all the work to recreate the things that work
3 4 area's of combat *although space has been...interesting...follow up on that in the cons >.>* You can fight on land, sea, air, and yes, even space.
4 AI system for your creations to make your own fleet and evolving options to control the actions of your AI drones. I for example have my B-ship i control, with 4 fighters and a destroyer escort that are all AI controlled to escort my Big boat♥♥♥♥♥around. w00t w00t
5 Open minded and honest hard working dev team. Now as of now, the only 'dev' i know of, is Mr. Nick Smart. But he has been ON IT. I mean, I participate in alot of early access games. And this is the only one where the dev is constantly in the forums, posting on others and publishing his own, on a frequent basis. He is constant with updates, and is truly doing a phenominal job trying to keep the game in the direction his vision has for it.
6 Campaign system - ok this will be my last pro, as I don't want to bore anyone Ok so, the campaign, has some ups and downs of it's own. Upsides - harvest multiple resource zones, have multiple fleets, multiple battle fronts, simple interface to navigate around your fleets, simple dipolomacy panel to♥♥♥♥♥♥peeps off or make them like you, Pretty good map layout, difficult AI once you get about 1/2 across the map. Overall the campaign, I luv it. I know there are some things in the works so i'm going to list them in the cons section BUT, big disclaimer, they are already on nicks workload and I can't wait to see what he hits us with when he starts evolving them.
MK so, Cons. I'll be honest, not alot of huge game crippling things i have found. There are some nuisances but, the dev's actively working on them and, i'm not an impatient guy so, w00t w00t can't wait to see them fixed. Here they are
1 MP (creative) is a little buggy. The host is the only one who tends to see all the action going on in the map. For example, if a cannon has a prediction piece on it, and you are the client, you won't be able to see the line drawn to show where your round will go. YOu also can't see the power, speed, drag, so on so forth. Now, do'nt get me wrong, the client can still do everything the host can, but the downside is, he won't SEE everything he's doing. Creative is basically no resource costs, on the campaign map, where you and all connected players can just, build.
MP (AI fight) is a neat concept, but it can be hard finding games up unless you have buddies who have the game to get on at the same time. Basically, you build a ship with an AI interface. You load it against someone elses, and you both watch the ships fight to the death, with no involvement from you. It's great to do to see how your creations stack up against other players. Neat little game mode.
2 AI in campaign is, well, garbage >.> As in you can just flot over to a ship, SHOOT the AI mainframe, and walla you have a new ship. Now if you decide to not do that, it can get hard granted if you up the difficulty it does get pretty rough, BUT you have to have a high end machine to handle the big boys, and that means you may be annoyed with the scrub ships your stuck on depending on your gaming monster which takes me into
3 Frame rate can get pretty low when alot of stuff is going on. Another *disclaimer* is that nick is already working on moving to a different game engine, in order to improve this. But as of now, if you aren't sporting a hot rod, and your just cruising with a sedan, you may want to keep your block count a little low to keep from getting to choppy.
4 Getting to space *this might be restricted to just me* Now i have been having the hardest time getting a ship to leave orbit and actually get into space. The only way I have been able to get into space is to, well, build in space. I've been trying to build jets with ion thrusters that could leave the planet go to space and come back in, but i've had no success. Again, this could be a just me moment, but it shouldn't be that hard to leave orbit if you already have the engines to get you to max altitude in the first place. which rolls me into
5 the playable field, while awesome, is also kinda limited. Now it's cool because, you can really chew someone up and they can't get away from you b/c the deepest the water gets is like, 50 meters, and the air goes up as far as 500 meters, and your weapons can easily reach 1000 + meters. So, ya, they can't get away unless they just run, horizontally, str8 away from you. However, if your on the 'oh♥♥♥♥♥♥i gots to go' end of this, ya, it sucks. You have nothing going for you as the height/depth of the playable area is pretty small and therefore you have to just go for speed to run for your life.
The last 2 cons, are the only ones on my list that I honestly don't know if the dev is working on, and to be honest, if he didn't change it, i wouldn't be heart broken. B/c yeah, it sucks to not be able to go higher or lower in order to increase my survivability, but it has led me to make more interesting designs with a little more armor to take those hits. And the space thing, meh, i can get over that, i'll just keep building in space.
End of discussion Game review - Overall, i've been in 18 Early access games, and so far, this one and space engineers are the only 2 that truly paid off. This one is STILL in early access, but still is truly on point and moving forward at an amazing pace. Again, great dev, great gaming community, evolving game interface and AI systems make it a truly unique experience. Again, if you would like to play a sandbox game, and bring some idea's to the table, or just enjoy the game, this is a great pick. and hey, it'll be going in and out of sale frequently, so get it when it's cheap. I could easily see this game going for 40+ once it's finished. great game. If you happen to get it, by all means send me a message to do some building together, or to blow each other up, i'm always down for both!!

Have you ever designed a kick♥♥♥♥♥sailboat in Minecraft and wish you could take to the seas with it? Have you ever thought Kerbals were too peaceful? Have you ever wanted to design a plane that used cannons as a means of movement? Me neither, but in From the Depths, YOU CAN!
From the Depths is a sandbox physics game with some rts elements thrown in for good measure. Build a ship, watch it sink. Build a better ship, one that moves! ....Then watch it get blown up. Build a gun, then build a ship around it! This is, in essence, what FtD is all aboot.
In career mode you can take your designs and put them to the test. Capture resource nodes, battle pirates, and build your empire. Switch from game view to map view and position your fleet. Instead of rolling the dice when two ships meet, go back into physics mode and battle your enemy head on. You can manually control your vehicles and bases, or you can use the modular AI pieces and build an AI to do it for you.
Speaking of modular, this game features modular engines, cannons, lasers, missiles, etc. Instead of placing a gun block where you want a gun, you can build your cannon from many modules that altar how the gun works. Range, reload time, damage, armor penetration, explosive rounds, accuracy, etc.

Ah State of Decay, what an overlooked game and absolutely in the running to be my favorite game played in 2015. I honestly have no idea when or where I got this game, but I decided to give it a try over vacation and was instantly hooked.
I was expecting a generic zombie openworld survival game and the graphics and lighting effects were almost painful for long period of gaming. The first was quickly revealed to be only a tiny sliver of State of Decay while the latter was easily fixed with a shader mod from the Nexus. If anyone reading this has ever played with and enjoyed the Wasteland Defenders line of mods for Fallout 3 and Fallout New Vegas, stop reading this review and BUY State of Decay! Yes there are zombies, yes you hit them in the head with shovels and wrenches, but at the core State of Decay is much more about bringing together a group of survivors and managing resources and manpower to survive the zombie apocalypse. Scavenging is a primary advancing mechanic and you have to intelligently decide how to spend resources, balancing better functionality with the ever growing demands of your home.
As if the main game wasn’t awesome enough, the DLC Breakdown adds a never ending survival mode which in my opinion is the absolute best way to play the game. I have sunk a ridiculous amount of time into this game and I plan to sink many more hours.
As a last little note, the game has moments when you’ll think to yourself “wow what a glitchy mess” but I have never found them to be a deal breaker. The content is there and State of Decay is absolutely worth it.

So, all these zombie survival games coming out recently, I wanted to play SoD again.And I have to say, this is one of the greatest games I have played and I played A LOT of games.
State of Decay is a open world zombie survival game with a basic plot.You have a party of people that you can add people to or people from it can die which is pretty nice.At the beginning, there are some mandatory missions to discover the whole world but then, the game really opens up.
You can control any party members and there is this "trust" mechanic.If you bring resources into the HQ, you gain points that you can then use to get items from the base and interact with people.Game world is pretty large and nearly every building can be entered one way or another.
One of the best mechanics that are included in this game is, changing bases.You have a single home base and some little safe zones that you can create by clearing the zombies in it.Changing bases is really neat, you can relocate to gain tactical advantage or get closer to an area that you would like to invest more time in.The bases are upgradeable with a lot of stuff.
Weapons are what you would expect from a zombie game;mostly melee with a few firearms and explosives.Melee combat is pretty satisfying to say the least.Animations are done well though they can bug out sometimes.There are finishers and stealth kills included.By the way, there is a stealth mechanic and it works decently;it's not really deep but it serves it purpose fully.
There are drivable vehicles around the area and they control okay, pretty good for taking out hordes.Mentioning hordes, there are special zombies around, basically L4D specials.Kinda hard to kill but provides some diversity so it's ok
Now for my most hated point of the game;the performance.Since this was a XBL Arcade game before it was ported over to PC, it drops FPS sometimes, like when you are running through a horde.I have a really good gaming pc, so it's minimized but it can cause some problems on lower rigs.
Overall, it's gonna be a 8/10, 2 points gone for the performance and sometimes repetitive side missions.

I was very much a late adopter of Dark Souls, though it's definitely a game I wish I'd picked up years earlier. I know that it has an infamous reputation for being an incredibly challenging game, but what those people sometimes won't tell you is that it's also intensely rewarding. Dark Souls has an incredibly high skill ceiling and even after 240 hours playing it I still feel that I have much to learn about the more nuanced aspects of the game's mechanics. The online and offline experiences are so closely linked that I rarely find myself having to go out of my way to switch from one mode of play to the other. On the topic of the game's online elements, I personally believe that the fact that invasions and co-op are still fairly active speaks volumes about the game's quality. After all, it isn't just any old game that can retain a solid player base after 6 years and 2 sequels have passed.
To summarize, Dark Souls in an incredibly engaging, challenging and rewarding game. I have no reservations in saying that I'd recommend it wholehearted to not just fans of RPGs, but video games in general.

This is quite a weird game. There are certainly major issues: there's no mouseover help for much of the GUI, the GUI in general leaves much to be desired, new game elements are introduced too quickly (several each stage), the game itself is quite short, and the story not as good as Creeper World 3's, but in terms of weirdness there's something about this game that I liked.
Perhaps it's just that nothing is really explained, there's a bunch of random jargon like redacted space that is never really cleared up, and most of the time that's annoying but here it's kind of superb in its relentlessness. In some ways confusion is the highest state of mind, because confusion creates and precedes curiosity, which creates and precedes knowledge. So, in effect, games that confuse the mind are the greatest games of all, and this game is certainly confusing.
For instance, I beat the game, completed every story mission, and still feel like I don't know a thing about it. I can't even tell you if the game is well balanced or not because I often had no idea how I won, I was flying by the seat of my pants and I couldn't tell you what the difference between a Cruiser, a Destroyer, or a Joven ship is. I don't know if my strategy was any good, but my strategies did seem to eventually work, but they were probably nowhere near optimal. It's just a baffling, but interesting, game.
Basically I'd give it a recommendation if you enjoyed Creeper World 3 and if you want a game that's basically like that, but has a less interesting story, but instead has much stranger and more confusing gameplay. If you haven't yet played that game by the same developer, do that first.

"Ace Combat is finally on the PC!!" Is probably what you're thinking when you see this right? Well unfortunately, this isn't the Ace Combat game anyone wanted on PC. Why is that you ask? Well if you've played any AC game pre-AH, then you already know the answer. If you haven't, then allow me to explain why.
DFM is a feature that's supposedly the game's main selling point, which turns the game into an on rails shooter. It's activated when the L and R bumpers are pressed (playing on a 360 controller) when you're in close proximity of an enemy aircraft (green circle flashing). DFM is completely optional to use, except when combating lead targets. Lead targets requires the use of DFM as they're nearly impossible to shoot down without it; even with the CFA-44's EML cannon (OP weapon, more so in AC6).
Strangereal is the main setting of all the AC games pre-AH. In layman's terms, it's a world with fictitious nations based on their real world equivalents. A lot of people liked the idea of dogfighting in a place that isn't the same ol' boring real world Earth setting. The same people absolutely hated the change of scenery to a real world setting for this game.
The abridged version: NATO task force vs a separatist Russian movement armed with a stockpile of bombs with the yield of a nuclear bomb (only they're not). Lamentable, derivative, and boring as some people would say.
Any of the UH-60 Blackhawk door gunner escort missions, the AC-130 gunner mission, and the Heli gunship missions.
The game itself is absolutely gorgeous. Everything from the environments to the planes themselves. The only downside is that the graphics options are severely limited to AA, Vsync, and resolution. But the sight of an enemy plane exploding into pieces with copious amounts of oil splashing everywhere never gets old. Oh, and the occasional pilot falling out of the cockpit too.
Despite being heavily reliant on DFM, the game itself is actually really fun to play. Just remember to change the control scheme from optimal to classic. Because on optimal, you can't roll your plane.
There is a wide variety of planes to choose from in Assault Horizon; fighters, multirole craft, and even bombers believe it or not. Each and every plane has their own special paint schemes; some are unlocked at the start, some are unlocked when you finish the game, and all are customizable. Oh, and there are Idolmaster themed jets (returns from AC6) as well because Namco.
It's not the best Ace Combat game available, but it's worth playing at least once. So yes, I recommend you try it for yourselves.
Addendum: If you plan on buying this for the multiplayer, then DON'T. Multiplayer for the most part is a graveyard.

This game reminds me how much I don't like the Recommend\Don't Recommend system of Steam. This is one of the sad cases where I actually enjoyed a game, quiet a lot even, but am still aware that it isn't much good and is actually not a game to recommend to anyone.
I'll start by stating that I didn't play any other installment of Ace Combat and therefore I don't look at this game as a fan of the series, but simply gave this specific installment a try. I'm also not too experienced with flight games in general.
Horizon Assault is a very arcadic game in almost every sense of the word.
The story is, as you'd expect from this type of games, very predictable, generic, unsurprising, and not that vital for the game.
For a moment the game may seem like a flight simulator but it's definitely not, It's good at making you feel AS IF you're flying an aircraft, AS IF you're doing big stuff with the scripted explosions everywhere.
And that's actually one of the strong points of the game, it's very good with BOOMING stuff, with making you feel that YOU are booming stuff, and it gives you an addicting sense of action and thrill, although with completely unrealistic mechanics at times (e.g. aircraft "heals" itself automatically while flying), but who cares, it's a video game.
The game's soundtrack also adds a LOT to the game, and as one who really cares about music in video games and is giving it a lot of attention, this game has one of the best tracks in video game soundtracks, in my opinion, with a combination of symphonic music with some electronic\rock touches every once in a while. Splendid, really!
Unfortunately there are also reasons for you to stay away from Horizon Assault. Controls aren't most comfortable ever… Binding different keys won't help much. It can get confusing at times and at the beginning of the game I felt like quitting because I simply couldn't get hold of this DAMN helicopter. As soon as I got the hang of it, it started to get fun, though, but fun it really different and is a matter of perspective. And many people won't find this game fun at all.
The gameplay can get extremely repetitive and frustrating. The developers tried to keep it varied and in a way they succeeded in it, but it's still starting to feel generic and monotonous at times. Another thing which many people would hate is the Dog-Fight System, which is presented as an optional way to hunt your enemies but is actually your only way of getting through this game. And it can be horribly frustrating as well.
So, are you going to enjoy this game? That's really a matter of one's taste and expectations.
I enjoyed it, mostly, and if you can enjoy some intense action sequences with things getting blown away with dramatic music in the background and some clichéd "saving America" story, it's possible you'd enjoy this as well.
It's possible you'd hate it, if that's not your kind …
Another note, out of the three times I've tried playing this game in multiplayer mode, I've managed to find other players to play with only once. So, my guess is that the multiplayer scene of Horizon Assault isn't very active. There's also no way to play over LAN, so, I could be wrong but I believe Horizon Assault pretty much leaves you with solely the single player missions. You should keep that in mind.
You can get some limited fun out of the game but is it really worth it? No unfortunately

This is an open world zombie survival game in which you take care of a community of survivors in hopes of surviving the pandemic.
In your community you have strength in numbers so you'll want more people but with more people you need more supplies to take care of them so you'll need to go scavenging for said supplies looking in whatever places to find the ones you need. All item drops are random, as you can find a shotgun in a house one time and in another play through you find a flare, and once the items placed around the world thats is, no more items spawn unless you reset.
Each person you bring into your community is playable after you become friends and each one has their own set of skills that you can train up such as small guns or large guns, unarmed combat or using blunt weapons, it all depends on each person.
The zombies are pretty simple in that they only want to kill humans and will follow loud sounds such as cars, gunshots, running, then there is the special zombies, some are easy to kill such as the bloaters or the swat zombies, and some not so much like the tank zombies or the ferals, they all can be killed in diffrent ways (mostly by car).
The game has a story line and it's all about you surviving and trying to get out of the town you are stuck in, along the way you get to meet some new people which won't become part of your community but will help you in diffrent ways such as givving you cover fire, droping off a new car, all at the cost of influence, thats the money of the game, you help people out and they will be more open to help you.
Something to note is the game plays while you are away, by that I mean when you turn off the game it takes remembers when you turned it off and the next time you turn it back on the game translates that into game time so it will take/give you items based on if the other people in your community went on supply runs or not, the largest jumps for this is 3 IRL days, after that it cuts it by a large amount.
There is plenty of missions you can do but after awhile it gets a bit dull having to go after yet another swat zombie or another supply run.
PROS
Open world.
Zombie survival.
World changes at all times.
CONS
Short story.
Lack of diversity in missions.
Doesn't explain the time jumps well.
All in all this game is an awesome game that you should check out if you enjoy zombie games or open world games.

My second foray into a Souls game, and I'm at odds with myself over which I prefer - DS2:SotFS, or DS:PtD.
Souls games have rich stories and environments to explore and interact with. You are always aware that you are a small being in a place that doesn't really care for you; the lands have enough problems of their own. There is a notion that the Souls games are particularly difficult - if you are cautious, if you have played a tabletop RPG with someone who likes Gygaxian traps, if you understand that you're not all-powerful and magnificent, then you can quite happily get through these games. Deaths in the game teach you a lesson; except for when they don't. The only cheap deaths I encountered in my playthrough were due to glitches and getting stuck in walls.
As a port, this is shoddy. When I first bought the game, there was no controller support. I played for half an hour, then left it alone for years. I decided to check it out on a whim, as I figured I could just configure my Steam controller to sort it out, and was glad to see Xbox 360 gamepad support. I started a new game, and heard my computer fan screaming - if you buy this game, you will have to do a tiny bit of work to get it running. The fixes are in the community guides, and they're easy to implement, which makes it disappointing that the publisher hasn't patched it in already.
In comparing DS1 and DS2, I found that DS2 was much easier to pick up. The leveling system, tooltips, and tutorial are all better than DS1. I was much much more into the story of DS1 though. DS2 did not have the full direction of Hidetaka Miyazaki that DS1 has, and it is quite evident in the art of the storytelling and worldbuilding.
Some parts of DS1 feel rushed - there are enemies reused from earlier sections (which are essentially reskins), the areas feel more on rails, and there are little touches here and there where you understand that the studio was under pressure from their publisher to finish the game early. But overall this does not impact upon the enjoyment of the game.
It took me about 50 hours to go through both the main game and included DLC. I went through at a slow pace, taking time to enjoy everything, and did not use a guide - I wanted everything to be fresh, and to avoid spoilers.
Sadly, due to the game being older than others in the series, there was absolutely no interaction with other players. I personally didn't mind this, but I do not count my experience as being holistic.
I absolutely recommend this game - but do I recommend this one, or Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin?
If you are new to these games, then DS2: Scholar of the First Sin should be the first port of call - it'll set you up with the tools necessary to get through DS1, and the narrative of DS1 will become that much richer for having gone through DS2 in the first instance. SotFS has more of an active playerbase, so you'll get to have more fun with the PvP and Coop aspects.
But wow, the story of Dark Souls, of Lordran and its characters, it kept me invested until the very end. I was sad to finish the game, even though there is replay value (your character is carried over into a new game, and there is a spike in the difficulty). Going to go and sit and enjoy the memories captured in my screenshots before I turn hollow.

As note before reading this review, I have completed all 3 games in the series so there will be references to the other two.
Dark Souls as a series is a well crafted series although it's steep learning curve often times drives away the audience. I was able to overcome this learning curve and found the real charm of the series. If you can run it, I recommend get the DSFix mod for this game, it gives more framerate and makes the game more enjoyable in my opinion. It has its bugs, but what games and mods don't? Now, some things about the game. The game has a lot to offer in terms of gameplay. It centers around survivability, difficulty, and exploration. These all come together with its mostly polished game mechanics to create a well made game. Yes, I understand the game is annoying and quite hard, but it is not impossible. The point is to give you a sense of satisfaction when you overcome a difficult situation. Some people start at out good at the game, others like me have to take a while to truly learn. Eventually though, everyone creates their own style in how they play the game and weapons, items, and armor allow for many play styles. Keep in mind when you play this though, this was the first game in the series. With that being said, I think it shows as there were situations in which things could have been better thought out but are forgivable in my opinion. Please do not misconstrue my critique for hatred. Yes, there were many times where I was very mad at the game but it was a new type of game and they couldn't get user feedback until it was fully released. The two games that followed this one each tried to rework how the series worked. It's hard to find a perfect balance on the gameplay so that it is most enjoyable. Like the others, it includes: decent graphics, polished mechanics, optional areas and endings, side quests, replayability, good audio/music, exploration, risks & rewards, and DLC (they are harder than the main game areas). One thing in particular that I like is that you are never truly helpless. There are times where you get put in situations where you can't get out of them and you die for some stupid reason, but you are the core reason they happened. They give you the necessary items, you just have to learn how everything works and adjust to it. The important thing is that you keep learning, that is the key to mastering the game. Another thing that I particularly like in the series is the parry system. You can counter attacks instead of blocking or running away. Not all shields allow this but if you can master this technique then it provides extra damage. It is one of those high risk, high reward situations that can be quite handy but also broken. SPOILER: You can parry the final boss and it is very broken as it makes him very easy to defeat. Now another thing I do and don't like in this game is that a couple bosses require you to die in order to progress the game. I think it is a neat thing about the bosses but honestly, it just makes it kind of annoying. That is the reason they took it out in the two following games. They learned from their mistakes and tried to redo things. Now with this being said, I think you should still give this game a chance if you want to play any of the three because each game has its own charm to it. None of the games are the same, they each differ in major and minor ways. As long as you persist in your playthrough, you should be fine. A lot of people give and like to say the game is too hard which is why you will hear so many hard things but honestly, it isn't that hard. It just takes time and patience to learn the game. Do not give up on the game, that is the biggest mistake you can make. I hope this review gives you a little insight on the the game and that it helps you choose to play it.

I really wasn't pleased with Thinking with Time Machine, not in the way that Portal 2 or other mods seemed to flow and satisfy me. It's free and relatively short, so it's only the large download to stop you, but I didn't enjoy the puzzles. This is definitely a mod, visually polished but still rough. Considering the developer has a sticky in the forums to remind players of the time machine controls, the tutorial clearly doesn't demonstrate the new mechanics and controls properly.
Most of the puzzles involved jumping on your time-traveler's back to reach things, recording yourself standing in place for awhile to open doors, and passing cubes to yourself through lasers. I expected more in line with a mod called Prometheus, which had multiple tasks to complete spread through the map. I also would've expected puzzles using portals, but it seems like half the maps don't allow any portals. None of the puzzles really made me think, as the main challenge was to execute the recordings and movements instead of solving puzzles. The story had be somewhat interested, but as soon as it was introduced, the mod was basically over.
If you are running low on puzzle games, give it a shot. I didn't feel it was worth my time, as I really didn't enjoy any of the puzzles.

Yorkshire Gubbins is a point-and-click adventure game clearly inspired by games made during the heyday of the genre in the mid-90s. Thankfully, the game eschews referential meta jokes about that era of gaming and instead uses the conventions and tropes of the genre to deliver a fun, charming (but short) experience. Retro-inspired games can often feel exploitative of nostalgia, but this is a straight revival and that appealed to me as a fan of the genre.
The game is really nice to look at. The "big pixel" art style used for the character sprites is reminiscent of the scaling artefacts seen in ScummVM or Sierra games, but remains expressive throughout. The sprites' idle animations and fancy shader effects help the world look alive and engaging.
Speaking of, this is a fully voiced game and the voice acting really adds a layer of cohesion to the game. It's possibly the single strongest element in YG. It's really good and a pleasure to listen to.
Story-wise, the game's episodes work well as self-contained units of silliness. There's the expected item retrieval quests and character distraction subplots, but there is no overarching plot or dramatic tension. This makes sense considering the game's two episodes and tutorial can be completed in one sitting but it might frustrate some players.
One aspect of Yorskhire Gubbins that feels limiting is the fact that all objects and characters are present on the same plane of depth. On the one hand, it means there's no pixel-hunting, but on the other it makes the world look flat and takes away from the sense of exploration. The game works around that limitation to deliver a fun experience, but it might become a problem for longer and more ambitious future episodes.
But really, the reason I'm writing this review is the setting. I didn't have the grace and foresight to be born an Englishman and, for that reason, I have no great familiarity with either Yorkshire itself or how it's depicted in British media.
I was a bit apprehensive that the game would rely heavily on regional stereotypes and tropes to get its laughs and that these would woosh over my head.
Having played the game, I'm very pleased to report that this isn't the case. Yorkshire is to the game what the fantasy genre and sci-fi are to Simon the Sorcerer and the Space Quest games, respectively. It's the substrate on which the game's humour grows - but it's not itself the joke.

Yorkshire Gubbins is the debut Steam title from developers Stairfall Institute, published by Green Mesa Ltd.
In Yorkshire Gubbins -- what there is of it so far, anyway -- you control Steggy, a lass from Yorkshire with a penchant for droll comments and an affinity for pie making. In the introductory episode a robot introduces both you and Steggy to the workings of the game's interface in Verb School, and at the bargain price of only 20p, too!
The game proper begins after that, with the episode called Humble Pie. This sees Steggy foiled in the last stages of preparing her entry for the Yorkshire Pie Competition when she finds a serious problem with a key pie ingredient: her Special Meat is in fact only normal meat in a Special Meat wrapper.
Pixelated point-and-click hilarity ensues as you guide Steggy through various encounters and simple inventory puzzles in search of some real Special Meat, and a chance at pie greatness.
The graphics in Yorkshire Gubbins are chunky pixel graphics. They're really chunky: too chunky to really enjoy in full-screen at HD resolutions, and much more chunky even than something like Lucasarts' The Secret of Monkey Island (the original), from the 1990s.
The game only includes a small number of characters and locations. Locations are somewhat bland -- but then again, the game is set in a town in Yorkshire! -- but the characters have all been infused with some personality. Each character has an idle animation, and in-game objects are drawn well enough to at least be recognisable.
The interface is extremely simple and SCUMM-like: a series of nine verbs, each of which can be applied to selectable objects on the screen. The cursor is a set of large white crosshairs and interactive objects or characters are indicated by partially formed sentences at the bottom of the screen, using the currently selected verb.
The game has minimal music, but what is included fits the game and setting perfectly and is well produced: simple ditties using only a couple of instruments. I don't recall any sound effects, but there may have been some.
The big appeal to the game's audio is the fully voiced dialogue, mostly consisting of Yorkshire accents. (I admit, I'm not familiar enough with Yorkshire accents to know if these are real, but they sound pretty convincing to me.) Every line of text in the game is spoken and the voices mostly sound professional and work extremely well. I did hear a few places where it sounded a little muddy, and a couple of voices that didn't sound quite as convincing as the rest, but overall it was well done.
Subtitles are optional. I kept them turned on and noticed a few places where the spoken text was different to the written words, which I always find a bit jarring. The grammar was mostly excellent; I only noticed a couple of errors across all three current episodes.
There are limited options: three volume levels each for music and sound, fullscreen / windowed mode toggle for graphics, and a single special effect filter: "Steggyvision', which appears to be a sort of bright blur lighting effect for characters and interface elements. I can't imagine any modern PCs experiencing performance issues with the game.
Yorkshire Gubbins is a traditional point-and-click adventure game. The game takes place in the top three quarters of the screen, with the bottom quarter being reserved for the simple interface: nine verbs, selectable by word, and a small inventory area. As with any point-and-click adventure, your goal is to find your way to the end of the story by solving verb- and inventory- based puzzles. The gameplay offers nothing revolutionary; indeed, it is obviously heavily influenced by the classics of the genre, such as the SCUMM-based Lucasarts games of the 1990s, and it does a good job.
The core of every good point-and-click adventure is its puzzles, and Yorkshire Gubbins follows the rulebook here, too. There's nothing outlandishly difficult and, so far at least, you shouldn't need to resort to a walkthrough. I did find one puzzle that was a bit fiddly and required a bit of the old "use everything on everything in the scene" tactic; though I knew what I wanted to do I just couldn't work out how the game wanted me to do it.
The game is divided into episodes. Currently there's a short tutorial of about 10-15 minutes' length, a single episode of somewhere between 60-90 minutes, and a 'bonus' prequel episode with a play time somewhere between the other two. Even though the game is not marked as Early Access, the developers are being generous and planning to offer a few more episodes free to owners of the game over the next year. So while the game as it is now only provides about two hours of play, you can expect more over the coming months.
The script is well written and the game's main drawcard is its humour, which I found entertaining; it didn't fall flat like many other comedy games and it even made me laugh out loud a few times.
Pros:
+ Sense of humour
+ Great accents
+ Steam Achievements
Cons:
- Pixel graphics are a bit too low resolution for modern displays
- Variable voice acting quality
- Very short (so far; more is coming)
Yorkshire Gubbins is a very welcome addition to the point-and-click adventure genre, with comedy that's light-hearted and fun. At the moment there's not much here, but what there is is well written and funny. The promise of up to another four long episodes over the next year adds to the appeal. Yorkshire Gubbins made me laugh out loud more than once, which is quite rare in this age of memes and in-your-face slapstick.
If you like point-and-click adventure games and you appreciate good humour, then pick it up and take a look.

I like games where you complete everything in a good time waster. This game fits that. It is not boring, but not exactly exciting either. I got this game in a 13-game boxed set from Wal-Mart. After two hours, while I haven't completed everything, I've seen everything the game has to offer.
The game has three modes: Manage, Dispatch (Had a different name, but I can't remember it), and Missions. In manage mode, you buy upgrades using 'budget' (currency you get in Dispatch and Mission modes). These upgrades include more cars/trucks, the ability to make your 'RAS Rangers' go on patrols, better gas mileage, etc.
Dispatch mode is the mode you play the most. It's endless, where you dispatch 'Rangers' (repair cars) and tow trucks (though It seems you can unlock helicopters and other such things later on) to red icons before the month is up. If the cars/trucks don't get to the targets before time is up, it affects your final score, which is based on a 3-star rating (this rating system is also used in the Missions).
In Mission mode, you assume a 3rd person camera and can go around a client's car, checking the tires, engine, fuel level, wipers, power steering, and other such car bits to repair the client's car. Most missions have extra broken things (for example, if the main problem is a broken radiator, a tire may have too much pressure, or a windshield wiper may be stuck). If you can repair the car with the least amount of unnessary operations, you get 3 stars and extra budget.
All in all, I reccomend this game if you like a good time waster that's sort of fun. Don't know how much this game is on its own, but in the $20 13-game bundle it's certainly worth it.
Edit: Made an 8-minute-long video showing all aspects of the game that you unlock after 6 hours of play.
Edit 2: Changing this game from Recommended to Not Reccomended. This far in, I've bought everything in the store and just have to finish the fourth region of the game. However, the last level has to be repeated 50+ times (the meter goes up 1-2% each time). This may not be so bad if it weren't for the fact that it starts to spew breakdowns faster than you can dispatch units, leading to up to 100 (occasionally more) breakdowns on one level, not to mention the helicopter missions, tow truck missions, and heavy truck missions. In the end the game is an absolute slog. Completionists should NOT buy this game, and completionists are the only people who would play this game at all. So who should play this game?

Another excellcent game from this studio that's a little hard to classify.  It is different than the creeper world series but still feels familiar.  Instead of fighting creeper moving along the surface, you are fighting against particles that flow / shoot out of locations.  The particles travel through space based on the terrain, fields and natural forces.  There are also some other obstacles such as plasma (slows your ships), emergent (powerful somewhat random moving ship killers), mines, turrets and even enemy ships and ship like particles in latter missions.
To battle this you have a small fleet and a limited land vechicle to fight this.  Each scenario defines what ships are available and each ship has a role (i.e. capturing spawn points, blocking/ramming, ranged fighting, killing ships, clearing plasma, speed, etc).  It makes for a very rewarding experience, slowly fighting back the particles and using your ships to the best of their abilities.  Very puzzle like and less RTS like.  It should also be mentioned you can build your own ships and use them in missions in sandbox mode or even make them the default ships in your own missions made with the editor.
Overall I found this game easier than creeper world 3 (only creeper game I've played so far).  The story is also a bit on the short side but there are user made missions, hard missions and random missions which still gives a lot of content.  Overall, well worth your time if you are into unique strategy experiences.

tl;dr: Novel content that you absolutely need to try.
It's basically your childhood dream in game form: Dynamic ships with volumetric, fully destructible hull which is simulated per-piece, no immersion-breaking health bars, only that giant hole in your ship which went straight through your lathe module. The enemy, despite being a mass of particles, is surprisingly relatable and seemingly intelligent (in the sense that you will rage at it because it destroyed your HQ while you were trying to hold it off elsewhere, or it managed to take out that mission-critical energy mine). There's also enemy ships with a rudimentry AI, but even those can be devasting opponents. Storyline is excellent and has ties with previous creeper world games, but you don't need those to enjoy this game.
The game also includes a full ship editor, where you can build out your hull block-by-block then litter it with guns, energy tanks and support modules. There's also an in-depth mission editor with a fully-scriptable 'PRPL' module for creating complex custom maps with original behavior. If you're not one for building a map, there's a mission generator capable of making just about anything you want, and they play like an actual story mode mission, with a (normally) balanced progression, minus a few novelties usually present in most custom maps.
Combat is surprisingly in-depth: Ramming with heavily armored ships works just as well as missile spam, and the hull+modules-to-build-time ratio really helps balance it as well. There's not a huge variety in weapons, but the ways in which you can combine those weapons lead to specialized ships and rich strategies. You can design a huge mothership with twenty of each module, but you need to defend it for a considerable amount of time due to the steadily increasing time-per-hull-cost ratio. Or you can go the route of several smaller ships, or even several ships which combine into a larger ship.
The game isn't bad in terms of performance either: obviously, a massive particle simulation isn't exactly easy for your CPU but it runs fine on my mid-range gaming laptop. Graphics look great, although they're not as impressive as say, GSB2.
All I can say is that this would be EPIC as a game engine for realtime player vs player ship combat. There's already fully-featured enemy ships controllable via scripting, but what could beat real multiplayer where you have to build your fleet up, organize your particulate and proceed to the all-out in a war of epic proportions.
My only complain is that it would be nice if tankers would refuel ships within range of an energy mine if the mine was unable to provide them sufficient power.

Compared to it's predacessors, Particle Fleet is a dissapointment. There is very little strategy involved, the story is forced (painfully so), and the level variety leaves a lot to be desired. Every mission its the same thing. Turtle up in the energy well, capture more energy wells, make a massive fleet, destroy particle nodes. Rinse and repeat.
Creeper world, the games predeccessor, had much more variety in terms of obsatcles and weapons the player was up against, and in response the player had to adapt. In Particle fleet, there is no adapting, because you are only allowed the ships you are given, and even the particles themselves don't really seem that dangerous when your ships can take a truckload of them inside your own energy wells. You can create a custom fleet, sure, but for most, that won't make the game any harder.
As for the story, I don't mind so much its shorter than it's Creeper World counterparts. I do mind that it was poorly developed with an ending so forced only a "first draft for sale on Amazon author" would be proud of it. And before fan boys begin commenting "well you only didn't like the ending because..." No. That type of ending is fine so long as it is done right. This one isn't done right. It's pointless, senseless, and it practically gives a middle finger to the player. Perhaps I wouldn't have minded so much if the gameplay was interesting, but it wasn't.
TLDR: In short it's Gun platforms vs. Particle effects, and that's it. Compared to Knuckle Cracker's earlier outings, this game just feels lazy and/or a cash in on an idea they were too far along to give up on but didn't want to take all the way. Knuckle Cracker games used to be a guaranteed purchase from me. After Particle Fleet, they arn't anymore.

First thing most people may think when they see the block system in the game is to think of this as a game like Minecraft. Trust me; calling this Minecraft would be like calling "Space Engineers" Minecraft. Honestly Space Engineers would be a far better game for comparison to FTD than Minecraft. Does Minecraft have missiles, space-ships and lasers? Didnt think so.....
You can basically build just about anything from Submarines to boats to spaceships in a pretty wide variety of ways, Land structures and vehicles are also gonna be in the game in some time. The engine is very versatile, and the game is  VERY stable for a Pre-Alpha game; seriously ive run into more or less no major issues so far. The campaign mode is aimed to be a very strategic mode where you basically command fleets of vessels (designed by you and made using resources harvested by you!) against the AI factions and there own respective fleets; each faction having unique designs, tactics and difficulty.
Now onto the frequent complains that negative reviewers are making about the UI and control system. The Control systems basically designed to give a high amount of fine control over block placement; giving control over all 3 Axis using a combination of WASD keys and the mouse, which helps when your making complicating designs. It also makes it easier to edit componnents that are deep inside the constructs hull; letting you reach and change them easily without having to strip off parts to reach it directly. Despite its versatility and varied usage I really dont think it takes too long to get the hang of the control system; but if you really cant stand it the game also offers a much simpler "Look and place" build mode. Building stuff and making it work is a lot easier than people keep saying it is; while at the same timing perfectly optimising something to run via the AI system can be a very interesting challenge for those that wanna have a go at it.
tl;dr: Its a lot easier than most people keep saying it is; and if you played Space Engineers (or another similar build-style game) and liked it then youll most likely love this.

It's kinda like Minecraft and Kerbal Space Program had a baby which had all the ingrediants to fail horribly and fall into the pit of clone games that are all essentially "Minecraft with a slight twist", however the baby turned out to be the Mozart of block building games, even in alpha stages it is incredibly fun and rediculously engaging.
During the campaign you can feel how innefective a one man army is so your first priority is to automate your ships, planes and fortresses and once that's done this game transforms from a complex block builder, to a full blown Real Time Strategy. It has no real constrictions to the way you play, you can build monstrous battleships that are almost unsinkable, hitting harder than a Sunday morning hangover, or squadrons of ultra nimble fighters that can outpace missiles and bullets with ease, though personally I go for edge of space motherships that rain down molten pain from a distance. The ability to craft a cannon piece by piece is something I've never encountered before, taking into account what kind of weapon would be appropriate for the craft you can fully customise the weapons capabilities from the range, to the accuracy, firerate, caliber and ammunition type, or opt for a laser or missile system with just as many options.
Another wonderful thing about this game is the developer's 100% commitment, I've seen on the forums more than once, someone having an issue getting something to work correctly or encountering a bug of sorts and the developer promptly replying, first to appologise, then to explain how to make something work or to say that he will fix this in the next update, which he seems to always follow through with. The developer's liveliness in the community is reason enough to buy this game as he listens to suggestions and responds almost always saying that he will add this as a feature, or that it may damage the balance and it may possibly come as a feature in the future. With this in consideration it honestly feels like a game "by the people, for the people".

OMG.  What looks like a low priced and fun little word puzzle game is nothing but utter frustration.
Why?
Ugh, this is an absolute "perfect example" of why you should NEVER make a game, especially of this nature in a language which you are not well versed in.  Good grief!
The game asks you to make smaller words using the letters in any order from a bigger word that it gives you, however it doesn't recognize tons of even the most obvious English words like "is" "if" and "or".  In my short time with this game here is a list of words that the game didn't recognize as valid English words (I was playing the game using the ENGLISH language option)
NOT VALID ENGLISH WORDS (According to this game):
---------------------------------------------------------
mad
Is
his
as
beg
if
got
..Notice how the word "got" is NOT a valid word according to this game, but the word "get" IS recongized as a word and this game will give you its definition of any word should you simply click on it.  According to this game, the word "get" has this meaning: "a return on a shot that seemed impossible to reach and would normally have resulted in a point for the opponent".
So words like "is" and "if" aren't valid English words, but words like "pe" is fine and has the meaning "the 17th letter of the Herbew alphabet".
Stay FAR away from this nonsense of a game, at least if you speak English.  NOT recommended.  I know this game doesn't know that the word "not" is actually an English word, but trust me... it is.
---------------
One last interesting note about this game:
This game recognizes the word "S H I T" as a word and it has this meaning: "something of little value"
...I'm so glad that this game understands what it is worth.  Little value.  And nowhere near the low price tag asked for here on Steam.
It's a pretty solid game, little slow-paced at times but definitely not the slowest.  7/10

Ace Combat Assault Horizon is quite entertaining if you like arcade combat flightsimulators without the depht of a real flightsimulor. Within minutes you are able to handle te plane like a pro. If you have a joystick I recommend to use it, because it gives this game a little bit more like a simulation feel.
Positive:
+ During the storyline you'll get the chance to control different kind of planes, helicopter and control even as a gunman or bomber (precision bombing).
+ Gamepad and joystick compatibility.
+ Lot's of actions.
+ Customization in colors of your plane.
+ Different choices of airplanes.
+ Graphics (in game) and sounds are fine.
+ It is an entertaining game and I have enjoy it.
Negative:
- Lack of more simulation and realistic feel and depth to this game. It's very arcade!
- Most of the time the actions come's way to quickly after eachother which you'll get tired of it and wondering when the end will comes.
- Dogfightmodus which you can trigger if you are close enough to an enemy is way to arcade and unrealistic. Ok somtimes it's spectacular because it triggers other animations and events, and most of the time it is also easier to shot the enemy down but this doesn't feel and look right.
- No fly-by or rocket cam.
- No free flight modus.
- Bought this game last week and finished it already within 3 days.
Note:
If you are looking for a realistic simulation game like I was, then this isn't the game you want.
However I do have enjoyed playing this game and finish all the different kind of missions with satisfaction..
If you are looking for an arcade combat flightsimulator with lot's of actions, then this game will do the trick.
But frankly, the game is not worth the money (yet). I bought this game for 20,- Euros, wait till it's 10,- Euros is my advise.
Despite all this I will recommend this game in this genre. This game do meets all the facets of an arcade player, it is an enjoyable action game and controls are great with full gamepad and joystick compatibility.

The online and offline experiences are so closely linked that I rarely find myself having to go out of my way to switch from one mode of play to the other. On the topic of the game's online elements, I personally believe that the fact that invasions and co-op are still fairly active speaks volumes about the game's quality. After all, it isn't just any old game that can retain a solid player base after 6 years and 2 sequels have passed.
To summarize, Dark Souls in an incredibly engaging, challenging and rewarding game. I have no reservations in saying that I'd recommend it wholehearted to not just fans of RPGs, but video games in general.

Luck-based trial and error and error and error and error, effectively lacking interactivity.
This reminds me of Time Gal, where part of the fun can be seeing all the different ways your female protagonist can die over and over again in cutesy ways. The problem is that victory in Long Live The Queen is completely luck based, and even if you get near the end then restart, powered by the knowledge of what's to come, you'll still not get all the way through.
The idea is that you train your stats, while constantly receiving situations (these aren't randomised, though that can be slightly different paths depending on outcomes) that test these stats. If you trained one or two stats high enough, you pass. It might matter, it might not, it might change something in a few turns' time.
But there's very little give. Even if you die and reload a save from a few turns back, you might train the stat high enough to pass, only to soon die again for not having another stat. So you have load an even earlier save to train both the stats high enough, but then you die earlier because one of the stats you didn't train wasn't high enough. It's a cycle that isn't fun.
The idea had a lot of potential, but it only works if there are several ways to an ending (early deaths don't count as satisfying endings), which would be based on your personal approach to being a leader. Instead, you just get killed off unless you have certain stats up to certain levels by a certain point in time, without being given any clues.
To get to the end, you'll likely need to follow a guide to the letter. But then what's the point of playing?

Nice idea and it may have a lot of endings but after few gameplays you pretty much give up. The endings are all based on stats which you pretty much just end up either guessing, lucking out or looking up a guide.
