The "Crack" in "Knuckle Cracker" is the sound of this developer knocking it out of the park again. I have been following and supporting this fellow since 2008 with Creeper World.
Each one of his games expands the Creeper universe, while bringing new gameplay and playstyles. Particle Fleet continues in this tradition, creating a game that is familiar but fresh, easy to learn but with amazing depth and adding ever more customization options.
Particle Fleet is worth full price, no question. Support this guy and show the rest of the gaming industry how it should be done by voting with your wallet. Your money will buy you a game that was 100% complete, bug-free and polished Day One. Every feature is there and unlockable from the moment you load it up. There will never be any DLC or microtransactions, and from past experience I can tell you the developer will support and improve it until the moment his next game comes out.
Oh and you're probably going to lose dozens of hours to this game, fair warning.

Particle Fleet: Emergence is my favourite new game. It takes elements of a classic RTS and adds some constraints for match-like play that are very well balanced.
You begin with a set of ships, but none are built. By capturing and holding energy mines, you can use that energy to build ships. However, you've always got a set number of ships you can build. That means you don't "build ships", per se - you have a ship allotment of, say, 10 ships, and each ship can either be built (and in play) or not built (destroyed). There's no overwhelming force possible in this game - you've got a small number of pieces to move around.
That's hugely important to the gameplay, where the particals you battle swarm in patterns. You block those patterns by positioning ships where they can destroy the particle advance before it goes through your defensive lines.
You can speed run the maps (some players finish levels in 6-7 minutes), but a slow, long match is just as fun. You can gradually move your defensive lines up to the enemy and have a good long battle if you want. That 90 minute match might get tedious, but fortunately you can speed up the game 4x to skip by time if your ships are only slowly gaining ground.
There's a story campaign with 15 missions that help introduce the different game elements and ship designs. It's light fluff but walks you through a lot of great map designs. After that, there's a set of one-off maps (some user-submitted, from the looks of it) that aren't realistic (from the story/lore POV), but give fun scenarios to try to play in.
THEN there's the online map index where you can download and review maps submitted by other players.
THEN there's also the map editor, which is fully capable of building any map in the game (including the campaign maps). You can design any game map to your heart's content, and design specific ships to supply players with.
The overall AI is pretty good. The particle behaviour is interesting and challenging without being frustrating.
This was one of those risky buys where I wasn't sure I'd like the game, but it turned into my favourite in a long time. If you're a fan of slow RTS games like Supreme Commander, or if you like tower defense games, you'll probably find Partical Fleet: Emergence holds a lot of appeal for you. Fans of hardcore action games will probably not enjoy this as much - it's definitely more of a strategy game than an action game.
Good game, very enjoyable!

This is a 2D space strategy game where you have to conquer territory. You build your ships and then move them around the map to conquer new territory and defend existing territory. In the early levels there are no enemy ships. Instead, you are battling against swarms of red dots (Particulate) which are constantly attacking your ships and conquering territory against you. Later on the enemy ships start appearing and then you're really in trouble.
Each level contains points on the map:
The action happens in real time but you can control the pace by speeding up, slowing down and pausing, giving you time to think when you need it and to skip ahead to save time when you want things to move along.
There is a generic RPG-like story (in the Story missions), with characters discussing what's happening in the game at the time eg. "hey we just found so-and-so, this could be used for such-and-such". You get the idea. It's not a bestselling novel but it's worth reading for the tips given. There's a skip button if you can't be bothered with it.
This game is about beating situations and creating/sharing levels with other players. You cannot play directly against other human players.
If you're looking for a slick, fancy space game with glitzy ship designs, this is not it. This is crisp, functional 2D pixel graphics whose primary purpose is to display the territory and items clearly. Think of it more as a chess board than eye candy.
Cheery, upbeat space adventure theme. Nice enough to leave on but not something you'd feel like adding to your music collection.
There are 3 main sections each with a set of levels. The first one you play contains the Story Missions. The first half of the Story missions take a couple of hours and they are very easy. You can just build all your ships and send them in a loose bunch to conquer every strategic point one by one, without knowing or caring about the differences between the ship types. I was starting to think there was no challenge in this game but then eventually it did get more difficult and became increasingly necessary to learn the strengths and weaknesses of the various ship types and deploy them accordingly.
There are other Steam reviews talking about the lack of challenge but I suspect these are people who have yet to play the later levels, and have certainly not graduated to the many user-contributed levels. Yes, there is an easy phase but if you want challenge there is plenty to be had here.
There are stats everywhere: timings, ratings, popularity of levels, you name it.
This game is all about configuring levels and ships. Even during the main missions you have the option to either accept the default ships or build your own before starting the mission. Once you've completed all the main missions you can create your own levels using the in-game editor, share them and download levels from other players. There are currently 200+ player levels.
The developer is building a strong reputation and loyal following by being very communicative with his users and implementing suggestions. This is a good sign, especially for a game that revolves around user-contributed customisation.
I played on Linux with midrange graphics card and it was all smooth and perfect, no glitches found. It should run fine on low-end hardware due to the modest graphics. Menu and settings are all quite elegant and everything is fully configurable. No complaints at all.
It's one of those games where the in-game levels are only the start. These basic levels are more than enough to justify the price, but once you get involved in the community the content can be endless. So excellent value.
Achievements, Cloud, Stats, Level Editor but strangely no Cards. It's a new game so maybe they will come later.
Space games are usually geared towards fancy spaceship graphics and planets etc. The space theme here is only incidental, it would work equally well on land, sea or whatever. It's a pure strategy/puzzle game where you have to be aware of your ships' abilities and think about your moves.
I found the early 'easy' levels to be a lot of fun while getting used to the game, then it declared "right, that's enough of the nursery, time for big school!"
Love it, thoroughly recommended.

As a pilot and FSX/X-plane user, I can safely say that this game... is somewhat fun.
Is this game realistic? Hell no. But that's a good thing because real fighters only have like 10 missiles.
Am I vaguely annoyed to have to use "dogfight mode"? Well, a bit. But as the first game I'm playing with an xbox controller, I can't hit anything without it anyway. Speaking of which, the control scheme isn't very good: left/right stick makes you roll, then turn in that direction. However at least when in cockpit view when holding the stick to the left your aircraft is really (from your perspective) pitching up, making it a bit confusing when you're trying to track enemies - imo, the thumbstick should've controlled pitch and yaw, with the shoulder buttons controlling roll - but I get that such a control scheme might ruin the fast-paced action (or people trying to perform sharp turns using rudder).
This game was from way back in 2010, but for any current/future PC flight sim games, there simply is no excuse for lacking the War Thunder style of mouse-aiming/steering.
In the gunner and chopper missions, I've found its best to use mouse controls, as you do in cod and bf and moh.
The graphics are... meh. They're alright considering when the game was made. There aren't a lot of visible graphics options but the game runs pretty smoothly on my (as of sept 2015) 3 year old laptop, EXCEPT: desync problems. thankfully the subtitles are in sync so at least I know what the hell is going on, but audio desync really ruins the experience a bit.
The interface is well made and easy to understand.
The campaign story is a bit underwhelming and cliched, and it shows the game's age. Definitely contains elements "inspired" by call of duty (although it could also be a fault of the genre). Also there is a hint of romance which is really weird, its like, there was no development of a relationship (its an arcade flight combat game lol), but in the end
I enjoy realistic experiences, but I think this game definitely lives up to the name of being the cod of air combat - the kills are satisfying although it is a bit repetitive. I hate that missiles were often useless. And being used to the degree of freedom offered in other flight games, the scripted arcade sequences really felt somewhat limiting - at the end of the game I had to go read the walkthrough to find out why the bad guy wasn't dying after taking 10 missiles.
Anyway. Fun? Certainly. Accessible and makes you feel like a rockstar? Maybe. If you don't know a lot about flying and just want a cool game, then this game isn't too bad an 5 hours (or 10 if ur a noob like me) to spend less than $5 on.

Stranded Deep is pretty unique. I find it very chill and relaxing. I truely feel a sense of adventure traveling from island to island on my thin yellow life raft, oar in hand braving the elements. One such time I can remember being halfway to another island and suddenly getting caught in a huge storm. I paddled in what I hoped was the same direction for a few minutes but couldn't resist looking behind me to try and glimpse sight of my "home" island to get my bearings. After that point I was lost. The clouds were so thick I didn't know which way I was facing. Then as night came I was not only lost in the fog, I was also lost in the dark. I had mentaly maped out the nearest islands to my "home" but now was way off course. This was hillarious to me. It was like finding a brick of solid GOLD when I finally opened a chest with a COMPASS inside!  I eventually gave up on my mental map and grabed a piece of scratch paper and started maping my discoveries. I even started using real world triangulation to chart my discoveries with my new compass. I was hoping to have more of the game finished before reviewing, but it's pretty hard and I wanted to help spread the word about this hidden gem. I've had it on my wishlist for months and excitedly bought it the moment it finally came out. This game would be a bargain at twice the price and I feel I already got my money's worth in my first gaming session alone. According to the opening credits sequence, the whole Sun family pitched in to help make this game, which I thought was a nice touch.
There's 7 regions of puzzles and you have to solve a certain amount of puzzles in each region to unlock the next. Each zone has a new concept that introduces a little more complexity. The gameplay is relatively simple: you can move freely in 3 directions (provided there's ground there) or anchor yourself at one of the 3 tips of your pyramid and swing in an arc along the other two directions. This gives you a surprising range of options, even on a very small level. The goal is to use anchored swings to push other colored pyramids onto tiles of the same color and move your pyramid to the blue tile to finish. It's possible to brute force the earlier levels by just trying everything, but it pays to slow down and get an intuitive sense for how your movement is going to affect the pieces around you.
This game is nothing like the developer's earlier game, Yankai's Triangle. Triangle is procedurally generated and has very little variety. Yankai's Peak reminds me more of Steven's Sausage Roll, except it has a much smoother learning curve at the beginning. They both involve rotating your character to slide pieces into position and can get very difficult. I heartily recommend this game to anyone who enjoys spacial reasoning puzzles.

My experience with this game may have not been ordinary. Do not expect something similiar to happen to you. But last night, I had one of my best experiences with gaming in a very long time. This game is definetely worth the $9.99 it is right now, and it's full price.
"Miscreated is everything DayZ is not."
I will be going through and reviewing the differen't aspects of the game. Graphics, Exploration, Crafting and Inventory, Building, PvE, PvP and Community.
Graphics: YouTube does not give this game credit. If you have an uber beefy PC like me and you can play the game on ultra settings, you will  be amazed. This game was made in CryEngine, probably the most advanced Game Engine out there, the engine that was used to make the Crysis franchise, and Star Citizen, which is now using a fork of CryEngine. The original FarCry was also made in CryEngine. This game is breathtaking, the sunsets are majestic. The weather will make you think your in real life. The water move with your player, and reflects the surroundings. Your character leaves footprints on dirt roads. The attention to detail in this game is like no other. It is hard to believe this game is made by a small company, I believe this game is actually indie, but the graphics in this game rival today's AAA titles. The only complaint I have is that  the game doesn't have a very bleak color pallette, which doesn't very fit the postapocalyptic theme. Nor is the environment very pretty during the nuclear winters, but the winter thing is very new, and will probably change.
Exploration: This is where I start talking about my personal story in the game. I was playing the game, and started talking in chat a little. I gave out the area I was in. One guy offered to team up, and I was like "sure". I didn't have anything valuable on me, and completely expected him to kill me. But, when we met up in Sultan, he didn't kill me, we just walked around looting for a while. After a while, we heard some shotgun shots in the distance. Not to long later, we ran into another player. Which is quite normal, since Miscreated's map is much smaller than DayZ's, but is so much more dense. The play didn't say anything, but wasn't hostile. After a minute or so, the player with the shotgun showed up and blew my head off. Luckily, Sachtika survived, and I spawned near Sultan. We were reunited quickly, and this time with one of his friends. Sachtika knew the map like the back of his hand, and we ventured into the forest. Soon we wandered into a Fallout Shelter, which there are  multiple, inside we picked shrooms, and fought two headed dogs and other mutants.  Afterwards, we climbed to the top of a mountain and enjoyed the beauty of the map. Than we climbed back down and went to a plane crash, which we looted for some basic commodities. Next, we went to a vast cave system, filled with glowing blue mushrooms, there we climbed down, and swam in the water at the bottom to enter the different parts of the cave. The cave seemed to be some sort of abandoned refugee camp from during the apocalypse. The cave was filled with guns, but also mutants. Sachtika mentioned that there are four caves. Finally, we started to head towards the central city. Which got us stuck on the highway. A few time we got trapped on cars with wolves behind us. We finally got to the suburbs of the city, which was filled with mutants, and really gave us a reality check, because we had been safe for quite a while. Sachtika and his friend are from Quebec, Canada and taught me some French Canadian slang. We also made some dirty jokes. We finally entered the city, where we looted the strip malls. We found an underground parking lot, than discovered an entrance to the sewers, which was suprisingly mutant free. Once we emerged we accidently attracted a bunch  of mutants with a flashlight, and ran up a tall building so we could easily pick them off. We ended late at night, after midnight, and logged out in some tents on the roof, for roleplaying purposes. The next time we do something, we plan on raiding the police station, which apparantly filled with weapons, but also players.
Crafting & Inventory: The crafting this game is so much more fleshed out than DayZ's. Instead of derpilly dragging items ontop of eachother, and constantly going to Google. Miscreated has an actual crafting tab, than is organized into sections and even subsections, telling you what you need for every recipe. You can even find crafting notes acroos the world to unlock new recipes. Most of these meant for the building system, which are pertained on that server even after death. You can even mix drinks in this game, like whiskey and cola, which is always an added bonus. Furthermore, you can use a burlap sacks to kidnap players after knocking them out, and even tie them up with duct tape or rope. The inventory system is quite different than DayZ's, in both good way and bad ways. Certain items are automatically put in special slots that do not fill up you inventory, this being clothes, weapons, and backpacks. Which are also assigned to hotkeys. This game also has a weight system, which can be fun to manage, but sadly you can increase your weight capacity. One thing that definetely bugs me is that everything is the same size in your inventory, which kind of takes away from the immersion and realism.
Building: I haven't gotten into this system yet, but it seems to be quite good. You make a claim sign, and within a certain radius you can place buildings, which does pertain to physics, unlike Rust. From what I understand, at the moment they cannot be raided, unless you leave the door open, meaning you can have something to come back to even after you die. Which is good, because a lot of zombie survival games lack this, usually being you have to completely start over after death. Currently there is no way to put a bedroll in your base to always respawn there. The game also has a clan system for shared bases.
PvE: I like that this game has mutants, which have the ability to be so much more dangerous than zombies. Having mutant humanoids, giant mutant humanoids, mutant dog, and two head mutant dogs. The humanoid one are sadly pretty easy to outrun and outsmart currently, making them only a threat if you get cornered or snuck up on. The mutant dogs cannot be out ran as easily, but are quite weak. Normal wolves are quite dangeroud though, usually you will find yourself climbing ontop of a car and shooting down to kill them. There is also a lot of food an water in this game. You can also probably go as long as an hour without both. It's nice that it is not quite as annoying as it is in DayZ, but it almost feels like a non existant obtacle. There is a radiation system in the game right now, but it is not really fleshed out yet, but has a lot of potential for having a Fallout like feel. There is sadly no temperature yet, making campfires useless except for cooking, but it can be expected soon with the new winter system.
PvP & Community. This game community is not quite as shoot on sight as DayZ's is. I have heard it as 50% of players are cool, and the others will kill on sight, or kill new spawns for cans of ravioli. Some players will even offer to trade in chat. But the player count is much denser in this game, so don't go thinking your safe. I haven't gotten to involved in the PvP yet, I will update this when I do. I am not sure whether this game has serpentine-ing or not.
Lastly, but the developers of this game just seem to care more about this game, and aren't working on random side projects like Mini DayZ or Ylands. This game gets updated on  what seems a monthly basis. I have not ran into a single game breaking bug either yet nor hacke. This does not play like an Early Access game.
I personally give this game a 10/10, but my experience was not normal, so for the average player, I give this game an 8/10.

Absolutely the most tense and terrifying game I've played. I first spawned at night during a rain storm, no clue how to open the inventory, no idea I had a flashlight either. I spent the whole night crouching in the bedroom of a two story house, listening to a nearby mutant panting, afraid to move, only catching a glimpse of my surroundings through the illumination of lightning strikes. The next morning I venture out into the daylight confident and reassured of my skills, having figured out how to open my inventory. I wander up to a house on a hill and start looting. Almost immediately I hear footsteps... It was another bambi, fresh faced and looking for fable 2 gold. I quickly announce my presence, accidently waving my newly acuired axe in the process, the clearly frightened bambi quickly drops his brand new bow on the ground and types a message... "I'm friendly" What a relief. So I inform him how to use voice chat and we decide we had better work together. We head for a water tower close by and climb up to gather some intel about where to go next...
Thus began my adventure in Miscreation and a lovely new friendship. 35 hours later and I still love it, although it is harder to find friendlies and dying to a feller with 1 more bullet than me is common, the game is still fantastic and fresh. Each new spawn, a new adventure. I highly recommend this. Get a buddy to watch your back and have a blast.

TLDR: Yes.
Dark Souls has issues.
While most entertainment experiences go out of their way to encourage your interest, it feigns indifference to your attention.
Introducing itself via bizarre and meaningless cut scenes you find your protagonist in a pretty dull dungeon. “Oh look, a man with a sword viewed from third person” you observe with a mounting sense of déjà vu. “No doubt I have a healing potion and a sense of manifest destiny somewhere in my bag too” and reach for the reset button/cyanide pill. But Dark Souls IS different - not that it is keen to show off. Like Usain Bolt winning the Dad’s race on sport day mumbling something about how he probably jumped the gun, Dark Souls’ initial coyness infuriates and astounds with equal measure.
Dark Souls also has a reputation for being challenging to a point some distance beyond fun. From Software appear to be if anything encouraging this with the “Prepare to Die” rider added to the PC version of the game. When combined with the cult following it has acquired it’s hard to lose the feeling that you’re being invited into exactly that kind of religious order, in which you’ll be expected to defend a game that you derive no pleasure from beyond a feeling of superiority over the Skyrimmers.
Lastly but less significantly Dark Souls has some technical issues. Frames per second rates struggle along in the high teens at points as it tries to render the distant and yet unseen architecture (obscured by darkness or some other monstrous emanation). The camera also seems to be unashamedly on the side of the skeletal hordes, zooming and clipping through walls to reduce the chances of survival more than seems fair. Some of this can be addressed with programs such as DSFix and DSCM but these are really just a band aid.
All of the above would fairly lead you to sideline Dark Souls into the ‘I’ve got better things to do with my time’ category. Trust me, you don’t. If you can overlook the occasional rough edge and ignore the reputation of this being unfairly hard, you’ll enjoy one of the best games ever made.
First up, this is not an unfairly hard game. It is challenging and yet completely fair. I realise this make me sound like a fanboy or as though I’m in an abusive relationship with Dark Souls (“It only kills me when I deserve it – but it still loves me!”). Bear with me however, as this game will teach you how to be better, just not through tutorials or a shallow difficultly curve. These methods work, but crucially there is no fun in winning an easy fight. Every fight in Dark Souls is rewarding precisely because there is a decent chance you’ll die if you’re not fully awake. Death here is a lot less final than tradition demands outside video games however and you’ll respawn intact (albeit a little hollow) empowered with a little more knowledge about the world around you.
Eventually you’ll be wading into battle against titanic beasties with the knowledge that not only are you now wielding The Sacred Axe of Fliddle-Fladdle but crucially your struggles have honed your skills to a sharp edge. It may take 5 hours – it may take 500 but you will get good enough and Dark Souls will always be ready to teach you.
All of this process takes place in a glorious, varied world packed with environmental and sentient perils. These combine in myriad ways to create thousands of memorable experiences everywhere from gothic churches and gloomy woodland dells to gleaming marble cities and poisonous swamps. It appears however to be impossible to describe the way these areas connect without using the wonderful neologism ‘Metroidvania’.
It’s impossible to adequately convey how complete and ambitious this game is (I haven’t even mentioned the original and subtle integration of multiplayer) without rambling on so I’ll leave it there. Sufficed to say Dark Souls has the ability to colour your experience in every future game and make all other RPGs feel a little… hollow.

Starting out in From The Depths can be a discouraging experience, the amount there is to learn may seem overwhelming but is met with some of the most rewarding results I've come across in the vehicle crafting sandbox genre. This is a game that requires patience to be put in but gives back in copious amounts, learning the usage of every tool is key to creating the most enjoyable experience as you'll have plenty to use at your disposal.
First and foremost, every player from the curious new builders to the most seasoned of engineers will want to delve into the playable tutorials and building guides supplied by the game as you'll quickly find the learning curve is no joke. Although it may seem tedious at first the more patient of players will begin to slowly learn important hotkeys and shortcut tools such as copying and reusing large sections of previously created vehicles that will make your building endeavors quick, seamless, and enjoyable.
Creating vehicles is way more than just their visual appearance and basic form, you'll have to get into the guts of each machine and engineer their inner-workings putting you in full control of everything from connecting series of logic up to thrusters, distributing equal amounts of power evenly across your ship, to creating your own missiles and ammunition as well as defining their behavior. The limits in From The Depths are determined solely by your own creative capacity.

Aside from the vehicle creation and building mode, there are some ambitious features to battle it out in including a progressive campaign that expands with each update and quick skirmishes you can set up for testing your new creations in the heat of battle. Terrain in the game varies from sea, to land, to air/space giving you lots of types of traversable landscape to consider when creating your specific dream vehicle.
The campaign itself is impressively engrossing for those well versed in the mechanics of the game throwing you into the world with a starting base to gather resources from and expand off of as you fight for survival and resourceful territories. This campaign mode is already very addictive and continues to grow rapidly with each update, promising the addition of more enemies, factions and objectives to spice up your survival in this free-form sandbox adventure.
Currently in development is the story based mission mode but it already features a couple of the basic starting missions which I found to be some of my most exhilarating moments with the game. The few story missions we have already do a great job of setting you up with some pre-determined scenarios, getting you into an operable pre-made vehicle and dropping you into the midst of a full-scale battle. These missions are a really excellent way to get a glimpse at what all-out war looks like in From the Depths.
Considering the complexity of what you can do and the scope of freedom you have doing it, From the Depths is a game I feel deserves way more attention and hype from sandbox and crafting enthusiasts. For me it's certainly the next biggest sandbox game on the market and one I've already put more time into than KSP or Space Engineers, and the prospects shown from constant updates and a very close relationship between the developer and the community make it even more important to get involved early to watch something already engrossing turn into something huge.

Aright, so here's the thing. This is a great game IF you're willing to sink obsessive amounts of time into it. This is by no means a casual game as there is simply too much content to be absorbed across any number of ten minute sessions. If one isn't willing to make that committment to learning, this game is not for them.
Reasons to play this game:
+Excellent physics, especially for a voxel box-esque game.
+Build literally any sort of vehicle you want. You want a spaceship that doubles as a submarine? No problem.
+Story missions that test the depths of one's abilities.
+Fully customizable weapons platforms. I don't think of my laser guided missiles so much as missiles as they are long range sea mines that happen to fly.
+Intuitive and shockingly convenient vehicle automation.
+Nowhere as resource intensive as one would think it would be.
Reasons NOT to play this game:
-Steep learning curve. Building more than basic boats and engines is not for the faint of heart.
-High time commitment.
-Build interface is clunky and plays less like a game than a 3D drafting program.
-Controls frequently inconvenient and limited in customization.
-Stock vehicles for story missions seem unabashedly bad. Namely one critical, otherwise easily fixed flaw, like leaving the driveshaft of a gigantic drill completely exposed...

Epic. Just epic.
I tend to shy away from Early Access nowadays, given the recent disappointments like Starforge or Towns, but this definitely hit the sweet spot of EA.
The sheer scope of the premise, given with the activity and apparent competence level of the developer made this pretty much an instant buy. It also has a pretty good AI (one that even the player can use, too), so it offers a ton of replayability already. A campaign with resource gathering, diplomacy, hell even a working RPG system with levelups are there to tamper around with. Didn't even factor in things like multiplayer or co-op, which are still pretty much a work in progress.
Also, the physics are pretty nice. Recoil has an actual impact, parts breaking off of your vessel can make you lose control, and weight will make you sink to the bottom of the ocean, whereas airtight compartments on a metal ship will keep you afloat, unless breached and flooded with water.
If you like Kerbal Space Program or Starmade, or if you like the big, humming multiblock machines of certain Minecraft mods, you're probably going to love the hell out of this. Oh yeah, there's space, too. Orbital cannons raining down fiery death on submarines are possible and encouraged. And don't worry, the graphics are going to get an overhaul, too. Awesome game, well recommended. If you liked the creeper world series, this similarly fun to play. Great replay value and the graphics are definitely a whole lot improved since creeper world 3.
For those new to it, the levels in the campaign are usually easy to figure out but the real challenge is in beating the level quickly. So, you can grind it out for an hour or figure out how to do it in a few minutes. This makes the game attractive for casual playing as well as for hard core strategists. To win, you need to optimize strategy and resource usage and make use of all the various strengths and weaknesses of your own and enemy units. What adds fun is that the enemy is beautifully rendered particles that move and cluster in all sorts of complex patterns. It can crowd you and and you counter with guns and armor to overcome it. You beat the game by by taking out particle emitters and gaining control of the energy resources on the map.
With creeper world 3 there have been lots of users that ended up writing new levels and using the built in scripting language to tweak the game dynamics or even introduce new game modes. This game has similar potentia and comes with all the tools to do thisl and there already loads of community maps. You'll do the campaign in about 10-15 hours and then move on to the user provided maps, This is where the real fun starts. These unlock after you complete the first ten levels, which sort of function as a tutorial as well.
This price for a game like this is a bargain. i wish the firs two creeper world were also available on steam.

Watching one of the developer's beta videos sold me on buying this game, and it was well worth it.  I haven't played any of the dev's previous games, but this one is fascinating.  You control a fleet of ships fighting against the "particles", a non-intelligent enemy seemingly governed by a physics or rule base.  In addition to the 16 mission campaign, there are an additional 9 missions from the dev, plus 100+ user-created ones on the user exchange, created using the built-in mission editor.  The game also includes a ship editor to create your own ships, and the "simulator", which is a very customizable random map creator.   The UI on the assorted editors and extras needs some improvements. butthe amount of stuff provided in the game is a tremendous value.  And that's not even considering the awesome soundtrack.  I'm not normally one to pay much attention to the music in a game. butthe music in Particle Fleet is great.  Even my son kept on commenting on how much he liked the music while I was playing the game.  I'd buy a stand alone soundtrack if they offered one.
So it's a good value, but what's the gameplay like?  I loved it, personally.  It's a bit hard to describe, but I'll try.  You build the ships in your fleet using energy from energy sources you control.  You use those ships to destroy enemy structures, such as particle emitters.   The enemy particles form hazards and threats you must overcome, but it's much more like puzzle-solving strategy than what you'd find in a RTS.  The difficulty is generally not that hard is you take your time and plan ahead.

Overall, I'd give this game an 7/10. I'm taking into account that a lot of people who play these types of games are completionists, unlike me. Make no mistake, this game is a completionist's wet dream.
While I did enjoy the story and background tidbits scattered throughout the game, my main criticism is that it involves little to no skill whatsoever. It wasn't about planning carefully which skills to invest in, based on clues or common sense. It was about playing through the game enough times to memorize which skill needed to be raised by which point. That took a lot of the fun out of it for me. Who wants to sit and takes notes while playing a game? I found a lot of the events and decision-making points to be completely arbitrary.
At its highest points, the game is interesting and well-written, with nice touches of realism (magical girl transformations not-withstanding). At its lowest, it's a malignant, faintly tedious chore for myself and players like me.

This game is more or less a shot-for-shot remake of the old Impressions City-Building Series (Caesar, Pharaoh, etc.), but set in the Wild West.
Which is good in theory, but there are a lot of good reasons that gaming's evolved past this since the last of those games came out in the early aughts. Resource management is a nightmare, houses will downgrade all the way from big mansions to little shacks because you had a temporary timber or alcohol shortage, non-renewable resources run out practically instantly, there are no options to automate the trade system to keep from running out of key import resources (or sell your resources you've set to export)...every place the designer had a decision to make about game flow, they made the wrong one.
Basically, this game would've been very good in 1999, but it's not 1999 anymore and there's no excuse for this kind of design even in a casual game.  I wanted to like it, but it simply isn't very good. More frustrating than fun even for big fans of the genre.

This review was originally a comment I made replying to someone about whether they should buy Starbound since they like Terraria. Still basically is a review of the game though.
Terraria and Starbound are without a doubt similar. They're both pixelated 2D sidescrollers trhat have you craft, explore, and fight monsters. In terms of a sense of progression however, Terraria takes the cake. Terraria has many bosses and dungeons that you have to complete in a sequential order as you progress through the game. Starbound, while having dungeons and bosses, is far simpler in practice. In Starbound the major in-game dungeons are story content that is unlocked after doing the same object scanning quest for that dungeon's respective race. The dungeons themselves while somewhat aesthetically pleasing, feel quite boring in my opinion. You go through their not-so-challenging obstacles and enemies to a final boss that is for the most part mechanically simple and thus, easy to beat. Hit the boss when it's armor is down, fight waves of enemies until the boss arrives and then shoot it, Switch the switches until you can use a device to damage the boss. Starbound just isn't interesting in that regard.
After you reach the game's hub world and beat the first story dungeon is when you get the ability to explore all that Starbound's procedurally generated universe has to offer. You go to your ship's bridge, and sit in the captain's chair to open the starmap. There you'll see an endless number of stars for you to warp to, each star with it's own tier and and different planets based on the star's tier. You pick a star, warp to it, then fly to a planet or moon of your choice. Different planets have different difficulties, worldgen dungeons, and species, so you have to make sure you're ready for that planet's mobs and climate. Along with the different mobs come different dungeons. Science facilities, prisons, and egyptian style temples, Starbound has quite a bit to offer. These dungeons are scattered on different types of planets so looking to the wiki is helpful when trying to look for something specific. Compared to the worldgen dungeons of Terraria, Starbound's dungeons are again, inferior. You'll be mining underground, or exploring the surface and see them. When you enter them they have mobs and loot to either collect or kill, then you leave. So long as you have equipment that's for that tier of planet/star they aren't too challenging, although the same could be said about Terraria and it's dungeons. Terraria has places like the hives, Jungle Temple, and the Dungeon with their rather challenging enemies, rare loot, and sometimes bosses. Something that the Starbound dungeons largely lack aside from the occasional miniboss. Starbound does have something that Terraria doesn't when it comes to exploration, and that is villlages. Like with the rest of the game, different planets and stars mean different villages. The villages contain a single race and are decorated with blocks and furniture that reflects that race. These villages also have loot to reap and merchants to barter with. However, you can't break too many blocks in the village or else the village guards will try to kill you. Some villagers will also have rnadomly generated quest, although they're not very varied and don't offer a great reward, except for maybe a crew member if you're lucky. There's also in sapce mech combat that only really gets interesting once you get upgraded mech parts that I feel are a little too difficult to get considering how small of a role mechs actually play in the game.
Starbound's loot consist of randomly generated wapons with random stats, cosmetic items, potions, armor, etc., just like Terraria, but again Terraria has better loot. Aside from the unique weapons, the loot in Starbound isn't all that interesting going through the game until you reach endgame. It isn't like Terraria where you're scrrambling to find a magic mirror before your friends or get a particular item for your build. You're going through the game equipping armor that's better than you last, finding stronger weapons, and equipping some of the many cosmetic items that the game gives you. And that brings us to combat. Without a doubt, Terraria has better combat than Starbound. Terraria has wings, a variety of magical items, a variety of magical swords, and more. Starbound has a variety of gun types, but most aren't very useful at all, and all the swords, axes, and spears are essentially the same item aside from a random secondary ability given to it. The enemies in Starbound are also pretty lackluster. No matter what planet you're on, you'll usually see the same enemies you've seen on other planets. Starbound's enemies somehow are somehow less varied across planets than Terraria's are on just one.
I think Starbound wins in this category because of the matter manipulator, the block breaking and placing tool in Starbound. It allows you you upgrade it to have a longer range, break blocks faster, and increase the amount of blocks it can break simultaneaously. Another thing I feel I should note is that placing walls in Starbound is easier because it doesn't force you to fill any tiny seam in the wall, all wall blocks just seamlessly connect which helps save blocks.
Modding in Starbound is the reason I'm still playing it. Mods help to even the playfield between the two games and what allows Starbound (in my opinion) to shine. The Starbound mods that are currently availble help to improve the game in numerous ways and to add more content. One of the most, if not the most, popular mods for Starbound, Frackin' Universe, helps to fill the gaps between it and Terraria. It adds many planets, stars, biomes, and some bosses that really help to put a fresh coat of paint on the game after playing it a few times on vanilla. I highly reccomend getting the game and playing with Frackin' Universe as it really does bring Starbound in-line with Terraria (in my opinion)
Throughout the comparison it may seem as though I'm trying to paint Starbound in a negative light, however that isn't what I mean to show. My impressions of the two games are this:
Terraria - Quality > Quantity
Starbound - Quantity > Quality
There are a lot more mechanics in both games that I did not mention simply because this comment would be going on forever.
Modding is what helps to keep me and many others interested in Starbound, and all you have to do is subscribe to the mod on the Steam Workshop to play them.
Just to clarify, this is my opinion on the two games when compared.

Let me just say I'm glad I got this game for $6 on the humble bundle. There's unfortunately a lot of flaws with assualt horizon. Let's start with the story it's bland and generic with truely awful voice acting and I usually skipped all the cutscenes because they are just so boring. The pacing is not so good and it's all over the place during the gameplay and the story. The turrent sections are by far the worst part about Ace Combat AH as not only do the sections drag on for far too long but this doesn't belong in an ace combat game at all. What's worse is the helicopters controls are just awful and it results in a lot of cheap deaths.
Thankfully the rest of the game including the fighter stuff and the dogfights are just awesome and extremely enjoyable. The number of skins for your plane are insane and there's a good reason to go back and earn them. The flying is exteremly good and is very high odrelen and I love that the debree can fly in your face which is awesome and I wish more flight games did this.
Outside of that there are a few things I would like to mention. The PC port itself is good, the controls for both flightsticks and controllers are really good however the game sucks with a keyboard as it's almost unplayable. The graphics and the options are also good I'm glad the game runs above 60FPS and it looks quite good despite being a PC port. I'm happy to say that as of 2015 the game does not have GFWL anymore so If you were worried about this being in there then fear not it's been removed and replaced with steamworks. The music on the other hand is just terrible and Ace Combat games usually have an awesome soundtrack but AH is just terrible and not a single track stuck in my head.
So overall would I reccommend AH, for me if you can get past the awful turrets sections and the forgettable story then I think this would good flight game for you to pick up on the cheap. If you are into voxel building games (IE. Minecraft) and want a bigger focus on PVP then this game is for you. Much deeper and customize-able than games like Robocraft. While this game does have a fairly steep learning curve and Youtube tutorial videos are practically mandatory for some of the more complex designs like setting up your own AI control of your ships and building custom weapons once you get the hang of it the game is a blast. Anything from submarines, planes, and even space ships are possible in this game.
There are some features that really make this game stand out to me that I haven't seen done anywhere else like being able to design your own custom weapons and setup your own AI to control your individual ship or even your fleet. While there is a "simple weapons" tab which includes prebuilt weapons like small and heavy cannons, a missile and torpedo launcher, and ramming weapons like rams and drills the real meat and potatoes is the Custom Cannons, Custom missiles/torpedoes, and laser weapons. Simple weapons work fine early on against smaller ships made of wood but don;t have the versatility or sheer damage custom weapons are capable of.
Custom weapons aren't simply placed on a ship but have to be built using individual components. For example to build a cannon you start with the firing piece. Then you can add different types of barrels (recoil reduction, flash suppressed, etc) and can add a component which increases the barrel gauge. Then you can add components like ammo crates, armor pen and explosive shells, autoloaders that speed up firing, shot predictors, etc. These components all modify the weapon in certain ways like accuracy, range, and dps. Custom missiles are built differently but the core idea still applies and same goes for the laser weapons.
At this point you have a great game where you can build some pretty awesome combat vehicles but they didn't stop there.
The feature that makes this game stand above most other voxel style games is the ability to create your own AI for your ships. Using an AI mainframe and a selection of different cards like target prioritization and Naval AI you can program your entire fleet or just individual ships to act autonomously within the rules you set for the ship. If you have a long range missile boat you could set it to try to stay within a certain range from its target. These are just the most basic AI functions and can get very deep and complicated depending on the design. This means not only can you create an entire fleet of ships with AI, but you can create an enemy fleet using AI to do battle against. Campaign and story missions do a good job of showing this off in single player.
Multiplayer is planned and the option is in game but is currently not implemented but should be soon.

This is a brilliant little arcade style game. Incidentaly I picked this up in a Humble Bundle, but already before I start this review I'd say that it is definitly worth full price!
Luftrausers is an oldschool arcade style game, with focus on racking up as many points as possible, while sustaining a multiplier. To do this you gun down hundreds of planes, ships, and various modifications and bosstypes of these.
The game does however feature some progression, in that you will be offered various jobs to complete, and by doing that you will progressively unlock parts to your plane, which comes with more jobs to do. There is also colourschemes to unlock,  since the artstyle is uses a simple 4-5 colour pallette.
The unlockable parts gives a whole lot of vararity, and there's a bunch of different playstyles, depending on how you combine your plane. Personally I'm a big fan of the laser+melee body+booster engine combo.
Gameplay continues to be fun, and even after you have completed all jobs and unlocked all parts, there is more to do, a hardcore mode will unlock, which is really hardcore. You will basically die within seconds, and this mode comes with additional jobs to do.
Luftrausers is ultmatively a bunch of fun, with flying mechanics that feel really awesome, and gamplay that keeps on giving. It does however run in some wierd aspect ratio (most likely 4:3) and there is no way to make it wide screen as far as I have seen, but this doesn't really detract from the game in any way.
I would definitly reccomend this game if you are into arcade style games with scores and multipliers. Or if you just want to waste some time shooting thing out of a brown sky.

Luftrausers is the fairly new arcade shmup from Vlambeer, who is best known for their indie hit Super Crate Box. Super Crate Box, while a freeware and simplistic shoot-em-up game that probably isn't meant to have hours dumped into, was incredibly addicting and I ended up spending around 17 to 18 hours playing it total (not counting the occasional rainy afternoon I pick it up for a half hour before not touching it for weeks). Even though I haven't put that much time yet into Luftrausers, I'm already hooked. The gameplay starts off simple: you're a plane. You shoot other planes and boats. That's it. However, once you start really playing it and improving your game, you start unlocking new parts and start finding some more enemies, such as the blimp. And that's where Luftrausers shines: it's so simple, yet gets more "complex" as you get better. The gameplay, while pretty much the same thing over and over and over again, is enthralling and addictive--it's suffice to say that Luftrausers is one of those "just one more turn" ordeals. Enemy AI is well-done, often moving around and dodging your bullets, causing you to really make split-second strategical decisions so that you don't crash and burn. The customization is rich and adds a whole different aspect not seen in other Vlambeer titles, with dozens of engines, weapons, and bodies to scroll through and unlock. And the soundtrack is amazingly done, a truly beautiful symphony that adds to the "gotta move fast!" aspect of the game. My only gripe is the lack of VARIATION in the gameplay, but it's one that I'm not losing sleep over.
OVERALL, Luftrausers is a gem of a game, combining sleek and stylish bullet-hell gameplay with well-done customization and a brilliant soundtrack. If you love Vlambeer or shmups, this is not to be missed. 9.5/10

Super Short TL;DR: If you liked creeper world 3, you will like this.
Slightly longer TL:DR: While this game isn't a creeper world 3 sequel it shares very similar gameplay elements and can almost be called a spiritual sequal. The game is played by defending from and conquering never ending emitters of 'stuff'. In creeper world it was basically water (grey goo) that you held back with various towers. In this game you're holding back "space grey goo" and instead of using towers, you're using space ships that are each retrofitted with various types of guns.
More formal review: Creative take on the tower defense genre. Instead of fighting waves of enemies, you're tasked with defeating a map that has a bunch of emitters that spawn unlimited enemies. The enemies in this game have a mostly fluid behavior similar to fighting a flow of water if that makes sense. Pacing through the story is good with incremental upgrades, and after a bit of progression the game opens up additional non-story maps and a community portal that can potentially offer an infinite number of maps to play.  Instead of building stationary towers you build space ships with retrofitted weapons that you can strategically place and move around the map at will.
Highly recommended if you like tower defense game. If you have not played Knuckle Cracker's previous game creeper world 3 I highly recommend both, as the the games are very similar in many ways but different enough to offer a fresh experience.

This is a good game, with a lot of potential, like many early access titles. However, the game still needs a great deal of polishing. I have played this game a fair amount since it first came out (around 60 hours or so, Ive played a lot offline when I have no internet connection), and it has improved a good deal from what it was. But its taken 2 years for these improvements to happen. While yes, it is being created by fairly new indie developers, 2 years is far too long, and honestly, the game doesnt feel much different from when it came out. Yeah its polished a bit, but its still feels like the same game, just with more base building.
Movement is not at all smooth and most character animations need a good deal of work, inventory management has improved, but its still pretty annoying to work with. Shark AI has actually gone down hill in my opinion, they've gone from being realisticly curious when first encountered, to being a Terminator shark intent on killing you from the start.
The islands within the game have improved a lot, with a substantial increase in size and aesthetic appeal. But they still aren't the islands that I wanted when I first started playing. I wanted Pirates of the Carribbean or a Tom Hanks 'Cast Away' style islands. Large islands that you could properly explore, with lagoons and rock pools or cave systems. But I was disappointed by the size and variation of the islands. Every island, though different in shape, is really the same island with just more resources.
The game has been made using the Unity Engine, and Beam Team has done a great job making the game look good. Shadows, lighting and textures have been done quite well in my opinion, but in truth I would prefer the graphics be worse and actual gameplay be much better. I would venture to say that their work on the graphical side of the game has meant that the gameplay aspect has suffered greatly.
Overall, this is a good game, with a lot of potential to be a game that I and my friends would keep going back to for the survival experience. However, I cannot recommend it due to the infrequent updates, and overall gameplay quality. If you like supporting new developers, and love a good survival experience, then by all means get the game. But I would wait until they make some serious updates to the gameplay, or until the game leaves early access. Getting the game in early access was a mistake in my opinion. Having played a decent amount of the game, I am bored and tired of the game, and in all honesty, I probably wont come back to the game, even if it progresses greatly from its current state.
TL:DR
Adequate game, needs a lot of work, wait for early access to end

Overview:
1849 is a settlement management sim set in...  Well?  In the time of the California Gold Rush.  1849 can be played in both sandbox and campaign modes, with the latter involving building towns all around California to exploit natural resourses of the immediate area, and sell these resourses to other cities in California via trade routes. Once scenario objectives are complete, it's time to move onto the founding of the next city.  Trade routes are both ways, so if one city buys something your city has to offer, then you'll also be able to buy whatever it is that other city specializes in, and hopefully the item in question will be something your settlement needs.  But like many other management sims, it's much better to sell than it is to buy.
Graphics and sound:
The graphics are what you can expect for the money, but that ASSumes the player bought 1849 when it was on sale.
There's nothing that stands out as particularly likable concerning the sounds of the game, but the period music does help with setting the mood.  I'll listen to the music if I really do need a mood-setter, but I don't particularly enjoy any song in the game's soundtrack more than the other, so I'll mute the sound on the game, and play my own brand of music the few times I play 1849.
Positives:
1849 is an original concept for management sims, and there's not a great deal of gold rush era games in the first place.  If you're fascinated by the Gold Rush era, you should enjoy this game more than me if you management sims are your thing.
Negatives:
The difficulty curve in 1849 appears to have some randomness to it.  (Either that, or it gets extremely difficult very quickly!)  The first several missions in 1849 were pig simple, but fairly early on, you're still going to need to need playthrough videos or text walkthroughs to help beat one of the scenarios.  The way to complete one early scenario was one I never would have guessed on account of the scenario not requiring production or selling of the biggest money maker, which is your only means of completing this scenario.  Any management sim fan will tell you that there's nothing worse than a game that has only one exact way of completing a scenario, and while I can tolerate such a flaw in missions that are supposed to be extremely difficult at the end of a campaign, a player shouldn't have to go through it less than five scenarios into the game.
There's nothing interesting to speak of about the campaign.  There's no main character to speak of, nothing of interest comes up between scenarios except for a big ol' map of northern California, and the location of where you settle next.  In fact, the campaign just seems very boring in general.  It's been about twenty years since Railroad Tycoon 2 was released, and it featured very interesting insights to scenarios.  (Including it's expansion pack, which had interesting things to say about even it's far future scenarios.)
Remember Imperium Romanum which had all sorts of interesting facts about the Roman Empire that were revealed as you played the game?  This feature is totally absent from 1849.  My only interest in California may be in the Punk bands from there, but it would have been nice to have gotten lessons from the game as to the relevance of things like olive oil and cotton to the Californian economy when you're pretty sure that gold mining was the be all, end all of what made settlers want to settle in a state plagued by mudslides, earthquakes, fires, and lots of people who think the sun shines out of their behinds.  Random fun facts about the Gold Rush would have been nice, but about the only thing you're going to learn from this game, is that the campaign can be difficult, and is really uninteresting.  (Players may, however, have fun building up a city in a sandbox game.)
Conclusion:
Listen to your friends on Steam:  They are your friends for a reason, and they mean what they say when they say not to purchase a game!  I thought one friend in particular was just being overly critical about 1849 (and lacking in key information), but you can take it from me to save your money on much more fascinating games, because I make a more solid effort to inform players (usually friends) about games.  I do intend on completing the campaign someday just for the sake of having bought this game. (Edit:  I changed my mind, and decided to request a refund.)  You might have fun playing sandbox games just for the sake of building settlements from the ground on up.  (A challenge I sometimes enjoy, but far less after having played Banished.)
I cannot recommend 1849 in good faith to anyone.  There's far better games on Steam involving management for the same amount of money (even at 1849's sale price), and if you need the challenge of developing cities, just look for an established city building game to get your kicks.

1849 is a gold rush-themed city builder in the same vein as the classic Impressions series (Pharaoh, Caesar, Zeus, and Emperor). It's a little less complex than the aforementioned games, and the strategy is pretty much the same for each level, making it a little repetitive after a while. The UI has some flaws; first of all, it covers up too much of the playing field. There are only two 'advisors': population and economy. The economics advisor doesn't give you nearly enough information about where your money is going. When buying and selling goods, you cannot set a purchase/sell level, where anything below/above that number is bought/sold. If you run out of a resource needed for your houses, they will devolve; thus, you must keep an eye on how much stock you have in your warehouse. You can tag items in the warehouse to 'hoard', but only food and alcohol, not resources such as wood and fabric.
As someone pointed out in an earlier review, when you start the game, you're likely to think, 'Wow! This is such a small map.' However, you really don't need much space to fulfill the terms of the missions. In addition, buildings can neither be rotated nor moved once placed. They can, however, be deactivated to save money. Also, there is no indication of this in game, but

I have found myself getting more indulged with this game than I had originally thought I would. Yeah, it doesn't look like much at first but once you get deeper into things, it all flows smoothly with this game.
Let me start off by saying that this game has some different character development compared to other games. You find survivors and have them join your group where you find out who they were before the apocalypse. Characters have real world personalities and traits such as "natural born leader" or "idol fan" or "practiced photography" and this helps decide who is good at what and good where. Once you lose a survivor, in some morbid gore-tastic way, your "community" feels the loss and demands more attention on the home front. This was a really nice spin on the survival genre.
Next, the world itself is always reacting to the things you do or do not do (aside from the main storyline missions). You have to choose between what is vital or what is time pressing. Also, the world keeps going after you've quit the game, so building projects are finished in real time instead of waiting around for it to be done, and your community's morality fluctuates while you are away too along with supplies being gathered and/or side missions being completed.
Oh, and there are plenty of good zombie killing weapons for the taking! Sure, it isn't a Dead Rising sort of diversity, but it is good and diverse for the most part!
Sure, it isn't in first person, but it still gives poetic justice to the survival genre and still gives that personal edge fans desire.

Now for a few of the game's cons:
-The hit reaction is sometimes off at vital points.
-NPC's do not help much when it is really needed and often times get themselves killed.
-The Dialouge is extremely repetitive... every character uses the same sentences as other characters.
-Gameplay can get dull at times.
-PC controls can be frustrating as well.
All in all, this game is an amazing take on the whole "Zombie, Survival" genre (that is sadly overdone) and is a great buy for any fans of the genre.

A terrifyingly bad port of a terrifyingly good game.
Despite what you may have been told, Dark Souls is not as soul-crushingly difficult as the belligerent masses berating you to "git gud" would have you believe. No, Dark Souls is really more a game about exploration and experimentation. Most enemies and traps can be outwitted by simple observation and a willingness to adapt.
While the game may be called "Prepare to Die", and yes you will die, in fact you will die a lot, death is really just as much a mechanic in this game as swinging your sword, or chugging down a fiery, healing charge of
Estus. Though souls, the money and XP in this game, are lost upon death; items are not, and as long as you learn from your actions you can reclaim your souls quite easily.
The true difficulty of Dark Souls comes from learning it's mechanics. Uses of items, upgrading equipment, your next destination, even the game's story, are all told by the game's cast of NPCs which you'll come across as you explore, as well as through item descriptions, usually in somewhat ambiguous ways. There are aspects I would recommend looking into a guide to discover, for instance how to access the DLC, I do not blame you if you wish to keep one handy, as this game does hold quite the plethora of secrets.
I highly recommend using a controller rather than keyboard and mouse, as the standard PC controls are not very intuitive to say the least, to make things worse most in-game control prompts are Xbox format and nothing else. A mod called MouseFix does remedy this by offering a customizable k&m format. Another mod DSFix, as the name suggests, fixes most of the performance issues with the game, including graphic fidelity and framerate. I recommend anyone getting this port to download it, especially if you're wanting an actual PC game.
Overall, this game is one of, if not my favorite, games of all time. Getting past the bad port issues, it is a gaming experience I would suggest everyone to try.

Particle Fleet is an amazing game in the classic style of Knuckle Cracker. Simple, colorful art, cheesy storylines and well-designed enemies. As with Creeper World 3 before it, Particle Fleet forces the player to fight a war on many fronts at once, all while managing logistics with a simple, intuitive energy transfer system.
You have to be able to direct streams of particles, arrange land-capturing turrets for maximum effect, build walls, destroy enemy walls, destroy enemy plasma (slows you down if you try to drive through), repair your own plasma, take strategic energy points, attack structures (quite difficult since only one very short-ranged weapon can destroy enemy structures), manage a ragtag group of loose cannon particles who don't play by anyone's rules (emergent), construct and command a fleet of spaceships which you may have designed yourself, depending on your play preferences, and ultimately rid yourself of any particulate before moving to the next system to start the process again.
Along the way you'll have to pick up info crates and blueprints for new ships (you can't build as many of each ship type as you want, you have to have a separate license for each one), and may be assisted by some very powerful capturable gun turrets. Or those turrets may belong to the particulate, and you have to withstand their withering rapid-fire barrages while shooting them with a mining laser. But it's all worth it when it turns around and fights for you in the end.
One thing I particularly like is the Doppel. Doppels are adorable squishy conglomerations of jello cubes in the shape of spaceships that try to crash into you to do damage. They can also shoot particles at you. Despite the fact that the map editor lets you create friendly allied Doppel spawners, they don't feature in the campaign, which made me sad. You can't boss them around like normal ships, but their AI is usually enough to make them useful.
Epic soundtrack makes you feel like you really are taking on the apocalypse itself and saving the universe. Thought it was worth mentioning.
There are exactly two reasons why I am giving this game a 9/10 instead of a full 10/10.
1: As of this review's writing, the map editor is extremely buggy, prone to crashing upon creation of a new map or locking the save/finalize buttons so you can't apply changes you've made. This is really frustrating because I like making maps and if I put a lot of work in to find that I can't save it, it pisses me off.
2: The game ships with a custom procedural scripting language called PRPL (Particulate Reverse Polish Language, if the CW3 naming convention is continued here.) It's awesome because you can build your own custom objects in the game to do virtually anything, including new ship parts and enemy types. The documentation is still lacking, which is why I sort of dislike trying to make things with it. Of course it doesn't help that the language itself is the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of an object-oriented programming language and an assembly language, but hey it's not too difficult to learn so I won't give it too much crap.
Other than that, good stuff. If you like real time tactics/strategy, you're liable to develop a crippling addiction to this game and you'll never regret a second of it.
EDIT 1: I found prpl reference on the wiki. It may have been added recently or it might have been there the whole time (derp). Either way, I'm upping from 9 to 9.5. If Virgil continues to update this game like he has with his last game, I'll happily make it an official 10.

Alright, so, it's review time again, this time I'm reviewing Particle Fleet:  Emergence.  I'll say right away, I'm very, very pleased with this one, just as I have been with the previous game in the series, Creeper World 3.  This is made by the same developer, which means this has the same incredible amount of sheer creativity that CW3 had.  This is similar to that in that it's something of an RTS / Tower Defense hybrid, though the RTS bit is alot stronger than in CW3.  But it sure as heck doesnt play even remotely like a traditional RTS, no sir.
Particle Fleet hits you with a few major differences right from the start:  Firstly, you have no big base to build up... this is a major departure from CW3's "network", and an even bigger departure from traditional RTS games.  In each mission, you'll start by warping in your HQ ship, a huge thing that can set up your first Energy Mine, preparing the foundations of your economy.   One thing you'll notice immediately is that instead of tons of little units like in most RTS games, in Particle Fleet you have a small number of really HUGE units.  All of your ships are big.  Really big.  These arent the dinky yet numerous turrets from CW3, instead they're big structures covered in turrets of their own.   Also, these ships dont have health bars... they're destructible in a dynamic way, in that if something hits the hull in a specific spot, that specific bit of hull will be damaged/broken.  Damaging things essentially eat their way into your ships, popping turrets and eventually destroying the core if they reach it.  But the SHAPE of each ship can determine how easy or not it is for that to happen.
These ships are constructed around any Energy Mines... which are the source of your resources in this game.  Unlike CW3's all-consuming Network, Energy Mines can only be constructed in specific locations, and have a certain range at which they can project energy.  You'll use this energy to build ships and other things, and to recharge ships as they continue to use their turrets.  You also have Omnis, which look like little turrets themselves, but can be used to capture land, or do anything that your HQ ship or Lathes could do (destroying/capturing structures, breaking up Struc and landmass, other things).   These are interesting in that unlike, say, reactors in CW3, these can be used in a variety of aggressive ways, since they can be flown around similar to how turrets moved in CW3.
And that's one interesting thing about this game, is that your units tend to be very versatile in terms of how you can use them (with certain exceptions).  This means there are a ton of different possible approaches, and all sorts of playstyles that you could use, that are all totally viable.  What's more, these different ships are just real fun to use.  My favorite is the Hammer; a huge blocky thing with a massive frontal hull, and the core at the very back of the ship.  Having next to no ranged weapons, this thing is meant for blocking damage.... or ramming stuff.  I'll never tire of doing this, it's just hilarious fun.  Other units tend to be very creative and entertaining in their own way too, things like Grabbers for instance, which can direct blue Particulate around the map.  However, there are restrictions: unlike CW3 you cant just build as many things as you want.  For example, the default fleet allows you to have only two Lathes, only one Hammer, only two Grabbers, and so on.  And a max number of Omnis.  This may sound restrictive, but you'll soon find that you feel like you have TONS of units.... there's alot to keep track of.  And build order ends up being very important on tougher missions... you'll be making some tough choices here, which makes things extra interesting.  As always though, there are many approaches to build order depending on your playstyle and strategy.  Nothing is ever set in stone in this game.  I cant even tell you just how much I appreciate this fact.
About the Particulate:  This serves as the enemy in each map (the red ones anyway, the blue ones are on your side).  As with CW3, this stuff isnt even remotely like a traditional enemy force in RTS games.  These are massive waves of individual particles that flow around the map in a variety of ways... different varieties of particles have different behavior, but individual particles are very weak; these are dangerous in the fact that they're in huge numbers, and they just... keep.... coming.  Like CW3 there are emitters around the map that never stop generating this stuff.   And what's more, these are used in tons of interesting ways in each map... you never know just what you're going to get from these until you start the map.   There are other threats, of course, such as Emergent (funky cubes that roam around awkwardly) or Doppels (big groupings of particles that look and act somewhat like your ships), among other stuff.  The creativity of the enemy units/behaviors constantly amazes me.
And of course, there's alot of interesting mechanics here, such as Amp Gems (can be used to grab "techs" that can be switched out at any time, or can be attached to ships to power them up) and other fun stuff.   All these mechanics and things are just as versatile as your ships.   Oh, and did I mention you can make your own custom ships?  You can have a seperate fleet, choosing either your custom-made stuff, or the default fleet, and there are seperate scoreboards for both.
The campaign itself is pretty interesting, but it's also quite short:  This is very clearly a game where the vast majority of content is found AFTER that.   Like CW3 it's pretty much endless... you can get procedurally generated maps, or download maps that others have made via the extensive editor.  The campaign is mostly there to tell a story, slowly teach you about every aspect of the game, and generally prepare you for greater challenges ahead.   There's TONS to do here... one of those games you can get hundreds of hours out of.
And that time is well spent.  This overall is just a very fun, deep, complex strategy game like no other, with so many possibilities.   If you're up for a strategy game that really does something NEW and different, something that's just darned fun while having the potential for great challenge.... this is the game to get.   Oh, and consider grabbing Creeper World, while you're at it, if you dont already have that.  It's a fantastic game too.
Definitely recommending this game very highly.

From the Depths, despite its blocky appearance, is a startlingly original game. From the construction features to the customizable combat AI, almost everything in From the Depths is innovative, exciting, and easy to use. In practice, many games in the construction genre tend to fall flat in certain areas. Unlike these, From the Depths is already well optimized, intuitive, and fun. From the Depths construction mechanic is unique, allowing extremely complex ideas to be easily realized. Unlike space engineers and many similar construction games, FTD's construction system is fluid, polished, and robust. Creating complex vehicles such as airships and battleships is easy enough- play the game, familiarize yourself with the mechanics, and boom! There you have it. That's all the experience you need to build something cool in From the Depths. Building something that works really well, however, is more difficult. The good news is, you'll never runout of ideas because From the Depth's extremely in-depth armor and weapons mechanics allow for hundreds of viable strategies.  Hollow armor designed to absorb enemy damage and insulate the core systems? Check. A floating reactor, relying on its powerful shields to rain death from above? Check. A wooden sailboat? Check. Several hundred wooden sailboats? Double check. Combat itself is no less impressive. The AI works surprisingly well out of the box. Because vehicles in From the Depths rely on many individual systems to continue working, combat in From the Depths is always dynamic and interesting. Aircraft usually rely on their speed to outrun danger, casting their lot on large engines and light armor. Landing a hit on an aircraft's jets is often enough to send them into a tailspin. Knock out the engines, and the battle's already won. Target a craft's radar and sensors, and leave a battleship blind. If you're brave enough, it's possible to go one step further and knock out a ship's master AI control. Target the propellers with torpedoes, and leave your enemies paralyzed. The possibilities are quite literally endless. When played In first person, From the Depths can become a fantastic roll-playing game. Ignoring the campaign, From the Depths is a fantastic sandbox. Ignoring the construction, From the Depths is a damn good action-RPG.
What I'm trying to get across here is that From the Depths is fun. Like, really fun. Everything works, and the price is right.
Do yourself a favor and buy it.
