*WARNING: THIS REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS*
I honestly cannot recommend this game at all.
The idea behind it is very nice - I'm a big fan of strategy and a sucker for most types of upgrade systems so this game seemed very appealing. The concept behind the game in general is fairly appealing. The aesthetic is excellent and the idea, though not wholly original is at least a breath of fresh air.
However, the game is just horridly designed in several ways. Most of the skills you can upgrade dont matter at all, and its basically impossible to know which ones untill youve finished the game. Horse riding for instance comes up literally once in an optional encounter that I never even got to - so much for those 30 skill points. Figuring out which moods need to be prominent to level which skills is also a thoroughly frustrating process of trial and error, one which the game does not assist you in any way. Considering that leveling skills is literally the only game mechanic, it's baffling that it's so difficult to actually figure out the mood system. The UI in generaly is fairly lackluster.
This isn't a strategy game. The vast majority of the skill checks are utterly irrelevant and the designer seemed to go out of his way to eliminate any semblance of strategy out of it by making the skill requirements for events arbitrary. For instance, there's a magical duel that may come up later in the game with the leader of an invading country, for which you need a very high skill in all three portions of the Lumen tree - and also either a high skill in swordfighting or DECORATION. I lost my first playthrough because apparently in order to confuse someone with magic I need to spend at least 120 points in the expression tree to get a high enough skill in decoration. This kind of arbitrary unpredicable nonsense annoys me extremely. The amount of meaninful skill checks is bafflingly small, I counter 3 in my winning playthrough that actually had a noticable effect on the plot.
Its not only the skill requirements that are arbitrary, the events in general are really very poorly designed. As a particularly egregious example there's an invasion by a foreign fleet in the game and one of the ways to repell it is to channel magic with at least 3 lumens in order to wipe the fleet out. Obtaining the first 2 is very easy - you and the mentor you get by basically not being an idiot at week two - but in order to obtain a third one the only way I figured out was to go into church with a high sense magic skill, notice one of the nuns is a Lumen and then talk to your mentor about it. If you do not do this, your mentor will insist that there's only two of you - despite being fully aware of the third lumen in the castle. Why this is ridiculous is that when you bring it up with her, she doesn't think revealing her presence matters at all. She's very secretive otherwise and getting other information out of her requires high skill checks, but she doesn't mind at all sharing this major secret about the nun. Why do you need to figure this out for her to suggest the option? More importantly, why isn't it enough to merely FIND OUT her secret in order for the option to show up? Why do you need to have explicitly mentioned it beforehand? It's arbitrary nonsense.
I still played through the game and it was basically enjoyable - though unsatisfying and frustrating at times, but the real kicker is the length of the game. I finished playing this in around 3 hours. Once you reach week 60, thats it. Theres nothing. I was expecting the game to continue - hopefully with some new mechanics - but once you reach that point there's nothing but a very lackluster epilogue.
One might expect this sort of game to be replayable but the weekly events aren't random at all so one has to drastically adjust their behaviour to get a different kind of playthrough - which is still fairly similar to the first one. Considering the natural repetiton of this type of game and the numerous problems with the design made the prospect unappealing to say the least.
I don't undestand how 92% of steam users justified a 10 euro price tag for a few hours of clicking but I sure as hell cant. Since there is no strategy required to win this game - it's literally about figuring out which 2 skills actually matter and leveling them, along with making a few fairly easy dialogue choises - there's also no alternative strategy one might try to win and no replay value. One does the exact same thing again with different decoration. I ended up unsatisifed and wishing I could get my money back. Some may disagree but I genuinely think the replay value is not high enough to justify multiple playthroughs.
So in conclusion, though Long Live The Queen has a nice concept behind it, it's too short and utilizes it's mechanics too poorly to provide any really satisfying experience. The experience just feels thoroughly insubstancial and shallow. There's no real depth or complexity because of the limited nature of design. If you can get it for extremely cheap on a sale it provides a fairly enjoyable distraction, but it is absolutely not worth the asking price.

Where do I start? Well, I really like this game and have a ton more hours into it than it shows (I played another couple hundred hours or so offline when I had no net access) so I'll start with the bad.
Bad stuff that really sucks:
Cars randomly flip over and send you flying out the door, then land on the roof or sides and blow up for no reason at all. You can be driving down a section of road that you've driven down dozens of times before with no problem and suddenly your vehicle decides it hit something and flips, leaving you precious little time to pull out whatever you may have stashed in the trunk before it blows up. The car blowing up also makes lots of noise, which is guaranteed to attract lots of zombies, so you have to choose real fast between trying to save what was in the trunk or running away before it blows to avoid the swarm of zombies.
Zombies sometimes clip through doors and walls. Granted this is WAY less frequent than it was at first but it's still annoying, especially when it's a Juggernaut clipping into an house full of people you're trying to recruit and starts ripping them in half making the mission fail.
The AI is as dumb as a box of rocks, possibly even dumber. Do not waste influence recruiting survivors to follow you because chances are they'll just get themselves killed and you'll not only be out the influence you spent but you'll be out a survifor as well. There's a mod that enables NPCs to use guns while following you around and this does help somewhat, but it's generally still not worth it unless you're doing something specific like clearing an infestation or taking out a few hordes that are headed for your base.
There's a few other minor gripes I have but pretty much everything else can be gotten around with mods so I'll just leave it at that.
Good stuff that's really cool:
Permadeath. Get careless or do something stupid and lose your favorite survivor that you've spent days building up? They're gone for good. Granted there IS a savegame backup utility made by one of the SoD forum members that you can use to take the sting out of things like this, but it's usually more fun to play without it unless you're trying for something specific.
Semi-realism in things happening when you're offline. Did you forget to search for that person who was reported as missing? They may very well be dead when you log in next. Did you skip stocking up on food before logging out? Morale will be low when you log back in, people will be hungry or even starving, and some may even have left.
Tactical options. There are a TON of different ways to do the same things. Need to clear an infestation or clear a house before scavenging it? You can rush in with a powerhouse character using an axe or sledgehammer and take out multiple zombies at a time, you can lay mines infront of the door then taunt the zombies inside the house until they come out and walk into them, you could just say screw it and chuck a pipe bomb or grenade through the window, or you could roll up in a car and lean on the horn until they start coming out and just run them over. Find a building you want to loot that has a few zombies outside it? You could sneak up and stealth kill them, or just run up and beat them down.
"Special" zombies (freaks). Sure, most zombpocalypse games have them, but the ones here all have either a pattern you can learn or a weakness to exploit and aren't just massive bags of HP with stupid damage output and cheesy special moves. I won't spoil it by giving details but they're all easily killable with the right strategy.
Base building. Ok, it's not as big or involved as I thought it would be, but it's still got a decent amount to do. There are only a few locations you can settle in and most have a very limited amount of space to work with, but you may not have enough manpower to grab one of the bigger bases at first and have to make do until you recruit more people and scavenge enough materials to settle in one of them. Even the biggest bases still won't let you build everything so you'll have to decide what to build and what to skip.
Combat. There are big differences between melee and guns, especially when you get a survivor built up enough to start getting specialized skills. You can get a "bullet time" type skill that slows time while you aim with a gun, or you can get special melee moves that can decapitate, cut zombies off at the knees, knock them down in a circle around you, even specialize in wrestling and suplex them.
It's worth noting again that no matter how much you build up a character they'll still die if you get careless, so it's a bad idea to get complacent and take too many risks.
Vehicles are useful beyond getting from point a to point b quicker. Yes, even though driving itself has it's share of glitches, if you're far from home gathering supplies it's worth it to take a vehicle so you can load the rucksacks into the trunk and bring back several at once instead of having to run back to base with each one individually, or spend influence calling home to get people to run over and grab them and risk losing someone along the way.
Now for my opinions in general.
Story mode is a lot of fun the first time you play through it, maybe another time or 2 just to try things a few different ways or get some achievements you missed but it does get old eventually having to do the same storyline stuff over again. Especially the tutorial area.
Breakdown, what can I say? It's sandbox mode. Same map as story but without the story, and you can "reset" the map by fixing an RV and taking off, which restarts with a little higher difficulty. Lots of fun if you just want to explore every building, kill every zombie you run across, or just try out different bases and see how long you can last.
Lifeline is a totally different game mode altogether. Story and Breakdown focus on base building, recruiting survivors, scavenging for supplies, and doing things more stealth than gung ho. Melee is king in story and BD but Lifeline is the opposite, if you go melee you can easily get swarmed and die horribly. You have a very limited amount of time for each objective and the Zombie density makes it hard to scavenge without being attacked so your best option is usually grab a gun, some ammo, a spare silencer, maybe a couple molotovs/grenades and headshot your way through while using influence to call in supply air drops.
In Lifeline your base will periodically be attacked by massive hordes of Zombies and when the danger level gets high you better be dropping what you're doing and heading back because if you don't make it in time you're almost guaranteed to lose people. The traps are a very nice touch and the outposts that add usable abilities are as well, using them smartly can be the difference between a siege being a walk in the park and a game over. Drone strikes and artillery support are your friends.

As much as I love "choose your own adventure" games, I wouldn't recommend this one.  Why?  Because while you'd think your choices would matter like in other similar games, they really don't.  Most choices you face lead to the same exact results and I don't mean it as in the long run.  Let's say you have the choice between killing or not killing someone.  First run through you'll go with one choice and next one pick the opposite choices figuring the story would be entirely different but no.  If you choose to spare the person the game will let you but most of the time when you choose to kill the person, you'll either fail or be interrupted, effectively making the game painfully linear.
You can't choose your own adventure, it's already been chosen for you.

Straight on silly game by COG and it works wonderfully.  There are flaws (the ending achievements are mostly determined by one big choice at the end with your previous decisions not preventing you from choosing any option or unlocking ones from you) but the sheer ludicrousness of some of the things you can do and experience make the experience awesome and enjoyable. For example, there's a subplot about a pair of anchors who have a failing on and off marriage, a rural cop who has more ordinance than small countries, and school kids who will help you steal gold.
The supervillainy/heroics are closer to something like Darkwing Duck, rather than your standard DC/Marvel parody.  The story can get dark (and there's even a lethality score to help represent  your bloodshed) but even the darker aspects aren't explicit.
One thing I really apprecciated was the "planning point" system. While there are decisions that are locked behind your past choices (for example: If you didn'tenslave a character, you can't use them when an opportunity presents itself), there are also locked choices that require planning points.  You acquire them by showing your ability to gain resources or favors from NPCs.  Locked choices that require PP allow you to take flashier options to sometimes use all of the other options at once.  It's a fun mechanic and gives replayability to the game since there aren't enough points to cover all locked choices)
While I still feel that Choice of the Deathless is COG's crown jewel, Diabolical is a lot of fun and well worth your time. Now, to make the greatest chocolate factory in the world...and keep all the chocolate TO MYSELF, MWHAHAHAHAHAHA!

Diabolical is an oddity on steam. It's an interactive story with some stats management that could not have been done in a book thrown in. However you should know that there is no music or art in here - I mean literally nothing at all. Its pretty much just writing, so if that doesn't sound like a good time to you, don't buy it. The good news is that the writing in Diabolical is good, even when you take into account that it is really the only thing it has. If I played an RPG with writing that had the same wit and ingenuity as this, I would be overjoyed - it is, in my opinion, a good deal better than most video game writing though in general I find writing in video games to be lackluster, it should be said.
I would recommend you pick up Diabolical if you are looking for a lighthearted, original and casual experience, if you think you can get past the fact that there is nothing presentation wise aside from text.

If you're an Ace Combat fan and have somehow lost possession of every single last gen console you had, and now only possess a slightly decent gaming PC, this is basically your only way to legitimately play some Ace Combat (though there are more, potentially nefarious, ways to get you some AC action on your PC, and I'd highly recommend those means instead). So this game gets a recommendation simply on that factor alone.
Heck, it's still, even if just slightly, better than the Hawx games. For experienced Ace Combat fans that have somehow overlooked this game, here's the two biggest changes that have essentially gotten this game to be seen as one of the least liked Ace Combat games. Period. Even compared to the DS release. Here they are:
1. DFM (Dogfight Mode). This mode is more or less a cinematic close range battle between aircraft. You either press the C key on the keyboard, or two shoulder buttons on a controller (default settings) when you close in on an aircraft (except helicopters, and the range is around 2.5k feet if I remember) and you'll enter this mode.
While an interesting feature, the biggest problem going for it is the fact that it's forced on you, and it just smells of gimmick. It's forced in that this mode is your only way of taking down ace pilots. I'll say that again, this is YOUR ONLY WAY of taking down ace pilots. On normal, you might be able to get lucky and take down certain weaker TGR_Leaders, but on higher difficulty this is almost impossible. And some of the harder enemies give you absolutely no chance of defeating them unless you use DFM. It's gimmicky because....well, same reasons, really.
2. The helicopter missions. Yes, this Ace Combat game lets you use helicopters. No, this isn't a good thing. The controls of the helicopters are clunky (get ready to use and abuse the autoaim feature), you're basically a sitting duck (slow moving, and everyone has you as their target...oh and the missile dodging animation of the 'choper is out right hilariously stupid) and the levels are, in essence, boring. This is just a poor execution, as I do think that helicopters can play a good role in an Ace Combat title, if done right. The helicopter missions almost single-handedly would have destroyed this game. The only saving grace against this is the rarity of the missions themselves. Power through them, get on to the much better jet missions.
Other than these two MAJOR problems with the game (from a pure entertainment standard, as I've had no technical problems such as glitches or bugs), this is an overall decent arcadey flight game. And your only option for an Ace Comabt game if you only own a PC.

In Orcs Must Die 2, the orcs invade you and you must defend the objective from them. Or should I say orcsssss because there is so much of them! And they have friends: Rock golems, Trolls, Ogres, Kobolds (those damn Kobolds), Kobolds with explosives (wait, that's the same thing isn't-it?) and other weird creatures that want you dead.
Hopefully, they are somehow forced to follow a certain path like in a tower-defense game. But you're not above them watching them being killed by your traps, you're
the map, facing them with your arsenal of weapons and traps.
This game is awesome because there is a lot of level and you have to adapt to each of them to win. (Well, the same strategy may work often but if you see something flying, you'll want to be sure you can catch him.) To do so, you have lots of weapons, spells, traps and trinkets with passive effects to chose from. You'll probably have 2 or 3 favorites ones you'll try to take every time. (A wall that throws arrows, man, that's strong.) There is many different ennemies and most of them must be dealt with a different way.
In the first levels, you'll more often stay in place pretty easily slaying the ennemy forces. But as you go further in the game, you'll find yourself running and cursing a lot more. You always have to watch your map to be sure that your traps are strong enought to secure the other path, that nobody passed beside you while you were fighting, that nothing is flying to the objective. You will learn to seek kobold first, defend your guards from the ennemy that seek them, use items to slow a wave down just to have time to deal with an other one, etc.. Franklin Fargo, who just attempted suicide by jumping off a cliff in the sea, wakes up in a strange abandoned facility with machines, laboratories and an odd synthetic voice that calls you "subject 13".
An anonymous beginning for an interesting story. This is an "almost" classic point & click game, so expect lots of riddles and exploration. More of the first and less of the second. The strong point of this game is certainly its set of increasingly more difficult riddles, some of them are puzzles, some of them make use of "items combinations", and others are just item interactions. The locations, on the other side, are quite limited as there are around 10 places to see (one less one more, I didn't count some small "rooms").
Besides the main mandatory riddles and puzzles, however, there are some "testimonies", which are nothing more than yellow vocal recorders with audio logs that can help you to better understand the story behind these abandoned laboratories. Yes, they're just collectibles, but they're like a game in a game as most of them are so hidden you're going to melt your eyes trying to find all of them. I actually had to use a guide to find the remaining testimonies as some of them were really impossible to find for me.
The intuitive interface has a particular feature where you can move your head to look around every time you zoom on items or places of interest. This is fundamental when you're looking for items, interactive objects or particular details in your inventory because some buttons or testimonies are really well hidden and you have to literally look around every corner to find out what you're looking for.
The engine is Unity, no flaws and no glory in this case, everything works fine but no miracle has been done here. The soundtrack could have proven to be interesting but unfortunately there's only a fistful of tracks which can be pleasant, anonymous or excessively ominous, depending on the track playing at the moment.
Where does the game fail? Small glitches and unexplained riddles like the fishing pole in the first case and the final riddle for the latter: the first won't come down if you pull the string too much and you're blocked, while the second
. I understand that you have to "find out", but there has to be a better way than trial and error

1849 is city builder set in 1849 during the California Gold rush. I haven't played many city builders in the past apart from SimCiity2000, so my experience is very limited so far.
The graphics on show here are pleasant, there is nothing special, it almost looks like the same style in Theme Hospital, sort of plump looking characters, and some nicely textured buildings. Each mission in the story modes offer roughly three objectives, these can be as simple as trading a certain amount of a resource with a neighbouring city, or to reach a specific level of social hierarchy in your city. The missions can last anywhere between 15 minutes, up to an hour.
The audio is done very well too, a classic cowboy tune plays in the background as you have your bustling city sound effects playing too. I really liked the music, I found myself dancing in my seat at times without realizing it.
From the tutorial, right until the later missions, you are walked through every new aspect of the game. I found the tutorial here to be very well designed and prepared you greatly for the missions ahead. There is definitely a high difficulty curve in 1849 too, once you get past level five, there is a sudden change in difficulty, and the missions become more and more in depth and you have to really focus on managing all of your resources and trades as efficiently as possible. This isn't a bad thing, it's nice to see games offering the challenging content.
I am about three quarters of my way through I think, and I am up to almost five hours of game play, there is also a sandbox mode included too, which will end up probably having around twenty plus hours in total from 1849, which is a lot considering it is only a £10,99 game.
I didn't find myself encountering any technical issues, runs very well although it's to be expected as it could probably run on a potato.
Would I recommend 1849? Sure, it might not be everyone’s cup of tea, but coming from someone who hasn't really played city building games, this is probably one of the better ones to start out playing.

What strikes me most about this game is its sense of style -- and I don't mean something shallow here. "Style" goes not only for the graphics and music (though both are excellent), but also for the gameplay itself. Your warplane flies and tumbles in sharp but graceful arcs, allowing you to execute fun and deadly maneuvers to dodge seemingly impossible situations and bring down screen-fulls of enemies. The action is fast-paced and exciting without feeling mindless or overwhelming. While the basic idea of the game will seem very familiar -- in fact, Luftrausers would look at home in an old-fashioned arcade -- the actual gameplay experience ends up feeling quite refreshing and innovative.
The graphics are simple, but very attractive, and the game definitely has its own unique look. There's a lot of detail hiding in these sepia-toned visuals. A little aircraft carrier is visible in the distance, launching those swarms of fighters you're battling. As your plane explodes, a skull-shaped mushroom cloud is visible for a split second, only to be blown away by the wind. You can tell that the art department put thought and effort into their work.
The music is catchy, a kind of quasi-militaristic, but still fun, rhythm, and there's an interesting mechanic here. Your plane is composed of three different parts (weapon, body, and engine), and each has its own musical theme. The soundtrack for the game is actually the mix of these three themes put together (a mix that works quite well), and as you unlock new parts for each category, that element of the music will change, resulting in a subtly different, unique tune. It's subtle, clever, and another example of the game's attention to detail.
The customizable parts also work quite well to keep the gameplay fresh. Each part you unlock will work in a completely different way, and will require a different play style. One of the body types allows you to ram enemies, but is fragile to all other damage, and will require nimbler flight and faster reflexes; one of the engines lets you plunge underwater, allowing you to evade pursuit beneath the waves, or attack battleships from below. It works to keep the game fresh. There's tons of combinations possible as you unlock new parts in each of the three categories. And each combination has its own name, highlighting the customized plane's personality! There's that attention to detail again.
In short, it's a very fun, very stylish game, that seems quite simple, but has a many subtle details and fun quirks. It's perfect for quick but satisfying gaming breaks, but there's also enough here to keep you coming back, and to give you plenty of enjoyable gameplay time.

This game is very arcadey; by that I mean if it cost a quarter to play you would be out hundreds of dollars very quickly. It also has the feel of many modern mobile games (the good ones) in its "mission" structure, its simple mechanics, and its combinatory building of airplanes.
Basically you pilot a plane, shoot down other planes and boats, complete "missions" (i.e. destroy 10 boats total! destroy 3 aces in one combo! etc.) which unlock alternate weapons, bodies, or engines for your plane that have interesting abilities (this body makes it so you don't take damage running into other planes, this engine lets you survive in the water). These each come with their own missions to complete. The longer you survive on a level the more challenging it becomes; eventually an enormous blimp or laser-wielding super ships will appear. If you can destroy the blimp you unlock SFMT mode which is basically bullet hell. If you survive more than 30 seconds you're doing well.
I thoroughly enjoyed the arcadey aspect of the game. A single play is quick, but you want to immediately jump right back in. The missions are a nice way to give you goals to work towards. I like that each combination of parts is given a unique name. It can be brutally difficult (especially SFMT mode) but it is a lot of fun.

Played this game years ago and wrote it off as a cheap Terraria re-skin, gave it another go with the 1.3 update and became an instant fan. The mechanics have been heaily re-tooled, a more in-depth story has been added as well as numerous small details that make the world more fun to explore. The end result is an excellent crafting/sandbox/survival game built inside a unique and detailed sci-fi world.
NPC and biome variety are what really set this game apart from Terraria. Lots of different biomes, and lots of NPCs from different races/species to inhabit them. Any given biome can be colonized by building shelters and allowing NPCs to move in, much like Terraria. Unlike Terraria these shelters can be customized to attract certain types of NPCs, for example you build a room with a stove/fridge and a chef may move in, build a room with lots of computer equipment and a scientist may move in, and so on. Different NPCs pay rent to you in different ways, essentially making them another farmable resource.
Exploration is key as it allows you to understand what kind of environments certain NPCs will flock to, and what kind of crafting materials each biome contains. Exploration also plays into the storyline which essentially requires you to learn as much as you can about the different races that inhabit the universe, and retrieve artifacts specific to those races.
Retrieving a race's atrifact requires you to go through a non procedurally generated "raid" level which always ends in a (typically) tough boss battle, these story segments help provide the gameplay with more clear goals, how you achieve those goals however is entirely up to you.
Inventory managment and general control set-up is very slickly designed, but not without problems. Combat is generally well-designed and fun with lots of weapon and enemy variety, however there are obvious advantages to certain weapon types which means a lot of high-level weapons end up being trashed simply because they aren't the right type.
Overall a fun and chill space adventure game you can sink countless hours into without it feeling too repetetive, well worth the $15 price. The developers of No Man's Sky should look to this game for inspiration.

I got this game about a year ago from my close friend, and honestly I'm very glad that that happened.
The pros of Starbound are the countless worlds, galaxies to explore and the ability to customize your ship. The fact that there's a lot of mods in the workshop is a huge plus too, because:
+ FU adds new worlds and monsters, without which the game gets a bit repetitive after a while
+ Frackin' Races, adds pros and cons to every race which means that picking a certain race isn't now purely for the aesthetics
+ More chests, monsters, races etc.
The combat is easy and it's not hard to fight, even the big bosses. Side-bosses are okay too.
There could've been more varied weapons, but I guess the problem is that they're randomized, so when you get the same level weapons they usually just look different and have a different special power. Again, this can be changed with mods, but I still wish the game had a wider weaponry (maybe like Terraria?). Corridors and dungeons leading up to bosses (so Boss Maps) are ok and I have no issue with them. The assistants that can help you out with fighting are also alright, but that's crew members, about which I'll talk later.
The story is also alright - although you can easily guess the ending, the characters are fun and I liked all of them equally. The story isn't what pulls you in though, what pulled me in was the endless exploration and planets, plus all the crafting and building. The Cult Classic hardcore hit of 2011, Dark Souls. What was once a chance taken by Fromsoft by following up on their fairly successful PS3 exclusive Demon's Souls has turned into a major staple of the gaming industry and the very definition of a "hard" game. But is it worth your time? I say this, the original Dark Souls, is definitely worth your time and money.
Despite being the second oldest game in the Soulsborne franchise, Dark Souls 1 is actually still entirely viable in terms of online invasions and summoning 6 years after release. Admittedly, you have to use the Dark Souls Connectivity Mod and sometimes you may have to wait a bit, but you can reliably be summoned or invade people during daylight hours in nearly any area of the game. Oolacile Township is still a PvP hotspot and the Undead Parish is so populated with humans during the day you can invade nearly 30 times in one hour. If you are down to Sunbro then you can always get summoned for the Gargoyles, Quelaag, Ornstein & Smough, Artorias and Gwyn. As an added plus of being so old, many of the hackers and griefers have moved on to Dark Souls 3, although not ALL of them are gone. Occasionally you will run into the crazy insta-curse or infinite health invaders / hosts. But hackers are a part of any online game, and Dark Souls 1 has relatively few (Stay out of Darkroot Woods.).
The biggest draw to the original Dark Souls is the combat. It's probably the most polished combat out of any of the Dark Souls games, including the fast-paced Bloodborne and Dark Souls 3. While it may be slow, you are always in danger. Every fight is a risk. But that is what makes it so compelling, unlike other games which can be breezed through. It encourages you to think in a fight. Look for an opening, and take the advantage. Pull back if things are getting too dicey. Parry an easy hit to take an enemy out of the fight. Every fight in Dark Souls is a constant strategical game, learning the moves of a new enemy to exploit them for your own gain, all the while trying to stay alive under their punishing blows. This is the combat that made the Dark Souls series the legend it is now. It is worth trying out, if you can handle it.
Both in PvP and PvE, nearly any combination of weapons and armor you desire can be viable if you put the effort to mastering it. If you want to use a Great Scythe and Pyromancy? Have at it. Beefy tank with a spear and Greatshield? Sure, go for it. Naked dude running around throwing lightning bolts? You'd be surprised. This sort of accesability makes the game amazingly replayable, with every run a new experience and new combat style to master. This makes it vastly superior to Dark Souls 3, in which the PvP meta is basically "Medium Armor and a Straight Sword or GTFO". If you want to have a fun time with the combat, get Dark Souls 1.
Possibly what the Dark Souls series is known for the most is the absolute spectacle it makes of the bosses. Every boss is completely unique (Except for the Copy and Paste Demon, ffs Fromsoft) and is a great obstacle to overcome. They all have their own strengths and weaknesses, encouraging analysis on how to take them down with what you currently have. While you may die (And you probably will), each clash is a learning experience. You learn how they act, how they respond. You can take this information, and use it your advantage. "If I stand underneath him, he'll try and sit on me." You can use this information to bait out an attack, and then punish it. And the feeling of exhiliration when you finally land the killing blow on a boss is unlike nearly any other game I've played. Each run with a different build is almost a new challenge, and it never loses its charm.
Due to being over 6 years old, Dark Souls 1 runs flawlessly at 30FPS, 720p without any dips in performance on a modern computer. If that isn't enough for you, the popular community mod DSfix can boost those numbers to 60FPS and 1080p resolution easily, at the cost of occasionally falling through the floor. People have reported horrible FPS in places like Blighttown, but I have never experienced these myself.
The Souls series originated on consoles with both Demon's Souls and Dark Souls 1 starting out as PS3 Exclusives. This shows heavily in the control scheme. The keyboard controls for Dark Souls are a clunky, unwieldy device that is incredibly difficult to use and even if mastered, will still be inferior to a controller in every concievable way. With the default control scheme, it is impossible to keep your shield up AND parry, as that requires you to Shift + Tab, which opens up the Steam Overlay. TL;DR, buy a controller for your computer before you buy Dark Souls 1.
However, not every death you experience will be fair. Yes, you did have your shield up when that attack hit. Yes, you did dodge that attack. For every "legitimate" death, there will be a few "illegitimate" ones. While they are infuriating, especially if you have been fighting a particularly intense boss battle, you have to move on eventually. There is simply no way of avoiding these. I still believe that despite these atrocious results of broken hitboxes or glitches, the game is worth it in the end.
While people praise Dark Souls for not holding the players hand, I believe that at least giving them a road sign would not be unwarranted. The game does NOT tell you at all what you are doing and where you should be going. The only way to even find out what to do to progress is to talk to the strange homeless man sitting next to the bonfire. Even then, he still doesn't tell you where to find these objectives. The other problem is the sort of hub bonfire at Firelink Shrine. There are three different paths to take, but only one is the right one for your first time. The other two paths lead to mid / end game areas that will almost instantly result in your death, but will not indicate you shouldnt be going this way. This happens multiple times at branching points, and it constantly makes you question if you are actually going the right way or not.
I wont name names for the sake of spoilers, but many incredibly helpful NPCs DIE unless something completely random is killed by the player. Two NPCs are killed by others, which are not even hinted at before it happens and cannot be undone. These killings lock you out of getting ANY high level miracles like Great Heal or Wrath of the Gods, and can also disable Firelink Shrine PERMANENTLY until you reach a very mid-game area, about ten to fifteen hours later. Another NPC can be murdered by a parasite unless you unlock a shortcut by giving 30 humanity to a hidden covenant, therby allowing you access to the area to kill the parasite. These abrupt murders are stupid, and while many players never fall for them again past the first time, its the first experience that counts the most and these are just needlessly cruel and unfair punishments for something the player could NOT have known without googling it beforehand.
While normally very compliant, the camera in Dark Souls is infamous for being a fickle piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ Occasionally it will get stuck to a wall, ceiling, or other sort of random object and whip to the side. This often happens when traversing dangerously precarious walkways, causing the character to suddenly plummet to their death. This sort of occurance is uncommon, but it is not even close to rare and it is COMPLETELY the game's fault.
Dark Souls 1, like all games, has its faults. But in the end, it's a unique experience unlike any other, and its worth buying for that.

I was rooting for Vinci Games, I really was. I wanted to like this game so bad. My brain was screaming don't buy this game, but I decided to follow my heart and give it a try. I regret my decision so much.
Here are my reasons:
I dropped my gun and couldn't pick up another one, the optimization was iffy, I got stuck on a pipe, the game design seem to be limited to grab the keycard and hit the thing, and in the short time I played I managed to turn the entire game wire frame by hitting esc and when I pressed F2 the entire thing quit itself. It took me all of 12 minutes to want my money back, as this game does not offer a compelling story or fun game experience. It was ear destroying ambient noise, unappealing AI interaction and absolutely no depth in combat, with a complete lack of any other mechanic. Unlike the description, there where almost no dynamics, and I was not even slightly thrilled playing any part of this game. This game is so bland, it makes air control look fun. You just run around and hit the same 4 or 5 monsters the entire game, with absolutely nothing satisfying about getting a kill. Sometimes there is one on the floor, which does the same thing, and sometimes there is a big one, which does the same thing. You just pathetically wallop them with your flashlight until they crumple up and instantly disappear. If you want a good sci-fi horror shooter experience, you are probably just better off installing Doom 3 again, because this game seems to be a horrible mangle of concepts from different titles that got tossed into one giant unappealing mess of a game. This is possibly one of the worst games I have ever played in my life. Even worse than early access, because they are trying to market this featureless pile of dung as a pulse pounding horror game.

"Conclusion" is a game where you trod through hi-res (but bog-standard) scenery for 20 minutes. You follow a single path and pick up five notes on the way, which tell a sad story in broken English. Then it ends.
That's really all there is to it. The ending is probably supposed to come across as a stunning revelation, but since the game never let me build up a connection to my character, it did nothing for me.
Sadly, almost everything about this game is of horribly shoddy quality. The writing is bland and superficial, and the English translation is so bad that I'm not sure what is worse - the unintelligible phrases or the hilarious mistranslations (e.g. when he keeps talking about his "incontinence", but actually does not mean bladder problems, but rather his inability to stop drinking). I am not sure why the designers thank someone for the translation in the credits, because it honestly reads like someone just put the text through Google translation and never even tried to proofread. There are also voice-overs, but they are so muffled that they remain barely audible throughout. The developers implemented one single interactive gameplay element (picking up notes), and they did not even get that one right - on two occasions, pressing "E" did not put the note back, and I had to go on walking sideways because a huge page of paper kept obstructing the center view.
The one aspect of this game that isn't obnoxiously bad, is the scenery - it looks beautiful, but that's more because of the engine than because of the game's design. When looking at the details, it is clear that even here the devs did not spend much attention, for example there is a bicycle wheel with spokes that go right through the rock underneath.
I'm sorry. I really tried to find some redeeming quality somewhere in this game. There is none. I even went through it twice in case I missed something, only to confirm that the second "playthrough" was as dull as the first one.
This appears to be the work of a mapmaker, who thought they could create a game, but failed in practically every aspect. I would be more lenient in my verdict if there was at least something in the game that was worth building upon - a spark of creativity, an original idea, or something that looks done right. But the entire game is just dull, with shoddily implemented ideas and minimal mechanics. Asking money for this, even if it's just a dollar, seems bizarre.

The term "walking simulator" has never been more apt. I will now spoil the entire game:
There's a tiny bit of story from the character which you'll have trouble hearing because the audio level is very low and there's no subtitles. Basically, he got drunk and got into a car crash. But it's that kind of "clever" story where you start dead and don't realize it until the end.
What actually happens in the game? You're a guy who magically appears at a collapsed tunnel entrance. You walk forward down a road. You encounter a note but you can't read it. You encounter a tire you can pick up (but you can't move while holding it). You walk some more. Then walk a lot more. You encounter a bicycle frame and wheel, but you can't pick either up. You encounter a grave. And several more notes you can't read. You eventually find a wrecked car which is apparently so detailed that the game slows to something like 8 FPS when it's on-screen. Before you reach the car, the game cuts to a black screen that basically says, "sorry but our next game will be better" (paraphrasing).
The game has trading cards, but since you can "beat" it in 30 minutes, you'll exhaust the game's value long before you collect the cards.

Yes, ULTRA Street Fighter IV. What can I say about this game? It's Street Fighter. Its a 2.5D, 1vs1 fighting game with a large and varied cast of charactes. There's lots of combos, ex moves, supers, ultras, awesome art design and great music.
Picking up and playing the game is easy but becoming good is difficult. Easy to play, hard to master. Button mashing only gets you so far. You really need to learn the controls and master the combo moves. You have to learn when to strike and when to stay back so you don't get countered and punished. Just like any compeditive game theres lots of strategy and quick thinking involved.
Playing the arcade mode with a character gives you only one piece of the whole story. You need to play through it with all the characters to get the complete story, plus you unlock things like titles, costumes and taunts so it's worth it if you like unlockables.
Technicaly the game is outdated now that Street Fighter V is out but it's still fun to come back to it, especially for me. This was the first Street Fighter that I really go into, and I have my college roommate to thank for that.

if you look at my library, you will notice I have many games that focus on running a country, speciically a kingdom. However, the fact that this game has a branching story, rather then a sandbox, makes things very diffrent; it's not so much a simulation, or stradegy, but a puzzle. This puzzle requires a few things from you; 1) that you can observe what people say 2) that you can remember this across playthoughs (beacuse you will die) and 3) that dependent on these remembered things, you can modify your skills to fit the situations. The world, and background story, is cleverly placed into little statements you recieve upon "leveling up" your skills, making the story a interconnected part of the gameplay. You can be a tyrant, you can be a diplomat, I was a war-lord and sorceress; they called me cruel, but I did what was needed, and did so in a way that didn't stagenate the economy, nor put into danger many of my people. Has great replay value, and is definetly 2 gems in one game.

My niece is 5.  Much to her parents' consternation, she wants to be a princess in pink when she grows up.  They only grudgingly allow her to have pink princess paraphernalia.  They also limit her time spent in front of video games.  So when I told her I had a game about being a princess, my neice almost exploded with excitement.  "Do the princess game!" she shouted.  Repeatedly.
So I fired it up, and I read (some of) the text to her.  We went through trade negotiations and border disputes.  My niece was a little dissapointed in the amount of text, but liked the pictures.  She didn't understand why princesses had to deal with all these boring things.  "Being a princess is hard work," I told her, "The whole kingdom is depending on you.  You can't afford to just play around with dolls."
I went through the game and we watched Elodie grow into a capable swordswoman and powerful sorceress.  In single combat, Elodie was a devastating opponent.  My niece asked me if she was a good princess.  "Elodie crushes her enemies.  She sees them driven before her, and hears the lamentations of those left behind.  Yes, she is a good princess."  My neice was unimpressed.  But she did like Elodie's magical girl outfit the best.  Which is good because I never quite got around to maxing out those stats.
Elodie became queen through force of arms, magical might, and bloodshed.  My niece's enthusiasm for my princess game was tempered, though she still likes it.  "Boring princess game!  Play the boring princess game!" she says now.

I'm not in the mood to attack other civilizations after building my own city from scratch and I like a little more of a "story" when I build up my things, so I thought 1849 was going to be a nice panacea to my City Builder Sim illness.
Not the cowbell I needed.
1849 is very slow and frankly easy to win each level. However, it is time consuming. The majority of the time you've built the required number of buildings and you're waiting for them to accumulate the needed number of supplies to move onto the next section of California to colonize. The plot of land you're given is relatively tiny, given how much you can really move around.
Each game I was given an "edge" from completing a previous round. There was no right or wrong answer to what helps you, just whatever helps you in how you finish the objectives in the time alotted. This, I found helpful. It benefitted my playing style which is very kind because I have a certain way I like to set up my time management games. It also allowed me to experiment each level.
What drove me relatively bonkers was that nothing really changed from level to level. Usually there's something new introduced that makes a very significant impact, but this never happened in my course of playing. I had to use multiple important buildings because the reach was impossibly short and your town/settlement will go to hell in a moment's notice and you will not salvage it unless you can accomplish a few key things in the first few moments of establishing your settlement.
But once you figure out your pattern of play, you generally just sit there, wait for your settlers to upgrade their houses, and just keep refueling things.
It's perhaps the worst city building sim I've played and I was highly disappointed. Wasn't worth the price I paid. I've honestly just sat still most of the time and done absolutely nothing. It's also a bit dated-looking as well so there are prettier games out there for your money.
Maybe this could be a game to teach small children about areas of California during the Gold Rush, but I don't believe this could keep their attention too long. This likely plays better on a tablet or a phone, as well. Personally, I'm not a fan and even after forcing myself to give it a good go, it wasn't meant to be.

I really enjoy this game, it's addictive in a strange, perfectionist, control-freak sort of way. I love city builders but was looking for some a little more simple than a huge sim-city type deal and without the combat that other strategy games have. I never get bored with the diverse scenarios each map brings and the acheivements you can obtain.
I have had no major gameplay issues, and have no serious complaints. As far as suggestions may go, I was hoping for a little more financial control, rather than really just balancing the wage-rent ratio. It gets a little annoying having to manually go in and sell my products every 10 seconds, whereas it would seem like a nice addition to offer contracts to the other cities in the same way you sometimes get from completeing commissions- every month a certain number of resources is sent over automatically.
Also, the population(?) advisor lady gets on my nerves, it seems like people in every city want to expand insanely quicker than your set up or ready to handle regardless of the scenario. Obviously people in a vineyard paradise are going to demand nice things, but in small mining town scenarios people begin to demand luxuries that are not availiable for that map (cobbler, tailor, etc) and end up throwing a hissy fit and leaving. That sort of control of expansion and growth seems  like it would be nice to have as the mayor. It seems unrealistic that during this time period a small mining outpost would attract the rich, family-type crowd.
On the opposite end of the spectrum I have had issues with houses refusing the expand even though the conditions are met, but I have no idea if that is part of the game considering they were the first few houses I built and subsequent houses did expand quickly.
And one tiny thing that just upsets my OCD personality, is that you cannot rotate buildings. In my opinion, its the simple details that sets a game apart from a city-builder farming phone game. Even from the screen shots you see building stacked in clusters behind and infront of each other. This is a game that can boast time-period accuracy, but the concept of anyone, anytime moving into town and opening up a shoestore that directly blocks your front porch seems unlikely. It's purely an aesthetic annoyance, but seemed worth a mention.
Overall though, seriously I love this game. And it takes some serious willpower to walk away even for a second.

I tried this game again after deleting it last year and again this year.
Their idea of a boundless map seems like a small map to me, on tiny you can only fit 2 buildings on it.
All building are available at start (nothing to unlock). All buildings have the exact same 2 upgrade, 15% increase in production and +1-2 extra items per week.
You're restricted to 4-5 trade routes. Each trade routers gives you the ability to buy and sell 1 item. You can only sell low $$$ items. You will alway be able to sell atleast 1 raw resource and 1 manufactured. 2-3 of your trade routes will always be for either gold, metal, or some other limited quantity resource. Leaving you with 2-3 resources to sell items. The rest you just constantly stockpile into infinity. There will always be some resource you must buy that you can't produce.
You can't tell which buildings need upgrades and which don't unless you click on each one. Also when you run out of iron ore, you get no message on it what so ever, since it's expensive to run, you have to be constantly clicking on the mine to find out if all the ore is gone.
When selling resources, you can only sell 500 at a time. Then 500 again, and again. This really doesn't make sense to me, if I have 5k of wood to sell, why not just let me sell it all in one click?
The most expensive item in game is pickaxes, these are more valuable then anythintg else.
Lots of metals on the map = 2 locations that run out quickly and need lots of pickaxes and are expensive to run. Also stone is very rare and you usually have to buy it. You will always be able to buy pickaxes, stone, and iron ore.
You'll only need a couple of houses and everything else is industry, police, & fire.
When you run out of needed items, there's no warning, all you'll see is people moving out and then you have to figure out why.
The game doesn't allow you to go bankrupt, if you run out, you get another $500.
In every sandbox game there will always be one building you can't build.
This game is tedious and repetative. I completed some of the missions and did some sandbox play, but frankly it just gets boring after a while. All you're doing most of the time is clicking buildings to check upgrades and seeing what you have in your storehouse that has unlimited storage. Once you've built everything and that doesn't take long on normal speed, last game it only took 1 hour (if that) there's nothing else to do but start a new game.

The type of resources you can create/gather/mine/farm are pre-selected from the beginning and sometimes make no sense. You can't unlock new trade routes. You can't unlock new buildings. Sometimes getting off the ground is incredibly difficult, other times, building a massive city, that can quickly become unweildy because for instance, the lumber cycle, lumber -> boards -> furniture, is extremely slow, so you may for instance, run out of room to put lumber yards.

Probably the closest we'll get to Portal 3. Overall, a wonderfully satisfying mod.
Weak points of this mod:
- The story is very thin. Don't expect the carefully-planned plot of Portal 1 or 2. It sets the premise but that's about it. It's almost entirely superfluous. The ending is almost nonsensical, but in the end, it's about as sensible as the rest of what passes for a plot. Fortunately, the point of this mod isn't the story.
- It is also quite short. Expect about 1 hour play time. That's understandable, considering the small number of people who made this. But I really enjoyed it, so 9 levels aren't enough!
- The progression of difficulty is a bit out-of-order. The hardest level was about half-way through (level 6, I think), and thereafter things seemed to get easier. But maybe that was just my learning curve.
Strong points of this mod:
- This mod is well made, especially considering the small number of people behind it. The visual style is very nice--it is unique to the mod, but based heavily on Portal 2's graphics, so you still feel that you're in a different section of the same game. Everything is so shiny and smooth! The sound clips and so on are pretty much all from Portal 2 as well. I had no problem with glitchy graphics.
- The time machine mechanism is explained nicely with computer screens that have Bendy demonstrating various skills. Much like the original Portal, the first several chambers are very helpful in building up your skills for the harder levels later on. This is a very useful way of teaching how to use the time machine without changing the feel of Portal too much, because, unlike cube- and button-based testing, it's not at all obvious from the get-go.
- The actual mechanism of the time machine is *very* fun. I feel that it wasn't utilised to its full extent here--there is a lot more that could be done with it. But most of the chambers have multiple solutions, all requiring use of the time machine, so you can play to your strengths and figure things out in a variety of ways.
- Level design is very nice. As in Portal, the early levels make it fairly clear what needs solving, but later ones become more open-ended. Every level has been designed with the time machine strongly in mind. It's quite impressive, when you consider the potential complexity given by the time machine.
- It's free!
Considering the price ($0), this is definitely worth playing. I would absolutely recommend it as a fun mini-continuation of Portal 2. The graphics, mechanism, and level design are all at a very high standard, higher than most games that cost actual money.

Ace Combat Assualt Horizon Enhanced Edition. What can I say about this game that most haven't already said about it already? Well for one this is one of the only games I actually bought off steam on release because I was a fan of the ace combat from the Playstation era and I saw a bunch of previews as well a friend on steam had it. I wasn't dissappointed with the game. It met most of my expectations.
+ Gameplay - great gameplay. It simulates a good dog fight what you would expect (at least what I imagine an actually air combat dog fight would look like)
+ Variety of planes - This game has a whole selection of planes, and even helicopters. As well as a range of weapons from Air-Air missles and Air-Ground missles
+ Story isn't too complexe but it gives the game some plot that makes it interesting enough to want to see it through to the end.
+Graphics - The graphics are top notch for a game of this genre. The cockpit view is astonishing though I wished they'd make taking off and landing a bit more complex to give it an actuall sim feel. Though I didn't like the obstruction in some of the cockpits of some of the fighter jets as it made that view unplayable but I also liked how u could swivel your head and look around in that view.
Now some of the negatives. Albeit I thought and read at the time that normal difficulty wasn't the way to play this game as it made things a bit too easy. So I went full out and had it on elite. The first half of the game was exillerating as it made things intense and in Elite your jet didn't recover from damages as opposed to the other difficulty modes. So if you're looking for a good challange then I suggest you go this mode and its ment for veterns of the series.
This is a plus and some what a negative. The DFM or (Dog Fight Mode) its the selling point to this game but I think its more of a gimmick. Well on the higher diffuculty its a must to get into this combat mode as it makes taking down enemies a neccessity as without DFM you'd have to expend a ton crap of missles to take down one or two enemies. But overall DFM mode on easier difficulties made the game too easy, and to continue on my first playthrough on Elite it became so frustrating during the Spooky mission where you were in a B2 bomber doing bombing run and helping out ground units. I kept dying and it♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off that I stopped playing this game but eventually I came back and preservered and then I came onto another hurdle in Elite that frustrated me so much that I had to bumb it down to Ace mode, it was also another non fighter jet mission which seems to be a trend. I get that they wanted to expand on the story and give the series a change of pace but the combat in the chopter and the B2- and stealth bomber missions just made the game feel off and it broke up the pacing of the game. That's also a Plus for this game as you can set the difficulty at any mission. But that also leads me to one of the biggest negatives of the game:

These missions over stay their welcome imo. You're introduced early on to a black hawk chopper which at first wasn't bad but the missions length go on and on. When you think its done they throw one or two final objectives and thats through out the game its just in non fighter jet missions these become tidiuous chores rather than fun objectives.
Overall this is a fun game and it made me feel like I was actually pilioting and dog fighting. The fights were intense and the wide range of vehicles makes it enjoyable.
I give this a 8.5/10 its worth a buy and I haven't really bought any game off release besides a couple but this is one of the games I would happily purchase full price again.

I see a great deal of "Not Recommended" in the reviews, and it seems a great many of them tout faulty controls as a game breaker. I will tell you right now, the default controls are designed to appeal to the kind of person who has never played a flight simulator. If you go through the control menus, you will find an option to revert to a more traditional flight simulator. Something to take the majority of the game "off the rails" as it were. There will still be the occasional track shooting section, as the gunner of an AC-130, or a Blackhawk, but the meat of the game, the flying, will feel considerably more natural. This was a mistake on the developers part, to default to a more infantile method of control scheme, while bearing the relatively trusted name of ACE COMBAT, but to err is human.
That being said, if you are looking for a tight, hardcore, physically sound, flight simulator, you will likely be disappointed. However, if you are a video game enthusiast, and are looking for a fun experience, this game is certainly worth a try. The game opens powerfully, focusing primarily on a hyperbolic view of dogfighting, but quickly spreads out to encompass other methods of flight to simulate. Before you know it, you'll find yourself in the seat of an AH-64 Longbow, as new mechanics are introduced. Then, you will make use of the aforementioned AC-130. Make no mistake, this is an attempt to broaden the horizons of the series, and draw in a more "action-phile" crowd. As I've seen, video game elitists hate things like this. I hope this explains the majority of the negative reviews, but if you're on Steam, you've seen the state of the internet, and you know that some people like to gripe, as they lack other methods of communicating.
The tl;dr of it, I found this to be a fun game, full of amusing content, and wrought with controller breaking challenge. Admittedly, the story is bland, but I defy you to find a war game that has a truly scintillating and hereto for untold story. Take a chance, make sure to change the control scheme, and test your mettle. I wasn't disappointed, and I don't think you will be either.

Oh Orcs Must Die! 2...what can I say after way too many hours of playing?
Pro:
1) Great mixture of Tower Defense and 3rd Person Shooter
You really have to think of a strategy for every level and, especially when playing the Sorceress there are hardly levels where the same strategy works twice. This is a really nice change from OMD 1. So you have to use your brain in every level. The third person shooter part adds nicely to it as you cannot lean back in the beginning and your very own skills are also needed.
2) Co-op!
You can play with a friend in this one and especially for Nightmare and Endless it is a load of fun, especially when aiming for high scores or just randomly picking traps and weapons and seeing how far you get.
3) Replayability
Collecting skulls, getting high scores, beating the map with War Mage and Sorceress, trying new combinations of traps and so on and so forth....you can replay a level a hundred times and it will hardly ever get boring
Cons:
1.) Co-op
Yes, this is a Pro, but especially in War Mage and if one of the players is experienced, Co-op gets old and boring rather fast as it offers no real challenge. Even Nightmare can get too easy. So personally, I think there should've been an additional mode or something comparable to make Co-op a little more challenging.
2.) No real changes
OMD 1 was great. OMD 2 is great. But there are hardly any REAL changes. Half of the game even uses the same general map layout as the first game. I'd love to see differences and new experiments, maybe commanding the Orcs for a while or something.
Conclusion:
Especially during a Sale you just cannot go wrong with the game. You can use the demo to try it out and see for yourself whether or not you like it, too.
Fun way to spend some time just like the prequel, and the multiplayer makes this game 5x as fun! I reccomend getting it if you can convince a friend to buy it too :)

I want to point out that I only played the co-op campaign and have no knowledge of the single player experience.
That being said there's a few reasons why I absolutely loved this game.
The beginning was absolutely frightening, being thrown in an open-world styled creepy town was amazing to explore together. It really had that creepy, lonely vibe going on and it was great to explore that in co-op.
The puzzles weren't that easy, but also not impossible, so I thought adding these types of puzzles definately threw the horror experience in a fresh direction.
The first encounter with the "monsters" was absolutely frightening and gave us a great scare/laugh when we had to figure out the mechanic of the game and how we were to overcome these threats.
(This footage can be seen in this link, should you be interested in a preview of the game:
)
The only downside I can note is the fact that there's only 2 types of monsters and therefor only 2 mechanics that one must apply. The game became rather predictable after a few deaths and the monsters lost their scary aspect.
BUT with the new patch a lot has changed: random spawning locations, enhanced pathfinding and so on, so the playthrough should be a lot more interesting compared to when we did it because we played the game pre-patch.
The creators informed me that they will first fully enhance the game and polish it the best they can and I feel like that's a great mindset. I bought the game in sale (€5,93 instead of €8,99) and it was totally worth the money. We completed the co-op campaign in about 4 hours and had tremendous amounts of fun playing it.
Bear in mind that this game was developped by only 7 (or 8, can't remember exact) people and I find that they did a great job!
I will definately keep up with their work and play their next upcoming games.
TL;DR - Absolutely worth it if you want a good puzzle/scare game with a good difficulty/challenge to play with a friend.
(I have no knowledge on the singleplayer, but I assume it uses the same mechanics. Being alone might make it a lot scarier though, definately worth a shot too!)

Great game overall. It also has the makings of something even greater. The base game can be fun and interesting, has replay value since most survivors and all loot is intelligently randomized, so one time you may find a good medic and a bunch of drunks along with an abundance of heavy firearms. Another you might find mechanics, cooks, and farmers, but nothing but .22 pistols and a random assortment of melee weapons. You might decide to live at different locations or utilize different strategies for survival. Kind of fun to see how different things pan out.
Breakdown DLC takes the normal game but makes it far more challenging. Survive in the same map, then when you've exhausted your resources, move on to a newly repopulated version of the same map taking only supplies and a hand full of survivors, only every time you move on, things get harder. More zombies, more specials, less cars, less resources, less to find all together. Go for as long as you can, or as long as you want.
Lifeline DLC was a bit lacking. Fairly short storyline. You can extend it out but you'd just be doing the same things for longer; surviving sieges on your base as you manage to rescue and evacuate civilians here and there. Map is interesting but small in terms of areas to explore.
Can't wait for the Year One Survival Edition.

Stay Close is a pretty interesting concept. Although it didn't really offer what the trailer showed us, it still felt like something good. It's not a really story driven game, so if you're looking for a story this isn't the game for you. But it did bring something new to the table. You're thrown in a city without any clue as to what you're supposed to do and It reminded me of Silent Hill in a way. You have to aquire certain items to "clear" a level. Yes, it's been done before I'm sure, but you have to micromanage two different creatures at the same time, there are different areas to unlock by completing the objectives, and it has a functional coop mode. On top of that, the monsters are very different from eachother (the complete opposites). One is attracted by light and one is stopped by light. This game is even more appealing in coop since you can work as a team, and if one player dies you die as well hence the name "Stay Close" you really do have to stay close. Yes, you will definitly get scared a few times there's no avoiding it. It's been a very interesting game so far. Only thing I'm not fond of is the riddle parts, where you need to solve a riddle to "unlock" the next level. It kinda slows the pace of the game and maybe once or twice had to google the riddle like an idiot. And after the first part, the creatures tend to get repetitive since they are the same all over again (although I've only played through 2 levels so far). Maybe add more variety there. Other than that, I think it's worth taking a look at it. If you have a friend to play with it's an even better experience. For an indie game it feels pretty good. I'll give it a 7/10.

Subject 13 is a quaint little game. I think it's a little pricey for its content, but otherwise a rare gem that is definitely worth consideration. I've broken my review for it down into positives and negatives so you can weigh if you think it is worth the money.
- Really ingenuitive puzzles that will wrack your brain, while still having logical elements. A puzzle halfway through the game involving a compass really didn't make much sense to me, but the others were all well-designed.
- A brilliant twist on your standard point-and-click adventure game with items; you actually have to examine the items in your inventory such as containers and revolve them in a three dimensional space in order to find secret compartments and such.
- The dialogue has full voicing with believable actors.
- The art style is rather unique, and a refreshing change from many other games released recently. This certainly helps with the immersion in the game.
- There's both Steam trading cards and Steam achievements. The achievements are both reasonable and logical, and have a good balance between difficulty and obtainability.
- The game is too short. Puzzles are a key aspect to this game, and without using any in-game hints or resorting to any sort of walkthrough, I was able to complete the game in under 5 hours. For a game priced at NZ $24, that's not really good value for money.
- There are a few game-breaking bugs. You have to 'zoom in' to see the majority of puzzles up close. For some reason, occasionally you will be unable to zoom out afterwards. This means you will be stuck looking at the puzzle, even if you have already solved it. You will be unable to progress through the game without saving and quitting, which will sometimes set you back a fair distance. In conjunction with this, there is a secondary bug in the third chapter where the testimonials will sometimes disappear or not spawn at all after reloading a checkpoint. This would be an annoying bug in itself, but coupled with occasionally being forced to restart a chapter, it can be devastating if going for the associated achievement!
- The weak storyline. There was no general objective. Having completed the game, I still haven't discovered 'the real story', as advertised. While progressing through the puzzles, you run into distorted images of your dead wife. There's absolutely no explanation of why you keep seeing images of her or information regarding how she died. For the matter, there's not even a backstory to the protagonist or an explanation of how he ended up in the facility on the island in the first place.
- Poor graphics for the release date. I personally am a fan of the classic art style, but the game should definitely not be advertised as having "stunning 3D rendering" as a "key feature". When you're using over 10 million polygons per scene whilst running Direct X 12 (like some other games released roughly the same time), *then* you can advertise "stunning 3D rendering".
This is a quaint game built by a small-time solo developer, rather than a large company. While the price is a bit high in relation to the length of the game, Subject 13 is definitely a game that you should give a chance if you can grab it on special. The puzzles are a step-above those in similar games that have been released by fully-fledged companies, and the high cost will hopefully go to cover the developer creating some more gems in the future.

An adequate puzzle game, nestled in disappointing packaging.
The puzzle types are standard (some inventory-based, some sliders, etc), though a few do stand out as novel twists on the formula. Unfortunately, the lack of a save system means that you will have to play through the entire game again to revisit those gems. (Achievement Hunters beware: one achievement is granted for completing a certain puzzle quickly, so take longer than the threshold and prepare for your full replay)
The game appears to auto-save whenever the voicework kicks in... Oh, yeah, that checkmark under "Full Audio" is overstating things. While there is "voice acting" (more on that in a moment), it only occurs alongside scene transitions or via a specific kind of item. The rest is unvoiced... which I failed to notice right away, missing some helpful tips in the bottom right corner as I was experimenting with the 3D perspective.
That said, the game might actually be improved by silence. The sound quality is perfectly fine, but the performances are flat, merely reading the lines aloud, so characters experiencing fear and stress come off as pleasantly calm... Bye-bye immersion... Also, I imagine that the script itself was translated into English, which would explain some of the stilted dialogue and odd syntax.
I did experience some minor bugs... or, perhaps, amazing superpowers on the part of the protagonist, as he could occasionally see through solid objects or interact with items that were left two screens ago... but nothing gamebreaking.
In the end, I would recommend for puzzle adventure gamers, who have not already been turned off by any of the above. The puzzles were fun, the graphics were fine, and the story was occasionally intriguing, though it does end on a bit of sequel bait. Wait for a sale though...

Long Live the Queen is somewhat hard to quantify, in as much as I think it's part of a genre, but since it's the only example of the genre I personally know, I can't really say what that is.  You've got sim elements and, I guess, text adventure elements?  Anyway, it's fun, if a somewhat strange kind of fun.
The basis of the game is this -- you control (for a definition of control) a princess with the goal of having her survive a full year to be crowned queen.  The main way to accomplish this is by setting her lessons (Which increase the skills she'll need to survive and thrive) and picking dialogue/action options at the appropiate prompts.
And unless you're the kind of person who reaches for the walkthrough alongside the game (in which case perhaps this game isn't for you), you're going to fail, probably multiple times, before you ever see a coronation.
It's not as bad as all that, though.  Even a full, successful playthrough doesn't take a ton of time, so where the game ends up shining is in the value to replay it.  There are a lot of endings to this game, both in the form of epilogues and deaths, and finding them can be a ton of fun.
This isn't an action game, or a game to make you excited.  It's a game to bend your brain around, excersize strategy and long-range planning, and in general spend a lazy afternoon with.

If you like the Sierra city-building games of the past (like the Caesar series and such), or even if you're new to this, then you'd probably like this game too, if you could tolerate some of its flaws. I am hoping that by posting this, they could address and fix said flaws.
First, the lack of multiple placement and demolish. Every time you want to place a house (or whatever), you have to click on that gold button on the lower right. You can't just place multiple buildings. You can't drag-and-place. This becomes an issue when you want to prevent homeless people from placing tents all over your empty lands by placing "doodads" on the vacant lots. Imagine using multiple clicks to place over 20 doodads, one by one. It gets frustrating. When deleting a building, you have to click on each building, then delete them - it's a 2-step process. You can't just select something once, then delete multiple buildings. Also, you can't drag-and-delete.
Second, UI issues. You can't resize them. Also, certain UI elements pop out when you're placing certain buildings, which can interfere with placement. Sherrif and similar buildings do that.
Another one is trading. It could be a chore. You can't set up something that will allow you to get or sell a resource automatically and to a certain amount automatically. It's all manual. For example, I can't import and maintain 500 lumber automatically, and I can't also export boards until I only have 500 left automatically. Because of this, you always have to monitor resources you need that you import and and export, then do it all manually, with many clicks.
These are just a few things that could be deal-breakers for some people. To sum it up, I still recommend the game (I'm still playing it, despite the flaws), but if you do not like all (or any) of what I mentioned, then this game might not be for you. You have to be very patient with this game.
