Alright, Conclusion is done and dusted. Conclusion itself is basically a very short walking simulator. Some of the steam reviews claim it took 5 minutes to complete. That is definitely not tru. You simply cant alk fast enough in the game for that to be a reality. About a half hour with examining all the items and taking in some scenery is more accurate.
This game is all about alcoholism. Unfortunately, I couldnt really tell what the narration was trying to say as all the voice work was muddy beyond comprehension. However, from the pieces of your car found, the bloodstained and broken bicycle and gravestone, bottles of alcohol, and the handful of notes you can read, I'd say somebody hit a bicyclist and then crashed, possibly to their own death. That is what I assume at this point anyway. Perhaps the audio will get cleaned up at some point and we will get better clarity on the topic.
As it stands, the story was negligible and would rate about a 3 out of 10
The gameplay in Conclusion is consistent with most walking simulators. Walk around, jump here and there, and examine the occasional object/page note. So, that all checks out.
However, there is no cursor or anything indicating when you are in the proper position to pick something up, and some of the objects I encountered were frustratingly difficult to actually pick up and examine (if I was able to at all). Having some sort of reticule woudl have been ideal.
Additionally, there was an aggravating amount of screen tearing and stuttering. This game was incredibly poorly optimized. This was already obvious given the 10+ gb file size, but it was in full evidence throughout my play through. Moving forward/backward was fine, but once you started actually looking around, and especially if you are moving and looking around, you were confronted head on with the poor optimization. Not the best use of the Unity engine by any srtetch of the imagination.
There was also an interesting dynamic where you could explore freely to one side of the road consistently, but not the other. So...feel free to explore one side of the map. We dont really want you to see what's hiding on the other side though.
Again, I feel the gameplay in Conclusion was subpar for this genre or any other. A 4 out of 10 in this category seems appropriate.
The graphics in Conclusion were by far and away the high point of this game. Conclusion is a beautiful game. I took many screenshots in my play through that could easily be used in monthly Steam competitions and woudl make very nice wallpaper/background shots as well. The developers dont have the mastery of the Unity engine that you see with games like Dear Esther or The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, but they did a good job making the world seem vibrant and alive
I think a 7.5 out of 10 is an papropriate rating for the graphics in Conclusion
The audio in Conclusion was poor at best. The ambient sounds such as your footsteps, for example, were poor stock samples from what I can tell, and the voice acting was muddled beyond comprehension.
This was perhaps Conclusion's greatest failing, as you really need to be able to hear the voice acting to have the story fully revealed to you (or so I imagine, not having been able to determine what was being said enough to know if it really had anything to do with the game or not)
This was a 1 out of 10.
Ultimately, for a sub $1 game, your expectations should probably be tempered a bit going in, but that doesnt excuse some of the glaring deficiencies in this game. At the very least, the developers should have includede a reticule and the audio tracks should have been clear rather than muddled and indistinct. Especially considering the file size, which is actually larger than a lot of AAA titles out there right now, I expect better work. The graphics drove my rating up a bit, and so in Conclusion, this game deserves a 4 out of 10. Not the worst use of your time, but definitely one of the bottom rung examples of a walking simulator out there right now.
I would like to add a note of encouragement to the developers though. You show promise. You just need to iron ourt some of the key elements to your game so future games you hope to release wont suffer from the same issues.

Whilst I appreciate that two people join forces to develop a video game there's no excuse for skipping quality control. I'm also looking at you Valve since I really do not understand why you don't nudge the creators of such game so that they notice they still have to do some work before the release of their game.
The trailer already shows the horrible voice acting  Conclusion has. The comments your protagonist makes on the way simply cannot be understood as you can barely hear him. You are asked not to hurry but listen... if you wait before proceeding to the first loading screen close by you can hear the sound of a (probably) fatal car crash. Then you control Neil who has no idea how he got to the bridge and what happened to him.
Looking at the various personal belongings and car parts along the way can easily make you understand what happened. The problem is that it all takes 5-10 minutes to get to the end of the level and while initially you start at 60 FPS the value is gradually decreasing. Alt-tabbing and starting a new game do not help - I've finished the last couple of minutes around 10 FPS.
Also, the game is simply too big: you download over 10 GBs but for what purpose? Clearly, the mountain and other surrounding areas are vast but you only have one or two sections to be able to wander off. And for what purpose? I guess for obtaining one or two missing achievements but even those that pop-up you have no idea what you did for them.
Naturally, the notes you find along the way are meant to hint at what's going on. Neil's life has been full of issues due to alcoholism. If only these thoughts were in proper English. If at the end you state the seriousness of the game and mention that it's based on true events at least take the minimum effort to carry out some quality control!
The conclusion is that Conclusion is a bad game. It's short, unoptimised, does not know what it wants to be and as much as I appreciate that the creators - as they claim - will use the income for their upcoming game I'll make sure to steer away from that one if it is looked after in a similar manner.
PS: That was a quick comment and comment deletion on somebody's part. I guess this game is upvoted just like similar games with same quality. Do not let the upvotes fool you - they are probably the friends of the developers.

NOTICE - THIS REVIEW WAS WRITTEN USING GAME RESEARCH AND ALSO ME EXPERIENCE AFTER 3 HOURS OF PLAY.
No, this is not worth buying, whether it be full price or on sale. Ace Combat is a series that has yet to join PC and is a series that may not ever join the PC even though flight games are right at home here.
Firstly, the game's port is bare bones. The game did not work for me at first and I had to keep restarting Steam and validating the system files etc. Alongside that, there are very few options, the game doesn't look that great even on the highest settings, and the game can crash if you alt-tab. However, in it's defence, the game does run well on my GTX 960, but that is by no means a low end card.
The game is breaks down in to two chunks, on rail turret sections and dogfight sections, both of which are very dull and last way too long. The on-rail shooting sections are about as fun as they sound - click the mouse to make an explosion, do it again until the section ends...which takes a long time. The sections can last about 20 minutes at times, and if it is shorter, it certainly feels like they go on forever. The dogfight sections are pretty much - get behind the target, lock on, shoot them with missiles, maybe lock on further to get more accuracy and watch them explode. It is boring, goes on forever, and feels unrealistic. You also get a minigun which is useless and does no noticeable damage to the enemies, and you can't tell if you are hitting them because there are no hitmarkers.
As for the story, I didn't get what was going on and I didn't even know who I was fighting because the game bored me so much I didn't care to get far in the game. There is also mouse acceleration in the on-rail shooting sections and no mouse control at all in the flight sections, so if you REALLY care to play this game, a controller is reccomended. The world also looks like they ripped a world from Google maps, as the skyscrapers, ground and even the explosions look very low resolution. The planes do look decent however.
The game is boring, the PC port is mediocre at best, and levels last way too long, and judging from other reviews, this is not what Ace Combat is really like and I am taking their word for it as I haven't played any other games in the series. Do not buy this game even if it is on sale.

In Spooky Heroes, you are a knight who has decided for whatever reason, to leave the safety of your home and try to solve the mystery of the hordes of spooky creatures rampaging villages, roads, and attacking anyone in sight. tl;dr If you like this kind of game (pick-your-own, number crunch-y, visual novel and kind of dating sim-like), it's a very nice example of what it is. Otherwise, you're probably not going to like it.
Initially,I sucked at the game and hated it. Then, I used a couple of walkthroughs, lightbulb moment happened and now I quite like it. It's a text-based game with consequences, but it's not as straightforward as that.  If you're slightly mathsy: instead of 'do x and y will happen' it sometimes feels more like x + v + u * w means y is very likely to happen, and maybe z too if your character feels more depressed that day'. It makes it almost realistic. In a way.
It's still not going to appeal to everyone, though.
My pros:
- Outcome engine well designed, and well-disguised, which prevents the game from feeling simplistic despite first appearances.
- Art is cute. Music doesn't irritate me despite the repetitiveness.
- The dating sim element is more interesting than most and doesn't feel tacky or forced. Except for the bit where she can get forced into marriage, of course, but I'm talking about gameplay here.
- This is basically a quick hit if you like achievement mining. I like achievement mining.
My cons:
- It's a visual novel-style game. For many players unfamiliar with them, or maybe text-based RPG games, I think it's not going to feel that engaging. Having to scrutinise a balance sheet of skills every round might not be that appealing to some either.
- Wasn't the most intuitive game for me - had to rely on walkthroughs until I actually understood how to not keep dying by week 20. But that's probably my fault.
- In terms of replayability, it can get very repetitive after a while. But I'm on something like my 35th playthrough.

I bought this game as part of a bundle and to be honest, I expected very little from it. Steam has recently become inundated with tons of anime visual novels, and the vast majority of them hardly look interesting. In addition, when I learned it was a stat distribution game, I had even less hope for it. I don't really care about distributing stats, especially if there are tons of stats. However, I try to play every game in my library, so I figured if I hated it I would have some Steam Trading Cards and it would be done. Thankfully, LLTQ exceeded my expectations.
There are a lot of stats (since there are many classes you can study) but game lets you know what stats you'll need in order to pass a test. You can easily explore different paths by utilizing the huge number of save files or by scrolling up with the scroll wheel. (However, you can only rewind up to the point after you select which classes to study in.) I was also blown away by the number of endings. For example, even if you end up marrying the same person, the ending will change depending on your other choices. Some other nice features of the game include the outfits Elodie can wear, which are both cute and actually affect your stats. In addition, the music is always a simple piano arrangement, but the music always fits what is going on in the game.
This game isn't without fault, though. First of all, even for visual novels, this one is visually underwhelming. There's a grand total of 4 backgrounds, and the vast majority of time, you're going to be stuck looking at the castle. There are also no cutscenes except for one brief animation and one cutscene at the very end. Practically everything that happens is simply told to you. Even fights have no pictures or animations save some flashes of white. The character portraits are are cut off at the shoulder, so that's all you will see of any character that's not Elodie. In addition, the game is pretty feminine, so it might not appeal to everyone.
If you can look past the boring visuals, LLTQ is enjoyable visual novel. Have fun dying and long live the queen!

Simple concept, upon which can, has been and will be built increasingly complex mechanics.
Depending on the mission you have limited amounts of ships, energy sources and land units. Your enemy has emitters which spew out particles that move around the map and damage your stuff. You move your ships close, have enough firepower to kill newly spawned particles and bring special units in range to kill the emitters. Simple, right? Now add to that virtually infinite possibilities thanks to the built-in map editor and scripting language as well as the option to share your maps with other players.At the same time you can do any mission with a custom fleet instead of the intended one.
The story, while not bad, is not exeptional. The story missions are well crafted to slowly introduce new elements to the player while not forcefully slowing down veterans.
Besides the story there is a random map generator as well as maps hand crafted by other players (currently, 24 hours after launch, already several dozen. Additionally you can play around with the ship editor and design your own awesome ships.
If you have played the previous Creeper World games, then this game offers far more dynamic gameplay while at the same time allowing for far more customization.
If you like strategy games in general, you should try it out, if feels different to other strategy games and might just satisfy an urge you did not even realize you had.
If you don't really like strategy games you should still try it out for the same reason: it is different to almost all other strategy games.
If you absolutly dislike strategy games, why are you even here? That strategy tag should tell you everything you need to know.
A really nice meal or a game that potentially can keep you busy for hours upon hours, you choose.
tl;dr: If you do not hate strategy games then try this one, it is basically it's own subgenre.

Never before have I been so confused by a video game. The trailer does not represent the final product in nearly any way.
Seemingly the game has been changed since the early stages of the development process and it has turned into a game with similar gameplay elements to various indie Slenderman games. You're tasked with finding items / areas (similar to the page system in Slenderman), while avoiding the two monsters in the game which have opposing triggers to gain their notice, creating occasional situations where both monsters are in the same narrow passage, making progress impossible.
The first enemies, which appear to be vortigaunt (from Half Life 2) wannabes have little sense in their AI but do have interesting design as well as eyes that glow eerily in the dark. The aggressive mannequins (which share the same audio clips as the only other enemy in the game) are easily glitched and manipulated which can make an encounter either impossible or an annoyance where monsters must be kited away from certain areas. Quite often during my coop, 2.2 hour experience with the game, the mechanics of both enemy types were easily manipulated to the point where the enemies became 'broken'.
Cyrus' writing is awful and clunky while being riddled with grammatical and structural errors just as Jane and David's are, with character names being inserted after their place at the top of the text box again or sentences being repeated. The riddles offered by Cyrus' did nothing to enhance the feeling of horror, instead serving only as bizarre roadblocks to progress through the game.
Even with a friend to laugh your way through with, this is not worth the $5.93 (on sale) price tag.

So I really like this game! First off, I have a very real irrational fear of open water and sharks. Sure all people "fear" sharks, but I get the sweats, and shakes. I repeat over and over again that I can't move, and I quit and restart rather than get bitten/eaten. Don't get me wrong, it's ark, but no dinos. I know this is still a early access, but I'm just aching for more. So here are my pro's and con's.
Pro: Hands down it's fun if you like sandbox survival games. The sharks seriously keep me paranoid. I always enjoy the building aspect, but I really like that there is also furniture. The water looks so freaking real! I get itchy and fearful just from how realistic the water is. I can spend endless hours creating my base, and exploring. Every time you start it's a new world. If you die, and go back to the save point, things may not happen the exact same way. It may not rain, and shark might not appear! Hands down I like the game and would recommend it to others. I "hear" that co-op is on it's way, that will be dope, however before I star that idea and get excited about them developing that; we need to address the con list, and there are many!
Con: Wonky, the menu (craft) closes every single time you create something. I love that you can't hold 45 things at once, but it's also my greatest annoyance. As of yet there is not a chest to store items in, and what crates you do find can only hold 3 items. The smoke is like a puzzle, you sometimes have to walk back and fourth to get items on the shelf of the smoker. Unless you're holding sticks when you interact with the fire a second time, you'd never know you have to add more sticks to get it going again. It's locks up often. Save your game often (Must have a shelter to save). My computer is a Goliath, and this game is a snail by comparison. However you'd think this game was David, it locks up my system and I have to power down. It freezes up a lot. It takes 8 wacks to take down a tree, another 8 to seperate the trunk, and another 8 to make 4 sticks. If you have hit the tree 12 times, stop what you're doing and go to another tree, because your ax/knife is about to die if you keep going and the tree will yield no wood. Look up how to use the tanning rack, because you'll just stand there like a fool waiting for the leather to dry. It wont!
Final thoughts: I don't want them to saturate the game with "easier" machanics, I like that you have to be active to survive and thrive. The sharks are terrifying, I've yet to go diving because I'm terrified. Co-op will be dope. I look forward to the bugs being fixed. Please input a chest into crafting!!!!!!!!!! I give it a B+ all around, but I've only got 24 hours in. It's worth the price, but you have to have patiences.

Pros:
-A pretty nice character creator that gives you decent liberties to play a character you can believe in.
-Excellent level-up system that rewards persistence and knowledge of grinding-favorable areas you've visited before.
-Assuming you start the game with the MASTER KEY starting gift, massive leeway to traverse the starter areas in the order you please.

Dark Souls is a franchise I have been holding out on for many months. It had me intimidated until one day I finally decided to try it out. A year later and it has become one of the franchises I treasure close to heart. Once you take the 30 years to create your character with a really jacked up face and neon red skin color, you are immediately dropped into a world with seemingly no explanation besides "Hey youre a piece of beef jerky here's a key and get out". Once free you soon discover the series' most iconic symbol: The Bonfire. These are basically checkpoints that allow you to return to at any time (via Homeward Bone, Dark Sign, or by dying).
This game will not hold any punches, once you're out it immediately throws at you a small taste of what the rest of the game will be like. Basically, you're going to die a lot, which is something that has made this franchise popular and infamous for. The difficulty of Dark Souls is what sets it apart from every other RPG game. Its contextual but at the same time really complex. Picking up a random weapon and hacking and slashing your way through the game will only take you so far until the game punishes you for being too careless or too aggressive. The idea of Dark Souls is to take your time and not just beat the game, but learn it. You'll hear from many Souls Veterans that the franchise isn't hard at all, and they are right to an extend. Dark Souls is a difficult game, yes, but its difficult as it teaches you to learn from your mistakes so you do not do them again.
The world design is possibly one of the best designed in its class. To decrease the amount of horizontal travelling, the world is layered upon itself so that it is large, however, not tedious to navigate as fast travel is not available in this game until over midway through the game, and even then only few Bonfires are available to fast travel to.
However, not every game is perfect, Dark Souls, while one of the best RPG experiences I've had, struggles from many drawbacks and minor inconviencies that definitly do end up piling up.
For starters, the game may be too daunting for newcomers wanting to try to learn the game but by being too curious or too experimental, time is ended up being wasted or characters can be accidentally poorly levelled. Forcing them to either give up the game or start a new game from scratch. This issue would not be prevalent in other RPGs but as for Dark Souls, there is no save slots. Meaning you can't just reload an older save and try again. Everything done in this game is permanent, all NPCs killed, all items used, all bosses killed, weapons upgraded, is all permanent. The only real solution is to try to not be too experimental or curious unless you are sure what you are getting yourself into.
Another issue is the weaponry and PvP. I bundled these two together as they do go hand in hand. There is a ton of weapons to use in the game and you'll always have access to a wide variety of swords, axes, bows, greatswords, greataxes, halberds and Ultra Greatswords and even more. I haven't even told you about the number of scorcery and hexing catalysts that cast offensive magic, and some that cast miracles for defensive spells and even Pyromancy. However, there is clearly some weapons that just do not feel worth getting or using at any point in the game. There's definitly some favor to certain weapons that do end up being really good for PvE, including the infamously overpowered Black Knight weapons. Fortunately, some of these weapons can be found very early on like the Claymore, Halberd, and the Zweihander. However, translating into PvP, even more weapons feel unworthy to use. PvP in this game is way too stiff and clunky, and weaponry is definitly more limited as you'll have to get familiar with the "meta" of the game for invading and doing co-op. Fortunately, not many people play online anymore as many people prefer to play offline and replay the game over and over because Dark Souls is one of those games where it just gets better with every playthrough
All in all, definitly one of the best RPG experiences I've ever had the pleasure to play. However, if you do plan on getting this version, make sure to download a mod called "DSFix" as it fixes many bugs and fixes the framerate for the game.

The black sheep of the Ace Combat franchise. I was EXTREMELY hyped for this title prior to release. Ace Combat 5 is my favourite game of all time, and I thought this would kick the franchise back into gear again. How foolish.
Cons:
- The gameplay is nothing like the earlier games, so die hard fans will find almost nothing of value here.
- The infamous and bizarre dog-fighting sections play like some on-rails arcade shooter.
- There are enforced helicopter sections (admittedly a little fun sometimes), enforced third-person gunner sections (again, sometimes fun) and awful bombing missions with overly-complicated recommended flight paths.
- The colour scheme is mostly grey/dark green.
- The over all combat is ultimately tedious due to over powered nature of your plane.
-  The story is forgettable at best. Nothing compared to the grand and bombastic entries into the Strangereal lore in earlier games.
But, for all of that. there is some light to this.
Pros:
- The port is solid (I'm only judging this after 30 minutes of playing, but nothing has crashed and there are minimal frame drops. Graphics settings are sparse though.)
- There are a few jaw-dropping moments, usually involving something to do with ejecting from the craft.
- The later missions get extremely intense. The penultimate one is actually fantastic.
- The gameplay is solid if you enjoy what it offers. Planes are responsive and destroying enemies is satisfying.
- Nagase from AC5 makes an easter egg appearance.
- The main theme is Ace Combat-esque, and thrilling for it. Also has a couple of other good tracks, like the free mission hangar OST, which serves as a nice throwback to the PS1 days of the series
Most of my negativity is just from being so heartbroken that this essentially damned the franchise. I don't want to be an♥♥♥♥♥♥and not recommend it for that reason. If this is your first time playing Ace Combat, give it a whirl.

It seems that folks either really really like this game or really really  dislike it.  For myself I found it to be a lot of fun and very polished.  It's an RPG in the sense that you progress characters, equip them, make decisions, and can genuinely immerse yourself in the overall story and environment. The game also involves some strategy and tactics... you build your base, choose which missions to take on, select which upgrades you want at your base, and at times will likely be put in a position where you begin studying the map to figure out the most strategic locations to set up outposts or move your base (and rebuild).  The majority of emphasis in this game though does seem to be about third person combat... which in my opinion is done well.  Typical WASD movement - though I think you can customize... I think there is also support for gamepads/controllers if that's your preference.  To be honest, the game could be (and I think it is) a console game, in that most of the decisions via conversation that you make are "selected" in drop down menus etc.
This is not simply a base-building game where you can avoid combat... it is an action game that has elements of base building, rpg and...zombies.  I'd personally recommend the game for anyone who enjoys games like X-COM, Jagged Alliance etc (tactical) though this game is NOT turn based, and I believe the two I mentioned above are....  It's a very unique game in my opinion, but I'd love  to see more like it (the expansions for this are also great - but you may want to try the main/core game first).
The game probably isn't for everyone, but I think most people will find something to enjoy...

Shadow of Mordor is aslasher action game with RPG elements. In this game you play as Talion, a ranger who has been killed and cast away in the shadow between life and death. His “self” is then melted with a powerful ringwraith and this final entity is a powerful but cursed undead creature who wanders across Middle Earth seeking revange for the murder of his family. The game has access to the source material from the movies, so the orcs are going to look ugly and twisted, just like in the movies, Sauron’s appearance is the same and so on.
Combat in this game is just awesome. It uses a free flow system, similar to the Batman series: while you are attacking an enemie, you can instantly counter attack other enemies and also jump around, fire arrows, hide in bushes and do a variety of other things. The result is a very cinematographic combat, quite epic and similar to the Lord of the Rings movies.
The movement is also great, you can easly run and climb in almost any structure or building, similar to the assassins creed series. You can also jump from higher places with your dagger over the enemy for a satisfying stealth kill.
Game is really good and fun, shame that it’s kinda repetitive, I mean, you have two huge open world areas all filled with nothing but orcs. I guess the game would be just so much better if there was a city where you could interact with NPCs and such. Also most missions and stuff you do in the game require lots of grinding, só be prepared. But, gameplay wise, it’s almost perfect for a free flow slasher.

After sitting idly in my Steam library for years, I decided to finally play this game. I was so positively surprised, that I even bothered to complete it.
So of course ... of positive review.
As you already know, this is an open-world action game set in the Lord Of The Rings universe, in Mordor to be precise. You are a dead ranger whose body is paired with an ancient elven spirit in order to take revenge on the bad guys.
At first sight this looks like a good foundation for a story, but during my playthrough I felt the storyline not really interesting and at some point dragging on. Yeah your family was killed, I get it already, no need to remind me of it every singly cutscene! If you're a Lord Of The Ring fan you'll probably like it for the whole Celemrimbor angle, but if you're not you should expect to be underwhelmed.
Of course, what matters most is the gameplay and that is exactly where this game shines. You can play as the noble warrior, sword in hand, hacking away at uruks. Or the nasty backstabber, assassinating and murdering uruks left and right while moving unseen. Or the valiant archer who snipes away baddies from across the map. And the best part? You are not forced into one role, but the game allows you to switch and combine the three play-styles fluently. I cannot express sufficiently how good this combat system feels!
Imagine: you're sneaking on top of a high wall, a dozen or so uruks nearby.  You need to pass them. Of course, you could just sneak your way around, but what's the fun in that? You carefully lay aim and fire an arrow into a bonfire, the explosion taking out half of dozen of the guys. Then you drop down onto the unexpecting captain who is resting below, killing him instantly. You grab the other uruk standing close and brand him, forcing him to pick you side. With your bow you then take out the 2 guys with shields who were storming to you. Finally you finish of the remaining 3 guys with a sword. As a final act of gratitude you drain the uruk you converted earlier, refilling your arrows and making his head explode. All this in 10 seconds.
Or you could just snipe them all with your bow.
Or do a little sneaking about and assassinate them all.
Or convert more of them to your cause and have them wipe out each other.
Or attract some animals to the place to do the fighting for you.
Or convert another captain and order him to duel the captain in question while you watch from a distance.
Or ...
This is how an open-world combat game should be: not forcing you but giving you freedom!
Adding to the gameplay is the Nemesis system: a hierarchy of uruks, who get promoted, fight amongst each other and try to topple their own boss.
Is one of the warchiefs (the "bossess" in this game) to hard for you? Easy, convert a captain and order him to become that warchief's bodyguard. If he succeeds, order him to kill his boss. Now you have a warchief under your control.
Let me give this little example:
Near the end of the game I had one warchief left that I needed to take out, but I just couldn't do it. He had the most nasty combinations of immunities and hates possible (a "hate" strengthens an uruk and even allows him to heal to full health sometimes). We're talking about a guy immune to almost all my damage, who had a whole posse of uruks with him at all times, able to sniff me out whenever I was near him, who hated being low on health (!) and catacors.
So I branded his bodyguard when he was alone. And I branded another 3 captains and had them all become bodyguard as well. Out of those 4, I picked the bodyguard with the nastiest combination of stats (immune to nearly everything as well and he hated seeing his boss being on low health, lol) and ordered him to usurp his boss.
I went to the site of the battle and saw the combat begin. My guy was strong and slowly chipped away at the warchief's health, but he was being overwhelmed by the mass of lowly uruks nearby. ***Insert “Everything is proceeding as I have foreseen!” soundbit here.*** So I ordered the other 3 bodyguards to join the fight, all ganging up on the warchief. Meanwhile I was backstabbing the nearby archers and shooting some of the other uruks with my bow.
Result: the warchief died quickly, the first bodyguard became new warchief (under my control) and the other 3 were now bodyguards of the new warchief. All hail the king! Nobody even saw me ...
It really feels great, the freedom and options that this game gives you.
Is the game perfect? No, not at all.
It compromises of 2 maps, the first a bleak typical mordor-army base map and the second a lush valley. personally I found the first one a lot more boring that the second.
Also, it takes a long time before you get all your abilities. The game only really shines when you get full power and that is only at the second half of the game.
Also, this game is basically quicktime-event simulator 2014. I despite quicktme-events and this game just had too much of them. Even the freaking endfight was just nothing but a series of QTE's, which pi$$ed me off tremendously. To add insult to injury, the game then has the guts to end with a massive and unfulfilling cliffhanger.
Graphically, the game is a marvel. It looks very good and has very little popup.
It sounds good as well, both sound effects, spoken lines and music being of decent quality. What did get on my nerves where the lines of the captains, who all felt the need to spit out an introduction every time they faced me.
Imagine: you sneak attack a captain, which takes away half their health, immediately triggerering them to flee. Once a captain is fleeing, you can grab him to brand and make him yours.
However, as soon as the sneak-attack move finishes, the captain gurgles his pre-defined introduction, including a little cut-scene: "You ugly manfilth, I'll drink the blood from your skull". This takes you out of the flow of combat.
Followed by another cutscene, pointing out that the captain is fleeing.
*Great*
And that is for every single captain you meet ...
Despite those annoyances, the game is a marvel.
Note, that is true for the vanilla game. If found none of the DLCs really worthwhile.

I would argue that there are two games out on Steam right now that embody the core of A Game of Thrones better then the actual GoT games do. Long Live the Queen is the one nobody expects.
Behind the veneer of cute chibi characters is a story of ruthless political intrigue, desperate Sophie's Choice no-win scenarios and the ever-looming threats of conspiracy, invasion and death.
The 14-almost 15--year old queen must step into the very big shoes of her recently deceased mother and prepare herself in a crash course of political protocol, economics, strategy, diplomacy and magic. She must fend off coup d'etats, assassins, invading armies and encroaching magical demons. Over the course of the game the player will need to deal with power-hungry nobles with assasination or diplomacy, make strategic alliances and potentially commit to a loveless political marraige to maintain stability, lead armies and treat with diplomats to keep your nation safe and your line secure until you are old enough to take the throne and securely transfer power.
The game itself is rather short, but with a multitude of branching story paths which will change based on the decisions you make--and this is one of the few RPGs I've played where it felt like LITERALLY every single decision I made was important, from the decrees and critical decisions of state to even the smallest details of what classes I took and what I did on the weekends to adjust my mood to change the bonus modifiers for skills.
One truth about the game, though, is that you will die at least the first 5-8 times you play, there's no gettting around it. You will suffer horrible deaths described in agaonizing verbal detail (and cute chibi picture form) if you make the wrong decisions or don't prepare a good balance of skills to prepare for the events and challenges the game throws at you. That might get a little frustrating until you figure out and prepare a little for what's coming up at each bend.
Overall though it was an unusual and thoroughly enjoyable experience and I would love to pay for a longer such experience of political intrigue and grand strategy.

All in all, they added many new features to this game, but I think most of them made the game worse.

Seeing i poured more hours into this game than the average review-writing player, i figured i should write my own review as well. There might be spoilers.
So here goes:
I'm not a fan of most zombie games, which seem to revolve around "shoot millions of zombies to win". There is no "winning" State of decay. The zombies are everywhere and the horde is endless. The base game ends when your survivors manage to leave Trumbull Valley and you are left wondering "How long will they last without my help?"
And this is exactly what i love about State of Decay.
The game & DLC's in a nutshell:
State of Decay:
You and your buddy went on your annual fishing trip, while you were gone large swaths of the US have been overrun by zombies. You get attacked as soon as you tie off your boat. Fighting them off is easy enough but now need to figure out what happened and where you can find a safe place to stay. Jump in the nearest car and meet up with fellow survivors holed up at a church. Then the game begins for real and answers are gradually given.
Breakdown:
Same map, alternate storyline. Several weeks after the outbreak, you and Lily are the last 2 survivors of an enclave and you know you wont last much longer on your own. While you look for another enclave to join, Lily packs up and will meet you there with whatever supplies are left. Once settled it's back to basics: survive for as long as you can. You quickly realize resources are dwindling while zombie numbers increase. Eventually it's time to move on: you pack all equipment in the RV, load up your most important survivors and look for a new home. Your new home is on the exact same map, but with fresh resources and.. more zombies.
Lifeline:
New map. You are in command of the last military outpost in the overrun city of Danforth. You must secure your base, shore up your defenses and start the search for various survivors. The brass will direct you to high-value assets: scientists, doctors and their families whose expertise might be crucial to find an eventual cure. Along the way stranded survivors cry out for help and you're the only one with the means to respond. Your actions will decide the fate of not only Danforth, but possibly the whole world.
I'll do a short pros and cons but there are a few things i should really point out first. State of Decay is not about killing lots of zombies. It is about people trying to survive the zombie apocalypse. There are endless zombies but finite resources. Sure, it is great fun to smash your truck into a few zombie hordes or grab a machine gun and go on a killing spree, but that's not the intention of the game. When you're done a good truck will be broken, perhaps beyond repair. Or a lot of bullets will have been wasted on ever respawning zombies. So when you clear an area of zombies, you damn better scavenge as much as you can.
When you scavenge you may find resources you can use to improve your base or tools for zombie killing. Food and various painkillers/stimulants are also often found. There are a few possible home sites (bases) in the game for you to eventually choose from. Each of them has certain requisites and advantages/disadvantages, but larger is better :). Always you have to make tough choices: will i go for a workshop to repair weapons & cars, or rather a field hospital to aid the people who will inevitably fall sick? No one wants to go down with Black Fever.. trust me. Maybe i can have both IF i sacrifice room for the workout area, but then all survivors will have less stamina and fighting skills.. Choices.
Over the course of the game missions will pop up: help scavenging, clear out an infestation, save a survivor, trade resources with your neighbours, kill a freak zombie.
Unfortunately most of these missions can be boiled down to a simple fact: your fellow survivors have the mental capacity and survival skill of a baked potato. You are the only one who's good at it, and it's up to you to do ALL the work. I found this annoying when i first played the game and put it aside for a few weeks for that reason only. However, if you accept that's just how it is, embrace it, and you'll still have a most enjoyable game.
A few other points of light irritation:
- Graphics: good enough for a game of this price, but definately not top notch.
- Controls: especially car controls feel sluggish.
- Clipping: zombies occasionally clip trough solid objects. Not a problem if it's just a regular zombie, a bit more annoying when it's a Big Un or Feral in an enclosed space.
- Useless survivors: Plenty of them and no "clean" way to get rid of them.
The pros:
Open world game: You go where you want, when you want.
Permadeath: Your survivor got ambushed and killed? He's dead, no reloading an earlier save.
Stamina & carry capacity: The game's way of saying you're just an average Joe, not Rambo.
Traits and Skills: The game's way of taking the "average" out of "average Joe"
Soundtrack: Composed by Jesper Kyd. 'Nuff said.
Mods: Don't like this or that? Maybe want to see more of that other stuff? Check out the modding community, or find out how to do it yourself. Besides tweaking Breakdown to make it more enjoyable, i also added myself as a playable character. Much fun was had.
All in all i found this a very enjoyable game and the DLC's are definately worth it. Has been on sale several times @ -66% orso.
Even grabbed back to it a few months after i finished it.

For fans of the game, this is the highly anticipated 4th game from Knuckle Cracker, and I'm sorry to say that it was over hyped.  Previous games in the series left me with a feeling of wanting to come back for more.  In PF:E I managed to get through all the story missions and a couple of the bonus missions in a few hours without failing once.
The game feels like it was finished in a rush to meet the release date and lacks the polish found in the previous games.
I am a big fan of earlier games and I like the developer, so I will continue to buy following games they produce, but this just missed the mark by a fair amount. If you're new to the series, this may be a quick and easy introduction to the style of play, but for now there is a bigger challenge, and a deeper storyline, to be found in the earlier games.

If you've played the Creeper World games, this is similar. The big difference is the de-emphasis on resource gathering and base-building, and a bigger emphasis on battle control. There is a unit limit. You can't win purely off of turtling into a strong economy, you have to turtle into taking objectives here and there.
There is much more emphasis on movement and putting your ships in the right position. The 'creep' can now react to your presence, so you have to pick your battles carefully. Sometimes your full army can only take one objective at a time; sometimes it can take multiple objectives at once.
For those who haven't played creeper world, try the free demo on Kongregate / the interwebs. If you like that kind of slow RTS where you have perfect information and the enemy AI is predictable, you'll probably like this game.

Quick Overview: If you like Assasin's Creed games, but get bored of them quickly and / or find collection tedious, this games sets a faster pace. It has a lot of the best parts of the first of the new Tomb Raider games (though not the puzzle elements) combined with many of Assasin's Creed's best characteristics, and fewer of both series drawbacks. The Nemesis and Branding systems are unique and enjoyable, and the logic behind Talion's power adds a layer of thoughtful immersion often missing from other similar games. Worth a try even if you don't like the games I mentioned, but has parallels in gameplay that are easy to draw. Oh yeah, and its LotR so the story is very solid.
I'm very happy with what I got out of this game, and there was still more I could have done after with the extra campaigns (I had gotten my fill by that point, and dabbled in each of them only briefly out of curiosity, but not to completion). Getting it on sale, I would say it is absolutely worth $20 for the base game, and each of the expansions would be worth another $5 each.
As I note in the Quick Overview, the game has a lot of components and mechanics reminiscent of Assasin's Creed mixed with the new Tomb Raider games (or Uncharted if you prefer, obviously without the modern elements). However, I found it did not get boring nearly as quickly as Assasin's Creed games. Any of the AC series I have played, I got bored of within the first 5 - 15 hours. I have never beaten any of them as a result. I found it became tedious, and the core gameplay, thoroughly enjoyable at first, grew chore-like in time. I had the same archs of "okay, I'm starting to be good on this" in Shadows of Mordor, but where Assasin's Creed simply didn't hold my attention, Shadow of Mordor re-engaged me at each of those moments with new mechanics. I could easily see someone only playing the first half of the game in Udun and still getting their money's worth, but my favorite parts came in the second half in Nurn.
Nurn contained one of the two parts of this game that really set it apart from AC, TR or Uncharted. The first you encounter, though, is present throughout and you encounter in Udun: the Nemesis system. Essentially, if you are killed by an Uruk, a number of things can happen. When you continue after that death, if it was a simple foot soldier or the like that killed you, they will earn a name and become a captain, gaining special characterstics and the ability to rise through the ranks. If a captain or warchief kills you, they will increase in Power, often gaining new abilities and losing old weaknesses. Also, depending on how you have fought them in the past, their dialogue may change. All told, you start to get a degree of attachment and depth to your enemies that is not often present in other games. A lot of people think of the Nemesis system when they think of Shadow of Mordor, and with good reason - it is a lot of fun and adds a lot to the game.
For me, however, it is the element introduced in Nurn that captures me (Spoiler Alert!). In Nurn, by progressing the main storyline, one of your abilities transforms into a better version, doing what it did before but now also applies a Brand. When enemies are Branded,  they are your allies. Captains and Warchiefs can be branded as well, with somewhat more difficulty, and given commands to rise through the ranks. You can assist them on missions to help them gain power and improve their abilities. In the next game in the series, Shadow of War, your most dire Nemesis and most 'loyal' Follower will follow from Shadow of Mordor to Shadow of War, which is a nice touch. I nearly put the game down after the first half in Udun, but the Branding system re-engaged me enough to pull me through to the end.
I could go into more specifics about abilities, missions, side quests and the like, but I think the Nemesis System, the Branding System and the points I made about the game overall are enough. There were a couple of missions that I felt were not super well tuned and tried to do something interesting with the mechanics, but ended up being awkward or frustrating. The side quests were sometimes a little repetitive, though they made an effort to mix it up as much as they could. The story is LotR so if you like that universe, you will probably be happy. Some characters are more interesting than others, but I would say its very good as far as game storylines go.
If what you've read here appeals, consider picking it up. I definitely didn't regret it, so hopefully neither will you.

For years with Dark Souls on the PC and 360, I have struggled with an epiphany. I absolutely despise
about Dark Souls 1 to the point where my fondness for Demons’s Souls and Dark Souls 2 may appear contradictory. Issues that I have with SoulsBorne as a genre are magnified in DS1 that I can’t help but think there is a reason why games before and after DS1 have moved away from imitating the qualities die-hards have praised.
As I expect from previous reviews not sharing the consensus with ardent defenders that treats it as Citizen Kane, I expect many won’t bother to read this review. If, however, you are still reading then know that even at its best moments the same issues exist. The purpose for writing this review is not to dismiss people from DS1 but to interest people who share similar issues to try other games because they may be more to their tastes.
When DS2 was released, fans of DS1 were torn; when DS1 was released, some fans of DeS felt it was a misstep; and I imagine if you found fans of King’s Field they might say the DS games are simplified. How can so many varied opinions exist?
The underlying truth is gaming tastes are relative to your experiences and the expectations they set for future installments. This is why the Souls-like genre is inherently flawed; the consensus for what defines these games varies from how much emphasis is put on level-design, bosses, combat, etc. As someone who had a harder time with DS before warming up to DS2, the virgin effect is something fans need to accept when they talk about difficulty. Returning back to DS1, however, what expectations does it set that leaves me bitter?
For starters, the health recovery system. To use a flask at the cost of wasting one is not the issue; it’s the system that shows its problems for both PVE and PVP.  As a beginner’s tool, kindling bonfires is so poorly explained that many players will start off not knowing they can get more rations. Even when you get enough to make the choice moot, the short time-frame of refilling your health means bosses are designed to pummel you into a cycle of usage and in PVP people have made up “honor” rules not to use them. In contrast to other systems, the various grasses from DeS instills a greater sense of scarcity and the slow, continual regeneration of lifegems—the flasks are also slowed—rewards both more reckless players who use that regeneration to be on the offensive as well as offering new players an alternative resource as an optional difficulty modifier.
The much-touted line of “It’s hard but fair” is nonsense when difficulty spikes come from boss gimmicks on top of “GOTCHA!” moments. In describing gimmick bosses, I am not referring to Ornstein and Smough that test both your reflexes as well as adding something different; I am referring to encounters that are only hard because they test your patience with being obtuse or they aren’t mechanically satisfying. Although boss-fights do not have to be tests of skill, the spectacle remains dull. DeS, however, had far more engaging bosses that were amazing spectacles or tough encounters. Even in DS2, the “Dudes in Armor” problem is something I can tolerate as, contrary to what many believe, DS combat is ideal for multiple enemy encounters when you’re not locked on (see Darklurker in DS2 and even DS3’s Demon in Pain & Below). As for the “GOTCHA!” moments, one only need look up Joseph Anderson’s videos to see how they offer only a cheap death.
Now you may agree/disagree with my assessments, but I think what I have shown is that there is room for interpretation of players and not one Souls game has managed to please everyone. These next two problems are something I believe are more personal, which will make my assessment at the start make more sense.
Once I believed the open-world of DS1 was its greatest strength that the game strangely ignores as you hunt the Four Lord Souls, arguably the worst of DS1, but after experiencing DeS and DS2 I am not fond of it anymore. Guiding the players on intended routes is not the problem; it’s how much unnecessary backtracking there is because it is a Souls game as well as how much freedom is restricted by false appearances.
As much as players complain about teleportation in sequels, many players forget the first time playing DS in wandering off you to where you weren’t meant to be and then you had to stumble back to find the intended route. Sure, eventually you get the ability to transport between bonfires; however, the beginning will make you second-guess yourself for direction and the “GOTCHA!” moments sting more. Even in levels like Blighttown that do make use of this emotion, which I am surprisingly fond of this level, it is mitigated by the sense that going back is a royal pain for a SoulsBorne game. As a result, the Souls’ level of difficulty is rather a hindrance because of the open-world design as both DS2 and DeS are benefited by the level of challenge by going different paths.
What I think is perhaps a far greater misunderstanding is the limitation of exploration in DS as you’re not free to go anywhere as much as you initially believe because the game must push you back towards the right path. If anyone has tried to encounter the Lord Souls before the two bells have been rung, then you are probably aware of a mysterious wall of light that prevents you from progress. The reality is the world only opens areas when you’re meant to go there, not because of the player’s choice. This is in stark contrast to DeS where you can choose any level you want but they were often far more linear as a result and in contrast to DS2 where can choose various paths that lead to other areas as well as mitigating the Four Lord door with using bonfire ascetics to farm enough souls. These aspects work with player-choice that, admittedly, are never as strong as the interconnected nature of Undead Burg but never suffers the plight that is running back and forth between areas to find your way.

Whenever I think about the possible merits behind the storytelling of Dark Souls, I am reminded of how much I enjoy the idea behind Hemmingway’s iceberg theory where you only see the top of a glacier and you’re left to imagine the vast depths it has beneath the waters.  However, it doesn’t take long for the holes to become more transparent it leaves in a book, and applying a similar concept to games is perhaps an even worse idea when you stop to think about it.
In the case of Dark Souls, there are three issues with its storytelling: (1) the lack of plot versus lore; (2) the player’s own connection to the storyline; (3) various oversights that go beyond reading lore-descriptions. The first two problems are attributed to the same issue of the player being insignificant to the world of Dark Souls, which, as much as I love Lovecraftian cosmic horror, it makes the actual narrative of Dark Souls hard to give a damn without motivation. Even DS2 addresses this issue by having the illusions of a motive for the player as well as offering simple choices with NPCs in and outside of combat to learn more through player agency. The third problem is a combination of cut-content, translation discrepancies and incompleteness that is inherent with designing a story that must be learned through peer-review rather than something you experience. Perhaps I’m too old-school, but I prefer my stories self-contained.
Not getting the full story as well as community engagement is rather the purpose behind these decisions but it’s ultimately indicative of realizing the flaws with its novelty before audiences grow weary. Some issues are more personal than others, but that dissatisfaction is what I believe makes DS1 age worse than any other SoulsBorne title. May you never bear the curse that has befallen me.

There are many things that come up when discussing what makes Dark Souls so great; these praises mostly focus on its challenging but fair difficulty and its fascinating world with lore awaiting to be discovered. Both of these are absolutely true and, if you're up to the challenge, Dark Souls is an experience I'd consider essential to anyone who loves gaming.
"Getting into" the series is always the hardest part. It is for that reason I want to take this time as an attempt to guide you, the reader, into what I consider nearly holy ground. I want you to experience and love this series like I do. And so, I present my Recommendation to Get Into the Souls-series
The number one thing circulating around the internet about this game/series is that it is abusively difficult and you have to take some sort of perverse pleasure in pain to enjoy yourself. This is hyperbole, don't believe it.
It is absolutely true that Dark Souls is challenging, I even said it myself, but the common perception that it's impossibly difficult to get into is an insult. Games like "I Wanna Be the Guy!" are masochistic, revelling in killing the player in as many unforeseeable ways as possible, but Dark Souls is not one of those games. Dark Souls is challenging, but wants you to beat it; it is the Dungeon Master that knows you can do it, but knows you have to earn it to really feel accomplished.
The number one thing I have to say is to not be afraid of Dark Souls. It is not a game you can lose, there are no game overs. The absolute worst that can happen is that you don't win beause you stop playing, or you never play it in the first place.
Dark Souls is a community game, from the messages left on the ground in the game itself, to friends who've played it and want to help, and to the numerous wikis on the internet full of advice. Do not be afraid to seek help when you feel yourself getting lost or frustrated, for there is almost certaintly another way around whatever is giving you a headache.
For instance, perhaps you can try summoning a helper (NPC or player), maybe there's a special trick to this fight, or an item hidden elsewhere that makes it much easier. For example, the game hides everything you need to kill the first real boss in a short few swings for you to find before the fight.
Dark Souls expects you to seek this help and it does not hold it against you. It understands that you can't just explain to someone how a bike works and then immediately push them down the steepest hill in town into traffic. If you feel the need to prove yourself to yourself, the oppurtunity is there to play it completely without help, but do not be afraid to seek help.
As an aside, my favorite way to introduce someone to the game is with them, sitting on the couch next to them while they play. Giving them tips when they seem to be getting frustrated, but letting them try and figure it out themselves. Also, one part in the first "level" is always hilarious, which is definitely a plus.
As described in the Greater Internet ♥♥♥♥wad Theory, people are jerks online, especially when they can stroke their ego about something (and boy do jerks love to stroke their ego about Dark Souls). I said earlier that Dark Souls is a community game, and most of that community is good. But absolutely do not stress about the jerks that do exist.
They'll try and tell you that you're crap at the game because you haven't run it naked with only your fists. Or that "that boss" isn't hard, you just need to gitgud you ♥♥♥♥in' scrub. Really, just don't let them get to you, they're sad little people and it's unfortunate that this is where they want to stroke themselves off.
Dark Souls does not care if you decide to level a few times before you take on that boss again, nor does it care if you end the game fully upgraded and a much higher level than average. Dark Souls is a challenging game, and it's just glad you won.
I hope that this helps you pick up this wonderful game if you've been on the fence about it. Personally, it sat in my library of games I know are good but am anxious about getting into for way too long, and I wish I'd gotten in much sooner. I don't want that to happen to you, if you want to see just why this game is so great.

1849 is a game where you need to manage one city, leading it to prosperity in a very unique setting! As the name suggests, it's set in 1849, during the California Gold Rush. Your main focus, as you can guess, it mining for gold, as well as other minerals, and building full cities out of it (seldom self sustained; lots of trading with other cities is involved).
I'll make it clear right away that I have never played a city management game before, so my standards may be different from yours, as I have nothing to compare it to.
But I've found the setting to be interesting, and the game's aesthetic seemed to add to it well enough, so I bought it, and finish it. Here are my thoughts.

As you can see from the screenshots, this is no Tropico or SimCity with full 3D graphics, weather, and the sort. Not at all. As this is from a small team, they've opted for a more old school graphic style, with prerendered backgrounds and sprites. It may make the game seem very static, but each building has a sprite associated with a work-phase, and the townsfolk are also animated and walk around the city, delivering materials, going to the saloon, etc.
I think it looks really cool, and certainly not something you see a lot of. Everything seems to fit the setting (although I'm nowhere near an expert), and gives the game an unique vibe that works very well with its limitations. One problem is how blurry the sprites look when you zoom in a bit too close... Then, it looks a bit too rough. But you never need to zoom in as much, and it ends up looking great, for the most part! Well done here.
The
was good, but at the same time, a bit too repetitive. I like the western country it gives, adding to the atmosphere, but it's the same few tracks over and over again... Yeah, it ended up feeling too monotonous for me. What I ended up doing, was googling some other western country music (similar to what I heard in the game), and I stick to that instead. Unfortunately, I didn't find a lot from that time, which is a shame. It would be great if the developers could give the player some directions regarding finding other music, improving the overall experience for sure!
The
were good for the atmosphere, but always ended up going overboard, leading to a cacophony of work noises or general gibberish. It can be annoying. I believe that each building played a sound, which lead to lots of different sounds being played at once, in busy moments... Since it felt like the same clip over and over, it wasn't very pleasant for me... But it's not too bad, you can turn it off easily.
Just another issue here, is the fact that there are no audio sliders of any sort. It's just SFX and Music On/Off (separately).
The game was clearly designed for an iPad, and the interface shows that a lot, creating problems that should not exist in a PC game...
Now, about the game's
. You have a campaign with 20 different missions, each consisting of a city. In these missions, you have a checklist of 3 different objectives needed to succeed. As you play, there will also be 2 "surprise" comissions from the Mayor. These are optional, but generally provide you with a small benefit, in the form of upgraded buildings for free (although only in that particular level). There
be achievements for these, but the only ones who work are in the last level. All the others don't register, so there's that...
At the start of each city, you'll also have 3 starting options, depending on your playstyle. Some give you more money, some open more trading routes, more food, mines, etc. etc. All things considered, they only seemed to affect the very beginning of each mission. Once you're set, they all play very similarly.
Different cities will have different trading routes, and different types of buildings you can build. This could have been great for variety, and increasing strategy, but it's flawed. First off, you have no infomation about it when you choose your starting conditions. This is
. Very bad. So many developers give the player uninformed decisions to make...!
Then, there are the comissions. There's also no information about these beforehand, which means that you'll be caught by surprise, usually with very little money, and having to change your whole approach if you want to meet those requirement. Why? Because the comissions usually ask for materials you have no use for! Half of the time you can't sell them, so you just build structures to get them in time, and then it's just wasted space. All for a few building upgrades... In hindsight, I probably would have been better off not doing them! Oh well...
The limitations imposed to you regarding the farms you can use also seems very arbitrary. There weren't any radical terrain changes to justify these, which means that it just felt a way of forcing you into different directions. The same with trading routes, I have no idea why I can't create more flexible paths to make perfect use of my resources... Maybe it makes sense from an historical standpoint, but that's never explained. barely anything regarding the Gold Rush is explained actually, which is disappointing!
Then, you have the Sandbox Mode. This sounds fun, right? Just building you city, endlessly expanding! ... Well, not quite. You see, you'll be able to choose different areas on the map, some larger, with more coastal area, more minerals, etc. But they're all pretty limited levels. And there's no objective at all. I understand what Sandbox means, but even some comissions would have been very welcome! There are not even random events that can happen to throw you off guard (at least none that I've seen)... So, it ends up being very laborious. You simply repeat what you've done during the campaign, but this time, with no goal. Just mindlessly clicking things, reaching for infinity... I really do think this was a missed chance. Comissions would have helped with variety, perhaps some bandits would increase robberies, earthquakes, I don't know... there are lots of possibilities, but I've seen none of them, so yeah.
I'd stick with the campaign, and no more.
Aside from all of this, the game just lacks challenge, as well as options. First, there's no automated trading. Which means that you'll have to buy everything manually (and selling), making it hard to keep a constant economic balance. Then, even if you want to check your stock, you'll have to open another menu to see that, with more tabs and clicks than it needs (because I'm playing this on a mobile device... Oh, wait.)...
Each road must be built one by one as well, as well as every building. I think it would have benefited a lot from a selection method to construct more than one at once. Or even giving shortcuts to the different buildings. I have lots of buttons on my keyboard, and none of them seemed to do a damned thing! There's a lot of clicking through menus here, unnecessarily so.
The lack of challenge comes mostly from the lack of good objectives, and monotonous progress. There are no events to make your life harder, you just keep building until you're infinitely rich! The only difficulty was in the comissions (mostly due to omission), and maintaining a large mansions at the end. That's because each requires a plethora of different resources that you'll have to constatly keep trading for. Without automation, it's very easy to let things slip while you're doing something else, and then everything downgrades because they're lacking shoes... Or newspapers... Because that's what defines a mansion.
Sorry if I couldn't explain the mechanics all that well, but I've tried to focus on the negative points that I've found. I did not enjoy the game very much due to this lack of input from the player. It's just managing time and money, with no risk or reward. It's not awful, but not a great game!

1849 is like a grown-up version of Sim Town set in the old west.
It has simple gameplay mechanics, yet is still challenging, especially when it comes to completing commissions on time. The main story only takes about 15 hours to complete, but the game has good replay value if you're the type of gamer that likes to go back into beaten levels to try to complete tasks you couldn't before or try again with more challenging starter resources. The sandbox mode allows for further messing around too, but I can't figure out how to save a custom town before proceeding to a new one.
It features some nice isometric artwork and a solid soundtrack that doesn't loop too quickly (although, the sound effects do sometimes get repetetive).
I agree with other players on the point that it would be nice to have a feature that automates trading at a pace that you could customize, since micro-managing trades for resources that you need a constant supply of can become REALLY tedious. The Nevada DLC features a railroad trading system that automates trades, but the quantity traded cannot be customized, so it actually limits the size to which you can grow your town/city.

Before getting into the juicy bits, I'd like to provide a bit of background to what led me to write this "in-depth" review. At the time of writing this, it was only a couple hours beforehand that a friend of mine mentioned a new horror game with co-op has released; that game being Stay Close. I'm used to being badgered by the same friend to play a game of questionable quality, but that usually entails that said game is free, or a couple dollars at the most. I haven't heard of this game until that moment, so I can safely say that what you're currently reading is not something I typed out while blinded with the hype of a follower of the person(s) who have made this (for better or worse). My friend and I also did our best to go into this game as blind as possible, meaning that this review is pure, unadulterated, semi-biased-but-in-a-good-way opinions. Now with that out of the way, let's get down to the nitty-gritty.
As soon as you click play, you get a wide command window and another, smaller window with the game itself. The main menu is easily understandable, so at least it takes low effort to get into the settings. The settings themselves are a bit barren; nothing too spectacular. You have sliders for the usual graphic settings - shadows, texture quality, meshes and models (don't quote me on those two), even some for motion blur and FOV - that range from Low to Epic (Get it? This game runs on the Unreal Engine, made by Epic Games!) Also some checkboxes for stuff, but I wasn't paying much attention since the game runs mostly okay with graphics automatically set to Medium on my PC and I wasn't expecting to write a review after finishing to completion. The game itself looks fine graphically from what I've seen, but I will say that the flashlight felt almost worthless in some areas due to how dark it was. Perhaps I should have checked for brightness or contrast settings.
As for audio settings, well... at the time of writing this, there aren't any. At all. The only way to change the volume is by doing so with Windows or whatever OS this game lets you run it on. Maybe the audio menu is hidden somewhere? It's loud enough to hear most of what happens, but the first few minutes I played were spent looking behind me because of really faint footsteps
Good thing you don't have to worry about finding the checkbox for subtitles though, because there isn't any voiced dialogue whatsoever! At least the ambience is fitting.
For controls, there's only a really few amount of keybindings. WASD for movement, left shift for sprint, and mouse 1 for your flashlight. Was there controller support? I couldn't tell you. You're a nerd if you use a controller for a first person game anyways, so it doesn't matter.
Note: I haven't played single player which is supposed to be marginally different from what happens in multiplayer and I'm not significantly invested in Stay Close enough to play it just to write out an extra paragraph at best, so if you're a loner with no friends or if your friends refuse to buy this game/accept this game as a gift and you want to get your spooks on during October, you should probably look elsewhere.
So you or your friend clicked host game and after waiting forever for the game to finish loading, you find yourself in a pitch black room with a little entrance that leads to the words "Stay Away". If you're there with your friend, congratulations! You made it in record time compared to my friend and I what with the troubles we had. That dark room is, based off of my best guess, a lobby for you to wait in for a friend to connect. Once one person passes through, the other is stuck in there until you restart the entire process. If your friend crashes and needs to rejoin, you need to restart the process as well. Hopefully, this will only be the most glaring issue that you come across.
Upon going through the "Stay Away" entrance thingy, you're teleported to a well-lit back alley in a sanctioned off part of a city with not really much to do in terms of exploration. I thought the setting was nice, at least - night time in the city, boarded up buildings and flickering street lights, 4 body bags laying in that alley you start in and then no mention of what's up with them - very rustic. Very aesthetically pleasing. The thing is though, I had no idea where the ♥♥♥♥ this city was located. Some signs I passed by were in chinese, others in plain english, and all I could do was be irked by this inconsistency that isn't explained at all. Since most of the area is blocked off by fog It's time to explore what little you can.
Anyways, most of the gameplay and story that I can describe can be dumbed down to walking around in this city, doing requests for an old man named Cyrus while solving some of his relatively thought-provoking but overall easy riddles, and also coming across notes that don't have an effect on anything except world-building. Speaking to Cyrus reveals that all is not what it seems (surprise!) and that the characters that you and your friend play as are a couple who don't know where they are or how they got there. You solve a set of 3 riddles and then he sends you on a fetch quest to get a compass to an apartment where you encounter your first monsters.
The monsters themselves are nothing special; The first one is a feminine, mannequin-esque statue-but-also-a-living-thing that chases you unless you keep your flashlight pointed at it. I think it's called a Creeper? At this point, all I can think about is that it's a possible reference to Doctor Who, or maybe it's supposed to be unique and different and not at all like those statues but ends up being so. It might unnerve you for maybe 10 minutes or so until you get adjusted to it. As for the other monster, it's the direct opposite: a living thing with pink flesh, almost alien in appearence, that just so happens to chase you when your flashlight IS pointed at it; let's call them chasers. How convenient!
It's great and all that these two monsters exist, and you probably continue on in the game into the park looking for a different couple, an uncared for building that is apparently the city entrance in an attempt to find a key, along with the subways, thinking that there will be some more great and challenging attempts at scaring you, but there isn't. These two monsters are all you will encounter for the entire 2 hours of this story. I wouldn't be so rough about it if it wasn't so easy to take advantage of the AI of these things. For example, the Creepers will reset and go back to what is defined as their home point once you run a certain distance, as do the Chasers. It ends up just being management and memorization of their positions. It becomes stale. Not exciting. Not fun.
So, what happens when you reach the subway, which is the final part of the game? You meet Cyrus for one last time who summons a train to get on and he tells you what essentially amounts to, "Thanks for playing my game, you can go home now." So much for that unique twist. All I can say is, I expected nothing, and yet I still can't help but feel disappointed.
So, like, yeah. It could definitely be a lot better. I watched the trailer after completing the game, and the best way I can put how this game is in its current state is that it's like scraps. Maybe this game accidently forgot its Early Access tag, maybe some content updates will bring it to a level of quality that I'll miss out on, who knows? There are already plenty of horror games that do what Stay Close does, but better.  All I know is, I wouldn't spend $9 on it in its current state. $6 is pushing it.

Σίγουρα δεν είναι το παιχνίδι που θα μαγέψει την πλειοψηφία του κοινού, ούτε και o τίτλος που θ’ αποσπάσει διθυραμβικές κριτικές απ’ τους mainstream reviewers, όντας επί της ουσίας κομμένος και ραμμένος στα μέτρα των παραδοσιακών θιασωτών της κατηγορίας των adventure games. Εκείνους σίγουρα δεν θα τους απογοητεύσει κι εκεί έγκειται η επιτυχία του.
The feeling "Subject 13" finally leaves is that it meets the expectations of its 647 backers, as well as those of anybody else who has previously played one of Cuisset's games. It may not be the adventure game that will charm the majority of casual gamers, nor the one that mainstream reviewers will appreciate, but it's dedicated to true fans of the genre, due to the smart and difficult enough puzzles it includes. It won't disappoint them.
