I really wanted to like this Subject 13 because I'm generally a fan of puzzle-solving games, but I feel like there are too many rough edges here to ever settle in and enjoy it fully.
I got off to a rough start because the controls are not intuitive. The game's launcher has an option to customize controls, which is misleading because it's mouse-only. As a result, I spent the first several minutes mashing buttons on my keyboard and becoming frustrated because nothing seemed to be working. Further frustrating is that it's possible to accidentally click through the tooltip that tells you to how to navigate the controls. My first ten minutes in-game were completely wasted. I started over twice before understanding that holding down left-click over some items on-screen opens a wheel menu at the cursor.
A lot of the information you'll need to complete the puzzles isn't visible in the default camera view, so you'll have to contort your view somewhat in order to find the key items you need. The camera controls are only unlocked sometimes, though, which leads to frustratingly inconsistent controls. Mousewheel down is a particularly frustrating example - sometimes it means "zoom out", sometimes it means "leave this area". Eventually you'll figure out how to work with the controls, but even after several hours in-game it doesn't feel familiar.
Probably half of the key items you'll pick up present their own puzzles that you have to solve before you can use them. If you spend enough time examining each object (and checking the help/tips) you can probably figure out how to use it. Prepare to spend a lot of time figuring out what obscured detail is preventing you from taking an intuitive path to your goal, though. Have you ever had to use a socket wrench on a ladder before? I haven't. But your character will, and not for any good reason either. The game wants you to make twisting motions with your cursor to turn keys, unfasten bolts or open lids, but these motions feel out of place with the point-and-click style of the rest of the game, and they frequently don't work correctly on the first attempt.
The puzzles cover a pretty wide range of difficulties, from 4x4 sliding-tile-puzzle to Mayan kind-of algebra, but for the most part the game has a help/tips system that gives you a new clue every few minutes so that you don't get stuck. It'll also let you skip a puzzle once, so that if you get completely stuck the game's not ruined. You can only use it once, though. Unfortunately, some of the puzzles don't make any sense, and the only way I was able to get past those was either by brute force (combination locks) or by looking up the mechanics or solution, both of which really spoil the fun.
Some of the mechanics are downright bad. There's more than one instance where you'll have to scour the screen for a nearly invisible button or item, and you won't be able to progress until you find it.
At some point in the game there's a large cylindrical minesweeper-type puzzle that I just can't get past. I've uncovered every non-trap square and marked every trap square, but I don't know what's missing to trigger the completion and after three attempts on just that puzzle I'm not sure that I care enough to try again.
I don't know whether I'll ever finish this game. I feel like I gave it a good effort, and if I'd been able to finish it I think it might have been a good buy at $12.99. As-is, I just feel frustrated.

I wanted to like this game, because I'm a fan of Portal and puzzle-solving games, and the premise seemed interesting.  Sadly, I found this game quite boring to play.  The biggest issue for me was the severe limitation of movement.    It is basically a pixel-hunting point-and-click adventure, reminiscent of the "Escape"-style games.  Each chapter is basically a room you have to escape from.  The voice acting is terrible, and the journal entries you find along the way did little to make me care about the characters or the facility.  Compare that to Portal 2, where the humor and the post-apocalyptic story kept you going at a fast pace.  This game is glacial. If you miss a tiny little clue, you are basically stuck, and can't continue or do anything else until you find it.  This game might be worth $5, but I paid $13 and I felt robbed.  Poor story, boring puzzles, weak characters, and almost no freedom of movement.

The pseudo-3d approach is a bit annoying at times, with some puzzles reliant entirely too much on finding the exact angle needed to locate something, and the object interaction is clunky at times, especially when you know what you need to do, but are forced to follow the game's tortuous logical processes.
The story is not wholly original (although the cake reference was amusing) and even though I'm only about half-way, I will be pleasantly surprised if it works out differently to what I am expecting.

Luftrausers is an arcadey style game where you are put in an 'endless' arena, trapped between the seas below and the clouds above, flying around and shooting enemies that spawn semi-randomly.  That's about it, really.  But it's a hell of a lot of fun.
The controls are tight, the guns all feel around about as powerful as they should, each different engine and body and weapon has it's own niche that changes how you play, while still letting you learn from your general experience with all of the rest of the gear.  The unlock system is pretty good, and I was able to unlock all rauser parts within a couple of hours of play.
There are a lot of tiny details that make the game top knotch.  Each rauser combination has its own name, often humerous.  The music changes based upon which gear you equip, with each slot of your rauser changing one layer of the music.  After unlocking all the parts you begin to unlock alternate colour schemes, which make the game look different, and can call attention to differnt parts for the game, for instance enemies might be highlighted in one scheme, where your rauser is in another, or the bullets are in a third.  The running theme is: while you can change a lot of things, it is the same game at its heart.  And it's a damn good game.
If you like score attack games and competing against your friends, this is a must buy.  If you like arcade style games, I think it's well worth the $10.  If you want to support games with good design, or don't think you'll play it more than a few times, I still think it's worth paying for on sale.  If you're only interested in games for the plot... you might want to look elsewhere.
Overall, a rausing success of a game.

This game starts very fun with polished controls and a great visual style. I enjoyed it for the first hour, maybe two, but in the end the sudden drop off in entertainment made me to not recommend this game. It wasn't without other issues as well...
The game lacks a good progression/unlockable balance. There is overall goals and levels. But. Also each item (weapon/armor/boost) you unlock comes with it's own unlockable goals. This is honestly the only reason you would bother using most options beyond a one time try to "see what they are". Basically the system forces you to use items you don't prefer if you want to stay on track in your progression. But if like most people you find a weapon/armor/boost combo you prefer and ignore your other unlocks? Well, you run the risk of grinding your overall level progression up... Which changes the spawn rates of enemies. And that's where the balance is quickly lost when you start missing specific item goals. There's one "right" way to progress but even if you did it and methodically unlocked each upgrade's goals as you got them without wasted plays? I still doubt it would stay balanced! And let me be clear, this is not a complaint about difficulty...
I like a challenge and this game gives it when you get a lot of enemies on screen at once. But the spawning balance just ruins a reasonable chance at a goal and turns it into a lottery. Luck isn't a challenge, it is just luck. Skill goes out the window. And you do get to the point where you tap out. The goals you have left indeed become purely luck based or based on enemy spawns that rarely if ever cooperate. The game goes from a steady two hours of fun challenges of unlocks and goals to a test of  your willpower to grind and grind with items you don't like until you literally get lucky and win the lottery.
Which I guess points out one last flaw. Without the goals this game loses all of it's appeal. All of it. With runs so short it isn't rewarding in any way to just play for "fun" without a goal. An average run is well under a minute. This makes playing it like an arcade game just going for a high score both pointless and ultra repetitive.
I definitely had some fun playing it. It was a challenge at times and the gameplay felt tight. It was a pleasure to look at stylistically too. But then the fun ended. Abruptly. Completely. Beyond being a throw in game in a bundle I wouldn't recommend it. The price is way out of balance with what you actually get; A way out of balance short game.

Orcs Must Die 2 is a fun little game in solo or co-op, though it has some problems. There's no real tutorial and the hint scenes are busy and unintuitive, but at least the story mode has a reasonable progression and learing curve. The co-op mode reduces the amount of abilities each person can cast quite a bit making teamwork necessary, even more so because the game can be paused by either player.
There is a nice option to respec (basically sell purchased items) but no option to sell a single aquired item... which means if you screw up your loadout you need to do it all again. This gets really annoying when you have a bunch of stuff! I just cannot understand how this was not caught by playtesting. It drags down much of the game when you're trying to experiment. Also, be warned, the voice chat sucks (it's always on) and was also not thought through.
There are important upgrades behind an additional paywall. I'm okay with appearance options costing but when something like the guardian trinket (very important for endless or nightmare mode if you want to use archers\etc) is locked behind a paywall, I'm not happy. Finally there are times losses feel very cheap, including when bugs lead to them.
That said, for the price I paid (about $4) I certainly got enough enjoyment out of it to recommend the game (and it is addictive). It's funny at times and a neat puzzle game that involves squishing orcs, so it can't be that bad.

For me this is the most realistic open world survival games out there, and one that could really happen to anyone in a similar unfortunate situation. There are no zombies or dinosaurs of course, but that doesn't detract from the game at all IMO.
What there are are some very nasty sharks, and what those bad boys can do to you puts them almost in the same category - especially the Great White and Tiger sharks - they'll really mess you up bad and even a machete might not save you because once you've spilt blood then those things just won't let up.
You'll be washed up on a tiny Pacific Island in a chain of such islets, another of which you can see. There are resources enough to get you going and you should be able to stave off hunger and thirst whilst you build your first fire and shelter allowing you to save the game.
Pretty soon your mind will turn to supplies as you struggle to cope with the tiny amount of resources on each island (thank god for coconuts), and you'll see the tops of masts from wrecked vessels sticking out of the sea within swimming distance. However between you and the wrecks there is a very dangerous peice of water - you may be lucky and make it, or you may not! Even if you're lucky you'll still need to be careful of how long you can hold your breath as you swim around the innards of the wreck. The rewards can be great if you're prepared to take the risk. Or pehaps build a raft to get you there? Mind you a Great White might be no respector of even a raft...
The game plays well and the graphics are very good when turned up. The UI is probably the easiest to use of any survival game I've played too. I love the cyclic day/night effects, the weather and nice little touches like the bats coming in to roost on the few trees. Underwater swimming is nice to look at as you pass corals, rays and various fish - but just watch out for those sharks!

Sometimes planes can take 2 missiles and explode which is usually the fastest some standard jet planes can go down, but sometimes planes can also take up to 4-6 missile hits and a barrage of guns only to explode after we see some stylized collateral damage.
The story is also uninspiring when compared to past Ace Combat games. Anything interesting in the plot could've been seen a mile away with as the game tries to hold your hand through its already weak plot.
The game tries to make up for its lackluster gameplay by expanding on what you can do in the game: bombing and helicopter assaults. Helicopter missions are a bit weak while the bombing ones are actually interesting althought there is only a total of 1 bombing mission in the game.

Note: I'm burning through my Steam backlog and trying out every game I have so this is based on about an hour of gameplay.
I'm a big fan of Ace Combat on PS2. Now I haven't played an Ace Combat game in many years before today and sadly, the series looks to be in worse shape then when I last saw it.
Firstly the presentation: The overall presentation and feel of the series I remember is gone and replaced with a more Tom Clancy-ish / Call of Battlefield modern military cinematic style; which wouldn't be so bad if this were some other game. The story is pretty generic and forgetable as are the characters; but then I never played Ace Combat for the story so it's not that big of a deal. Just a little bit of a let down.
The Combat: It feels dumbed down. I remember having more control over the aircraft previously. Dogfighting  now comes down to switching to an on the rails mode briefly while AI controls your aircraft following the enemy. It does provide a more cinematic experience I guess but I didn't buy this game to watch a movie. Don't get me wrong, I enjoy arcade style action, but that's not what Ace Combat is about for me.
Other Issues: In order to integrate variety into the game, helicopter and turret missions have been added. The helo controls just awfully and I HATE turret missions in any game so there's that. Besides, why would Ace Combat need anything else besides the aircraft missions? This really hurts the game in my opinion.
Overall Ace Combat: Assault Horizon is not the worst thing I've ever played but it's certainly not worth 20 dollars. The Fighter Jet missions are still kind of fun despite being dumbed down and the aircraft all look pretty cool. I can not recommend this game based on the price, but if you can pick it up under 5 bucks, it may be worth an afternoon.

This game is a disappointment. The single player story is weak, specially when compared to previous titles such as Ace Combat 5 or ACZero (6, the first title on the 360 and PS3 and directly previous to AH, had a pretty short story as well); it feels like the story has been completely cast aside in favor of the multiplayer, which is also extremely poor and mostly dead by now. It feels shallow, and the characters are very dry, with bad voice acting to match. The helicopter missions, one of the new additions of AH, are absolutely terrible, with sketchy controls and no real way to control the heli's nose; on the other hand, the C130 attack plane is very fun to play with.
The real world setting made more bad than good to this game - you won't see any of the fantastic boss battles you had on the other games, such as Scinfaxi and Arkbird from AC5 or Excalibur from ACZero, since those were made up technology; instead in AH you'll have unimpressive fights against a cruiser ship and occasionally shoot some missiles off air, and that's it. The battles against other aces (which are too few to actually cause impact on the players) are heavily scripted rail shooting sections, with little to no skill involved.
Over all, this game feels like a huge letdown for the series, with many things that made the series great being cut off, in favor of poorly thought and badly realized features. 4/10, a waste of money if you're expecting an actual Ace Combat game.

Pros
* Bombing is neat
Cons
* Ridiculous anime skins for the planes

The cons are pretty much endless
All in all, don't waste your time or money on this game. It wasn't worth the $60 when I got it and its not worth the $20 now. If you must spend your money on this series, at least get a game that will be worth it such as ace combat 4 or 5. I would recommend 'Ace Combat 5: The Unsung War'

Overall, SOM is an OK game, 3 out of 5 stars.  The story just isn't that compelling unless you're SUPER into Tolkein.  The combat system is great, because it's basically the Arkham games system, which is great.  However, unlike the Arkham games, SOM is too overpowered.  In the Arkham games yeah you collected gadgets and techniques, but it wasn't to be a supreme fighter, it was to counteract the new enemy types that couldn't be taken down by standard punches and kicks.  In SOM, there really isn't a variety of enemies, and the few that they are, can still be taken down easily by the standard moves.  That's why the added abilities just makes the main character OP in my opinion.  The animations are fantastic, always get to see a cool way for an Uruk to die.  The challenges and the discoverable items were boring, again, unless you're SUPER into Tolkein.  Take Tomb Raider, when you find something, it's engaging, and has to do with the story, in SOM they're just there for the sake of finding them mostly.  Basically from a cutscene, animation, fighting system standpoint, the game is great, but the meat and potatoes of it as a whole fell through.  Blah story, almost no chance of ever dying or feeling a real threat to your life.  The nemesis system is cool in theory, and actually works out pretty well, but without that actual fear of dying and therefore stacking the nemesis system against you due to your failure, it too falls short.  Get it on sale like I did, not worth full price, but it is worth a try.

Quick Overview: If you like Assasin's Creed games, but get bored of them quickly and / or find collection tedious, this games sets a faster pace. It has a lot of the best parts of the first of the new Tomb Raider games (though not the puzzle elements) combined with many of Assasin's Creed's best characteristics, and fewer of both series drawbacks. The Nemesis and Branding systems are unique and enjoyable, and the logic behind Talion's power adds a layer of thoughtful immersion often missing from other similar games. Worth a try even if you don't like the games I mentioned, but has parallels in gameplay that are easy to draw. Oh yeah, and its LotR so the story is very solid.
I'm very happy with what I got out of this game, and there was still more I could have done after with the extra campaigns (I had gotten my fill by that point, and dabbled in each of them only briefly out of curiosity, but not to completion). Getting it on sale, I would say it is absolutely worth $20 for the base game, and each of the expansions would be worth another $5 each.
As I note in the Quick Overview, the game has a lot of components and mechanics reminiscent of Assasin's Creed mixed with the new Tomb Raider games (or Uncharted if you prefer, obviously without the modern elements). However, I found it did not get boring nearly as quickly as Assasin's Creed games. Any of the AC series I have played, I got bored of within the first 5 - 15 hours. I have never beaten any of them as a result. I found it became tedious, and the core gameplay, thoroughly enjoyable at first, grew chore-like in time. I had the same archs of "okay, I'm starting to be good on this" in Shadows of Mordor, but where Assasin's Creed simply didn't hold my attention, Shadow of Mordor re-engaged me at each of those moments with new mechanics. I could easily see someone only playing the first half of the game in Udun and still getting their money's worth, but my favorite parts came in the second half in Nurn.
Nurn contained one of the two parts of this game that really set it apart from AC, TR or Uncharted. The first you encounter, though, is present throughout and you encounter in Udun: the Nemesis system. Essentially, if you are killed by an Uruk, a number of things can happen. When you continue after that death, if it was a simple foot soldier or the like that killed you, they will earn a name and become a captain, gaining special characterstics and the ability to rise through the ranks. If a captain or warchief kills you, they will increase in Power, often gaining new abilities and losing old weaknesses. Also, depending on how you have fought them in the past, their dialogue may change. All told, you start to get a degree of attachment and depth to your enemies that is not often present in other games. A lot of people think of the Nemesis system when they think of Shadow of Mordor, and with good reason - it is a lot of fun and adds a lot to the game.
For me, however, it is the element introduced in Nurn that captures me (Spoiler Alert!). In Nurn, by progressing the main storyline, one of your abilities transforms into a better version, doing what it did before but now also applies a Brand. When enemies are Branded,  they are your allies. Captains and Warchiefs can be branded as well, with somewhat more difficulty, and given commands to rise through the ranks. You can assist them on missions to help them gain power and improve their abilities. In the next game in the series, Shadow of War, your most dire Nemesis and most 'loyal' Follower will follow from Shadow of Mordor to Shadow of War, which is a nice touch. I nearly put the game down after the first half in Udun, but the Branding system re-engaged me enough to pull me through to the end.
I could go into more specifics about abilities, missions, side quests and the like, but I think the Nemesis System, the Branding System and the points I made about the game overall are enough. There were a couple of missions that I felt were not super well tuned and tried to do something interesting with the mechanics, but ended up being awkward or frustrating. The side quests were sometimes a little repetitive, though they made an effort to mix it up as much as they could. The story is LotR so if you like that universe, you will probably be happy. Some characters are more interesting than others, but I would say its very good as far as game storylines go.
If what you've read here appeals, consider picking it up. I definitely didn't regret it, so hopefully neither will you.

Remember back in the 90's when Street Fighter II came out, then was followed by constant rerelease after rerelease, so much that you could make a game based entirely on each character having all their versions playable? (They did, by the way) Well, Ultra Street Fighter IV is that to Super Street Fighter IV Arcade Edition, which in turn was that to Super Street Fighter IV, which started all the way in Street Fighter IV. And to think just a few decades ago, there wasn't enough Street Fighter to go around!
So what's new this time? The Street Fighter IV series' main gimmick is that the graphics have been brought into 3D while maintaining a 2D axis, sort of like Street Fighter EX only closer to the 2D games. The vibe I get from this series, after the Experts-Only vibe I get from Street Fighter III, is "Introducing the New Gen to Street Fighter". Indeed, when this series began, the roster was basically Street Fighter II Champion Edition + some new guys, a new boss, Akuma and Shen Long.
That's my biggest praise and yet, biggest gripe about Street Fighter IV: Of the cast featured in just this entry, only 9 are new, and one is from Final Fight, one's a Super Akuma, and the third's basically a replacement for Juli and Juni. Call me nuts, but I miss something like Street Fighter III, where each cast member save a few veterans for newcomers are brand new, with unique fighting styles. Street Fighter IV's newcomers are alright, but of them, only C. Viper, Hakann, and Juri stand out. They've got some interesting playstyles, but not very compelling designs. I guess if this were the best I could come up with after waiting for a decade to make it, I'd stick to familiar faces, too.
The familiar faces translate fairly well to 3D. I will truly miss the fluid animation of Street Fighter III, but IV has a great aesthetic. Fireballs in particular look wonderful, like wisps of ki energy. This does very well for the powerpuf Super and Ultra Combos involving them, in particular Dhalsim's Yoga Catastrophe. On the other hand, the movement can sometimes feel a tad artificial; one need only compare the Street Fighter III characters in their debut game to their appearances here to see what I mean. There's also an interesting detail in that when you complete Arcade Mode once, you can set each character's voice language to either English or Japanese. If you miss your Yatta, but wonder why Guile has to speak Japanese to hear it again, that's your solution.
As for the Arcade Mode, the end boss is rather challenging, but not unfairly so. An average player who knows what he's doing can probably defeat the arcade mode in two tries, give or take. Of course, since this is a Street Fighter game, there are four "powered-up" versions of specific Shotos to face as secret bosses; having taken on only one of them, they are a real challenge, good for someone who wants a test of their power.
Ultra doesn't add much on top of the base Super Street Fighter IV: Arcade Edition, but what it adds is nice. Five new characters are added, although four are simply reused assets from Street Fighter X Tekken and one plays similar to Cammy. Still, three of them are veterans, so it's worth it if you're a fan of any of them. Also added is the ability to use both of your characters' Ultra Combos instead of having to pick one, the tradeoff being the attacks are weaker. There is also a special Omega Mode for Vs. Mode that offers unique alternate versions of select cast members while also simultaneously changing how certain moves affect the Super Meter to an extent. Combine these variants with the bundled Alternate Costumes included with Ultra's standalone edition, and you practically have new takes on familiar faces, which end up breathing new life into the old cast, and even turn one much-maligned character into less of a copy of another. Sadly, this mode cannot be used in the Arcade Mode or in select Online Modes, so make of that what you will.
By now, anyone who's played a Street Fighter title before knows what they're doing. This game is the very definition of "Welcome Back, Street Fighter!", a way to introduce the lil' whippersnappers to fightan' games like they used to make. Still, what Street Fighter does it usually does well, and IV is no exception. If you'd like to introduce someone to Street Fighter, or 2D fighters, you can't go wrong with this.
One more note: the PC Version actually runs smoother than the console versions. Framerates are much better and load-times are nonexistent. I haven't tested the online mode, but so far this PC release knocks it out of the ballpark. I picked this up during Black Friday because I needed something to keep me company while I was away from my consoles... I'm selling the console version I had in favor of this. Great job, again, on the PC Port, Capcom!
If I had to give Ultra Street Fighter IV a grade, it would be 4/5. Not quite on the level of Third Strike, but still a very solid game, one I'd easily recommend to someone who wants to get into fighting games. Go gift it to someone, and who knows, maybe you'll like it, too!

There are many things you can do in starbound, you can follow the main missions, do sidequests from the many different NPCs or even trade with them, each with their own unique design, home, village, etc.
There's a large amount of different stars, each with different planets depending on the star type. Gentle stars, Frozen stars, Temperate stars, you name it, it's there.
The planets all have different types of metals, crystals, materials and different species of intelligent life as well as wildlife.
You can colonize, terraform, and explore them all given the right equipment to do so. The weapons in this game are phenomenal, each have different types of elements and abilities. Swords, spears, boomerangs, guns, and a wide variety of throwing weapons.
I honestly cant put it into words how great the building system is. There are so many amazing things you can build in this game that I can't even list it. The possibilities are limited only to your imagination.
I highly, HIGHLY, recommend this game. All of this for only $14.99 [$10.04 during steam sale.]. The game only gets better and better with each update and I'm absolutely ecstatic for what the developers have in store for the future.

But in case you need more convincing, let me tell you what's what. Ace Combat is not - and never has been - a flight sim. It's a long-running franchise hailing from Japan, eminently focused on high-speed arcade action. It has always had very, very little at all to do with reality, save the inclusion of detailed plane models based mostly on real-life military fighters and bombers.
As a flight-sim enthusiast, some would consider it a crime for me to admit that I really do enjoy arcade flight games. They're a great fallback for those times when you want to splash some bogies, but you don't have the time or the inclination to go full-real (or even semi-real, honestly).
I've played Ace Combat games for years, since I was a kid, and it was probably Ace Combat among other games that helped foster my later interest in more authentic fare. I started with Ace Combat 2: Electrosphere on the original Playstation, and let me tell you: the title of that game says it all. Ace Combat has a track record of featuring crazy, wonky, way-out-there fantasy elements, up to and including the absurdly massive flying superweapons that are a genuine staple of the franchise.
Ace Combat was never about being serious. It was about flying around a surprisingly well-modeled, realistic-looking plane incongruously stuffed with 200-plus anti-everything missiles, and blowing things up with reckless abandon. This and Armored Core was where it was at back in the day, and it was a glorious time to grow up in.
Now, AC4 tried to shake things up a bit by introducing a "relatable" "story" with "characters" and such. And it's fairly poor. Thankfully, it doesn't detract from gameplay too much, as the background chatter is easy to tune out, but if examined at length...oh boy. The writing was chunky and oftentimes silly, and the low-grade-anime-quality voice actors delivering the lines made for a very embarrassing experience.
"Yeah, we won! Now let's sing our dramatically overwrought national anthem as the camera pans dramatically around our planes! YEAH!"
But AC5 didn't improve its horrible dialog and hand-wringingly bad voice acting. In fact, it made it *worse,* as "story" became an increasing focus. And then AC6? Oh my and dear me. Just go YouTube the intro, or look up "dance with the angels - " actually, no. Don't do that. You'll die of embarrassment. Actually, you should, because the sheer temple-drilling horribleness of that dialogue atrocity is actually important to this review.
For years, the core gameplay never really changed between sequels. It was all about going from one target to the next, getting a lock-on, and then double-tapping the missile button to launch precisely two missiles, and flying off to the next enemy. It's fun, for a while, but without any real evolution going on in the background, franchise fatigue was inevitable.
So what did they change? Is this game "Call of Duty with wings," as so many reviews claim? Ha, well, the answer is that they changed everything, while actually changing nothing. Let me explain in brief.
The "innovations" consist of one central new "feature:" Dog-Fight Mode. That's right. "Mode." As in, one of the core aspects of air combat is now a "mode." There's also a differently-named variant for ground attacks, but it's the exact same concept: press a combination of two buttons, and you lock into a more or less on-rails scripted sequence where you keep your target or targets centered while your missiles lock on.
I don't even really mind the system in theory. Really, they HAD to do something to change things up, because even as a long-time AC fan, I was getting bored of the one-button double-tap missile fest the game had stubbornly been for years.  What they were trying to achieve with DFM was to add some depth to air battles, make them more dependent on timing and reading movements. It actually plays much better in practice than it sounds going by my description of it. But here's the problem: occasionally, the game uses DFM as an excuse to pretty much put you through an on-rails theme-park ride that's scripted to the end. Don't balk too much - after all, Grand Theft Auto has been doing the exact same thing for years with every single one of its "dramatic car chases," and it's a million seller. But let's be honest - it still sucks.
DFM is actually okay on its own. It's got flaws, but the core idea is sound. It takes all the concepts of energy and g-forces and simplifies the crap out of them so as not to burden the core arcade experience with excessive realism, giving the occasional dog-fight a fraction of the intensity and strategy of the real thing. The enemy suddenly peels left, so you have to slow and follow to keep from losing him. He dives and burns, so you have to throttle up to keep pace. A lot of scripting is required, sure, and all of these maneuvers do constitute a sort of timing mini-game in all honesty, but still, the nature of the game's AI would ordinarily prevent exciting dog-fights from actually taking place to begin with. So in that regard, it's nice to have a sort-of-dog-fight experience every once in a while.
The problem is when DFM triggers a heavily-scripted setpiece, as mentioned above. It tends to happen at least twice per mission, and you have little to no actual control over the events. Your subject plane becomes temporarily immune to all damage until a sufficiently exciting number of explosions occur within your relative field of view, and the setpiece is over.
It's fun the first time, sure, but if you eat a missile (or two, or three) and die, and one of those setpieces occurs after your last checkpoint, be prepared for your next DFM attempt to trigger the exact same pseudo-cutscene again. It will do so the next time you die, too. And the next time.
Thankfully, most enemies can be defeated the old-school double-tap way, but you're still avoiding an entire facet of the gameplay. It sucks because these scripted moments, when they do occur, detract from the good the devs achieved, and all but ruin the feature completely. Regular DFM battles are just fine.
The ground attacks, though, are boiled crap. They force you on a linear path, often against ALL COMMON SENSE, and it becomes a game of struggling with the lock toggle to send your missiles to the right target. It's just plain horrible, and unlike DFM, it's straight-up forced on you. Do it, or mail your fission, 'cause it's game over.
The devs know all about the importance of cushioning a bad landing. In case their grand gameplay experiment failed, they needed a scapegoat to blame for the negative reviews. And so: thematic shift! They hired a half-decent American writer to pen an actually coherent script, applied some color-grading to the post, and for the first time placed the game's events in the real world. So of course the new "direction of the plot" was the game's real failing. Oh, yeah, definitely. Don't worry, fans. We'll never do that again, we promise.
Sadly, this nonsense seemed to have worked. Most people hate the game because it's "too American," while claiming that the prior games' plots were so good, that they moved them to tears. "Dance with the angels." Search it. I'll save space in the review. Anyway, it's not the fault of the ill thought-out gameplay mechanics - it's because they Americanized it. Yeah, that's it. Certainly it, no question.
Anyway, in summary - I just can't recommend it. It's broken, it's frustrating. At one point, a dozen planes spawn right behind you when the game expects you take out a boatload of ground targets in less than two minutes. Another has you struggling to shoot down an ICBM whose exhaust causes unavoidable damage. Sucks if you get THAT checkpoint while already critically damaged...like *I* did. Time to restart a 30 minute mission!
...or not. Save yourself the trouble, and save yourself the scratch. This game needs to go dance with the angels.

Orcs Must Die 2 is the sequel to Orcs Must Die (obviously) and as lazy as it sounds I would recommend reading my review of that because this game is essentially the same again. Not that that's a bad thing! The formula works, hell in this one they even improved a few things.
This time you can choose between 2 characters to play as, the apprentice or the antagonist from the previous game. Each of the characters has their strengths and weaknesses, the apprentice carries on as he did before but now gives you the choice of crossbow, blunderbuss. The crossbow being the same as the last game and the blunderbuss causing far more damage but having a much longer reload time. The sorceress has less health than the apprentice but more mana and she can control a Orc and make him fight the others for a short period. As well as that some of the starting traps are different depending on which you choose as well as a few unlockables later.
Speaking of traps there are some new ones, all of which are entertaining to see unfold, the levels also sometimes have environmental traps built in which you can take advantage of.
This time there are far more unlockables to collect, costumes that change your abilities, rings and trinkets to enhance the way you play and of course the upgrades.
Like the first game it's repetitive as hell, but what do you expect? And also like the first it's difficulty seems to ramp up out of nowhere.
I recommend this game to those who have either played the first and want more of the same. If your new to the series... Well start here. It's a better game really, since it's the first one plus extras.
I'd say £11.99 is a little steep though considering the first is essentially the same minus a few parts. See if you can find it a bit cheaper or on a sale. Anything below £10 is a bargain really.

An excellent buy in or out of sale months, and my personal favorite game on Steam (perhaps that I've ever played).
Pros:
-A pretty nice character creator that gives you decent liberties to play a character you can believe in.
-Excellent level-up system that rewards persistence and knowledge of grinding-favorable areas you've visited before.
-Assuming you start the game with the MASTER KEY starting gift, massive leeway to traverse the starter areas in the order you please.
-Fair difficulty progression as the game goes on.
-Some of the best story any action RPG has to offer, but you have to work your♥♥♥♥♥off to piece it together.
-Online play system that operates on a risk/reward basis (you can summon help but at the same time be at risk of being invaded by other players wanting to kill you)
-Death is not the end of the world: get back up and go get those souls back!
-Wide pools of weapons to choose from, pick your favorites and run with them.
-Bosses that challenge both your reaction time as well as spatial awareness.
-Allows replayability by followup playthroughs in the New Game Plus system, that pits the player agaisnt more powerful and rewarding foes.
-DSFix mod makes the game look delicious in comparison to console versions.
Cons
-Multiplayer has been waning in recent years. It's a shell of its former self, but not dead.
-Framerate drops in Blighttown.
-Almost necessitates use of the DSFix for a good, proper visual experience. (Oh no, I have to download third party software that even the devs said was good!)
Iffy (could be considered Pro or Con)
-It's hard. If you don't have patience, this could make or break the game for you.
-There will be that ONE type of enemy or boss that has it out for you specifically. Other people might say its easy, but you find it the most infuriating thing ever. (Or the greatest challenge of the game?)
Overall Rating: 10/10

The way the game builds a meta-narrative by constructing the narrative around the game's implicit rogue-like formula, using symbolism and game mechanics within that rogue-like format (item pickups, enemies, etc) makes this game truly special. In a way, by using a meta-narrative to form the narrative, The Binding of Isaac's narrative can escape the postmodern crisis of "where do we go from self-awareness?" This brilliance, this elevation of the narrative from postmodern via the postmodern, thus propelling it not into a postpostmodern work but instead an EXmodern work (so to speak), helps inform the game's feedback loop on a subconscious level (after all, all games begin at postmodern because they're interactive, so such a magnificent break from postmodern, as is done by Isaac, is picked up on immediately-perhaps first sensually, before slowly worming it's way into self-awareness-and thus lends the idea of mindless entertainment a new edge). The narrative within this trans-meta-narrative structure, which is to say, the narrative's own narrative aside, the game deals with abuse and childhood psychology: how does abuse affect children? It feels tasteful in it's atmosphere and does a good job. Except for Afterbirth, which sucks. The portals as a meta-allegory fall short, feeling more a proof of concept than finished piece of literature. The update in it's entirety fails to capitalize on the meta-concept of DLC, too. Very disappointing. I haven't played Afterbirth but really, you don't need to either.

This was a game that pleasantly surprised me as a well conceieved work of art. Not only has it got some amazing game play, it's movement system and combo systems are also quite impressive. As city-builders run short these days, i decided to have a go at this game. When i first started it i had in mind all the older city building game i already played such as SimCity, Cities XL, the Anno series and Sierra games (Pharaon, Zeus, the Caesar series...), the last which apparently served as the main inspiration for this game.
Thus, i was not surprised of the game mechanics which mainly consists of starting from scratch with three objectives that need to be filled. You then start to build some houses and production buildings, and the way to proceed is as i said above based on Sierra's mechanics: citizens need a certain resource/building in order to upgrade their houses, and therefore increase the rent income. Run short of any resource and the houses will shortly degrade to the highest level it can attain with the remaining ones.
Production on it's side consists of running a production chain which may consist of one up to three buildings in order to well... produce resources. These resources can be either used to satisfy citizen's needs, be sold at trading routes or given to the few events (up to three per mission from my experience). Some other elements have been included such as crime or fire, with respectively the sheriff and fire brigade in order to fight against them.
At this stage of the review you are probably thinking "Well that doesn't look so bad, does it?". And unfortunately it does. Let me explain you why, in the same way as i described the game above:
You start each game with three objectives: there is absolutely no time-limit or constraint of any kind. There is no other way to lose the game then through bad management, which is nearly impossible after a playing for a few hours. You can start from three "difficulty" options at the start of each mission, but it does only impact the first few minutes of play.
The resource management of this game is very simplistic: The raw resources are produced at a steady rate, never influenced by seasons (grapes, grain and cotton all the year! ) nor resource availability (hunters producing without animals, lumber mills without forests...). Stock management has been dealt with by giving your warehouse an unlimited storage capacity. You cannot predict as well the resource supply and demand of your city easily, as no production and consumption summary is given, which means that you will have to over-produce all goods required to avoid stock shortage.
Trade is the simplest form that could be included. You pay a "fee" to open the trade route with a city, and then after you can import or export goods from there. Goods are imported/exported at a fixed price, with unlimited quantity. This means that you can sell the town next door 100k logs of lumber at the same price, and import 100k crates of beer, without any impact on future trade or product price. Production capacity and demand are simply not taken into account in this game. This lead to a "give me money" button that can be pressed once in a while, without thinking any further.
Wages and rents are also fixed, population satisfaction is simply not taken into account, and unemployment's only impact is the color of the total population indicator. Hazards like crime and fire are solved by having the relevant building, effectively leading the risk to 0%. Other natural hazards likely never happen, or even if they do their impact is so minor that you do not even need to take them into account.
One back side of this game simplicity is that a resource shortage (non-anticipable as said before) can lead to total mayhem. A  house degrading can mean worker shortage (which has no proper indicator), and this shortage can escalate to a complete desertion: some buildings required by citizens are shut down, leading to further house degrading, leading to further work shortage... A simple feature to give work priorities could eliminate this issue but it has not been implemented.
To sum up, this game is simplistic, terribly easy, and becomes quickly repetitive. I can say without any risk that after playing this game for 2 hours like i did you will have gotten all that this game has to offer. The only difficulties that can arise are not part of the intended gameplay but are the result of a lack of management tools and features that are included in most other city-builders.
Despite having the full california on the main menu and a large map when starting a game, you are confined in a tiny square without any opportunity to expand. That shocked me first but after playing for a while you understand that this space is all you need to have a working untouchable, steady producing money-farm.
To finish this review i wanted to say that i understand that this a new indie development studio, but i just took a look of the game description of this store page. "complex cities" and "deep simulation games" are not the words i would use to describe this game. On this opposite i would use the words "simplistic" and "casual". This is typically a game you could run on social networks or mobile phones, but in no way a city-builder simulation or resource management game.
Recommendation:
- For new players discovering the genre: This game could be an interesting first city-builder to play, but you will soon outgrow this game and regret buying it in the first place. If you want to start with a city-building game you should look for classics such as the ones i listed in the first pagagraph.
- For experimented city-building games players: Do not buy this game as you will feel robbed after playing for a few hours. Used to more complex management games it will feel like riding a car on a carousel after being used to drive a real one.
Sorry for the long review, but i didn't want to freely throw a bunch of critics without explaining why i came to these conclusions.

At first glance, you might think, "Eh, this looks simplistic."
Well, you'd be right. And wrong. True, you shoot and you fly; that's really it. The beauty of it however is how well realized Luftrausers' combat is, and it is marvelous. Weaving inbetween hails of bullets from all directions is an incredible experience, and after a while you start to get a handle on how to fly around and shoot at your foes. If that wasn't enough, the upgrade system is also well executed; with each unlockable feeling quite distinct from the next. Vlambeer really busted their creative noggins here (as they often tend to do).
The visuals are muted; true some might decry this as being a boring visual style, and while not popping with color it does lend a good deal of uniqueness to this title. Further, the art of your rather villainous looking comrades is quite striking as well, and fits the theme nicely.
If there was any con I'd have to conjure it'd be this; the nuke body is quite overpowered. I earned a couple achievements purely due to it's sheer power, and thus somewhat robbed me of more fitting gratification; though at the same time I'm not much of one to stress achievements in the 1st place, so being gifted one is certainly not the worst thing either. Plus, going too far towards balancing EVERYTHING can also make some improvements that much less apparent; so perhaps the diversity and power range is more a good thing than a bad one.
I won't lie; I picked this game up in a bundle for $10. Am I satisfied? A delightfully addicting tower defense/real time strategy hybrid-esque game, with show-stealing enemy (and sometimes allied) particles that can freely bounce around the map or clump together in a variety of formations for more orderly assaults. Mix the gameplay with custom ships/units and new features and gimmicks being constantly introduced, and you have a game that rarely seems to get old. If you've played any of the Creeper World games, you'll feel right at home here. If not, go ahead and try it out!
In addition, like the Creeper World games, Particle Fleet features a substantial custom level creator, complete with its own scripting system, which allows for the creation of some fairly elaborate levels, alongside a customizable random level generator. As such, there's tons of replay value, and there will be even more as the community begins to make more levels.
The two weak points to me are really more nitpicking than anything. In the story mode, the grammar used by characters can be a little...off, sometimes. Nothing major, but it can be noticeable if you're the type to pick up on that. The other minor issue is that the music, while great and suitably epic feeling, tends to loop often enough to be noticeable. Once again, not a big deal.
In conclusion, Particle Fleet is a fantastic game that I highly recommend to anyone with a taste for tower defense or RTS games, and it's definitely a more-than-worthy successor to the Creeper World series.

Like any platformer game, Alter World has your character set to reach from Point A to Point B, and includes more obstacles and challenges as the level progresses. I encountered numerous puzzles that were incorporated: From world swapping, to catching moving platforms and activating switches. The former was the most distinguished, and the feature that I really liked.
It would constantly be introducing us to two worlds, and ones that are contrast to each other: One world is full of vegetation and life, while the other is full of gloom and death.
This goes to the graphics and art, which were also superb. Though it is 2D, there is a great amount of shading and texture in the design. The BG even has some simple, but nice animations. You’ll notice the spinning Windmills near the end levels, the comets raining down on stage 50, and flashing lamps at the level 40s. It’s these little details that can liven up any environment to a game!
I also found the music quite settling, and suitable to the theme of their respective level and world. Though at times, the audio can be a bit annoying when you’re constantly swapping between worlds, and the BGM is pausing and switching repetitively. There are also sounds that the character makes, and when they perform actions. Jumping and opening the door are some of these features.
The playability however, is where things get frazzling. Much of the negative reviews goes to the character’s choppy movements and lack of flexibility, to which I can agree. I find that my character may also freeze or bug out in mid jumps, which ultimately results in a restart of the level. This part can get frustrating over time.
Ultimately, the game does give an atmospheric experience, and a good taste of many themes and worlds inspired by “The Dark Tower” by Stephen King. I give it a thumbs up.

Thinking with Time Machine is a mod for the well known first-person puzzle game, Portal 2 but with the twist. You have to use a mini time machine on your left hand to solve the puzzles, where it creates a past you that will repeat the same actions you did when the time machine is on at the time (ah ha get it? I said the word time twice in that sentence. Nevermind).
Now the mechanics are great and work mostly quite well with the portal mechanics though they are not seen together until later in the game which is about the middle part. Some of the levels are cleverly designed but those are the ones in the first and middle part of the game. The end part of the game is very hard mostly due to the time mechanic being use here and the levels at the end are really confusing because of how the portal and time mechanics are trying to be combined together which makes it really frustrating. I also have to use a walkthrough guide to figure out the puzzles though I will admit I'm not the greatest at puzzles game but I'm pretty good enough to play and finish them. And when I was playing Portal 2, I was able to solve most of the puzzles without any help expect for some of the levels with the gel mechanics. I never felt so frustrated when playing a game ever in my experience of gaming that is not really my fault cause in TWTM you don't get a clear instruction of what to do though in the early levels you have to find a video ingame to show you an idea of how the game works while in Portal 2 you get a very clear idea of you to do and how the game works.
It is only about 2 hours long so it's pretty much a short but fun way to cut down some time if you want to (ah ha get it? I said cut down some time cause the game is about time travel. But anyway, at the end while I have some parts of the game I don't like I still had a good time with this mod and I really enjoy the mechanics they are very clever. So if you want to play Portal with something new in it then Thinking with Time Machine is the mod to play.

For years with Dark Souls on the PC and 360, I have struggled with an epiphany. I absolutely despise
about Dark Souls 1 to the point where my fondness for Demons’s Souls and Dark Souls 2 may appear contradictory. Issues that I have with SoulsBorne as a genre are magnified in DS1 that I can’t help but think there is a reason why games before and after DS1 have moved away from imitating the qualities die-hards have praised.
As I expect from previous reviews not sharing the consensus with ardent defenders that treats it as Citizen Kane, I expect many won’t bother to read this review. If, however, you are still reading then know that even at its best moments the same issues exist. The purpose for writing this review is not to dismiss people from DS1 but to interest people who share similar issues to try other games because they may be more to their tastes.
When DS2 was released, fans of DS1 were torn; when DS1 was released, some fans of DeS felt it was a misstep; and I imagine if you found fans of King’s Field they might say the DS games are simplified. How can so many varied opinions exist?
The underlying truth is gaming tastes are relative to your experiences and the expectations they set for future installments. This is why the Souls-like genre is inherently flawed; the consensus for what defines these games varies from how much emphasis is put on level-design, bosses, combat, etc. As someone who had a harder time with DS before warming up to DS2, the virgin effect is something fans need to accept when they talk about difficulty. Returning back to DS1, however, what expectations does it set that leaves me bitter?
For starters, the health recovery system. To use a flask at the cost of wasting one is not the issue; it’s the system that shows its problems for both PVE and PVP.  As a beginner’s tool, kindling bonfires is so poorly explained that many players will start off not knowing they can get more rations. Even when you get enough to make the choice moot, the short time-frame of refilling your health means bosses are designed to pummel you into a cycle of usage and in PVP people have made up “honor” rules not to use them. In contrast to other systems, the various grasses from DeS instills a greater sense of scarcity and the slow, continual regeneration of lifegems—the flasks are also slowed—rewards both more reckless players who use that regeneration to be on the offensive as well as offering new players an alternative resource as an optional difficulty modifier.
The much-touted line of “It’s hard but fair” is nonsense when difficulty spikes come from boss gimmicks on top of “GOTCHA!” moments. In describing gimmick bosses, I am not referring to Ornstein and Smough that test both your reflexes as well as adding something different; I am referring to encounters that are only hard because they test your patience with being obtuse or they aren’t mechanically satisfying. Although boss-fights do not have to be tests of skill, the spectacle remains dull. DeS, however, had far more engaging bosses that were amazing spectacles or tough encounters. Even in DS2, the “Dudes in Armor” problem is something I can tolerate as, contrary to what many believe, DS combat is ideal for multiple enemy encounters when you’re not locked on (see Darklurker in DS2 and even DS3’s Demon in Pain & Below). As for the “GOTCHA!” moments, one only need look up Joseph Anderson’s videos to see how they offer only a cheap death.
Now you may agree/disagree with my assessments, but I think what I have shown is that there is room for interpretation of players and not one Souls game has managed to please everyone. These next two problems are something I believe are more personal, which will make my assessment at the start make more sense.
Once I believed the open-world of DS1 was its greatest strength that the game strangely ignores as you hunt the Four Lord Souls, arguably the worst of DS1, but after experiencing DeS and DS2 I am not fond of it anymore. Guiding the players on intended routes is not the problem; it’s how much unnecessary backtracking there is because it is a Souls game as well as how much freedom is restricted by false appearances.
As much as players complain about teleportation in sequels, many players forget the first time playing DS in wandering off you to where you weren’t meant to be and then you had to stumble back to find the intended route. Sure, eventually you get the ability to transport between bonfires; however, the beginning will make you second-guess yourself for direction and the “GOTCHA!” moments sting more. Even in levels like Blighttown that do make use of this emotion, which I am surprisingly fond of this level, it is mitigated by the sense that going back is a royal pain for a SoulsBorne game. As a result, the Souls’ level of difficulty is rather a hindrance because of the open-world design as both DS2 and DeS are benefited by the level of challenge by going different paths.
What I think is perhaps a far greater misunderstanding is the limitation of exploration in DS as you’re not free to go anywhere as much as you initially believe because the game must push you back towards the right path. If anyone has tried to encounter the Lord Souls before the two bells have been rung, then you are probably aware of a mysterious wall of light that prevents you from progress. The reality is the world only opens areas when you’re meant to go there, not because of the player’s choice. This is in stark contrast to DeS where you can choose any level you want but they were often far more linear as a result and in contrast to DS2 where can choose various paths that lead to other areas as well as mitigating the Four Lord door with using bonfire ascetics to farm enough souls. These aspects work with player-choice that, admittedly, are never as strong as the interconnected nature of Undead Burg but never suffers the plight that is running back and forth between areas to find your way.

Whenever I think about the possible merits behind the storytelling of Dark Souls, I am reminded of how much I enjoy the idea behind Hemmingway’s iceberg theory where you only see the top of a glacier and you’re left to imagine the vast depths it has beneath the waters.  However, it doesn’t take long for the holes to become more transparent it leaves in a book, and applying a similar concept to games is perhaps an even worse idea when you stop to think about it.
In the case of Dark Souls, there are three issues with its storytelling: (1) the lack of plot versus lore; (2) the player’s own connection to the storyline; (3) various oversights that go beyond reading lore-descriptions. The first two problems are attributed to the same issue of the player being insignificant to the world of Dark Souls, which, as much as I love Lovecraftian cosmic horror, it makes the actual narrative of Dark Souls hard to give a damn without motivation. Even DS2 addresses this issue by having the illusions of a motive for the player as well as offering simple choices with NPCs in and outside of combat to learn more through player agency. The third problem is a combination of cut-content, translation discrepancies and incompleteness that is inherent with designing a story that must be learned through peer-review rather than something you experience. Perhaps I’m too old-school, but I prefer my stories self-contained.
Not getting the full story as well as community engagement is rather the purpose behind these decisions but it’s ultimately indicative of realizing the flaws with its novelty before audiences grow weary. Some issues are more personal than others, but that dissatisfaction is what I believe makes DS1 age worse than any other SoulsBorne title. May you never bear the curse that has befallen me.

There are many things that come up when discussing what makes Dark Souls so great; these praises mostly focus on its challenging but fair difficulty and its fascinating world with lore awaiting to be discovered. Both of these are absolutely true and, if you're up to the challenge, Dark Souls is an experience I'd consider essential to anyone who loves gaming.
"Getting into" the series is always the hardest part. It is for that reason I want to take this time as an attempt to guide you, the reader, into what I consider nearly holy ground. I want you to experience and love this series like I do. And so, I present my Recommendation to Get Into the Souls-series
The number one thing circulating around the internet about this game/series is that it is abusively difficult and you have to take some sort of perverse pleasure in pain to enjoy yourself. This is hyperbole, don't believe it.
It is absolutely true that Dark Souls is challenging, I even said it myself, but the common perception that it's impossibly difficult to get into is an insult. Games like "I Wanna Be the Guy!" are masochistic, revelling in killing the player in as many unforeseeable ways as possible, but Dark Souls is not one of those games. Dark Souls is challenging, but wants you to beat it; it is the Dungeon Master that knows you can do it, but knows you have to earn it to really feel accomplished.
The number one thing I have to say is to not be afraid of Dark Souls. It is not a game you can lose, there are no game overs. The absolute worst that can happen is that you don't win beause you stop playing, or you never play it in the first place.
Dark Souls is a community game, from the messages left on the ground in the game itself, to friends who've played it and want to help, and to the numerous wikis on the internet full of advice. Do not be afraid to seek help when you feel yourself getting lost or frustrated, for there is almost certaintly another way around whatever is giving you a headache.
For instance, perhaps you can try summoning a helper (NPC or player), maybe there's a special trick to this fight, or an item hidden elsewhere that makes it much easier. For example, the game hides everything you need to kill the first real boss in a short few swings for you to find before the fight.
Dark Souls expects you to seek this help and it does not hold it against you. It understands that you can't just explain to someone how a bike works and then immediately push them down the steepest hill in town into traffic. If you feel the need to prove yourself to yourself, the oppurtunity is there to play it completely without help, but do not be afraid to seek help.
As an aside, my favorite way to introduce someone to the game is with them, sitting on the couch next to them while they play. Giving them tips when they seem to be getting frustrated, but letting them try and figure it out themselves. Also, one part in the first "level" is always hilarious, which is definitely a plus.
As described in the Greater Internet ♥♥♥♥wad Theory, people are jerks online, especially when they can stroke their ego about something (and boy do jerks love to stroke their ego about Dark Souls). I said earlier that Dark Souls is a community game, and most of that community is good. But absolutely do not stress about the jerks that do exist.
They'll try and tell you that you're crap at the game because you haven't run it naked with only your fists. Or that "that boss" isn't hard, you just need to gitgud you ♥♥♥♥in' scrub. Really, just don't let them get to you, they're sad little people and it's unfortunate that this is where they want to stroke themselves off.
Dark Souls does not care if you decide to level a few times before you take on that boss again, nor does it care if you end the game fully upgraded and a much higher level than average. Dark Souls is a challenging game, and it's just glad you won.
I hope that this helps you pick up this wonderful game if you've been on the fence about it. Personally, it sat in my library of games I know are good but am anxious about getting into for way too long, and I wish I'd gotten in much sooner. I may not have many hours of play on Steam just yet, but I don't think I'm exaggerating when I say I have already clocked at least 100 hours on this game ever since I got it on IndieGameStand, so I thought this game deserved a nice little review for all potential fellow players out there.
The premise of 1849 is a classic one, and the game may not have loads of different buildings to build or hundreds of different resources to collect, but rest assured that it has more than enough to keep you busy for a long time. The casual-looking interface hides a challenging city management simulation and everything in the game works together just perfectly. There are no electricity grids or traffic jams, but the simple yet challenging resource management and production chain systems are crafted wonderfully and the game stays engaging, inciting you to expand and to find the perfect balance between farms, factories, saloons and houses. Make no mistake, 1849 is casual and I love its refined simplicity because it makes the game so easy to pick up, but at the same time it plays like a true management game and it can get quite hard, and I love it equally - if not more - for that.
And as if the game mechanics weren't enough, the game is also set in a period of time that easily speaks to the imagination and that has been crafted beautifully in the visuals of each little part of the game. In every building, every tree and every person walking through the streets you can feel the atmosphere of the bustling town you're shaping where only moments ago was nothing but forests and meadows. Combine that with the challenges from the management mechanics, and it's easy to see why this game gives you such a rewarding sense of accomplishment but at the same time gives you the need to keep going and keep making your town better.
I got this game in the daily deal on IGS for only a few bucks, but knowing how much I've already enjoyed playing this game I would happily pay full price for this game that is quickly becoming one of my favourites.

Full Video Review -
Hello I'm Cosmic and welcome to indie city management game 1849 developed by SomaSim. The premise of the game is well, obviously its 1849, and gold has just been discovered in California. New towns are popping up left right and centre from mining towns to farming communities. Now I'm English so I'm not much of an old timey prospector type but dang nabbit we'll give it a jolly good go.
1849 is all about city building and management, straight off the bat those who played games like Pharaoh and the Caesar series will be instantly hit with a sense of nostalgia. I played the Caesar games extensively and huge comparisons can be drawn to it, its clear that 1849 was heavily inspired by those games. The game has both story mode and a sandbox mode. Story mode sees you progress through a variety of towns with different objectives as the Californian gold rush takes hold. You'll build mining towns, farming towns and towns for educated families to live in.
One you start, you start with a storage depot where all your resources will be gathered. You'll have to build homes for people to live in and start some agriculture as people need to eat. Building cost money, and you only have a finite amount. Housing is a source of income from their rent but production building cost money as you have to pay wages. As your town increases in standards and resources housing will upgrade to offer more people per house and more rent. However production buildings will far outweigh the amount of housing required which is where one of the more interesting game mechanics come into play.
Similar to the real world, no town is completely self sufficient. This means while you may have a town with an abundance of iron ore your town may have no access to the production of fabrics. Trading is a massive component of the game, each town  you play has access to several trade routes with other towns, these require money to open and you can then import the materials you need and export the materials you don't. Money management is a big factor, making sure you don't go bust is crucial which means making sure you have the best housing for rent and are regularly exporting your overstocks for cold hard cash.
On top of your standard objectives you'll also come across optional telegram missions where by you'll be rewarding for attaining certain objectives. Usually this comes in the form of exporting X amount of materials to town Y or making sure you have excess materials in your depot. The rewards of this missions usually help you out greatly and if you can achieve them, they often are well worth doing.
City building is very similar to the Caesar games, things like roads and and housing don't cost anything to place. Production buildings will cost varying amounts of money and you'll have to make sure you have enough funds to not only build the building but make sure you don't go bankrupt when the next round of wages come in. Speaking of production you have to follow the process the whole way through. Simply building a wheat farm will not feed anyone, you'll also have to build a bakery. Even further down the line as you unlock more complex industries, things like mines will require more than just money to upkeep but also equipment too, like pickaxes.
I really enjoyed the city building in the game, it is not as micro as some similar games but it captures the fun of the genre and makes the process simple and easy to use. Returning to the management side of things, you'll have to do more than just watch your wallet. As your town grows you'll have to deal with disasters such as fire in which a fire department will be needed if you don't want fires to wipe out half your town. You'll also encounter a human element, as more people influx into your prospering town you'll encounter unemployment and if you don't provide local amenities such as a saloon, people will become unhappy. Crime is also a big factor, 1849 was a tough time for folks and the lure of a prospering town full of gold is too much temptation for some. You will have to build a sheriff to enforce some law in your town, if you don't production buildings will start to get robbed which halts production and steals precious resources.
Overall 1849 is a solid indie city building sim that captures the fun of previous games in the genre. It's well designed and thought out and its progression is well paced but also adds a good challenge to each new town. While not a micro management sim and it doesn't have the depth of a bigger city game, its a well put together title that has plenty of value for money. If you enjoy games like Pharaoh , 1849 may be right up your alley but if your looking for a more in depth realistic city sim you may wish to look else where.

Overall, “1849″ has a lot to offer but does so in such a way to where you won’t need a lifetime supply of Excedrin Migraine to keep up.  It’s a somewhat casual experience but still can challenge even the most hardcore city-builder fans.  I suspect that part of the game’s design has something to do with the fact that it’s also available on mobile devices, though this isn’t necessarily a bad thing.  Don’t let the cartoony graphics deter you, however…there’s plenty of content here to justify its fifteen dollar price tag.  It would also serve as a great primer for tougher resource management games like those found in the “Caesar” series, I feel.  The campaign can be a little limiting at times with regard to the buildable structures available on any given map, but the sandbox mode helps to alleviate this problem.  All in all, a cute (but tough) “little” game.

-The menus use their own fixed button configuration for navigation, and you can’t change it
-MOM mode is poorly executed, and ultimately is tedious and frustrating to play:
--There is a timer, which when empty, results in an automatic loss; this discourages defensive and cautious playstyles, and encourages you to be risky and aggressive
--Armor mode allows the computer opponent to attack with infinite super armor and unlockable supers. This mode is supposedly balanced by having the computer follow a set of rules, so the player has a chance to win. The problem is that the computer can break these rules whenever it wants to, and will do so
--Winning against multiple opponents in row results in a streak bonus. The idea is that the higher your streak bonus, the more challenging the next opponent is to beat. The issue is, that instead of having the next computer use more complex AI patterns, the game will instead increase stat numbers to the point where you cannot beat it
--The only way to compete against the increasing stats of your opponents is to level yourself up. It eventually becomes such a tediously long grind to so, that you end up wasted large amounts of time for little reward
-Mission mode generally puts you in several instances with very little time to prepare yourself or react. I personally feel like it then judges your performance too harshly as a result; it gives you little leeway, and expects too much, especially if you’re a beginner
-Technical issue: “Guilty Until Proven Innocent” achievement has issues triggering
(Going through arcade mode with a DLC character [Sin, Elphelt, or Leo] may be the root of the problem which causes this hiccup. I suggest avoiding them to trigger this achievement)
Story mode mini-review:
~It’s decent overall.
-The production value is generally low, and a lot of waiting around and empty filler happens within the context of the story itself.
+Seeing the how characters interact with each other is nice, and the main plot thread tying the story together is solid enough
~The most surprising thing to me, was that for a game praised for its great character animation during gameplay, I counted one scene that had animation of that same caliber
-There is no game to play in story mode; it is essentially an anime to watch
