Mixing a martini on a plane and crashing into the ocean is an interesting way to start a video game. Stranded Deep is an interesting take on the survival genre. Like many titles within its category, there is no real goal other than maintaining your hunger, staying hydrated, and not getting killed off by an antagonizing force. Unlike most recent popular titles that have a heavy focus on survival, Stranded Deep presents a much more realistic premise. There are no zombies or fictitious monster varieties lurking around. As the title already implies, you might have already figured out that the main enemies are Stephen Spielberg's favorite fish,  the ancient aquatic wild life we all know and fear, sharks.
As soon as my in game character recovered from his hang over on the salty surface of this beautiful blue hued hell of infinity, I was allowed to begin the real game. The intro being somewhat reminiscent of Bioshock with its plane plummet into the sea, the follow up however, is a far different experience. You start with a few basic tools including a life boat, an oar, a pocket knife, and a water bottle. The game is kind enough to spawn you close to an island, a gaming design choice that was most like attempting at getting the player acquainted with game and setting up as early as possible thus giving a fair chance at surviving.
After paddling my way to the small reclusive island and embarking on a small expedition to tour the tiny island, I realized the game wasn't over saturated with endless and nagging tutorials that so many games of current trends typically put emphasis on. This was definitely a relief for me, as modern tutorials are over bearing nightmares. I figured out the game mechanics after several minutes on m own and later with the help of the internet. In exploring the island, I had time to realize the beauty and polish that Stranded Deep had to offer, the graphics are amazing, especially taking into consideration the game was made by an indie team of developers. The immersion is fantastic as a result. A more objective based gamer might ask what the point of this game is. Is it another Minecraft wannabe? The answer is no, it's more or less Tom Hanks: The Game.
The game can be a great distraction due to the fact you really get lost on these islands and zone out working to survive. I spent hours cutting palm trees down so I could get lumber, in turn used the lumber to build fires and make spears to stab at my endless crab leg buffet. After a while the island I was occupying started to bore me, so I packed my things and set  sail on my trusty neon yellow, octagonal companion to find a new sand berg to settle on. I paddled for nearly five minutes straight taking breaks to drink coconuts I had shucked. Shortly afterwards a creepy ambience of music started to indicate the arrival of a shark. Looking over my raft and observing how realistic this situation was combined with my irrational fear of sharks, I couldn't help but to feel a slight panic. This game was serving its purpose better than I could have imagined. Instead of panicking I simply pulled my spear out that I had made before embarking, and gave that tiger shark a poke to the face he would not soon forget. This turned the sinister shark into a fleeing fish. Not long after this encounter, I had arrived on the beach of a new island.
Shortly after arriving on the new island I realized it wasn't all that different from the one I had worked so hard to migrate from. One of the main faults of the game is the lack of variety in locations, the only two being the open sea or small palm tree infested island, which in a way is what the game is going for so it's not a game breaker. I ended up settling on that second island building a small settlement. A storm broke out with rain drops hitting like vertical bullets, I had to built a bed and shelter to see through the night. The following day I took time to search the shallows, and in a fruitful turn of events I discovered a sunken ship. I swam down to the rusted vessel and looted lockers and crates for supplies that surpassed my cheaply made tools. This aspect of the game made exploration extremely rewarding. You could play it safe and stay on land and waste more time using♥♥♥♥♥♥quality tools from rocks, or you could acquire real manufactured metal based tools by diving into a claustrophobic metal maze that you might drown in or worse, be dined on. These game mechanics help motivate you as a player to explore and discover.
After outfitting myself with my newly acquired machete I decided it was time to try it out. I crept into the shallows and searched for another one of those punk♥♥♥♥♥tiger sharks. Not long after I had found the stripe covered coward in all of his ineffective camouflaged glory. I swiped at him, nailing hit after hit on him until he fled into deeper waters. I'm no Steve Irwin, but I went a little overboard and dove into the deeper waters after the shark attempting to get as many stabs as I could. After a dozen or more wounds were inflicted, the beast sank to his doom upon the sandy sea bed. Immediately upon witnessing the defeat of the creature I swam to its fresh corpse and dragged it to the shoreline. This game provides many options, one of which is to fillet a shark into steaks and grill them on the barbie. However, I was too proud of the work and effort put into hunting that shark, so I took it upon myself to make the shark into a trophy. I laid him to rest in an awkward and amusing position so that every time I had second thoughts about exploring the ocean out of my fear of sharks, I would remember that ♥♥♥♥♥ of fish taking his permanent nap back at my camp. Although I had conquered the tiger shark, the game had not yet presented me with a confrontation with the games most dangerous enemy, the great white shark. These ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s mean business, unlike their tiger shark cousins they can easily flip your raft over which might as well be a game over. My confidence and pride were short lived and I closed out the tab of the game like a whimpering child.
The controls of the game are solid, standard for the genre. Typical key bindings for a first person perspective game with survival elements. Crafting is the only unique aspect I had noticed. Instead of having a chart table come up over the game screen every time, you are just supposed to drop all the building materials into a pile and left click it. This triggers a building options window to pop up with multiple choices to select from based on what readily available supplies you have. For instance, if you drop several sticks, leaves, ropes, and rocks into a pile the box will provide you with different objects to build after left clicking it, such as a hammer, an axe, a raft, a bed, a fire pit, etc. It's a simple and effective crafting system with basic controls, thus speeding the games learning curve to a faster pace and making the game easier to get into.
Stranded Deep is not without its faults however, there were several instances in which the graphics would lose their textures or clip in and out of existence. Occurrences such as these can really break the immersion experience, that would otherwise be perfect in this game that has a heavy focus on that aspect. The game also suffers from a lack of wild life variety, especially hostile creatures. In the eight or so hours I have invested in the game so far, I have yet to have to experience confrontation with anything other than a tiger shark or a great white. From reading various forums on the game client the game is available on, Steam, I learned there are also sea urchins sometimes lurking in and around the sunken ships, but that's about it. There are marlins and humpback whales if you go far out, but they are more or less scenery that you can kill if you desire wasting several minutes devoting to the tedious task of repetitive stabbing. Also, what kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ climbs onto a whale and attempts to maul it to death?

Isaac and his mother lived alone in a small house on a hill.
Isaac kept to himself, drawing pictures, and playing with his toys, as his mom watched christian broadcasts on the television.
Life was simple, and they were both happy.
That was until the day Isaac's mom heard a voice from above;
"Your son has become corrupted by sin! He needs to be saved!"
"I will do my best to save him, my lord" his mother replied, Rushing into Isaac's room, removing all that was evil from his life.
Again, the voice called to her; "Isaac's soul is still corrupt! He needs to be cut off from all that is evil in this world, and confess his sins!"
"I will follow your instructions lord, I have faith in thee" Isaac's mother replied, as she locked Isaac in his room, away from the evils of the world.
One last time, Isaac's mom heard the voice of god calling to her; "You've done as I've asked, but I still question your devotion to me. To prove your faith, I will ask one more thing of you"
"Yes lord, anything" Isaac's mother begged.
"To prove your love and devotion, I require a sacrifice, your son Isaac will be this sacrifice. Go into his room, and end his life as an offering to me to prove you love me above all else"
"Yes lord" she replied, grabbing a butcher's knife from the kitchen.
Isaac, watching through a crack in his door, trembled in fear.
Scrambling around his room to find a hiding place, he noticed a trap door to the basement, hidden under his rug.
Without hesitation, he flung open the hatch, just as his mother burst through his door, and threw himself down, into the unknown depths below.

So why the positive you ask? What is so special about a simple game about some space ooze? It is more than that. This is the 4th installment of a series of games, each better than the last. One person putting out a game and not ignoring it after it's release. One guy refusing to take my money before it is in stores. No early access, no pay before you see what your getting. What back up, paying for a game usually means you pay, then play right? WRONG! Can we say free demo? That's right, a demo in 2016. You would think it was 1996 the way this guy operates. Maybe more gaming companies should take notice.
So here are the pros and cons....
Pros-
- A full story line that builds off of the 3 previous games. You should buy those as well, but not needed to enjoy the game.
- A fully working random map generator with user options enhancing the replay value indefinitely.
- A ship editor, you can make a ship from scratch, or many and even share them within the game.
- A map editor, also allowing you to share with others.
- Did I mention a devoper that isn't just grabbing your money and leaving for Timbuktu?
So here are the cons-
- The ship editor in general is pro, but also a con. It is clumbsy, it has no tool tips (what the heck does a port do vs a laser?) The deveoper has stated he plans to add that in a post release patch. Experimentaion will answer many of those questions. You can copy and paste from an old ship, but I still haven't figured out how to do that. I would say a complete rework of the ship editor is in order, but needless to say, it is adaquet for the game.
-Although some have pointed out some bugs, I have yet to run into any that are game breaking. While I put that under the cons, it is really a pro.
In all fairness, this game is worth the full price, it is simple to learn, but difficult to master. This is much like the three other creeper world titles. This one gets my full support and should be in everyone's library.

In a world rapidly being filled with generic and increasingly boring zombie games, State of Decay is a rare gem that gets zombie survival right. It's that game that makes you a part of the world you wanted to play in after watching a good zombie flick.
State of Decay is... just that zombie survival game I have been looking for. I was surprised that more people are not talking about it. Where some games get a little too caught up in humans fighting each other over resources in a post zombie-apocalypse world (like DayZ) or zombie slaughter simulation (like Dead Island and Dead Rising), State of Decay perfectly scratches that 'build a community of survivors and scavenge for resources' itch.
You get to choose a location for your group to set up in, manage your resources by scavenging, building base upgrades, and helping people out in the world. Even though the game has a story - and that story is interesting to play - I found myself just exploring, scavenging, and killing some zombies.
This is exactly the kind of zombie games I want to see in the future. Let's face it, the zombie genre is hot right now, and I am tired of the endless DayZ clones where you are in a zombie-themed minecraft world with the greatest danger being the other players. State of Decay gives you an open world that is exciting to explore. There are many buildings, and they are full of resources, and sometimes also full of zombies. The zombies themselves are trivial on their own, but in groups are quite deadly, and you have to take them into account when trying to figure out whether a place is worth raiding, or a route worth traveling down.
Overall, I love this game, and I hope we can see a bigger, multiplayer version of it in the future.

This game............ sucks. It's bad. Like really bad. If you don't want to read my entire review, here is a summary:
This game is exactly the same as those hundreds of terrible greenlight horror games on Steam. It is not unique, it is boring and it is garbage. It's like a kid's first attempt at making a game, and it is laughable that the devs are actually charging $9 for this crap. When I've seen Happy Meal toys offer a more fulfilling experience.
If you want me to list out all the terrible things in this game. Here is a few:
1. The monsters. This is a joke. Remember how I said how un-unique this game is? Well, the enemies in this game are the most cliched and pathetic excuses for horror enemies I've ever seen. The game offers a huge selection of TWO enemy types. A mannequin (never seen that before: Silent Hill, Kraven Manor  ) which you need to look at for it not to kill you (100% original. Not just like: The Weeping Angles or SCP-173). And the second enemy type is one that won't see you if you have your flashlight off (Which is like nearly EVERY HORROR GAME EVER). However, the game didn't even do that part right. At least in most horror games like Amnesia, you can turn off lights to lower your chance of being found. BUT IN THIS GAME, you can literally go up to the monsters and suck their d*ck, just as long as your light is off. They're completely static and don't even attempt to kill you.
2. It's stupid riddles. You're asked a total of I believe 12 riddles in this game in order to progress. Somewhat like a troll under the bridge sorta thing. However, this is honestly one of the laziest excuses at a bloody 'puzzle' I've ever seen. All the riddles you are asked, have NOTHING to do with the story. They offer NO explanation in the story, they offer NO personality of our characters, they have NOTHING to do with the game at all (other than to try to pad out your game time so you cannot refund the game). And the worse thing? They're all unoriginal. All the riddles in this game were completely ripped from online. The creators of this game didn't even TRY to create their own original riddles. They instead chose to steal them instead because their brains were rotted from Year 3's math homework.
3. The game is ugly. Visually it's gross. The game is too bloody dark so if your light is off you have no idea where you are going. The game looks like a collection of free-to-download assets all plunked down on a level editor. And the game uses so many stock-font choices it looks like the game was written using Microsoft Word 2007.
4. The story is non-existant. NOTHING, in the game, is explained. Nothing is resolved, nothing is revealed, nothing happens. What happened to that couple? NEVER FOUND OUT. Why are their monsters? NOT EXPLAINED. Whats with all the bodybags? NEVER ANSWERED. I'm fine with games leaving things open for interpretation. But there's a difference between leaving things ambiguous for analysis, and being too lazy to answer things yourselves.
5. The game is pathetic. This is how I feel about the game the most. It's pathetic. It's got pathetic graphics, it's got pathetic programming, it's got a pathetic story, the list goes on. The devs did not try. This feels like college students first attempt at making a game. WHICH IS FINE. But don't bloody dare to charge babies first game for $9.  Which ironically is higher then the production budget of the game itself. If this game was free on Indie GoGo - sure. That would be fine. But the fact that this game made it on the Steam Page, really says a lot about greenlight.
I could rag on the terrible things in this game for dozens of more hours. Such as how slow your character moves, the fact that enemies can literally be placed behind a corner so you have no idea there is one up ahead and you die, the terrible overworld which offers like 5 locations, the lack of music or overall ambiance. But, that would be putting in more effort than the devs did to this entire game.
This game is a joke. For all those horror nutters looking for that hidden unique indie horror game like myself, move along. You've played this game before.
And to the devs, listen, I don't want to discourage you making games. In-fact, I want to encourage you to better yourself from this experience. Just please, try something new, try to increase your level of quality. I've got faith in you guys and I hope you can better yourselves.
Unfortunately, this game is bad and if you somehow couldn't guess it, I strongly DO NOT recommend this game. 'Stay FAR' away from this game.

For years with Dark Souls on the PC and 360, I have struggled with an epiphany. I absolutely despise
about Dark Souls 1 to the point where my fondness for Demons’s Souls and Dark Souls 2 may appear contradictory. Issues that I have with SoulsBorne as a genre are magnified in DS1 that I can’t help but think there is a reason why games before and after DS1 have moved away from imitating the qualities die-hards have praised.
As I expect from previous reviews not sharing the consensus with ardent defenders that treats it as Citizen Kane, I expect many won’t bother to read this review. If, however, you are still reading then know that even at its best moments the same issues exist. The purpose for writing this review is not to dismiss people from DS1 but to interest people who share similar issues to try other games because they may be more to their tastes.
When DS2 was released, fans of DS1 were torn; when DS1 was released, some fans of DeS felt it was a misstep; and I imagine if you found fans of King’s Field they might say the DS games are simplified. How can so many varied opinions exist?
The underlying truth is gaming tastes are relative to your experiences and the expectations they set for future installments. This is why the Souls-like genre is inherently flawed; the consensus for what defines these games varies from how much emphasis is put on level-design, bosses, combat, etc. As someone who had a harder time with DS before warming up to DS2, the virgin effect is something fans need to accept when they talk about difficulty. Returning back to DS1, however, what expectations does it set that leaves me bitter?
For starters, the health recovery system. To use a flask at the cost of wasting one is not the issue; it’s the system that shows its problems for both PVE and PVP.  As a beginner’s tool, kindling bonfires is so poorly explained that many players will start off not knowing they can get more rations. Even when you get enough to make the choice moot, the short time-frame of refilling your health means bosses are designed to pummel you into a cycle of usage and in PVP people have made up “honor” rules not to use them. In contrast to other systems, the various grasses from DeS instills a greater sense of scarcity and the slow, continual regeneration of lifegems—the flasks are also slowed—rewards both more reckless players who use that regeneration to be on the offensive as well as offering new players an alternative resource as an optional difficulty modifier.
The much-touted line of “It’s hard but fair” is nonsense when difficulty spikes come from boss gimmicks on top of “GOTCHA!” moments. In describing gimmick bosses, I am not referring to Ornstein and Smough that test both your reflexes as well as adding something different; I am referring to encounters that are only hard because they test your patience with being obtuse or they aren’t mechanically satisfying. Although boss-fights do not have to be tests of skill, the spectacle remains dull. DeS, however, had far more engaging bosses that were amazing spectacles or tough encounters. Even in DS2, the “Dudes in Armor” problem is something I can tolerate as, contrary to what many believe, DS combat is ideal for multiple enemy encounters when you’re not locked on (see Darklurker in DS2 and even DS3’s Demon in Pain & Below). As for the “GOTCHA!” moments, one only need look up Joseph Anderson’s videos to see how they offer only a cheap death.
Now you may agree/disagree with my assessments, but I think what I have shown is that there is room for interpretation of players and not one Souls game has managed to please everyone. These next two problems are something I believe are more personal, which will make my assessment at the start make more sense.
Once I believed the open-world of DS1 was its greatest strength that the game strangely ignores as you hunt the Four Lord Souls, arguably the worst of DS1, but after experiencing DeS and DS2 I am not fond of it anymore. Guiding the players on intended routes is not the problem; it’s how much unnecessary backtracking there is because it is a Souls game as well as how much freedom is restricted by false appearances.
As much as players complain about teleportation in sequels, many players forget the first time playing DS in wandering off you to where you weren’t meant to be and then you had to stumble back to find the intended route. Sure, eventually you get the ability to transport between bonfires; however, the beginning will make you second-guess yourself for direction and the “GOTCHA!” moments sting more. Even in levels like Blighttown that do make use of this emotion, which I am surprisingly fond of this level, it is mitigated by the sense that going back is a royal pain for a SoulsBorne game. As a result, the Souls’ level of difficulty is rather a hindrance because of the open-world design as both DS2 and DeS are benefited by the level of challenge by going different paths.
What I think is perhaps a far greater misunderstanding is the limitation of exploration in DS as you’re not free to go anywhere as much as you initially believe because the game must push you back towards the right path. If anyone has tried to encounter the Lord Souls before the two bells have been rung, then you are probably aware of a mysterious wall of light that prevents you from progress. The reality is the world only opens areas when you’re meant to go there, not because of the player’s choice. This is in stark contrast to DeS where you can choose any level you want but they were often far more linear as a result and in contrast to DS2 where can choose various paths that lead to other areas as well as mitigating the Four Lord door with using bonfire ascetics to farm enough souls. These aspects work with player-choice that, admittedly, are never as strong as the interconnected nature of Undead Burg but never suffers the plight that is running back and forth between areas to find your way.

Whenever I think about the possible merits behind the storytelling of Dark Souls, I am reminded of how much I enjoy the idea behind Hemmingway’s iceberg theory where you only see the top of a glacier and you’re left to imagine the vast depths it has beneath the waters.  However, it doesn’t take long for the holes to become more transparent it leaves in a book, and applying a similar concept to games is perhaps an even worse idea when you stop to think about it.
In the case of Dark Souls, there are three issues with its storytelling: (1) the lack of plot versus lore; (2) the player’s own connection to the storyline; (3) various oversights that go beyond reading lore-descriptions. The first two problems are attributed to the same issue of the player being insignificant to the world of Dark Souls, which, as much as I love Lovecraftian cosmic horror, it makes the actual narrative of Dark Souls hard to give a damn without motivation. Even DS2 addresses this issue by having the illusions of a motive for the player as well as offering simple choices with NPCs in and outside of combat to learn more through player agency. The third problem is a combination of cut-content, translation discrepancies and incompleteness that is inherent with designing a story that must be learned through peer-review rather than something you experience. Perhaps I’m too old-school, but I prefer my stories self-contained.
Not getting the full story as well as community engagement is rather the purpose behind these decisions but it’s ultimately indicative of realizing the flaws with its novelty before audiences grow weary. Some issues are more personal than others, but that dissatisfaction is what I believe makes DS1 age worse than any other SoulsBorne title. May you never bear the curse that has befallen me.

There are many things that come up when discussing what makes Dark Souls so great; these praises mostly focus on its challenging but fair difficulty and its fascinating world with lore awaiting to be discovered. Both of these are absolutely true and, if you're up to the challenge, Dark Souls is an experience I'd consider essential to anyone who loves gaming.
"Getting into" the series is always the hardest part. It is for that reason I want to take this time as an attempt to guide you, the reader, into what I consider nearly holy ground. I want you to experience and love this series like I do. And so, I present my Recommendation to Get Into the Souls-series
The number one thing circulating around the internet about this game/series is that it is abusively difficult and you have to take some sort of perverse pleasure in pain to enjoy yourself. This is hyperbole, don't believe it.
It is absolutely true that Dark Souls is challenging, I even said it myself, but the common perception that it's impossibly difficult to get into is an insult. Games like "I Wanna Be the Guy!" are masochistic, revelling in killing the player in as many unforeseeable ways as possible, but Dark Souls is not one of those games. Dark Souls is challenging, but wants you to beat it; it is the Dungeon Master that knows you can do it, but knows you have to earn it to really feel accomplished.
The number one thing I have to say is to not be afraid of Dark Souls. It is not a game you can lose, there are no game overs. The absolute worst that can happen is that you don't win beause you stop playing, or you never play it in the first place.
Dark Souls is a community game, from the messages left on the ground in the game itself, to friends who've played it and want to help, and to the numerous wikis on the internet full of advice. Do not be afraid to seek help when you feel yourself getting lost or frustrated, for there is almost certaintly another way around whatever is giving you a headache.
For instance, perhaps you can try summoning a helper (NPC or player), maybe there's a special trick to this fight, or an item hidden elsewhere that makes it much easier. For example, the game hides everything you need to kill the first real boss in a short few swings for you to find before the fight.
Dark Souls expects you to seek this help and it does not hold it against you. It understands that you can't just explain to someone how a bike works and then immediately push them down the steepest hill in town into traffic. If you feel the need to prove yourself to yourself, the oppurtunity is there to play it completely without help, but do not be afraid to seek help.
As an aside, my favorite way to introduce someone to the game is with them, sitting on the couch next to them while they play. Giving them tips when they seem to be getting frustrated, but letting them try and figure it out themselves. Also, one part in the first "level" is always hilarious, which is definitely a plus.
As described in the Greater Internet ♥♥♥♥wad Theory, people are jerks online, especially when they can stroke their ego about something (and boy do jerks love to stroke their ego about Dark Souls). I said earlier that Dark Souls is a community game, and most of that community is good. But absolutely do not stress about the jerks that do exist.
They'll try and tell you that you're crap at the game because you haven't run it naked with only your fists. Or that "that boss" isn't hard, you just need to gitgud you ♥♥♥♥in' scrub. Really, just don't let them get to you, they're sad little people and it's unfortunate that this is where they want to stroke themselves off.
Dark Souls does not care if you decide to level a few times before you take on that boss again, nor does it care if you end the game fully upgraded and a much higher level than average. Dark Souls is a challenging game, and it's just glad you won.
I hope that this helps you pick up this wonderful game if you've been on the fence about it. Personally, it sat in my library of games I know are good but am anxious about getting into for way too long, and I wish I'd gotten in much sooner. Waste Walker is a darkly themed survival strategy RPG created using RPG maker. In the game, The world has transformed into a post apocalyptic dystopia after countries release bombs to annihilate each other. You are a survivor who is looking for your family after you got separated while you were scavenging. You will explore the wasteland of Ashen and meet people, fight bandits, kill mutants, scavenge for loots, and many more.
The world is big and very immersive if you ask me specially when you have the fog of war turned on. Some might find it annoying but I love how it adds this dark and lonely atmosphere that the developer wants us to experience. One problem though, the map may need a bit of work. It is somehow informative but I often find myself getting lost because there is no marker on where I am. But in a way still, it immerses me. I feel like in reality, I would have to look in to a map and try to see landmarks that would tell me my exact location.
The characters are alright, but maybe they can have a bit more life to them. Especially the ones that you can recruit. Maybe a little backstory or a quest that reveals their past or something. The main quest is too short and lack some depth. Side quests are also not that meaningful except for the XP and tabs(curreny in the game) gained.
As a game made using RPG maker, the games graphics is your standard 2D RPG graphics. Nothing that special, but I love some of the character skins. Specially the skin used by Corrosion.
The sound used in the game is sad and depressing, this is good because it reflects how a post apocalyptic world feels like.
Mechanics are similar to classic Final Fantasy games. You enter a battle you choose wether you fight or flee. You can use items or reequip your character during a battle. One difference is that you can see your enemies coming rather that the random encounters while walking inside dungeons.
A problem that I'm having with the game is that I can't open steam overlay during gameplay and I've checked my settings. Also when Im not inside buildings, opening the menu screen takes a long pause around 3-4 seconds.
Overall, I like how the game feels and how it portrays a post apocalyptic world. But there is so much that this game should improve. I'll give it a 3/5. Its good but I don't think many will like it but I still recommend it.

This is the 2nd game from Corrosive Studios that I played. My first game was called "Disgraced" and the gameplay experience was so wonderful that I bought the 2nd game, "Waste Walker".
Waste Walker is a open-world exploration of a dystopian, post-apocalyptic megapolis. There is a central main-quest, and a large number of side quests that are given by various colonists. As rewards, you get tabs (cash), food, gears and even NPC team mates. As an extra benefit, the game even throw in a colony building aspect as well, so that you can also spend time doing colony management with all the spare cash that you get. You can build up a super colony with will provide you additional food, gears, ammo, and you can even hire various personnels to make life easy for you. For example, you can hire scientists which will help you to reduce radiation, guides which help you with teleportation-like travel services, doctors which heals you for free, dealers to supply you with fixes, etc.
The game play is fun and fast pace. The game play is generally light-hearted, except for the ending of the main quest which has a dark overtone. However, it is still fun.
I would highly recommend ths game to any old school turn-based gamer who likes a good rpg with a bit of colony management. Thumbs up to a wonderful game.

I remember an experience I had playing this game shortly after it was released. I was on my raft heading back to a secondary base island after scavenging for resources from one of the far-off islands, a necessary errand since single islands didn't provide many resources and your backpack could only hold 8 things at a time. These were long journeys (~10-15 minutes) and required some intelligent resource managing to make it there and back in good health but with enough new materials to make the trip worthwhile. I began the trip in the evening and soon realized I had made a mistake when heavy rain began pouring down. To allow more backpack room I didn't bring my compass, so with my visilibity reduced to mere feet in front of me I did my best to maintain my direction of rowing. I was feeling pretty confident until the music began that indicates the proximity of a shark, and my heart began to race. Sure enough I saw a dark shadow in the water below me, circling around my raft and making occasional attempts to bump it over.  In short order I became disoriented and realized I had forgotten in which direction I had been travelling. My first thought was, my island was a tiny dot on the horizon, and the chances of me missing it are pretty high; I could try staying stationary and wait out the rain so I can regain my bearings, but the thought of being on top of a bottomless pit of giant monsters convinced me to redouble my navigational efforts and strike out in the most likely direction (which, very fortunately, were just barely correct enough and I eventually reached my intended island). My second thought was, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game has absolutely nailed the terror and challenge of this sort of nightmare scenario in a way no other game I've played has.
The reason why I don't recommend it is because in the years since then, rather than expanding on what made the game so unique, the developments have done nothing but bring the game half-way up to par with the survival genre generic standards, drowning its strengths in the cesspool of bloated crafting systems and meaningless item-scavenging that characterizes nearly every other survival game on the market. Instead of adding more ways to challenge resource-management and survival skills, or adding more risk-reward events and mechanics, there are simply more ways to build your house and hoard all the rocks and branches you can find, and more ways to blow up sharks.
It still has a lot of potential, but the developers don't seem to know what it is.

Bland, very bland. The game has the merest hint of a plot, the protagonist has zero personality, the backgrounds look like they've just been put together by copy-pasting various pieces of clipart, and the game feels like it was thrown together in "Klik and Play" in about five minutes. The movement of the character is very odd with absolutely no inertia, and the game is strangely unresponsive, often not recognising a keypress. Combined with the pixel-perfect accuracy needed makes this game pure frustration. I got to about level 28 but can't be bothered to finish it.
There's also precious little innovation in the level design. If they introduce a new concept or challenge, you can bet than the next three levels will be exactly the same thing but with slight variations...
I also don't understand why the developer is so keen to tie in the game to King's wonderful "Dark Tower" series. There are many, many, MANY games which feature a "switch back and forth between dimensions" gimmick, and none of them feel the need to do so. King wasn't the first to write about such a skill, and the game doesn't actually have anything to do with it besides the quotation on the opening screen. In the books, the characters can't travel back and forth at will - that's actually a key plot point - and doing so is incredibly dangerous because of the creatures that lurk in the Todash. In this game, you can flip back and forth as much as you like with no penalty, and it happens in a fraction of a second. It actually has more in common with Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams than it does with Dark Tower.

The fact that my first achievement was the "die 100 times" one should probably tell you a lot about my experience with the game.
Then again, I'm not a fan of puzzle games in general, so your mileage may vary.

Simple, but with surprising depth - and altogether an awesome ride.
Gameplay wise, your're essentially fighting red sand: it tends to clump together and fall towards disturbances (AKA everything that wants to live).  This in itself makes for interesting strategies, as it's possible to manipulate where and how you want the particles to "fall," so-to-speak.
The story does make references to the Creeper World games - also developed by Knuckle Cracker (which are awesome, by the way) - but you won't be lost if you haven't played them.
But here's a forewarning: the gameplay didn't really remind me of the Creeper World games, if that is what you're looking for.  That's not a bad thing however, and shouldn't detract from the game itself.
It plays exactly as you'd expect it to, given the promotional material, and is rather free in how you go about finishing maps.
Well worth the wait, and well worth the buy.

Similar to Creeper World in some ways, yet quite different enough to stand on its own.  If you're already a fan of Knuckle Cracker games, you'll feel right at home, without feeling like you're playing the same game again.  If you are new, it's time to get started!
Added Oct 3, 2016:
So I've been playing more.. I usually try to do a mission or two per day off, and I feel like that's a good pace to play at.
I really love this game, and I think it has enough strategy and depth to keep me thinking, without being so complex that I lose track of things or find myself getting overwhelmed with features.
The main game features a campaign with a number of scenarios that you must play in order.  If you're interested in the story, it will be slowly revealed over the course of these missions.  As you progress, you'll obtain more ships, 'omni' which are used to claim land for energy production, and new abilities.. such as being able to assign your 'amp gems' to overall buffs that increase your movement speed, energy efficiency, or add cannons and 'struc' walls to your stationary energy mines for defense, plus a lot more.
Also, as you gain new abilities and expand your arsenal, the enemies will unveil new tricks of their sleeves.  It'd probably be best to leave much of this unspoiled, but I'll just say that simple floating red particles aren't your only concern, they're just kind of the main staple of the enemy forces later on.
One of the coolest features, in my opinion, is revealed just a short time into the campaign.. friendly particle emitters, and the means to direct them.  These friendly particles can help you 'mire' land (the term for claiming the land, turning it blue, so it produces energy for you) and unmire the enemy land, harm enemy 'struc' walls and particles, give enemy weapons something to shoot at other than your ships, or even just bolster up your fleet from behind with a constant stream of good particles to help your fighting ships in combat.
Another amazing feature is that the ships are made up of little grid-shaped pieces.  These pieces can be structural/defensive blocks, weapons, engines etc, and being hit by something will destroy these pieces.  Taking some structural damage will leave the vital parts functional, but vulnerable.. if the weapons or engines get hit directly, they'll be destroyed, and if the main 'core' of the ship gets hit, that ship will explode and need to reassemble it from scratch.  If your ship is within range of an energy source, however, it will simply use some of your energy to repair itself.
Because of the way these ships are designed, you can use the in-game editor to create your own.  I haven't tested this feature much, but I believe user-made ships are restricted to non-campaign modes, such as user-created levels, and the randomly generated maps in the combat simulator.  I believe you CAN use these custom ships on campaign missions, but it will be in a sandbox mode, and only works on missions you have already beaten previously with the ships that are provided in the standard campaign mode.
Anyway, I think this is my favorite Knuckle Cracker game.  I liked Creeper World 3 a lot, but eventually certain aspects of that game became too difficult for me, and it wasn't 100% my jam because it's kind of tower defense.  Particle Fleet feels a lot more like an RTS, the difficulty curve feels fair, and.. I just like it.  It's fun.  I would absolutely recommend this game.

I will warn you going in, my friends; this game can be an incredibly frustrating experience. You will die a lot, as a result of failing checks that seem to come out of nowhere. However, if you push through this and keep replaying you'll find an
rewarding game waiting for you. It's a great feeling to finally pass a high level check for the first time, and seeing Elodie finally make it to her coronation is the best!
One thing I do wish is that there were an option to reread all the lessons Elodie learned so far on a given playthrough. It'd make it easier to catch foreshadowing, get a fuller sense of the world when you can read lessons which inform each other back to back instead of with potentially weeks of gameplay between them, and (when replaying) to realize that you've forgotten to do anything for a check that's coming up.
I'd recommend playing through your first time or two just picking whatever you'd like and seeing what happens, but after that here are a couple tips:
Okay, one tip for your very first playthrough: Don't keep chasing checks that have already passed! By that I mean a LOT of people have the instinct when they see a failed stat check to go "Oh no! Let's focus only on that stat for the next few weeks so I'll never fail with it again!" You'll see this happen in blind let's plays of the game all the time, and it's a good way to get Elodie dead.
Read the flavor text you get with your classes! Not only is foreshadowing and worldbuilding hidden there, if you see the description for one lesson mention something you'd need a different type of class to use effectively that's probably the game waving at you yelling "Hey! I'm gonna check for these back-to-back at some point!
Have an idea going in of what you want to accomplish. There is not enough time in the game to get skilled enough to pass every high-level check, so just pick a couple things you want to do and only worry about them. (Well, them plus surviving, obviously.)
By that same measure, don't feel pressured into getting your Lumen crystal just because the game keeps bringing it up! There is never once in the game that you NEED to use magic without any other way around it, so if there's some event you're focused on getting don't feel like you need to get sidetracked into pumping up your presence or accounting skills.
Having high enough intrigue by a point near the midgame will let you pick something you want your agents to focus on protecting you from. Whichever you pick can save you from one possible failure state later on. (More guards, for instance, will bypass the infamous
check.)
Divination is surprisingly useful, there're multiple points where Elodie will get a hint that can lead her to doing something that'll prove useful later in the game from it. But if you rely on it too much it can also drive you away from interesting plotlines.
Almost every failure state in the game has more than one way to avoid it. If you keep banging against one scenario you just can't get all the way through try going back to an old save and seeing if you can find another way through it. Some of the alternate ways can be very satisfying! I love watching Elodie using knowledge of trade route and internal affairs to logic out that something's fishy about
.

I was looking forward to playing this game. I enjoy minecraft type games. Absolutely loved Terraria V1.0.
The trailers for this game make it out to be a complete upgrade to Terraria and maybe in some ways it is. Unfortunately it has a major problem, gameplay and user interface.
The gameplay suffers from one of the worst feelings you can have in an action game. Unresponsiveness. Sometimes it wont register a jump and sometimes you wont attack. Things like this can easily get you killed and then you get sent back to your ship regardless of what you were doing. Depending on the difficulty this could mean having to trek all the way back to get your dropped items or just straight game over.
The user interface has got to be one of the most baffling things about the game. When you enter a menu it goes roughly to the center of the screen, is not see-through basically covering your character so you can't see anything. Which could kill you. Menu screens like your inventory have multiple tabs in them instead of putting everything you need all on one page that you can scroll through. To use anything you have to go through multiple steps which can also get you killed.
Here's what you have to do to eat food:
Open inventory
Go to tab containing food (Yes it has it's own tab).
Drag food from inventory into an equip slot.
Exit inventory.
Press the corresponding number to access the equip slot with the food.
Press the corresponding mouse button to eat the food.
It is important to note that you can't equip more than one food and eating the food will empty the slot meaning if you want to eat something else you have to do all that all over again.I don't see any reason why they couldn't have shortcuts to eat food with a single button. Or at least be able to go into your inventory and be able to use an item directly from there, why do you need to equip it?
Now this is just inventory. Crafting has it's own menu and each crafting table in turn has it's own menu as well. Unlike minecraft, terraria, dragon quest builders, etc. in this game you'll have 5 or 6 different crafting tables within 20 minutes or less each with only a few things you can build. It ends up being more of a mess of multiple menus that could easily have just been one menu.
Now I did only make it 45 minutes into this game and maybe it redeems itself in the long run if you can forgive bad controls and bad UI which i could not. I think this game suffers from trying to pile on content without ever working on it's core gameplay mechanics. This is the first game I have ever asked for a refund because while playing it felt more like a chore than an actual game and I never got the sense of actual fun. This is really a shame, I think the game could have been great.

This series of games has been a joy to play so far. My introduction to souls was DS3, I bought it during this year's summer sale and beat it in 10 hours. Even after beating this hard♥♥♥♥♥game, I still wanted more, and after getting half way through my second journey, taking all the paths I'd missed in my first playthrough I knew I wanted everything on steam with Dark Souls in the name. So I bought everything in the series.
Let me start by saying I disagree with many of the members of this community by saying that this is not my favorite souls game. That goes to Dark Souls 3. Does that mean this game isnt worth picking up? HELL NO! If you're like me and you loved Dark Souls 3 then you'll enjoy playing Dark Souls 1. It is still very familiar to the newer souls games in controls, gameplay, and of course, difficulty, and for those veteran Dark Souls Fans, I see why this is your favorite in the series. Experiecing this series like this for the first time is an awesome experience, that leaves you waning more, and for the developers, its hard to capture that feeling in any following games. This game's lore, and story, go deeper than any other game i've played, its crazy. The only game universe that comes close is witcher.
This game, unlike many other games in this genre, doesnt present the story to you, you have to find the story yourself. So if you just rush through the game without reading through the dialogue or reading the descriptions of things you find, you wont have any clue what the story is, or what anything you're doing means. I spent time researching the lore and story of the game while playing, and trust me, its way cooler if you do it that way. Each map, each boss, enemy, and item has a long complex backstory that in itself could fill a book. Its crazy the universe these guys created. The game is just as fun to read about as it is to play. The tone is dark and glim, downright disturbing at times. At one point you go into a sort of spider hole and discover people laying on the ground with giant spider eggs attached to their backs which you can assume are slowly devouring them alive, as you walk by they beg for you to put them out of their misery and if you hit them the eggs explode and disgusting larvae attack you. I can't say I've enjoyed playing the game very much. It was very frustrating, at times... But, it is very short (2 hours to beat all 77 levels, for me), and it has some unique touches, so I'll stick with a recommendation.
I'll talk about some of the aspects I did and did not like.
First off, the visuals. They're rather strange, not the clean look I'm used to in platformers. But the game gives all the information necessary regardless, so nothing wrong there.
I think it looks very nice! Certainly unique, even though it is a bit crude.
The backgrounds have an almost blured, handpainted style. Then you have a few more elements like plants or clouds on top of them. The cool thing (and one of the problems I'll talk about) is that they're animated. In a way you don't really see very often.
Crude, but I appreciated it for what it was.
The problem with it is death. Usually, this is a problem with the music, but not there, surprisingly! When you die, all the animations reset. This doesn't help at all in a hard platformer where you die a lot in short time spans.
As I said, it's usually a problem with the music resetting, and have to listen to the first 2 seconds over and over... the effect applies perfectly with the visual animations, here. It breaks the pace and heightens frustration.
Now, the music. It's not anything memorable at all, but something merely there to set the mood, I guess. Because of the light/dark world theme. The instruments change in each one, with each cool, though not unexpected, I guess.
Nothing impressive, but again, it's a welcome touch.
It seems randomly generated, almost akin to drone music than actual music. A matter of personal preference here, I guess.
Ok, now the problem with the level design, and the biggest source of frustration.
In some respect, I liked the level design. It generally started with a simple pattern, and repeated it with added complexity (and difficulty) for a couple of levels, and sometimes recurring in later levels. This was alright. A few different mechanics to keep things fresh, all good! (not amazing, but still good enough, I thought)
The problem is how precise the game requires you to be. The margin for error is really, really small, even in the first 10 levels, or so. This is a problem, because you've figured out what to do to beat the level, but then have to try many times to get the
right. That's the main challenge of the game, your timing.
You have to time not only the world switching mechanic, but also jumping over vines to a rather excessive precision.
The make matters worse, the game has several sections where you have to repeat the same jump several times (4-10x). This was infuriating for me, when I knew what and how to do, but because of the ridiculous precision requires, I failed in one of the jumps somewhere and had to restart the level.
It was needlessly difficult. By simply making vines smaller (even if slightly), I think it would have made the game much more enjoyable, focusing on level design rather than repetition over details. If anything, it's a lesson for the future - how much of an influence precision has in a platformer. The window seems too narrow, in this game.
The other big problem, for me, was how the switching mechanic obscures half of the level. So, you almost have to die to look at the whole level, several times. On top of that, memorization becomes very important. You need to keep the hidden half in mind when traversing the first half, etc.
At times, it was a welcome challenge!
At others, it was dumb. Why? Because the game has very quick sections later on, and it's almost impossible to "plan". For me, it was a case of repeating over and over and over... until I had the timing right. I barely needed to look at the level, since I got the hang of an abstract timing for button presses.
Oh well.
So yeah, not a very good game. But it seems to be genuine in its presentation, both in the visuals and the music, so I think there's still some value here, despite the frustration in the gameplay.
It's not a hearty recommendation, but you can get something out of it, and it doesn't overstay its welcome.
P.S.: There are people saying the controls are broken, and the character doesn't always jump when press the button. This is true, but it only happens in a very specific circumstance: when you're at the edge of a platforming. Like, really, really, at the edge. When you are, you don't really fall, but the character doesn't jump. Not sure if it's a hitbox bug or what, but take that in mind. It didn't affect me too much.
Although... with the precision the game aims for (and requires of you!), it does seem a bit of a blunder.

Alter World is a timing focused platformer game which features two worlds in one level. Each world will have different obstacle and (or) platform placement in it which will make you have to switch between world (by pressing space) to finish the level.
I really love the background graphics. It is drawn beautifully. However, the other graphics doesn't seem to match with these beautiful backgrounds which are changed after some levels. The branch obstacle looks ridiculous compared to the outstanding background and so is the text. The text which sometimes shown in each levels looks like lazily put in there without much effort.
I love the notes which are playing when you are in the level selection. It's more like i'm playing a piano rather than trying to choose a level. The in game bgm gives off a relaxing vibe which is very subtle and might left you fall asleep if not for the "frustating" gameplay.
This game has 77 levels in total. I also noticed that there are some levels which are reused from previous level with minor tweaking. Like i said before, the game relies a lot on timing, especially in mid levels. However, the game is still fun to me.
This game gives almost no room of error, especially when jumping through branches which can kill you if you are close to it. The same thing also happens when you try to gain speed before jumping (by pressing left + jump right before the platform ends).
To be honest, i didn't really get used with the controls, especially with space being the key to toggle between worlds. I wanted to change my space key for jump, but the game doesn't offer keyboard configuration. However, you'll get used with the controls after you play several levels.
There are two endings in this game, although i admit that there is almost no story in the game except a girl which is looking for her dog which accidentally goes to the other world. The first ending is just plain normal to me, although the second ending doesn't even give other conclusion except a screen which is saying "Controller Strongly Recommended" and some overlapping texts below it.
Pros:
- 77 levels
- Interesting concept
Cons:
- No keyboard configuration
- Too much relying on timing

text: $9.99 for an RPG maker game.  What a rip.

is a perfectly legit open-world survival RPG made in RPGMaker.
You take a role of a survivor who went scavenging for supplies and got separated from his/her family. That is the "main" storyline (though it could have - and should have - been expanded on; for a main quest chain, it was rather brief).
Sounds simple enough, right?
Well there's plenty of side quests to complete as well as a variety of NPCs who can be recruited to join your party and fight by your side in the harsh post-apo world.
As a survival game,
has a hunger/thirst system that can be turned off if you prefer. The "fog of war" and limited stamina (which serves as your typical sprint function) can be also turned on or off depending on your preferences.
Even the character creation process is pretty complex for an RPGMaker game.
The graphic is pleasant to look at, you won't see many of those usual generic sprites. The background music and sound effects are moody, as in adding to the whole apocalypse feeling nicely. The in-game weather changes are a nice touch, too.
It's clear that the developer,
, has put a lot of time and effort into the game creation, and it really pays off.
Grab it on a discount or for the full price, it'll be worth it either way.

Though I do recommend this game to anyone who is into the simple platformer, however this one does come with some of those caveats that can make or break a game. Pros:
Compelling story
Full voice overs
Beautiful graphics with cutscenes
Customizable aircraft models all rendered in high resolution with their own stats, compatible weapons, skins and pilot skills.
Real-time physics battle damage details - see the individual holes from cannon fire or watch an enemy plane be cut in half by a missile.
Compatible with a controller or flight stick
*Multiplayer is SO much fun and very much feels like a sort of Call of Duty in the air, with a skill system roughly comparable to COD's (*Unfortunately, Multiplayer is dead.  Like, completely and utterly dead.  But if you have ever managed to get into a completely filled 8 X 8 multiplayer game of capital conquest, you are very lucky.  It's a shame.)
Fully animated cockpit view for each plane
First in series to have playable helicopters, Heavy Bombers and AC130 - Playable in campaign and the non-existant multiplayer (except the AC130) along side and against fighter, multirole and light bomber aircraft.
New Air Strike Mode (ASM) streamlines bombing runs and works really well.
New Dog Fight Mode (DFM)(the single biggest issue of the game - will explain more in Con section) Allows for the developers to create some intensely cinematic, but scripted dog fights.
Bonus aircraft, maps, skins and multiplayer skill upgrades that were not available in console version.
Con:
Dog Fight Mode (DFM) takes all the skill out of flying and is mandatory for certain campaign enemies.  The controversial new flying mode that you can engage virtually anytime you are facing a target within a certain range allows you to automatically position your aircraft behind your current target (and DFM has no issue with breaking the laws of physics to accomplish this: causing the DFM engaging plane to magically straffe sideways, stop or impossibly accelerate as the plane automatically follows your target allowing you to shoot missiles and cannon fire at it from behind (which are magically stronger and more accurate in this mode).  DFM is cheap and annoing, but not always a death sentence.  DFM is possible to reverse by braking hard so the pursuing plane overshoots and you automatically flip and follow your former pursuer at the press of the two shoulder buttons on your controller when prompted.  Or the plane being chased can escape manually without using DFM themselves by accellerating out of missile range or turning sharply to evade the pursuing aircraft.  You can also "support" a team mate engaged in DFM when prompted within range which causes the supporting aircraft to automatically fly with the lead pursuing aircraft and share radar information: causing both lead and supporting pursuing aircraft's missiles to be more accurate and deadly while engaged in DFM with a support aircraft.  Summary: DFM is the biggest flaw of the game.  It is mandatory in the campaign, and puts anyone who doesn't use it during multiplayer at a huge disadvantage against even a novice who knows how to engage DFM.  Dog Fight Mode takes away the need for the pilot to skillyfully position and pusue their enemy and is an unrealistic and cheap over simplification of the controls which breaks the laws of physics to set you up for the perfect missile shot against virtually any locked on air target within range by automatically positioning you behind the target and then automatically steering for you so you can focus on getting a missile lock or lining up a machine gun strike while only having to worry about controlling the plane's movement except for the throttle to prevent overshooting the enemy.
Oh and theres the complete lack of multiplayer that's a pretty big con, which is frustrating for a game with some much multiplayer potential and replayability with the new customization system and new helicopter and heavy bomber aircraft types.
And another stupid♥♥♥♥♥con for this game is the fact that if you get targetting by a missile and you are in a helicopter, you can press the shoulder buttons to evade the missile when prompted by what else but doing a barrel roll.  Which looks dumb as hell to see an apache attack helicopter flipping around the battlefeild avoiding missiles.  I don't understand why they didn't just use flares or electronic countermeasures or something...
But, despite it's flaws, the game has huge, beautiful and detailed environments with beautiful and detailed planes flying around dogfighting with real physic based battle damage systems.  The Campaign is fun, and the multiplayer is like Call of Duty in the sky...well, if it is ever revived... which I'm afraid multiplayer for this one probably won't be ever restored. It's a real pity.  Don't get me wrong, I love this game, but I would pick it up when it is on sale.

I first discovered the KnuckleCracker games with CreeperWorld 1 on some flash games site.  At first the game looked pretty basic and simplistic, but I soon found out that was far from correct.  Fast forward a few more years to Creeper World 3 (CW3) and I was stunned not just by the game itself, but by the community of map builders.  Virgil (the developer of the games) had introduced a scripting language to allow players to create practically anything they could imagine within the world.
So, why do I even mention the past?  When Virgil announced the new game, Particle Fleet (PF), which is in the CW universe but with a different mechanic for playing I was quite excited.  I had discovered a developer who not only made highly enjoyable games (CW3 is one of my highest number of hours played), but was also incredibly connected to the community.  He is constantly listening to the fans of his games and does a great job of responding to bugs but also to new ideas.  Now, I'm just an average player who doesn't create maps for others to play (I tried once and I found out I sucked creating them), but I do play a lot of them and have been fairly active on the boards.  Thus I was surprised and more than a little excited to be given the opportunity to play a preview copy of the new game.  This is my review of what I've seen so far.
Much like CW3, the base game itself is quite fun.  There are a series of "tutorial" maps that ramp up in difficulty to introduce new game mechanics but are also fun in themselves.  The game mechanics are extremely fluid and intuitive.  It's very easy to pick up the basics of how to play the game.
Where PF truly shines is in the tactical area.  Once you get past the basic maps, there are a myriad of ways to proceed in each battle and your tactics will determine whether or not you succeed.  Sometimes you’ll want to use an overwhelming force to attach an enemy.  Sometimes you’ll want to divide your forces to distract the enemy AI.  Sometimes you’ll want to set up a mobile strike force to get in and get out to advance the overall cause.  Sometimes you’ll even want to send in a ship on a suicide run (all ships are robotic drones…no humans killed) to clear out some of the enemy for other ships to have space to operate.  At any given time you’ll need to evaluate the overall battle and determine the best tactics for the given situation. Sometimes, you’ll be wrong and will have to try to regroup to save the day.
As far as the AI goes, this game is a big step up from the CW games.  The enemy in CW, while difficult to beat, is ultimately a mindless blob.  The enemy in PF has come quite a ways from that.  For every ship you have, the enemy can create the opposite to attack you with.  The enemy ships will also probe your defenses, running away if they can’t get through.  Overall it seems like the enemy is much smarter in this game and that definitely makes for a more challenging test of your skill.
However, as fun as the game is right now, I also know that it will get 100 times better in the months to come.  Much like in CW3, Virgil has added a scripting language to PF to allow the players to create amazing maps.  We are still in the early versions of what will come out, but already there are some new ideas from players.  It is the player created maps that extend the life of a game like PF to a huge number of hours.  If the only thing you got were the base game, it’d be fun but over too quick.  With the map exchange there are literally countless possibilities for new maps.
Another addition in PF that is really neat is that there is not only a map editor like in CW3, but there is also a ship editor.  The map makers (or even just a regular player) can create their own ships to use in the base game or in maps that are created.
Also like CW, there is a procedurally generated map maker.  You can easily create a map to play on the fly and then share it with other players if it is fun.  With the number of variables that you can control, the possible number of maps is, practically speaking, limitless.
All in all, I highly recommend this game to anybody who enjoys playing a fun, tactical game.  The graphics are relatively simplistic, but don’t let that turn you off.  You’ll quickly forget about the graphics as you get sucked into yet another great KnuckleCracker game!
As a final note, I should mention that I was given the preview key.  However, I was going to buy the game regardless so just ended up buying a copy for my brother since I really like to support Indie developers like Virgil.  With as many hours as I put into CW3, and as many as I’ve already put into PF, I’m quite happy to say that it’s well worth the money!

Particle Fleet is the fifth game from Knuckle Cracker, after ChopRaider and the three Creeper Worlds.  It's also an amazing game.  If you like RTSs, buy it.  If you're not sure, download the demo and try it out.

TL;DR. A nice RTS, in the mold of previous games from the same developer, but different enough that you won't feel you've paid twice for the same product.
If you were a fan of Creeper World (any one of the 3), you may be disappointed. There is no Creeper in this game. "Wot?", I hear you say, "A Knuckle Cracker game with no Creeper? That's an abomination!"
Maybe so. But remember there was not always Creeper, and maybe there will not be always Creeper - in the CW3 story, there were references to other, long-forgotten races, the Ticon and the Seloi. Maybe they too have stories. Maybe there was (or will be, or always has been) things that were not Creeper and that were hostile. Maybe they were not explicitly hostile - after all, if we need a canoe, are we explicitly hostile to the entities that occupied the ecosystem of that tree that we need for the canoe?
OK, OK, you aren't reading this to get a lesson in philosophy or time-travel. You want to know about Particle Fleet. So let me see... what can I tell you? I've been play-testing Creeper World Particle Fleet: Emergence for more than 2 years now. Hence the reason I have a free copy.
It's definitely a Knuckle Cracker game, with all the elements of the previous games I love. Mort of a Tower Defense and Real-Time strategy game mixed in together. There's an enemy (the particulate, Duh!) with a few variants, such as Stunners, Struct, which is a static barrier, Emergent which is a mindless moving entity that is derived based on terrain dominance. Then there's an artificial Intelligence - and that, we'll have to wait and see where the game and the map makers take up. Don't be surprised if the Particles can build ships similar to yours and attack you in retaliation.
Not player vs player, but definitely a more variable and mobile opponent than what Creeper were.
Graphics? Well, you've never bought a KC game for it's graphics, unless you are a hard-core fan of retro graphics, in which case nothing has changed.
In Particle Fleet, you can, as in previous games, make your own maps, either using the menu-driven "Simulacrum" (now with 50,000 variables!*), or by hand-crafting them in the map editor. In both cases, if you finally have a mp you like, you can submit it to the community Exchange for other players to play and to tell you how brilliant a map maker you are.
But there's more! You can also make your own ships. If you don't like the weapons choices, simply chose Sandbox mode on any map, include a few ships of your own design, or one from a ship-maker you admire and play to your heart's content. Of course, if you play in Sandbox mode, your time is scored differently that if you play with the same fleet as everyone else. You can, of course upload a map with custom ships and have everyone play with your favorite ships.
* I exaggerated a tad.

In Luftrausers there's only one "level". You can play this level with a great number of different planes, and each plane has its own missions, for example: "Destroy 2 Battleships"; "Kill x enemies without taking damage". It's incredibly addictive, as you unlock new ship parts and tick off the missions assigned to each one. The controls are tight, yet fluid, and when you pull off deft maneuvers to weave through a hail of bullets, while at the same time taking down the swarm of fighters giving chase, you know you're a dogfighting ace.
The game is brimming over with that Vlambeer 'juice': screenshakes, masses of particles, crunchy explosions and tactile mini-pauses and slowdown. This is a game that feels great to play, and that's why a single level has kept me playing for hours. Granted, when the missions became very difficult, I started to feel like I was putting more into the game than I was getting out of it. At that point it was time to hang up my aviator's hat and goggles. But to have kept me playing so long with so little is testament to the mechanics and polish of the game.

3rd Person Single Player DAY Z inspired by the Walking Dead.
This is a very good game if you can get past the random bugs and glitches.   The game without the DLC is a basic campaign/story mode where you control a group of survivors.   The point is escaping the town you are in, but to do that you have to recruit more surivors, scavange for supplies, and survive long enough.   You setup a home base in one of the many locations throughout the city (Warehouse is the best South/West of map in town) and build things in your base like medical labs, sleeping bunks for extra people, storage, machine shops, etc.     The game also has RPG elements, each person has skills they can level up on a scale of 1-8, and you can pick a offensive and sometimes a defensive skill to specialize in.
Breakdown (DLC)
While some people think this is a dumb idea, it's actually very entertaining.  The problem with the regular game is that after you get to the end of the campaign the zombies don't really get harder.   Breakdown is like the Walking dead, it goes on endlessly until you die.   Rather than escaping the town, you get to the RV and leave and restart the town with the difficulty level increased.   Each difficulty level provides new challengers/achievements you'll want to get, which unlock survivors from the story line.
Lineline (DLC)
This steps up the action significantly as you control the military after the events of the campaign inside the actual big city.  Sometimes this DLC frustraits people.   You  have a threat level of 1 - 3, when it goes to 3 zombies will attack your military base and you have to fend them off like any defense/wave type game.   What gets people mad is that they feel you don't have enough time to scavange / loot / complete quests before the threat level gets to 3.   The solution so this is to assign your men to "thin the herd" which will delay the increase in threat levels and give you enough time.   You can do this through the base overview section in your options.
This game does have bugs and glitches, none that I found were game breaking, they actually make me laugh so hard I usually end up dying from it.   You can be driving a car with a flat tire and just get lauched staight up into the air for example :)  Always funny.   The glitches are few and far between and definitely don't ruin the game.
If you like zombie survival games and you haven't played this one you should already be buying it!
Oh, and on bugs/glitches.  I did mention it has some bugs, but it doesn't have 1,000,000 like the Standalone version of dayz.

Probably one of the best Zombie games put out in the last few years.
The best way to describe this really is It's San Andreas with zombies, an easy, lesser focus on maintaing your base/resource management and some decent writing. Just don't expect TellTale's The Walking Dead here, as while it's not a game with a tongue in cheek tone, it's not exactly the most serious game in town. Think Dead Island at face value but a tad more serious.
It's a bit of a rough game, it's not exactly the prettiest looking, the controls may feel a little wonky at first, but if you're up for a game about scavenging through areas infested with zombies, dealing with problems within your group, and every once and a while having some emergent moments like watching in horror as a runner gets litterally torn in half captain rhodes day of the dead style in the middle of the street after getting surrounded and downed by a horde.
The melee combat is a bit like a stripped down superpower-less Arkham Asylum that makes fighting hordes feel just as difficult and tiring as it reasonably should. While guns are by nature as much of a liability as they are a reward, the gunplay's fine, it's just that the crosshair is a bit too large to be reliable on higher resolutions for which i'd REALLY reccomend the Widescreen Crosshair Fix mod found here:
. Cars are similarily very useful and a bit of a risk, although they are the best way to get around the map, the game does throw some roadblocks every once and a while on roads to make driving a bit more difficult, although you can use mods to remove those if they annoy you.
There are a few mechanics that might "tick you off" a bit if you have seething hatred for them and so I'll list them below:
-Character Permadeath, if a character dies/Goes down three times, they're dead. No getting them back. Even story relevant characters can die but it will never make the game unbeatable.
-A persistent World aspect a bit like Animal Crossing although don't worry, you won't not play for a week to find everything in shambles. The longer you're not playing, the slower time moves and if I recall it caps at 3 hours.
-A level of repetition very late into the game, and light annoyance at times. I've seen the game be criticized for this, but at some point parts of the tasks might start to feel a bit repetitive, but this is mostly stuff related to scavenging necessary items and helping characters through emotional states.
The annoyance part I mentioned relates to stuff like having to deal with stuff rather constantly, there will very rarely be a moment that something won't need to be done for someone or around the safehouse. Someone might need saving(Outposts reduce the chances of this happening, increasing the area zombies won't spawn in.), someone might need help with their anxiety (Which always results in you killing zombies with them. It's a bit lazy and repetitive but with the amount of♥♥♥♥♥♥in this game already I can forgive it.), there's story missions to do all while you're trying to keep the safehouse running, everyone healthy and also trying to make towards your next goal and trying not to screw yourself further down the line.
The story itself is nothing special really, but it is written competently and while not every character feels like more than just an NPC, it does it's job fleshing most of them out. I can't think of a main character I could really call "bland and lifeless".
One last thing, but this game isn't amazingly well optimized for lower end systems. You should be fine if you have a moderate or high end rig, but if your computer lands more on the "toaster" end, you probably won't be able to tweak the settings too heavily to save your performance.
Honstly, if something irks you about the game, look through the mods there's probably going to be something there to fix it.
If you like zombie games just about at all, or what I described interests you, grab this game.
