Oh, Ace Combat, why did you have to do this to me?
I'm a big fan of the series, it's always been a blast to play, and yes there were low times, but never so much as this. Now, i'm not saying that the game is 100% terrible, it DOES have it's pros, but it has many more cons. I'll list them below;
Pros:
-The plane flight mechanics feel tight and responsive, sure they're not realistic, but we're not playing Ace Combat for realism, are we? We're playing it for the fun of doing crazy air stunts and gunning down people along the way.
-The sound design is nothing spectacular, but it does it's job. The guns and the music are serviceable. Now, the old Ace Combats had some great soundtracks with some spectacularly memorable pieces. DO NOT expect those here. But, at the same time, it's not terrible.
- The planes, while not being the highest texture quality you've ever seen, are pretty damn sexy. As are some of the spark and explosion effects, it does feel good to gun down planes out of the sky and watch them burst into flames.
Cons:
- The dogfighting system. Now, this one just relies on how you feel about the system. The dogfighting system allows you to lock onto an enemy and kep on their tail while firing at them. Alternatively, enemies can also do this to you. It does allow for some pretty cinematic chases, but ultimately after about three times it's already gotten old. What it actually boils down to is this: Lock onto the enemy. Wiggle stick a bit. Fire. Move on. Find new target. Lock onto new target. Wiggle stick a bit. Fire. Move on.
It makes the game just a million times easier and means that instead of having these amazing dogfights where you're doing all these crazy stunt mid air, it just means that you see an enemy...and now he's dead.
Most of the time.
In order to combat you doing this, the game suffers from the same artificial diffficulty that a lot of plane games suffer from, whereby your target will just perpetually fly away from you. Get an enemy into your line of sight, and all of a sudden they pull up. And up. And up. And then you pull up. And up. And up. And now you're just spinning a hundred times before you can lock him into your dogfighting system. No skill needed.
The next thing that annoys me is that the enemies can also lock YOU into the DFS (dog fighting system). It seems like a good idea, having to escape them, but it just boils down to doing exactly what the enemies do to you! You're chasing someone for aaaages and then BAM you're taken right out of it, so what do you do? Pull up until you escape. Now you can continue to chase NOPE YOU'RE BACK IN IT WHOOAAA CRAZY RIGHT? PULL UP PULL UP okay we're free again, now to finally chase that NOOOOOOOPE I'M BACK ♥♥♥♥♥ES.
-The helicopter missions. They're awful. You fly around a horribly controlled helicopter, gunning down floor enemies and the occasional helicopter. That's it. The heliocopter controls terribly, as i've mentioned, and the whole missions are just uninspired. Use these boring weapons and this boring helicopter and shoot some cars. Woo. Do that multiple times throughout the game.
-The turret sequences. OH? WHAT'S THAT? YOU DIDN'T LIKE THE HELICOPTER SEQUENCES? ALRIGHT WELL TELL YA WHAT, HOW ABOUT WE TAKE OUT THE WHOLE FLYING THE HELICOPTER THING AND JUST GIVE YOU A GODDAMN TURRET? Yeah, thanks developers. There's literally whole missions where you load in, and shoot a turret for about 20 minutes at some foot soldiers, and then move on. No variety, no challenge, no interest, nothing. Just point at people and click. You don't even get to move around on your own. Just point and click. Oh you wanna do something else? NOPE. POINT AND CLICK.
-The voice acting. It's awful. There's not much to say except that everyone is just Mr Generic McGenericson or Mrs Genericson and her Generic babies. Maybe it's not even that bad, but seriously it's so generic that I think it dulled my senses.
-The story. Spoilers, i guess, but hoestly just read any Tom Clancy novel and you've heard this story.  While the game is voiced by Mr Generic Genericson, the story was written by his superhero alter ego; JERRY GENERICMAN! American hero. He's the hero we need. Other people. They're the heroes we need. Terrorists have a bad plot to blow up some people! Quick; call America! Oh no, a Generic non-american bad guy who wants to do bad stuff. WE STOPPED HIM JUST IN TIME. BUT WILL YOU MAKE IT BACK IN ONE PIECE? Yes. Roll credits.
-The AC130 missions. Just fancier disguised turret sections.
Overall this game was a huge disappointment. Are you a huge fan of the series and you're just ACHING for more? Sure, pick it up on sale and just slog your way through it. Only have a slight interest? Just don't buy it. There are plenty of other plane games that you could get that are ultimately better.

Many people have heard of the Ace Combat flight arcade games, and hundreds of thousands of players around the globe are fans of the series. However, Assault Horizon was an anomaly. The game's producer, Kazutoki Kono, saw fit to try a different formula for the series, and the results were varied. I'm going to attempt an honest review with little bias from the rest of the Ace Combat series. First things first, imagine this game didn't have the "Ace Combat" name in front. Because it's not a part of the series at all. Got it? Alright.
: The game's story is tightly integrated with the missions, allowing for a smooth transition and preventing the player from getting lost (although it can definitely be intrusive at points). You are flying as Colonel William Bishop, a renowned fighter pilot, for Task Force 108, a multi-national task force including units from the United States, Russia, and even France. The plot is centered around Colonel Andrei Markov and his personal vendetta for revenge against the United States, as well as a rebel uprising within Russia.
Yeah, it's not anything we haven't heard before. If you've played any modern warfare shooter released in the last 5-8 years, you basically got it all. What it does do, however, is give us varied characters. To be quite honest, I loved flying alongside Russian and French pilots - they actually seemed more interesting to hear over the radio than your own American squadmates. But other than that, character interaction is really cringe-worthy and there isn't much development to speak of.
: Holy. Crap. Yeah, they're not the
beautiful thing, but Assault Horizon in 1080p at 60fps on PC, or higher, is probably the greatest thing to happen from Project Aces until
. The aircraft are all gorgeous, with fully-modeled cockpits and animated control surfaces. Explosions are a little Michael Bay-esque, but something I will never get sick of is seeing an enemy aircraft shatter to pieces from a charged missile hit or the individual holes I create with the machine gun. The level of detail in the environment completely sucks at close-up views, but in general the game is so great to look at.
: Obviously the meat of the game. Fair warning, I play on "Original" controls, which emulates "Normal" in older
games. The game is set by default to "Optimum", which emulates "Novice" in the older games and makes the game a lot easier (or a lot harder, depending on your playstyle). So if you have the game and it's not controlling the way you think it should be, take a look at the control setting and see if it's this you gotta look at.
Assault Horizon's gameplay is pretty great at its best times, but really flawed at its worst. Everyone by now is aware of Dogfight Mode (DFM), which allows you to initiate a close-range chase sequence between you and one enemy aircraft. Guns are more accurate and missiles can be charged for insane accuracy and damage, but you run the risk of the enemy aircraft performing a counter-maneuver to get behind you. A lot of people claim that this is an on-rails sequence, but for the most part that isn't the case. The player still has complete control of their aircraft and must stay locked on with the enemy to keep this sequence going.
Playing with fighter aircraft is the core of the game, and it works. You can still dogfight without DFM, but DFM is unfortunately required for some boss-type enemies - these guys have plot armor and are set up to give you a cinematic experience with additional dialog, you know the drill. It definitely retracts from gameplay a little too much, especially when the game cuts away from your aircraft to give you a cinematic close-up of the aircraft being destroyed. I stated before that I loved seeing this, but not in the middle of a big dogfight with tons of other units firing on me.
Assault Horizon also introduces, for the first time, gameplay with bombers, helicopters, and a gunship to the series. However, I listed them in order from best to worst. Bombers are pretty fun to fly due to their unique weight and power, and you get to perform a strafing run with dozens of bombs at your disposal in the unfortunately single mission you get to have them. Helicopters, however, are really difficult to control and the missions designed for them are really poor - they're insanely difficult and seem to be aimed at shooting you down unless you follow a specific path. The gunship is the worst - anyone who's played an AC-130 mission in other shooters are sick of these already. The (thankfully only) one mission designed for it is enough to fit into the horror genre given its difficulty in the number of SAMs and AA guns that are trying to shoot you down. There's also two missions that are on-rails shooter sequences using a Black Hawk's machine gun, and they definitely overstay their welcome in terms of time.
There are also a few glitches you may encounter, such as enemy aircraft flying through the ground (this has been a common bug in the entire
series) or cutting away from DFM at insane angles that you can't follow. But for the most part, thankfully the fighter/multirole missions are the core of the game and they do work, just with a few rough edges for sure.
: By the way, I didn't mention music or sound effects. These are gorgeous, and everyone on the Assault Horizon OST, from Rio Hamamoto to Hiroshi Okubo to Keiki Kobayashi and more, deserve insane credit. Also, be advised that there are two glaring bugs that no one has fixed since GFWL was removed: you can't rename aircraft skins or skill sets, and trying to access the leaderboards crashes the game. Additionally, the game will definitely tax on the processor for some computers. On an older machine, I couldn't run AH in tandem with a Skype call since it would lag every now and then. These are definitely minor things, though.
: Assault Horizon is definitely a flawed game but, for the most part in my opinion, it works. There are some things I didn't mention, like multiplayer (which is dead) and Air Strike Mode (which works just fine). I own the game on the PS3 and paid $60 for it, and I don't regret that at all because I felt it was worth it. Most won't, but the Steam version costs $20 when it's not on sale, and it goes on sale for $5 or less every now and then. So, for $20, I think it's worth a try. For $5 or less, though, it's definitely worth it. Just remember,
.

I remember looking at Mutant Storm when it first came out and being absolutely blown away by how it looked, how things moved in it. It was a genuine and very real inspiration for me thinking "one day, I want to do something like that" and well, I do now.
It wasn't just the game, it was that there was this really small team making arcade games at a point where it's generally accepted that the arcade is dead. Well, that's fairly good right?
And sure, looks wise even despite a couple of makeovers it looks sort of less inspirational now than it did in the early 2000's and we're in a post Geometry Wars world where everything subscribes to a similar sort of neon-particle explosion sort of thing and I like that, I really really like that but Mutant Storm looks like Mutant Storm and nothing else. It's clearly got Minter-spirations but it's very very "looks like a Pompom game" and that's the kind of thing we can all aspire to. Not necessarily looking like Pompom but making a game that's ours and unmistakably ours too.
The gameplay seems, now, rather tame considering. It's not easy but there's a rigidity to the waves and patterns that compared to a lot of what we see now is very much more considered. And that's fine, absolutely fine because it still remains a very good little game of shooting things. And what's a game like this if not about shooting things, right? Right.
So yeah, Mutant Storm. A classic and an inspiration to me. Still, after all these years. An essential, no doubt.

Playing Mutant Storm Reloaded is like falling into a nightmare or audio visualizers and 80s sitcom transitions. The abundance of hideous and unnecessary visual effects almost seems intentional to try to hide the uninspired mediocrity of a twin stick shooter hiding underneath. Blurry textures, a nauseous camera, laughable transitional effects between levels, and an overwhelming feeling that the developer lacked any real vision when creating their game make it unpleasant to play just a few levels, let alone "complete" the game by grinding through the seemingly endless supply.
A few ideas, like dynamically raising the difficulty based on your performance, are novel enough, but the implementation is so unclear and arbitrary that none of them can salvage an experience that was doomed from the start. I could forgive the numerous poor choices made with the presentation if the gameplay was at least moderately decent, but unsatisfying shooting, awkward level designs, and frustrating (and boring) enemies did absolutely nothing but remind me of how many other games I could be playing.
Twin stick wave based shooters are a dime a dozen, and Mutant Storm Reloaded ranks among the most prosaic and unquestionably substandard I've played to date.

I went into this expecting a typical anime dating sim/visual novel where I could wear cute outfits. But I didn't realize exactly what I was getting myself into.
This game is anomalous in the sense that it has nothing to do with dating, or Japanese culture, or trying on cute clothes, or just reading a story go by and indifferently making a few decisions. This is a really immersive, challenging game that requires you to balance everything you could've ever imagined as a soon-to-be-queen. At first, I went into this game thinking dating would be the most important thing to me, but I quickly learned I didn't care at all about dating. Well, unless it better secured my position as a queen. Only then did I care.
The outfits serve to boost your stats, so deciding when and where to wear them matters a lot more than what they look like. However, I really do like their overall design. The art in this game is wonderful. It is exactly what I enjoy when playing an anime visual novel - the right balance between lacking details and overbearing details. The colors are bright and stand out when it's something that matters, and otherwise they are faded or dark and recede into the background. I enjoyed the music a lot, but I could imagine other people found it annoying and repetitive. It is soft and unobtrusive unless something important happens, so I hardly ever paid attention to it. It was, in general, calming.
I have, so far, played this game for twelve hours. I just beat it. This game is, technically, very short. About 1-2 hours. But unless you read a walkthrough or got lucky, you will end up dying a lot before you live to see your coronation. Which I did.
The gameplay is faintly reminiscent of D&D in the sense that you level up your character, and then pass checks to keep going on. There are no attacks, no health bars, no choosing weapons (unless you count your tabard as a weapon...).
Tl;dr: This game is simple, short, but extremely challenging. The art is exactly what you should want/expect from a game like this, and the music is (mostly) calm but repetitive. Since there are about 1000 ways to go in this game, the replayability is spectacular (and looking back at my missing achievements, I am stunned by how much I never even had the opportunity to encounter, and how much I never even heard of). You do very little, but that very little escalates more than you originally realize. But you feel so spectacular when you finally reach your coronation.
I love this game. I am addicted, and I think this game should be played by anyone who enjoys anime, visual novels, and challenging stratey games.

First off I am going to assume that if you're even bothering to read this, you DON'T hate RPGMaker games. Or at least you're open minded to them. If you're not familiar with RPGmaker's engine you may want to familiarize yourself with it before proceeding.  Plenty of youtube videos to give you a preview out there.
So assuming you've made it this far, congrats!
So this game is a Sandbox...and a bigger one that it looks to be at first glance. I've been playing for a while now and there's still entire sections of the map i haven't even approached yet. Combat is tough, especially in the beginning, and best avoided altogether until you've gone up a few levels, and preferably found your first companion to fight beside you. ProTip: Get Kara. She's hawt.
Hunger, Thirst, and Radiation will be your real enemies during these early stages of the game.  Pick your battles carefully. Once you've got some experience under your belt, you can start tackling more combat oriented objectives, and start slaughtering psychos, mutants, and looters for fun and profit.
The base game has very little story, but then the story isn't really the point of the base game. the Deliverance DLC is another matter, but I haven't gotten to that yet so i'll reserve comment.
Fair warning...this game kind of tosses you into the deep end and forces you to sink or swim. Quest objectives don't come with convenient arrows to guide you along. You might get a vague "Go Northeast of here" and sometimes not even that much. You really need to read the initial quest giver's dialogue and refer to your journal entries.
You'll have to explore a lot and figure out what you're doing. The Map does not give you a "You are here" point of reference either. The only point marked is your house, which you won't be going to often since most of the action takes place quite a ways away from it. There is a community map that is quite helpful but even that will take some trial and error to get the hang of. These elements can be a turnoff to the more casual gamer, but certainly do add to the challenge of the game.
Overall I like it. Just stay out of the water. Seriously, even the puddles will kill you.

Waste Walkers is one of those gems that stands out from the crowd of the typical RPGMaker games. It is games like this that make me even bother considering any RPGMaker game. I’m a sucker for the post-apocalyptic genre, and Waste Walkers “did it” for me, but there was more to it than that.
I’m fairly picky with my gaming time. I have so many games in my backlog that if a game doesn’t grip me, I don’t play it longer than an hour. A very large percentage of games I buy don’t even make it past 30 minutes. A game doesn’t have to grip tight, but it does have to keep my interest enough so that I will progress through the story. Waste Walkers managed to keep my interest long enough that by the time I felt like I was done I was close enough to the end that I went ahead and finished it.
There are definitely some issues in the game, and other reviews already go into those in detail so no need to rehash. Some of the complaints have even been addressed. One of the big issues for me was that I had was some suspension of disbelief issues for quests and getting around on the map.
The main character is supposed to be from the town where the story takes place. My character should know where specific buildings are, at least places of business, the police station, etc. The character should also know where they are on the map in relation to the building they are next to. So a pip on the map would be really useful and even "realistic" since the character has been living in that city.
An objective pointer might not make sense for every quest, but maybe the map could have labels on at least some of the major buildings, or if you are tracking a quest and the quest has you go to a public building (like the bus depot, fire station, police station, etc.) then there should be an indicator for the direction to the building with relation to your current position. Since the quest givers are in “known” locations, it would also be nice to have a quest pointer back to the quest giver’s building, too. The player pip and pointers are to help simulate character knowledge that the player doesn't have, and there may be some other way to do this.
Luckily, there is a game guide that provides a map of the city with building names on it, so most of this particular problem only bugged me until I discovered that map. After that when a quest casually mentioned a building, I would scan the map for that building, and head over that way. It would just be a bit more convenient and "more realistic" if an objective pointer would do that for me, and certainly help me find things more easily if I knew where I was in the town by displaying a pip on the map.
So, really, I don't have much to criticize on the game. I would definitely recommend this game to anyone that is a fan of this style of game.

Waste Walkers is an indie RPG maker game set in an apocalyptic future filled with ghouls, hounds, bandits and such. You explore a destroyed city searching for your family and attempting to survive. You'll meet people here and there with side quests for you to do, found a couple of them and liked the small dialogues and the characters I met.
There's a ton of loot to use as craft or resell. For the time being I only have 2 crafting recipes and can only craft bandages and such but The crafting system seem elaborated. I liked the fact that the loot is varied and make the world coherent: you find cigarettes, sex magazines, destroyed books, ... I even found a condom! All the objects have an interesting description, sometimes funny, and flesh out the world.
In case you're worried about emptying the world (I managed to do it in some games, that's not good at all, believe me) I saw that the enemies and the containers repoped after an hour or so.
There's also a ton of options that you can modify: fog of war makes your view very small but makes for a better ambiance; Stamina to toggle free run or not; Survival to toggle hunger and thirst, you find a lot of food and realistically the hardest to find is water. You can deactivate everything for a more casual experience or activate everything for a bit of challenge.
The game is set up as a real RPG with attributes and skills and I really liked the skills system: you have 5 points on each level up to pick your skills and can choose active or passive ones, their cost varying from 1 to 5 points. And there's a ton of skills to choose! The battles are really hard at first so I went for passive ones that raises evade and such, and inflict status effects or riposte. That made the battles really easier: I inflict a ton of deadly effects and the enemies basically kill themselves when they manage to hit me, much fun! Interestingly there's an aggro system: you can equip one of your characters with special equipment and buy him special skills so that he becomes the most targeted person in the group. Or the opposite: modify him to be less targeted.
The bad: The game is very rough on the edges. The intro is really raw with barely a few lines, then the character creation isn't detailed; you choose one of 4 propositions, twice. Apparently you first choose your appearance, then an attribute bonus. Luckily I chose 'tough' which gave a nice bonus from what I read in the forum (+25% Max HP, +25% Morale.). The stat screen is filled with a lot of abbreviations, making it a bit confusing. Hint: MSV is the radiation level. There's also several different damages, like puncture. But there's nothing bad there in fact, it's only the profusion of it that makes it hard to understand in the beginning.
So yeah the beginning is very confusing and can leave a bad impression, but if you give it a chance you'll quickly get around it and discover a really enjoyable game. The more I played, the more I got hooked to it and started enjoying it. Went in the loop: have a couple of fights, loot everything and go back to the safe place to trade all that for pills to heal my radiation level, equiping and leveling my character and buying more combat skills. It quickly went into the 'I'll just make one more building', it's hard to stop. And it's the first time that I'm happy to find a rotten fruit in a container to quench my thirst :) Apparently the game is a single guy's work, so I'm rather impressed.
So yeah I do recommend the game. Give it a chance and you're in for some fun. Be your own caravan guy: kill, loot, sell, craft!

Another example of why it might be necessary for developers to have some kind of license before they just bash out "games".
The platformer genre has been around for 36 years, the first protoplatformer being "Space Panic" in 1980.  This is not a new genre.  So if you're going to release a game based on technology 36 years old, you should probably try to make it look like it's 36 years more advanced.   Alter World absolutely doesn't.
Very low quality (in before: "But it's arrrrtttttt") graphics.   Poor/fuzzy controls (on a game that does require reflexes).    The only thing the game has to differentiate itself is a "phasing" technology which you have to use to pass the levels by switching between two maps to reach all the required platforms to advance the levels.   This gets old quickly and is hampered by the fuzzy controls.

Luftrausers is a game with amazing mechanics that is sadly marred by some borderline unreasonable objectives later into the game.
The main draw of Luftrausers is the beautifully responsive flight mechanics that you get to play with. By cutting your engine, you are able to 'stall' in the air, allowing you to shoot in any direction as your craft is carried on by momentum and gravity. I cannot dexcribe how awesome it feels to arc over a battleship as you sweep your lasers across its hull, or blow a tailing enemy squadron out of the sky with a well timed cannon shot as you fall
towards the ocean.
And yes, you do have multiple weapons options for your 'rauser' (plane). There are a number of customisation options for the guns, hull and engine, which are unlocked by some algorithm tied into mission completion (see next paragraph). Though these seemingly offer different playstyles, and add something to the progession model of the game, I found that a significant number of 'upgrades' were rendered (sometimes immediately) obsolete by clearly better alternatives. For example, the nuke body will perform a screen-wipe upon your death, but these kills aren't added to your score. So apart from helping with a small number of 'kill [X]' missions, this body is outright inferior to the body that just buffs your health.
Though the game is designed to be like an old-school arcade game where the main objective is maximising score, for each customisation option, there is a short string of sub-objectives. This allows you to attempt up to three missions per round, with one tied to each part of your ship. These start out simple enough, but by the end of the game, they start to veer into RNG-fests that require you to kill high-profile enemies at maximum combo. (Kill an enemy to increase combo by 1, maxes at 20; standard combo fare.) But this requires you to get a max combo, sustain a max combo, and do the three-plus attack runs required to kill the target, all in one round. If that target never spawns (submarines, you scumbags!), then tough luck. I found myself quitting out of frustration after a while, because of the increasingly unreasonable missions.
Having made those complains, I am still reccomending this game. Why? Because
. I don't know how much life you'll get out of this game (it depends on your levels of perseverance), but it's cheap and the core mechanics are just that good.

Look, I'm only being realistic when I say: this game is probably too confusing for the vast majority of you. Is it a good fighting game? Abso-f*cking-lutely. But for anyone not playing Fighting games super seriously at a competitive level this is just not enjoyable.
It is also the most complex one I have ever tried in my life. You have like 3-4 meters to manage. Counter moves upon special counters upon even more different kinds of counter moves, cancels, slow-times, instakills, overdrives, reversals... There's just SOOOOO many mechanics. The only thing it lacks are combo moves. You can combine attacks any way you want. It is up to you to find out which ones are the good combinations.
The fact that it took me 2 hours just to get through the tutorial in order to understand and memorize anything at all, speaks volumes. And that taught me only the "basics". The game actually has a very extensive tutorial system, with missions where you can practice a particular set of mechanics, frame-timing, reactions, moves, etc. The weird thing about this tutorial is that it doesn't teach you how to play with each character. Instead, it teaches you how to play
properly. It teaches you the mentality behind it and gradually combines all the stuff you learned.
This game has a ridiculously high skill ceiling (and probably also skill floor). People playing fighting games at the very highest level will enjoy this, because it gives even them a challenge. This isn't Mortal Kombat, kids. This isn't Street Fighter. It's not Injustice (and that was a game which was already a bit too complex for my friend after playing MK and that game doesn't even come close to Guilty Gear).
If fighting games are like something like your "main" games, sure, go ahead, buy this. You won't regret it, I promise. For anyone else...

Trick & Treat is a very cute, yet short game. It's not the spooktacular game that most people would thing of when playing a halloween game, although some light horror elements are present (and I do mean light).
You play as Amelia, the maid of the young Charlotte, as the two of them attend a dinner party at a mansion deep in the woods. However Amelia and Charlotte quickly get separated from one another, with Amelia desperate to find her. Though it's ultimately story driven, much of the game is presented via logic puzzels. Each room is a riddle, and finding the answer allows you to progress. Some puzzles are even optional, but give more lore to the game if completed.
The main bulk of the game's story, sadly, is locked behind optional rooms -- with one even requiring you to beat the game before accessing -- but most of that is background information that isn't required to understand the game's story.
For a free to play RPG Maker game, I actually rather enjoyed it. I recommend the game to anyone who is looking for a cute game they can blow an hour or two on any night they feel like being spooky, without necessarily being scary or needing skeletons.

An overall good game! It's pretty short; I beat it in only two hours.
The game focuses on puzzles and they are actually pretty interesting and unique. I was stumped for a while on some of them. The game doesn't hold your hand and just tell you the answers either, but hints to you through enviromental clues. The fact that you have to explore and find things yourself, with no real hint to where some things are is refreshing too. YOU have to figure it out.
As for the genre, horror doesn't really nail it. There are horror elements in the game, sure, but I never really felt scared or have jumped at anything in this game. It's much more of a casual puzzle game where you can die in some cases. If you get scared by minor things like sudden pictures of not-so-scary things, then this game might scare you. It's a nice halloween game.
The music was fitting and gave the game an air of unease. The tracks fit where they were implemented, but I did go out and then back in to an area and the music dissapeared. Not sure if that was intended.
The plot was lacking; there was a story, but it didn't have much substance. If you are looking for something that has a lot of plot, this isn't the game for you to play, but this is a puzzle game, so it doesn't really need plot to be fun. As for the characters, they are kinda flat and baseless, but again, this game doesn't focus on that. There are a few unexpected plot twists at the end.
As for me, I enjoyed the game, as short as it was, and got the true ending on first play. It wasn't too hard, in the sense that dying is very easy to avoid if you pay attention to hints.
Personally I'd give this game a 6/10. It was short and sweet, fits the halloween vibe that it was going for, and has good puzzles. There are also extras you can unlock if you play again and get the true ending a second time, but that's for another time. I'll probably get back to this game again soon.

Meant to be played on a controller and don't even think of doing otherwise... They do give you a mouse/keyboard layout, but all the in-game tutorials and instructions are still designed for a gamepad.  They did the absolute minimum for this PC port possible.  I can't even exit the game because the PC version is so bad.  I tried every key I could think of and finally just gave up and CTRL+ALT+DEL the thing.
If you are determined to use the keyboard and mouse anyways, here's what I figured out.
Q = use key, the game will call it the "A" button however.  It closes prompts and picks up items.
E = Use estus jars.  Basically, this will heal you.
END = inventory.  Change weapons and items (later found out that you can quit the game from this as well.)
SPACE = Roll, dodge, AND RUN. Hold for run, VERY IMPORTANT
OTHER CRITICISMS
A lot of the game's challenge is based on treacherous terrain that kills you because of the often awkward controls.  There's a lot of "push-back" programming in the game.  If you hit a wall with your sword or get attacked, you might get pushed back a little.  This can easily knock you off a ledge.  And this game LOVES treacherous ledges.
There's one boss that will literally kill you the moment you start fighting him.  Not because I'm not supposed to attempt him yet.  I'm talking about the Stray Demon fight in the return to the prison.  Unless you watch a tutorial on how to kill him, he'll take hours to kill.  He basically explodes the room over and over again.  You have to figure out through trial and error that his explosion radius is thinner behind him.
There's very little direction in the game.  No one tells you, "you should go this way first, it's got the weakest monsters that you can probably kill right now".  Right when the game really starts in the firelink shrine, you can go one of three directions.  One of them is ridiculously hard now, and near impossible later.  Another is near impossible from the start. and the third is quite doable.
I personally really don't like being forced to accept death punishments.  If you die, you lose all your souls and humanity that you've saved up.  You can reclaim it if you recover your body, but if you die once more, it's all gone.  All this means to me is that I have to repetitively grind for hours on end to recover it all.  It's not fun for me.  That's why I recommend my "screw roguelike" strategy.  The games save file is in "Documents/NBGI/DarkSouls" Copy that to a separate location whenever you have a lot of souls and humanity that you don't wanna lose then copy it back if you die.  You might have to disable cloudsaves as well through the games properties on the steam library section.
Oh then there's the fact that if you misclick once and accidentally attack an NPC, you will permenently be aggroed to that NPC.  The only way to unaggro him is to spend an enormous amount of money at an NPC that only appears a third of the way through the game (which you will VERY likely miss if you didn't look it up)
I still don't know how magic works really.  I got some of it working.  Apparently you attune one magic at a fire and buy something somewhere else and equip it in your weapons slot.  I'm sure it won't be too bad once I figure it out, but figuring it out shouldn't be this hard.

Really fun single-player zombie survival game.  I've played through the main game and the DLC packs a few times each.  Storylines are good (with the exception of the Lifeline ending), and the gameplay is rock solid to keep you going back for more.  You build a community of survivors and build up your defenses and stockpiles while completing several side storylines in the process to recruit more people into the community.  There are so many small game features that make the game, from ability to drop several rucksacks into the trunk or bed of a truck, missions where you can take one or two other NPC's with you to complete, to keeping the balance of demands for food and ammo without that becoming the only thing you're trying to do...  This is one game I hope they revisit, expanding your ability to build and fortify the community (i.e. who wouldn't move into a Walmart sized building and fortify rather than a house?!) and keep the great features that made this fun to play.  If survival games are your thing, this is a great find at a great price.  Really enjoyed this series.

There is near to no genuine creativity to anything involved with the themes and world of this game. It is just, generic subterranean locations, generic creatures, generic humanoids. Either looking as they are, tweaked to look psuedo morbid, or something that is fictitious but is heavily based off something real. The entire plot using religious mythology as a crutch also in place of genuine creativity; with extremely crude and taboo themes and concepts added in to contrive individuality to the world and artificially shock the player with the subject matter. If it were not for the gorgeous music in the game, it would be completely void of any immersion or atmosphere of any kind.
The gameplay however, generally does not need the player at all to be involved. The chance of the player making any decent progress is exclusively dependent on their luck. Most significantly in the item drops they get. The game has no actual character development or customization of any kind, the player exclusively grows in strength by finding items, trinkets and consumables which are totally random. Many, many items and trinkets in the pool are useless rubbish or have very niche uses. Many of the consumables have potentially harmful effects. And quite a few items and trinkets actually are bad for the player to have. Yet this is the system the game uses to scale the players power as they progress to harder floors, completely random drops which have a completely random chance of being good, bad, useless or neutral.
Imagine playing a role playing game where everytime you level up, instead of getting new abilities and statistics bonuses; you are randomly handed a good, bad or neutral power up instead. And the game keeps getting harder regardless of whether it gives you something good or not, meaning if you do not get good rolls on your level ups you will not win. That is this game. This system, is pointless to be a part of. You might as well code the computer to play the game for you as your input will not make a difference regardless.
Players are not even allowed to know what the items they pick up do half the time either. Many items in the game have extremely vague descriptions, and or the item effect does not even trigger except under certain circumstances or it is passive. So players will not even understand their own assets much of the time. There is no sense of discovery or wonder from finding out or seeing your item effect trigger and learning its purpose. It is just arbitrary confusion that detracts from the game, up until the point where the confusion is banished. There is no joyful moment of discovery, it is just a basic element of game design being witheld from the player for the sake of contriving yet another false "unique" element of this game; not letting the player know their own build.
The randomization to survival is also caused by the presence of specifically overpowered and or obnoxious enemies in the game. Enemies that consistently shoot large shot spreads, enemies that shoot instantly, enemies that can teleport ontop of you, enemies that are invincible over half the time, enemies that are invisible and invincible over half the time, enemies that can leap or move great and sudden distances with no warning, floor damage which is the same colour as the actual floor, bosses with the same animations for different attacks, leaping or burrowing attacks with no telegraph on when the enemy will appear and strike, enemies and traps which can only be avoided if the player has enough speed. Some rooms are just flooded with these enemies, other rooms are just flooded in general, other rooms jump the player as they walk in, they are basically mandatory damage gates which show up randomly through the whole game. This game is filled with so much poor enemy design it is ridiculous.
It is made significantly worse by the scale of the game being off as well. The player has a decent sized damage received hit box and no dodge ability; while consistently fighting enemies which can shoot spreads of projectiles in tiny rooms, fill the room full of lingering ground hazards, shoot or explode into patterns of projectiles or just fill the room in general. A lot of the time, there just is not enough room to move around in to avoid many hazards. A lot of enemy attacks in general have no telegraph at all, yet the player has no dodge abilities and the rooms are crowded and already small the begin with. The fundamental scale of this game in comparison to the gameplay, is so ignorantly designed.
Even the boss rooms are undersized and sometimes the game makes them even smaller, just because it can. Many enemies depend on spawning more enemies as a crutch for spiking the difficulty; and the projectiles of some enemies have the same graphics as the ones the player shoots unless they get items that change it. So sometimes the player can not even tell what shots belong to who, which is a problem when half of them will hurt you. The game is so cluttered in general, in some situations it can become difficult to even tell or see what is happening which makes it quite difficult to keep track of enemy projectiles or even just the protagonist at all amidst the jumble of oversized sprites in an undersized room.
When the game is not being absurdly overbearing and functionally unbalanced, it slows down to toss some completely uninteresting and unthreatening enemies at the player instead. It often feels like the game is purposely trying to waste the players time by putting out fodder enemies that are often tedious to get rid of. Which is not to say that the base combat system of the game, running around shooting orbs at enemies, is normally stimulating. Because it really is not, at all, it just feels like going through the motions. There is no flare or dexterity to the combat, it is just shooting orbs and moving away from threats.
In all, an uncreative angsty world that gives players no real reason to try to progress. It just feels like some rebellious adolescent going to a religious school started scribbling up an uber metal taboo story on the back of his textbooks while he was bored and looking for a way to vent his hormones. But the story is not uncreative and angsty while minding its own business. The developer constantly trivializes serious real world subject matter as a part of the angsty world. Players can find various diseases including cancer as items, and they are boons. Players can also find depression as an item, players can also find references to razor blades in candy and also terrorism in items, and so on.
The sociopathic lack of empathy and exploitation of real world travesties is utterly disgusting. And it is made even more pathetic that the developer uses them as a crutch to compensate for his own total lack of imagination or any skill when it comes to creative thinking. In more then just this game.
But beyond that, the gameplay is bad. The progression system is asinine and the players actions make almost no difference, the combat is bland and generic orb shooting, the enemies are not articulate at all and lack numerous basic features which make enemies fair; and the game in general lacks any compelling or innovative features.
What does the game have, it has a lot of content. Much of that content being either uncreative, imbalanced, offensive or all of the above. In general there is almost nothing about this game that is actually well designed, thoughtfully designed, or creative in any way. Game is bad as a game, developer is bad as a person.

Pros:
+ Nemesis System: This is by far the most fun and unique feature on Shadow of Mordor, it provides different opportunities to different Captains, Vice-Captains, War-Chiefs etc.
+ Combat: You get three different trees to level up: Melee (Sword), Bow (Ranged) and Dagger (Stealth) which opens up a quite a few ways to kill enemies. You can mix up between the three and the minigames are alright I guess, it mostly depends on reaction timing. If you wanted a comparison I think the Arkham games combat is very similar to this one.
+ Characters/Personalities: I was gonna make this a Con because some characters are vague/boring; but I really enjoyed the dwarf's personality and many of the Uruks/Orks had their funny moments so I can overlook that.
+ Gameplay: Now there's ALOT of activities to do in the world of Mordor, personally I have mostly done the main missions and a few side things here and there, with all the activities it could easily take up over 30 hours.
+ Optimization: The game runs really smoothly on my rig even with demanding conditions like heavy rains etc. I had zero issues with the game so Im gonna list this as a positive.
Cons:
- Storyline: The story didn't feel that engaging to me, it was vague and lacked thrills. I can say I haven't enjoyed the game storyline wise, It was very average.
- Difficulty: The game felt way too easy, there isn't even an option to change this setting. If you will make a game this way like GTA, AC etc. at least try to make it challenging.
Do I recommend this game? Absolutely, but just wait for a sale and pick up the GOTY edition for 4 bucks, its an enjoyable game but not perfect.

This is a top-down, twin-stick, shooter. You choose from 8 levels of difficulty in the form of different coloured belts then dive into as many 30-second levels as you wish.
mode is a last-as-long-as-you-can romp. First off, the game throws you into a very tight arena-type room with little space for manoeuvre and challenges you to clear it in thirty seconds. You get an ominous siren after 20 seconds to signal that an indestructible nasty will soon arrive. The actual challenge from room to room rises well. One death ends the level (in
mode) making that 15 seconds delay to get back into the game seem VERY long.
Progress is displayed by showing which of the 89 rooms have been cleared and with which coloured belt. The game takes you to this screen every time you finish a room which is a great, at-a-glance progress system. The sound is ambient and tunnel-like. When entering a room you get that echoey industrial sound which adds a suitable edge to the game's atmosphere. Explosions and the deaths of enemies is satisfying especially those that require a number of hits to be dispatched. Rooms are lit with a Tron inspired neon-lighting theme.
Like most twin-stick shooters this is not a game you'd normally play for long stretches. However, for a fifteen or twenty minute blast it's a great pick-up-and-play game. There is a bit of back and forth screen hopping when changing difficulty but no biggie.
5/5

Mutant Storm Reloaded is an arcade actioner that shares quite a few simularities with another Steam title, Scoregasm. In short, Mutant Storm Reloaded is an average entry into the genre, one that is worth grabbing if you catch it on sale, but otherwise there are better titles in the genre.

Long Live the Queen is an interesting game which follows a girl named Elodie as she tries to live to see her coronation day. The game is heavily strategy focused and requires extensive attention to detail so that you may appropriately spend your time studying different subjects. I have four hours in the game and haven't managed to beaten the game yet; I highly recommend taking notes because there's so much to take in. Some skills are more important than others (ESPECIALLY LUMEN, which you'll unlock through gameplay), but every skill plays a part in some way, and a lack of any of them can lead to your death if you're not careful. That being said, this game is incredibly focused on strategizing and doesn't really encourage free choice at times, which is probably the biggest downside to this game.
On the topic of choice, it's really interesting to see the impact your choices have. Elements of both the game and Elodie's personality will change as a result of your choices. Characters can die if you don't study certain skills enough. You can become a cruel person by killing people. Even your mood or personality will affect how certain weekend excursions influence your emotions. Your choices will even affect which dialogue paths are presented to you, too. The game's incredibly well-thought out in that way, and I applaud the developer(s) for taking the time to do that. It's smart game writing, in my opinion.
As for the game itself, it's eh. Like, the game has some annoying bugs (especially when it comes to saving, since the game likes to forget which keys are bound to what, which makes typing save file names a huge chore). Also, the visuals aren't very high resolution, which makes the illustrations rather pixellated when you try to resize the game window or make it fullscreen. (Then again, my laptop screen's rather large, so this would affect that as well.)
Overall, despite the bugs and the somewhat unfairly unfair gameplay, Long Live the Queen is worth buying. You'll become so interested in the story that replaying the game in order to figure out a successful story path will keep you playing. The choices intermingle with the game's lore so flawlessly that it makes each playthough interesting.

I was looking forward to playing this game. I enjoy minecraft type games. Absolutely loved Terraria V1.0.
The trailers for this game make it out to be a complete upgrade to Terraria and maybe in some ways it is. Unfortunately it has a major problem, gameplay and user interface.
The gameplay suffers from one of the worst feelings you can have in an action game. Unresponsiveness. Sometimes it wont register a jump and sometimes you wont attack. Things like this can easily get you killed and then you get sent back to your ship regardless of what you were doing. Depending on the difficulty this could mean having to trek all the way back to get your dropped items or just straight game over.
The user interface has got to be one of the most baffling things about the game. When you enter a menu it goes roughly to the center of the screen, is not see-through basically covering your character so you can't see anything. Which could kill you. Menu screens like your inventory have multiple tabs in them instead of putting everything you need all on one page that you can scroll through. To use anything you have to go through multiple steps which can also get you killed.
Here's what you have to do to eat food:
Open inventory
Go to tab containing food (Yes it has it's own tab).
Drag food from inventory into an equip slot.
Exit inventory.
Press the corresponding number to access the equip slot with the food.
Press the corresponding mouse button to eat the food.
It is important to note that you can't equip more than one food and eating the food will empty the slot meaning if you want to eat something else you have to do all that all over again.I don't see any reason why they couldn't have shortcuts to eat food with a single button. Or at least be able to go into your inventory and be able to use an item directly from there, why do you need to equip it?
Now this is just inventory. Crafting has it's own menu and each crafting table in turn has it's own menu as well. Unlike minecraft, terraria, dragon quest builders, etc. in this game you'll have 5 or 6 different crafting tables within 20 minutes or less each with only a few things you can build. It ends up being more of a mess of multiple menus that could easily have just been one menu.
Now I did only make it 45 minutes into this game and maybe it redeems itself in the long run if you can forgive bad controls and bad UI which i could not. I think this game suffers from trying to pile on content without ever working on it's core gameplay mechanics. This is the first game I have ever asked for a refund because while playing it felt more like a chore than an actual game and I never got the sense of actual fun. This is really a shame, I think the game could have been great.

A surprisingly well excuted use of the RPG Maker engine to produce something more than the usual fare. Mechanics are about as would be predicted for the engine and genre, extended to include welcome survial elements (which I believe can be turned off? Wasn't intrested in doing so myself but do recall seeing that).
The setting might be said to be like Fallout, but unlike Fallout which takes place many decades after an apocolyptic event, Waste Walkers places you in the role of a survivor shortly after whatever happened (it seems to be one of the mysteries of the game) happened. Resources are scarce and heavy enough to make you concerned and wish to create stashes around the city, but not so far as to panic. Combat is very challenging but not impossible, and the survival element is reinforced by some encounters consistantly costing more resources than they reward, making 'fight or flight?' an important question throughout the game.
The two things I felt could have contained more content was the novel and guide found in the Pepper's edition. However those are accurately presented as non essetial content that in no way impacts the game (much like a sound track dlc, they're just additional files of interest to some and not game content) so it's a minor grief of mine.
All around though if you were looking for a lower end post apocolyptic survival game and/or an example of the RPG Maker engine being pushed to produce something different than the stereotypical content people have come to expect, Waste Walkers is worth a shot. Kinda looking forward to the author's next project as well.

Been trying to post a review for the new DLC through the usual method, on the DLC page, but Steam doesn't seem to want to let me so... figure I'll try adding it to the end of this. So this is for the Deliverance DLC
Key for DLC provided by the developer for reviewing purposes, which was really nice of him. Thanks to Corrosion!
Deliverance plays as a separate game from standard Waste Walkers using the same engine. When you load Waste Walkers a Steam dialog pops up to ask you which of the two games you wish to play. I'm a bit torn as to if Deliverance would have been better posted as a separate game (perhaps billed as a sequel), rather than as a DLC to Waste Walkers, but I can definitely say that your experience in the base Waste Walkers game is not effected by having Deliverance or not.
Rather than creating your own custom character as in Waste Walkers you start as the character Screw, with a few stat points and skills already taken as well as his own backstory. The skill system is the same as Waste Walkers though, so you'll quickly be setting up your own style of character anyway within a couple of levels.
Combat is much more difficult than in Waste Walkers in a good way, early on guns beyond the pipe weapons that fire improvised ammo made with nails are nearly impossible to find even in the shops prior to completing a certain story mission.
After a few plays I was finding tabs (the currency of the Waste Walkers world, similar to caps from Fallout) were easy to come by in standard Waste Walkers, while in Deliverance I was doing more to manage them so that I could afford what limited armor and weapons was available for purchase. There's also a great deal more crafting going on in Deliverance, with almost all of the vendors offering a few schematics for sale to make items of varying usefulness. First aid kids, survival kits and med packs were probably the items I found the most useful to craft, allowing me to carry a few more effective items rather than a larger number of minor supplies.
Deliverance has quite a bit more writing and character than Waste Walkers, and while it could still use some polish (odd moments such as a character walking wounded into a room she was expected to be found in, rather than being found wounded in the room could have been staged to make a touch more sense) it shows a major step up from the previous entry. NPCs are a bit more fleshed out and human in their interactions, and events flow together in a cohesive manner. There's quite a few more quests as well, though perhaps a few of those from NPCs at the base area could have been spread out by delaying them until later in the story. Felt as though a glut of them were presented at the outset, then as I progressed through the main story there weren't as many minor side quests to pursue.
So overall a good amount of fun, and if I were to pick one thing I'd like to have seen differently it'd be having Deliverance as a separate game from Waste Walkers. The difference in overall quality and enjoyment is significant enough that it almost feels awkward having it as a DLC.

Addicting and endless, this game has had me trapped for hours. A bit challenging, but the right combos can let you breeze through certain bosses and stages in such a satisfying manner. Definately got my money's worth with how much I've replayed it and I still have only made a wee dent in unlocking everything.
There are a few tips and room/item info that you might have to look up, but there's a nice wiki you can always go to after playing through a few times. Item descriptions can be a bit cryptic but I think that makes it more interesting in the heat of the moment.
PROS
-So many item combos/synergies + stage randomization and endings keep you on your toes and interested
-Enough challange to be interesting but not too overwhelming. Can always keep resetting until you get a good item on the first stage if you're still shakey on fighting.
-Crazy amount of items give you something to do when unlocking all of them.
-Lots of Seeds and mods to play around with along with the buyable DLC.
-I loved the first BOI and had tons of fun with this one. I was initially worried about it being just a nicer-looking reskin, but there is enough new content to keep things fun (and I'm really tempted to buy the DLC). If you were on the fence like me for a while, I'd give it a shot, especially if it goes on sale!!
CONS
-If you're new to shmups, I miiiight not recommend you buy this, but it depends on how much of a challenge you're willing to take if you're not used to this kind of thing. Could try introduce a friend through co-op and see how it goes.
-Tons of items means a lot of 'junk' items can end up cluttering the item pool in treasures/treasure rooms. Some seem a bit unneccecary sometimes.
-I've had a friend complain about lack of story. (I think there's enough lore and interesting enemy/character designs with the tie to religious themes to pick through, but we just ended up agreeing to disagree)
OVERALL
Tons of fun, lots to do, not getting old to me despite 50+ hrs of gameplay and I'm still eager to jump in again.

First things first: if you have not yet played Portal 2 to the end do not play this, since there are some spoiler in this mod.
This short mod is centered around a specific mechanic: you can record yourself and your actions (including shooting portals) and play that record back, so you can interact with your pre-recorded self (even physically), unless you move through an energy barrier that would also despawn your portals.
The leveldesign for the most part is good, consistent and the mod ends after it has shown you its potential without repeating a certain part of a puzzle you just solved too often in the following rooms. There are only 2 rooms that are flawed: one were you're supposed to use a Aerial Faith Plate to get somewhere high up (which I think wasn't tweaked enough and therefore didn't work as well as in the original Portal 2) and the last segment before the ending where you could find a relatively easy solution to the room which was most likely not what the modders had intended (in fact, I think I saw what they thought you should do, but there was an easier option available that didn't require any exploitation or trick to it).
Since it's only a mod, there's no real voice acting to be found (as I remember you get to hear playbacks from the original at best or chattering noise at one point), but that's to be expected.
For the low price of >>nothing*<<  (*if you own Portal 2) I definitely recommend giving this a try, it's well put together and there's fun to be had if you're into some puzzles that will have you think somewhat outside of the box.

Blazing Beaks is a great buy if you can play with friends due to the multiple multiplayer and coop modes. If you are buying it, like me, for just the story mode, single player, then it squeaks buy as a good deal. (Video Version of this Review.)
Not that there is anything necessarily wrong with this title, but it has a very been there, done that feel to it. I liked the relic system, where you pick up a relic that causes some negative effect till you find an in game shop and can trade it in for something good. This offers a difficult choice of picking up the items and dealing with the negative effect for a later payoff. I also liked the first boss and found him to be a challenge. The randomly generated levels have a lot of traps, and the monsters also leave a varity of damaging effects too. This makes attention to your surroundings and placement key to survival. The weapons in the shop seem a tad expensive as money drops are on the rare side early on. One thing I didn't like was the characters you can choose from, as I found a lot of them to simply be ineffective choices. One character for instance drops a bomb whenever hit, but with such fragile characters this makes no tactical sense. Overall the game is well done with good art and fun rogue-lite twin-stick shooting.

Although this game has some problems, and I came into it a couple years after it's initial early access release (which, is a dreadful long time), I feel like I have to recommend it. Why? It has a great atmosphere, is a true survival game (without zombies or murdersome gangs of ten year-olds) and, barring a few minor changes, is nearly a complete experience.
I've put about 19 hours into the game at this point and, unfortunately, don't feel like anything is much of a challenge anymore. I have a heartiful stock of smoked meat and fresh water, have a decent home with plenty of storage and have wiped out all the animals on the island. Unfortunately, I've also deforested it, but jumping over to other islands is easy. The sharks are a little worrysome, but I haven't even been attacked by one yet. I do start to move in zigzag patterns when they come near - I'm not sure if that's why I've survived them - but it definitely doesn't feel like a threat. Besides, I just save prior to leaving my island and can just reload if I run into trouble.
Outside of continuing to... survive, I can't say I feel like I need to dominate all the islands or build anything spectacular, or anything else of long-term value. What would make this have more long-term appeal for me would be a renewing animal population and/or animal husbandry, the ability to bring animals back to your own island, a way to plant trees (and not fruit trees in a harvesting plot), increased danger from the marine environment, storms that have real-world effects such as structure damage (like in Mad Max), enhanced action animations to replace the somewhat cheesy fire starting and the chopping mechanic that feels a little like you're cheating, and, well, heck, even though I don't always like the roaming gangs of murdersome ten year-olds, some form of optional multiplayer.
As for what's good: The atmosphere is wonderful. The graphics are good; I won't say I was stunned, but there's at least nothing that detracts from gameplay. The lighting effects are good and lend to the atmosphere. There have been quite a few points where I just stopped what I was doing to look up at the sky for a bit or made sure I was up for the sunrise in the case of a late night. The point of view is wonderful in that you can see your body when you look down - you're viewpoint is from an actual head, not a floating one with the rest of you being invisible. Another great thing is that to cook a piece of meat, what do you do? You throw it on the fire! Of course, you can build a spit or a smoker, but in the end, putting a piece of meat on a fire actually cooks it. That's a touch of realism that's missing from most of these games.
So, all-in-all, I recommend this game. It's not quite to the point of long-term playability that I'd like, but I suspect they'll be getting there soon. They seem so close. I'll update my review if I see this not taking place, but, for now, I like the game, see its potential and can't wait for it to get there. I'll still be playing here and there in the meantime!
UPDATE
-------------
I didn't realize I wasn't receiving experimental updates and, when I turned them on, I got another 20 hours of play out of this. I hit the bar again, but the expiremental updates are great. I appreciate being able to build a more solid, even if only superficial, structure and really love not having to look for empty buckets. I'm looking forward to what comes next and still recommend this game.
UPDATE
-------------
After the initial glee that came along with the addition of the experimental features, I quickly found myself tapped out again. I just don't feel like doing anything else in this game. I built an awesome house on an island, have a healthy stock of food and water and otherwise have no need to stray. After you've completed the initial hurdles to your survival, continuing to do so becomes a piece of cake.
It does seem like the developers are continuing to address various issues and make small tweaks and additions, but I haven't seen anything approaching what I outlinted in my initial post. Once again, I find myself hating the Steam recommendation options of "yes" or "no". I'd still recommend this game, but only for short-term playability. Don't buy this expecting that you'll be content to smoke meat for the rest of your days.

Waste Walkers, developed by Corrosion Studios, is an open-world survival game created with RPGMaker. Now, I won’t beat around the bush; this is one of the most expansive and intricate games built on this engine, and it’s sure to steal more than a few hours of your time.
The story is fairly standard for a post-apocalyptic setting: The world has been destroyed by nuclear war and mundane life no longer exists. Normal people who lead normal lives must struggle to survive against the war’s aftermath. You’re put in the shoes of a survivor, separated from his/her family. Vague leads and shady individuals are your only guides, and you’ll take whatever you can get to find them.
As stated previously, this is a big game with a lot of stuff crammed inside. The map is littered in side quests, NPCs, monsters, and all sorts of things to explore. Just about every structure has an interior ripe with loot, and believe me, there is a lot of stuff to loot. In fact, a lot of your time will be spent away from the main quest line; mastering the maddness in this shell of a city.
Before going any further, there’s something that should be made clear. This game does not hold your hand. Apart from a short tutorial explaining some basic mechanics, you’re on your own. A lot is left for the player to figure out, and if you’re the type of guy who needs a big, shiny objective marker leading the way, you might want to give Waste Walkers a pass.
You’ve got your typical array of survival mechanics, such as a hydration and hunger bar, topped off with a radiation meter; however, food and water is in large abundance, so keeping healthy is not much of a challenge. What really makes this game difficult is combat, especially in the earlier stages. You start out weak and pathetic. Maintaining ammunition is a challenge at first, and trading punches with every beast crossing your path is NOT a good idea.
Waste Walkers is a game that encourages patience, and with a variety of different survivors to recruit, armor to find and weapons to wield, it won’t be long before you’re ready for a fight…. In fact, maybe you’re a little too ready; after you’ve leveled up and found some decent loot, Waste Walkers challenge goes down the drain. Just about anything will die within a few hits, and the tension slowly dissolves little by little.
Like I said, the game offers little hand holding. I started up Waste Walkers with the wrong frame of mind. I spent a few hours running around aimlessly, getting lost and dying over and over and over. I got so frustrated that I was tempted to quit altogether. To properly enjoy this game, you’ve really gotta know what you’re getting into. Take things slow and try to familiarize yourself with the map, the enemies, the loot, the world as a whole. But trust me; Waste Walkers can get addictive once you know what you’re doing.
I can only recommend this game to those who are well acquainted with the genre, or to those who want to be. But if you’re willing to take the risk, you’ll be in for one hell of a ride.
This is a swell game with a lot of effort put into it. It is challenging and atmospheric and I look forward to seeing what I run into next on my wasteland adventures!

Right off the bat Waste Walkers captured my attention with a rather different approach to an RPG game than I've been used to lately. Whereas most stories start off by telling you that you have to go here or there to progress — WW did not. Waste walkers spins it's tale through the derelict buildings throughout the Ashen City, and playing with the Fog of War on gives off an eerie Silent Hill vibe.
The first few hours of the game are a breath of fresh air in comparison to what you'll encounter in the usual gamut of RPGs. You have a journal, a map, and some quest text. That's all you'll get for the rest of the game, and it's also part of the charm of figuring out what you have to do next. Careful planning and ammo conservation are key in the early game, and you run the risk of dying very often early on if you're not paying attention to your surroundings.
Environment and music are something the game pulls off well. Each area has a careful attention to detail, and the 30+ buildings that I've explored all have a unique touch to them. From the Cinema to the Police Station — all of them have a special look and feel different from the other areas. Where the story itself is scarce the environment picks up the pace with minimalist storytelling done through the range of NPCs and monsters that roam the Ashen City.
Combat is rather barebones once you really get down into the nit and gritty, but I have to say that it didn't really detract from the game in any way. Managing supplies/needs, health, and inventory doesn't feel like a chore. After a while you'll be able to tell what's worth taking, and what's worth leaving behind amidst your limited inventory space. The base mechanics of the game just work. They don't need the extra flair of 40 skills and abilities that all do the same thing. Maybe a little more push towards using debuffs, or forcing weapon proficiency skills on the player would give choosing a weapon type a weightier decision, but it's a minor gripe if anything.
The only real complaint I would have is that late-game scaling gets a little weird, and it's entirely possible to trivialize the combat if you've managed your resources properly. Better enemy scaling would provide a more clean transition into the late game, but it hasn't hindered my ability to enjoy the game.
8 hours in at the time of reviewing, and I'm still having a lot of fun with it. As of late I've been drawn to RPGMaker games due to growing tired of games giving me a story in hour long exposition with a cutscene. Waste Walkers is a gem for me, and I can see myself enjoying it for quite a bit longer. Give it a try. The developer certainly seems to have put a lot of love into the game and it shows.
Best of wishes to Corrosion and his future endeavors. I look forward to seeing what you do next.

It's impressive for a game made in RPGmaker, but the more you play it, the more its flaws start to stand out.
First, let's start with the good. It's fun to roam around the city, especially at low levels and alone when every encounter can be potentially life-ending. Combat is unforgiving when you don't have a gun or the ammo to use it, meaning that you need to be judicious where and when you fight. It also has a nice post-apocalyptic vibe to it.
So that's what's good. Past a certain point, the open exploration with little guidance starts to become frustrating. One of the selling points of this game was that you can establish your own colony, which is nice and thematic. However, I've spent eight hours on the game, crawled over the map, and found nothing. None of the characters have ever mentioned it to me either, so I guess I could keep playing if I just wanted to crawl the map endlessly looking for it.
Speaking of which, the map they provide in the game is fairly useless. Unless you're standing at the margins of the map, it's hard to get a real sense for where you are until you've effectively memorized the relations of where everything is anyway. I know that might be realistic, but in a game where things are abstractly rendered at best, it makes finding your way around really difficult. Why not a coordinate system?
Quest marking, or even writing it down in the journal you have would be a tremendous help too. There's something infuriating in finishing a quest and then not remembering where the quest giver was, leading you to wander the map just to find them.
Scavenging is also too effective. My strategy of looting every container and reselling what I didn't need (revolutionary, I know) left me with so many tabs that I could effectively buy everything my main character needed and have plenty left over. My safe was stocked to the gills with everything I could ever need, although the fact that it doesn't sort goods at all for you means that finding anything was incredibly difficult.
Maybe if I was anal retentive I would need to buy everything for my NPCs, but only one of them can fight with you at a time, and some are far, far better than others. (Was Nadia supposed to be useful? I got her up to level 5 and she never did more than a point of damage). Once you get a gun and enough ammo, which is easy because money is no issue, just make you sure you have an NPC who can use one, and fights will never be a real challenge again.
The story is nothing to write home about. A man kidnaps your family, you go after him, revenge, blah blah blah. Not bad, but nothing special, and its non-linearity makes it easy to forget it ever happened.
This game was fun for a while, but I happened to buy it when I desperately needed short distractions. Under normal circumstances, I wouldn't spend $10 on this, so unfortunately I can't recommend this.

Although better than some RPG Maker games i've seen and tried, Waste Walkers unfortunately is one of the few games i will be refunding and therefore can't reccomend.
The game itself runs smooth with only the occasional dip from 60 fps to 30 (which is annoyingly constantly displayed in the top right hand corner) when opening containers or inventory etc, which is good compared to most RPG Maker games these days. I also didn't experience any CTD's or similar during my play time.
The general Fallout/Stalker style gameplay of surviving and exploring is there, but unfortunately it just wasn't any fun, and for £6.99 that's not gonna fly, maybe at about £1.99 it would feel like decent value.
Ignore the feature list on the store page as it's all made up of the devs warped opinion of his own  game (brilliant sounds, beautiful environments etc etc, none of which are even close to the mark) and pure fiction (equivalent to 90KM of land to traverse (its actually only 120x120 meters with roughly 100 buildings)
A lot of the tiles (floor sprites, building sprites etc) used are of low quality and make the general game world look ugly and messy (unfortunately not in a good post-apocalyptic way).
The world itself is tiny, it took me 64 seconds to walk from the very west to the very east of the map and 70 seconds to walk from the very north to the very south. There are multiple buildings scattered around, some of which are enterable, but most of which consist of 1 floor with a few rooms seperated by ugly looking walls and doors.
Followed the main quest for the hour that i played, felt very bare bones and generic in terms of actual story, on about the same level as a short story written as a homework assignment.
Standard key binds are pretty bad and the controls screen shows no way of rebinding, however pressing f1 brought up a window allowing me to assign keys to a gamepad (doesnt work), rebind keyboard keys and also turn on/off the music etc. None of this mentioned in the controls screen however. Also, when playing in full screen the mouse cursor can dissappear off to the right and off the bottom of the screen, which at first made me think the mouse just didnt work in Waste Walkers.
"Developer" also likes to tell people their feedback is just plain wrong and that he has done everything right, even down to the fact that the controller support is borked and his reply was "well i decided to put game "features" in instead of fixing game pad, anyways this is on PC and all PC players use the keyboard and mouse", as well many other examples which you can see on peoples reveiws and in the games forums on steam.
TL:DR - At a price point of £7 i simply can't recommend Waste Walkers considering its super small world, poor story, poor tile/sprite choice and a Dev who tells you your feedback is wrong, the way you played his game was wrong and that he has done everything correct. Avoid.
